title: For Kemi, being the Nasty party is not toxic but a badge of honour | John Crace | The Guardian
description: The Tory leader says the party’s plans to cut people’s benefits are no more than ‘common sense’
Author: John Crace
Headline: The Tory leader says the party’s plans to cut people’s benefits are no more than ‘common sense’
Content: Kemi Badenoch being interviewed by the BBC’s Laura Kuenssberg on Sunday.Photograph: BBCView image in fullscreenKemi Badenoch being interviewed by the BBC’s Laura Kuenssberg on Sunday.Photograph: BBCThe politics sketchConservative conference 2026For Kemi, being the Nasty party is not toxic but a badge of honourJohn CraceThe Tory leader says the party’s plans to cut people’s benefits are no more than ‘common sense’Sun 4 Oct 2026 13.13 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 16.25 EDTShareIt’s a thought. A bold one. Possibly a career-ending one. But a thought nonetheless. When Theresa May told the Tory conference in 2002 that under Iain Duncan Smith theConservativeshad become “the Nasty party”, many members took that to mean they had become undesirable. Within a few years, David Cameron had moved the Tories closer to the “hug a husky” centre and by 2010 he was prime minister.Kemi Badenoch takes a rather different view. For her, being the Nasty party is a badge of honour. An aspiration. People had had it far too good with austerity, Brexit, Covid and the Liz Truss mini-budget. The country needed a reality check; a return to old-fashioned unpleasantness. A taste of genuine hardship. People had got far too used to getting something for nothing. Especially the physically and mentally ill. What they needed was a short sharp shock of intense labour from 8am to 8pm. That would make them feel better. And anyone found skiving would be banged up for a short time in prison. Say 10 years.And take a bow, her cheerleader-in-chief. The man whose sycophancy consistently goes above and beyond the call of duty. We’re talking, of course, of the shadow home secretary, Chris Philp. He had chosen to mark the beginning of Tory conference with an interview to the Sun in which he had identified himself as a one-man vigilante force. For the next four days, he had personally guaranteed that Birmingham would be a crime-free zone. The Philpster would be on guard night and day to arrest all shoplifters and to check up on people who hadn’t paid their TV licence. From now on he would be a superhero. BatTwat.For Kemi, the beginning of conference was marked with the traditional BBC interview with Laura Kuenssberg. One where she would try to be the cosiest version of herself. The nasty leader with the heart of gold. A woman who could say in all honesty that “this was hurting her more than it was hurting you” as she removed someone’s benefits. This was Kemi returning in triumph. A year ago, her position as leader had looked ropey. Now the Tories have had a long, hard look around and concluded there actually isn’t anyone better.“Is this a return to the nasty party?” asked Kuenssberg. Kemi was trying not to phrase it in precisely those terms. Nasty was only a word to be implied. Rather, she would prefer it if we could use the words “commonsense” party. Common sense, as in it was plain to everyone that something had to be done. And that something was to pick on the poorest and most vulnerable people in society. For years now, these parasites had been lounging around and getting fat on benefits. Asking themselves not what they could do for the Tory party but what the Tory party could do for them.To illustrate her point, Kemi proudly drew Laura’s attention to her rather desperate pamphlet The Right Way, which the Tories have published as their new credo. Six principles of Conservatism to get them through the bad times. To remind them they are right even when the country thinks they are unelectable. Kemi’s Kemistry, as she hopes we will call it. The first rule is that Kemi never makes mistakes. Asked to name anything she has changed her mind about, she comes up with nothing. The laws of physics will change long before Kemi. She wants us to think of The Right Way as her foundational document that will be spoken of in hushed tones for decades to come. It will be lucky to survive until tomorrow.I’m not buying into the ‘Keminaissance’. If the Tories lowered the bar any further, they’d be Reform UK | Frances RyanRead moreWe then moved on to Kemi’s latest big idea: to give everyone who makes more than £100,000 a year unlimited free childcare. The case was unarguable, said Kemi. Free childcare was totally wasted on people on the minimum wage because they couldn’t be trusted to spend the money wisely. It would probably all be wasted on Happy Meals at McDonald’s or a Sky subscription. Let’s face it, it was just chucking good money after bad. Most working-class kids were bound to end up on benefits anyway, so why encourage them from the moment they were born? It’s time they learned to be self-sufficient. What a contrast with the top 5% of the country. They could at least spend their benefits on something worthwhile. Like baby yoga.Kemi was also keen to keep pensioners happy. We will retain the triple lock, she said. Even though half the shadow cabinet know it’s completely unaffordable. Old people definitely had to be kept sweet, as they were about the last section of the country who actually voted Tory. Not that this was any factor in shaping current policy. Because Kemi had just published The Right Way, in which she had declared that her principles were whatever she wanted them to be on the day. And, by the way, this would all be paid for by cutting benefits for the 10 million scroungers who were cheating the system. Could you verify that figure? Laura asked. Kemi shook her head. It was just a well-known fact that she had made up. So no need.Badenoch returns to Conservative conference much stronger than a year agoRead moreAfter going on to say she would be building 50,000 more prison spaces for all the criminals BatTwat arrested in the next four days, the interview meandered to a close. In the studio, Penny Mordaunt declared it to be the best interview a Tory leader had ever given. Penny is beside herself with joy at having passed the test to be admitted to the MPs’ candidate list. Answering yes to questions such as: “Are you mad?” and “Are you happy to trash the Good Friday agreement?” It was Penny’s performance in the Sky reality show The War Game that swung it. As defence secretary she couldn’t wait to start a nuclear apocalypse. Come friendly bombs.Over in the conference centre, the complex was strangely quiet. Maybe the news that everything is going swimmingly for the Tories hasn’t yet filtered down to MPs and members. Even the main hall wasn’t full, and there was nothing going on elsewhere. But those who were there seemed happy enough. Perhaps they are genuinely delighted that things aren’t going even worse. That they are still only four points in the polls off their disastrous 2024 election result. That it doesn’t matter that the so-called Keminaissance exists largely in their imaginations.But on we go. A party the country still regards as toxic is determined to double down on its toxicity. Desperate to track ever further to the right and abandon its centre right to Labour and the Lib Dems. It feels like madness. But this conference is all about Kult Kemi. There is even an AI slop, sub-Beano reproduction of the Bayeux tapestry. A series of tableaux leading to the moment Kemi saves the world. She looks on beatifically as several easily identified journalists take dictation. Curiously, I’m not one of them.Explore more on these topicsConservative conference 2026The politics sketchConservativesKemi BadenochBenefitscommentShareReuse this content

title: The AI industry is booming. Women are getting left behind | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Women hold just a fraction of new AI jobs but are overrepresented in roles with high risk of AI disruption
Author: Arielle Pardes
Headline: Women hold just a fraction of new AI jobs but are overrepresented in roles with high risk of AI disruption
Content: ‘AI is creating some of the fastest growing, highest paying … jobs in the global economy. Women are just strikingly underrepresented.’Composite: The Guardian/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘AI is creating some of the fastest growing, highest paying … jobs in the global economy. Women are just strikingly underrepresented.’Composite: The Guardian/Getty ImagesReworkedAI (artificial intelligence)The AI industry is booming. Women are getting left behindWomen hold just a fraction of new AI jobs but are overrepresented in roles with high risk of AI disruptionSupported byAbout this contentArielle PardesSun 4 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 09.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere’s a common fear among people who work in Silicon Valley: snag one of the fast-growing, high-paying jobs in artificial intelligence, or get trapped in the “permanent underclass”, a phrase describing the fate of those who won’t have upward mobility in the age of AI.The phrase usually describes a future in which AI automates human jobs. But for women in tech, it’s starting to look like the present.“A lot of people say: ‘Oh, AI is lowering barriers, it’s equalizing the playing field for women,’” said Urvashi Batra, co-founder and CEO of Prioriwise, an AI platform for IT service providers. “I actually think it’s the opposite.”Batra said people take her less seriously as the founder of an AI company than her male co-founder. When pitching investors, she and her co-founder have learned that they are more likely to get an investment if he does the pitching.Women made up only about a quarter of new hires in AI roles in the last year, compared to 50% of new hires in non-AI roles, according to a recentreportfrom LinkedIn. In executive roles, that number drops to just 13%. At the same time, LinkedIn’sresearchshows that women are more likely to work in roles with high exposure to AI disruption, like customer service, meaning they are also at higher risk for job loss due to AI.AI jobs, whose postings have doubled since 2023, come with a salary premium, on average paying more than twice as much as roles that don’t involve working with AI, according to LinkedIn’s research. But women who do have jobs in AI are disproportionately concentrated in low-paying roles, like data annotators, said Sarah Steinberg, the head of global public policy partnerships at LinkedIn. Across all AI occupations, men have $45,000 higher median pay than women, partly due to the types of jobs they are likelier to have.“AI is creating some of the fastest growing, highest paying and most consequential jobs in the global economy,” said Steinberg. “Women are just strikingly underrepresented.”The ongoing trend could produce the greatest gender pay gap in generations and leave women out of building a technology that shaped the economy, advocates for women in tech said.“What we’re witnessing is a sort of backsliding,” said Brenda Darden Wilkerson, president of AnitaB.org, a non-profit devoted to advancing women in tech jobs.Initiatives to promote women in the tech industry have been ongoing for years, with mixed results. Women now holdabout one-thirdof tech jobs in the US. Butresearchhas found that women leave the tech industry at a much higher rate than their male counterparts, citing factors like non-inclusive cultures and barriers to advancement.‘I’ve seen so many women fall through the cracks’Women working in AI may face even greater challenges. “AI moves extremely fast, and the pressure to keep up is immense,” said Jayeeta Putatunda, an AI engineering lead at investment firm Turing. “I have seen throughout my career so many amazing women I know kind of fall through the cracks.”Putatunda said it’s not uncommon to be the only female engineer on a team, and that when women are outnumbered, they have to speak up louder to make their ideas known. Mentorship in the AI field, especially by other women, can be hard to come by. And the breakneck pace of AI advancements means anyone working in the field should expect to put in long hours in order to keep up.“If you have very ambitious career goals in this field, there will be seasons when you work beyond normal hours,” she said, noting that a culture of working 12-hour days to keep up was not uncommon. “I don’t think there is always a neat shortcut around that than to put in the hours.”Those kinds of work expectations can make it impossible for everyone to stay in the field. “I went onmaternity leave for four months, and by the time I came back, there were completely different frameworks and levels of models,” Putatunda said. Getting caught back up was overwhelming. She said it was only possible with the help of supportive co-workers and a husband who equitably split childcare.“That is one way women get pushed out of AI,” she said. “They don’t lack the interest or ability to keep up. They may lack the infrastructure that makes keeping up possible.”The AI industry is so new and fast-moving that it should in theory be more meritocratic. No one has a decade of experience working with a model developed one year ago, which should mean everyone has a level playing field. But instead the field has indexed more on personal networks and other loose signals, according to some women who work in AI.“Companies are hiring at a breakneck speed, but they’re finding people through the same networks, the same referrals, the same filters that they’ve always used,” Wilkerson said. “Generally, that’s not given women the same sort of exposure they should have.”When people have tried to address these tech industry problems in the past, the solutions have largely come down to giving women more mentorship and implementing diversity programs with goals around representation. But in recent years, companies have aggressively scaled back their diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) programs, largely in response to a political climate that discourages them. That has left fewer companies with institutional programs to hire and promote women.The political climate has made it more challenging to get AI companies to support initiatives focused on women, said Felicia Newhouse, founder of AI Powered Women, an organization that promotes women’s participation and leadership in AI. Newhouse, a product marketer who has worked in technology companies for two decades, points to the Department of Justice targeting corporations with DEI programs, claiming the initiatives violate anti-discrimination laws. Companies like Accenture, Deloitte, IBM and PayPal have all agreed to pay multimillion-dollar settlements under this enforcement.“It is getting harder to go into companies being called AI Powered Women,” Newhouse said. “And our advocates inside those companies are also struggling with having women-focused initiatives.”Still, she said the risk that women are left behind in the AI workforce was something that kept her up at night. “We’re talking about who captures a major new source of economic mobility,” she said. “The deepest risk is that a participation gap becomes a power gap.”Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)ReworkedfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘It’s OK to love somebody when they’re not perfect’: how John Cena conquered Hollywood – and why he refuses to abandon Vince McMahon | Movies | The Guardian
description: By embracing the role of amiable lunk, the wrestler turned actor has become an unlikely, and very modern, leading man. But does his relationship with the WWE, and its controversial former owner, risk tarnishing his brand?
Author: Sasha Mistlin
Headline: By embracing the role of amiable lunk, the wrestler turned actor has become an unlikely, and very modern, leading man. But does his relationship with the WWE, and its controversial former owner, risk tarnishing his brand?
Content: Mass appeal … John Cena.Photograph: Joe PuglieseView image in fullscreenMass appeal … John Cena.Photograph: Joe PuglieseMoviesInterview‘It’s OK to love somebody when they’re not perfect’: how John Cena conquered Hollywood – and why he refuses to abandon Vince McMahonSasha MistlinBy embracing the role of amiable lunk, the wrestler turned actor has become an unlikely, and very modern, leading man. But does his relationship with the WWE, and its controversial former owner, risk tarnishing his brand?Sun 4 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 10.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleImust admit, I was apprehensive about meeting John Cena. The WWE wrestler turned actor has built an enviable Hollywood career playing idiots – capable idiots with real heart, but dimwits nevertheless. Still, Cena is obviously nobody’s fool; fools don’t rise from humble beginnings to become their generation’s answer to Hulk Hogan or The Rock. Would the Cena who appears on my computer screen be the real one? Or something closer to the comic-book characters he embodies so well: guileless, silly and fond of a deliberate misunderstanding?It is immediately clear that this is no manchild. Perfectly punctual, he greets me with a lavish formality befitting a man who made his film debut as the title character in The Marine. Within a minute he has volunteered, unprompted, that “a core value of mine is respect”. Cena, 49, is speaking to me on behalf of Matchbox: The Movie, a film extension of the Mattel toy car brand for Apple TV, and for 45 minutes he is generous, funny, complimentary and elusive without ever being evasive. It’s a genuinely radical thing for a man built like a chest freezer – having only recently retired from wrestling after 26 years – to be so relaxed about being ridiculous, and in an age of such joyless online strongmen as Trump, Musk and Andrew Tate, his buff charm is welcome.John Cena is a company man. The word “loyalty” comes up often, and about everything from his friends back home to the wrestling to the US itself. Admirable, no doubt. But Cena’s loyalty has drawn him into some uncomfortable positions, and for 20 minutes our good-natured chat about reliability, discipline and what it means to owe everything to something bigger than yourself has set us on a collision course with one of the most disgraced figures in modern entertainment.View image in fullscreenCar trouble … John Cena in Matchbox: The Movie.Photograph: Jasin BolandIn January 2024, Vince McMahon, the all-powerful chairman and CEO of WWE, resigned from the organisation and its parent company TKO Group Holdings following a slew of sexual assault allegations and pending lawsuits that made his position in the company he’d spent his life building untenable. The final straw was a suit filed by a former WWE employee, Janel Grant, alleging that McMahon sexually assaulted her and pressed her into sexual acts during her time at the company, sent explicit images of her with other men without her consent, and passed her to others – in one instance, the filing says, to help secure a wrestler the company hoped to sign. McMahon denies all the allegations and in June, the litigation between him, the WWE and Grant was transferred voluntarily by all parties from the federal court into confidential private arbitration.McMahon was a mentor to Cena, and as well as sponsoring his career, provided him a second family amid the travelling circus of 00s wrestling. “I have no guilt nor shame about my friendship and my relationship with Vince McMahon,” he says, swiftly followed by “you’re obviously going to put this in [your] article”. He’s right, of course. What is strange isn’t that he foresaw this line of questioning – it’s that Cena took such an unequivocal stance in the face of something so potentially damaging. He is audibly proud of the association, revelling in the idea that he’s abiding by his principles in the face of what he calls “the storm”. “It’s OK to love somebody when they’re not perfect,” he says.Cena was born in West Newbury, Massachusetts, in 1977, one of five boys in a household that watched every dollar. His grandma and grandpa lived in an adjoining house. “There was a lot of ‘How are we going to pay the bills, how are we going to keep the lights on?’” Cena says. He worshipped the movie action men of the era – Schwarzenegger, Stallone, Willis – but he also loved hip-hop, which in suburban Massachusetts made him a target for bullies. Bodybuilding was the answer, and it doubles as an origin story – the boy bullied for dressing like a white rapper, growing up to become an icon for the next generation of suburban youth.Still, when I raise it, Cena is quick to correct the emphasis: the bullying wasn’t the point; his response to it was. “I didn’t treat hostility with hostility,” he says. “I got bullied for the way that I dressed, so I dressed more outlandish.” The muscle was a visible deterrent. “I’ll just project a physical sense of: Man, I don’t want to press my luck with that guy,” he says.After college, he drove to California in 1999 with about $500 to follow Schwarzenegger’s playbook to bodybuilding glory. He worked on the shop floor at Gold’s Gym in Venice Beach for six dollars an hour, and for a stretch, slept in the back of his 1991 Lincoln. A wrestler who worked out at Gold’s steered him towards the industry and in 2000 he made his debut in WWF (now WWE) as The Prototype, a robotic character whose deliberate speech was a clear nod to his idol Arnie. He was paid $250 a week “which meant I spiralled into debt”. To Cena’s credit he understood that the short-term loss had the potential to lead to long-term gain. “I’ve been pretty astute at understanding when luck arrives,” he says.View image in fullscreenLord of the ring … John Cena at a WWE event in Toronto in 2024.Photograph: WWE/Getty ImagesWhat followed was a 24-year stint as a WWE superstar, a period Cena describes without irony as “service”. “You can’t fake that,” he says. “If you’re in the business of bullshit, somebody’s going to see through it.” He stumbled on a character that stuck: a jersey-wearing, battle-rapping white kid from Massachusetts, who literally went by the name John Cena. Despite some distrust from fans – over his general clean-living, wholesome persona – and fellow wrestlers who initially ostracised him for not engaging in the hard-boozing that was par for the course, the gimmick worked. In fact it was so successful that it led to the slightly odd ongoing situation where Cena doesn’t own his own name.“John Cena is who I am as a human being,” he says, “and there is a company – WWE/TKO – that has invested hundreds of millions of dollars in the intellectual property of the character John Cena. And rightfully so; they have earned their share of ownership of that.” In Cena’s words he read and understood the agreement and he thought it was fair. However, the lingering sense that a career at the top of WWE requires a deal with the devil prevails (Dwayne Johnson onlygot his own moniker, “The Rock”, back in 2024, and now sits on the board of TKO). But Cena explicitly rejects the idea that he has had to make sacrifices along the way. “I prefer to use the word choice … When we say yes to something, we say no to everything else.” In effect, he gave up his name for the rare chance to live his dream.And for more than a decade he did. Cena was beloved throughout the 2000s and early 2010s primarily as an avatar for a certain brand of flag-waving, white masculinity that was firmly in tune with the climate of post-9/11 America but is maybe less so now. Donald Trump was a recurring presence in WWE during this period, memorably shaving McMahon’s head after besting him at WrestleMania and even “buying” flagship brand Raw as part of the pair’s staged rivalry. The DNA of today’s toxic masculinity can be seen in the WWE’s Attitude era: Muslim performers were painted as would-be terrorists; female wrestlers, known as “divas”, were sexualised, fighting in “bra and panties” matches; and scandals around steroid abuse and traumatic head injuries were raised in lawsuits.double quotation markRather than trying to take the reins of a movement or be the poster child for something, I’m just trying to be meThe miracle of Cena’s career is that the man who spent a decade as the straight-faced embodiment of American masculinity proved to be equally good at sending it up. After a handful of underwhelming action and sports film roles, he was cast against type by Judd Apatow for the 2015 romcomTrainwreck, playing a musclebound hunk whose attempts to be threatening just sound homoerotic. Then as the pumped-up Peacemaker, first in superhero movieThe Suicide Squad(2021), then in the comedyspin-off seriesnamed after the character, Cena managed to strike a balance between serious man and silly goose that would be tricky without a healthy amount of self-awareness. This quality was on full display during Cena’s small but charming turn as a merman inBarbie, a commitment to the bit that was all the more admirable given his agents tried to talk him out of the role.Matchbox, his latest film, is a vague attempt to recapture Barbie’s magic in the more contained format of a traditional action comedy. Cena admits feeling relieved when he read the script and found the cars to be “so far down the list of things they were doing with the IP”. He plays Sean, an undercover operative whose entire life is a performance. When I wonder aloud whether the part sits close to the bone, he eagerly connects the dots himself: “How does someone who thinks they’re always being watched act in a public place? That I got a little bit of familiarity with.”Cena’s onscreen persona is an intriguing model of masculinity: the strongman remade as softie. What’s more, his wall-to-wall presence in the childhoods of millennial men makes him a far more credible advocate of positive manhood than a Joe Rogan or a Jordan Peterson. But he is reluctant to assume the mantle. “Rather than trying to take the reins of a movement or be the poster child for something, I’m just trying to be me,” he says, before offering his own diagnosis of why so many people are in the business of selling a personal vision of masculinity. “The appetite for a certain kind of manhood is just supply and demand,” he says. To the people clamouring for it, “my advice would be: go get it”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenHero move … John Cena and Danielle Brooks in Peacemaker.Photograph: HBOPerhaps Cena’s lack of desire to be cast in the role is emblematic of why it would suit him. The system, he says, “is real fragile … if I say I’m going to be the showcase of masculinity and the supply-and-demand chain pivots in five minutes, I’m shit out of luck.” He is keen to underscore how much he “loves the United States and admires its military force that makes the vow to, under the ultimate sacrifice, protect that piece of paper that says ‘We the People’. To me, that’s extremely heroic.”Cena’s own heroism came into question in 2021 when, while promotingFast & Furious 9, he referred to Taiwan as “a country”. The Chinese audience took offence, and he filmed a contrite apology in Mandarin, a language he had been learning for six years in an attempt to grow the WWE’s presence in China. In the US, the grovelling video read less as an apology than a capitulation to the weight of China’s economic might. The fan backlash was so intense that he told James Gunn he’d understand if he had to be fired from Peacemaker. He takes full responsibility for the episode. “Just because you know the language doesn’t mean you know the culture,” he says, admitting, “I got way too overconfident. I thought I was the smartest guy in the room.” Part of what frightened him was the very real possibility of “the termination of employment that I love”. The same reflex to remain loyal to the brand has carried him, without complaint, to numerous events in Saudi Arabia. “WWE offers a universal language of diplomacy,” he says. “So, to your question of: ‘Hey, the thing that you’re in is sometimes criticised for the moves that it makes as an entity – is that difficult?’ Of course it is, especially when you believe in the entity.”For a man who prides himself on saying yes, it is revealing what he has time and time again said no to. Cena does not want children, and the reasoning is entirely in keeping with his sense of discipline: they’d simply require too much of him. From 2002 to 2015 he was home “about 15 days a year and even now it’s maybe 70”, he says. “If I said yes to children, I have to say no to everything else.” His engagement to fellow wrestler Nikki Bella – his co-star on the reality show Total Bellas – collapsed in 2018, in large part over whether to have them. Cena, who’d had a vasectomy, offered to reverse it, but the relationship ended shortly after.“I really enjoy my life,” he says. Cena has granted more than 650Make-a-Wishwishes, more than anyone alive. He sees his ability to do so much work for the organisation as inextricably linked to being child-free. “If I have a family of my own, I don’t have those 650 moments … I’m flying with just my partner on this one.” Cena married Shay Shariatzadeh, an Iranian Canadian tech product manager, in 2020, after meeting in Vancouver while he was shooting a film. They had only been together a year but he’s said he would have proposed after three months. “I have a loving connection that people don’t see,” he says. “I don’t need the world to totally know me as a person.”Wrestling With Trump review – the president gets an almighty smackdown!Read moreHe remains on the WWE’s books as a “brand ambassador”, a reflection of his gratitude to the company, but also an unresolved transition back into civilian life. Next up, he will star in One Attempt Remaining, a comedy from Kay Cannon (director of Blockers and the writer-producer behind the Pitch Perfect series). He plays one half of a divorced couple who is forced to team up with his ex in order to track down the lost password to a crypto account worth millions. Whereas Dwayne Johnson has become a brand bigger than his wrestling fame, you get the sense Cena will never fully escape his WWE persona, his screen performances a callback to the exaggerated version of himself he’s been playing since 2002.Perhaps that’s what it is to be a company man: not an empty suit or a servile mouthpiece but a person so thoroughly committed to the brand it is simply who he is. Present, punctual, polite and perfunctory. The job is done and it’s back to the gym.Matchbox: The Movie premieres on Apple TVon 9 October.Explore more on these topicsFilmWrestlingCelebrityinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: I was disorganised and overwhelmed. Could a daily to-do list turn my life around? | Life and style | The Guardian
description: Whenever I thought about getting a handle on life – decluttering, sorting my finances, improving my health and productivity – I felt defeated. So I tried this month-long experiment to feel more in control
Author: Sammy Gecsoyler
Headline: Whenever I thought about getting a handle on life – decluttering, sorting my finances, improving my health and productivity – I felt defeated. So I tried this month-long experiment to feel more in control
Content: Illustration: OXOlaterre/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: OXOlaterre/The GuardianLife and styleI was disorganised and overwhelmed. Could a daily to-do list turn my life around?Whenever I thought about getting a handle on life – decluttering, sorting my finances, improving my health and productivity – I felt defeated. So I tried this month-long experiment to feel more in controlSammy GecsoylerSun 4 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAlvin and the Chipmunks was my wake-up call. A Blu-ray copy of the film had stared down from my bookshelf for years, accumulating dust, when one day a shard of sunlight landed on it, as if directed by a higher power. This prompted some uncomfortable questions. Had I watched it? No. Did I intend to? No. So why had I let it linger there untouched for such a long time? The answer is simple: I’m a disorganised mess.Zooming out, things weren’t much better. I had a mountain of clothes that needed to be hung up or put away, cupboards stuffed with God knows what, plates and mugs that I had never used … The thought of sorting everything out was overwhelming.My mind wandered to other areas of my life that could do with some scrubbing up: my finances, health and general productivity. There are 24 hours in a day but, more often than not, they flitter away and I’ve hardly achieved anything.I am not the only person who struggles with the constant demands of modern life. Hence the boom in admin nights, where strangers gather in cafes and bars to blast through their backlog of unpaid bills, unanswered texts or unneeded subscriptions.My first step, though, was to pick up a notepad and pen and do something I hadn’t done in a long time. I made a list, and immediately felt a little better about myself. As Vicky Reynal, a London-based psychotherapist, puts it: “We all have something in our minds about the kind of person we want to be, whether that’s ‘adulting’ while taking more responsibility, or looking after ourselves to the best of our ability, and sometimes a to-do list can help us move a step closer.” So began what I hoped would be a month-long journey of self-improvement.Day 1“Sort out clothes.” This is the first item on my to-do list. And what a mammoth task I’ve set myself. My clothing rail has two dozen smart-looking white wooden hangers to give my setup a sleek, curated look. But this is undermined not only by the shabby old garments hanging off them, in a sight to make Miranda Priestly gag, but also by the heap of clothing that sits in a compartment above. The lower layers are neatly folded but the T-shirts, trousers and shorts near the top are scrunched and rolled up, slotted into random gaps to maintain the structural integrity of my fabric Jenga tower.View image in fullscreenBreak down tasks into smaller steps to make them manageable.Photograph: Creative Images Lab/Getty ImagesThe first step is to dismantle this heap, which, I’m ashamed to say, is almost three feet high. “Oh, I was looking for that” and “I’d wondered where that was,” I mutter intermittently as I sort through it.My word, there is a lot of hideous stuff. For years, I have bought clothes only if they are in the sale and, aside from a few gems, I’ve amassed a wardrobe full of one-hit misfires, worn once before being tossed on the pile or shoved on to a hanger. Among them is a multicoloured denim Tommy Hilfiger jacket that Andrew Lloyd Webber would probably consider a bit much even for his Joseph.I am about halfway through, with two bin bags full of clothes for the charity shop, when I realise I have taken on too much for one day. This is where I learn my first lesson: break down each task. “A good to-do list is achievable, realistic and has concrete objectives,” says Reynal. “When you break down tasks into small steps, they become more manageable and less frightening.”Day 3Starting my day with a to-do list is not only becoming part of my morning routine – it is helping me form one again. Instead of jumping straight into work emails, I put my phone and laptop aside and, notebook in hand, think: what do I need to do today? This is much easier without the constant barrage of notifications.I squiggle down the basics: make coffee and eat breakfast. It may sound silly, but as I tick off every task, no matter how insignificant, it gives me a push to keep going. I then write up a list of my work tasks, including a few I would normally leave until they became urgent, and feel calmer for it. It is the most productive working day I’ve had in ages. I also jot down some other things I’d like to achieve today: spend an hour reading, go to the gym and buy some more bin bags for my clear-out.I finish sorting out my clothes after work. A gym session follows and, just before going to sleep, I fit in an hour of reading. I tick this final item off my list and get another hit of dopamine.Day 7View image in fullscreenSammy filling out his to-do list in Barcelona.Photograph: Courtesy of Sammy GecsoylerToday is my first big test. I’m in Barcelona for a weekend trip, and surely a holiday is a time to unwind and leave the pressures of normal life behind? But I don’t want to fall back into bad habits, so I’m pressing ahead with my daily to-do list.As I lie on my hotel bed, however, I realise filling it with tasks is a bit of a struggle. “Read for an hour” is the only substantial one. The rest are things my mum would tell me to do: put on sunscreen, eat dinner, get souvenirs.I place the notebook in my backpack in case something else pops into my head, but I get carried away with having fun instead.Before I know it, it’s 2am and I’m in a nightclub. Out of nowhere, a pang of guilt hits me. I haven’t opened my notebook for hours and most of my tasks remain undone. I consider whipping out my copy of The Grapes of Wrath to fit in the reading, but reconsider and press on with the night.Day 10I’ve been ill ever since I made a noisy exit from the nightclub at 4am, and an angry local doused me with cold water. For the past two days, my notebook has been untouched. I know I have a valid excuse but I can’t help feeling bad. Reynal had warned me that to-do lists can be destructive, especially if they are too ambitious or you “beat yourself up over what you didn’t achieve that day”. Even so, I can’t help thinking of all the tasks mounting up.Day 15I’m much better now, and excited about tackling my backlog, which includes finishing sorting out my home and getting on top of work emails. As an experiment, I’ve also ditched my notebook in favour of an app called Todoist.In the morning, I log my tasks on my phone but notice that I am wandering towards other apps, my focus on the day at hand beginning to dwindle. Nevertheless, I crack on with tackling my bookshelf, which has more than 100 books plus 50 DVDs, video games and that damned Alvin and the Chipmunks Blu-ray. It’s the first thing tossed into a bin bag. Among the other tat I’ve accumulated are three copies of The Day of the Triffids, none of which I’ve read, stacks of magazines, some of which date back at least five years, and a few 1,000-page doorstoppers that I’m never going to read.View image in fullscreen‘I crack on with tackling my bookshelf.’Photograph: Grace Cary/Getty ImagesSome things are hard to let go of and I feel a conflict between the person I thought I might one day become (an incredibly well-read master of the zeitgeist), the reality (I crack the spines of about a dozen books a year) and who the lists are making me (ruthlessly organised and productivity-driven). I take a step back and return some of the more ambitious titles to my bookshelf. Although I want to be more productive, it’s not at the cost of believing that I’ll get around to War and Peace one day.Day 18My digital to-do list isn’t really hitting. Starting my day off in the virtual realm allows my thoughts to sway and old impulses to take over: namely succumbing to notifications and doomscrolling. So I’ve reverted to my notepad, and oh, how I’ve missed it. The quaint squiggle of a pen focuses my thoughts once more. Reynal says it’s a matter of “personal preference … Some clients tell me of the satisfaction they feel from physically crossing something off a list. But these days apps can throw confetti at you and help you feel equally in touch with the emotional feeling that comes when you achieve something.”I spend longer than usual collating my list and use today as a bit of a reset. To help me along, I invite some friends over for our very own admin night. According to one study with which Reynal was involved, attending one of these a month could save you £2,400 a year, especially if you use the time to focus on budgeting or find cheaper utility providers.Two friends show up at about 6pm and we get ready to knuckle down. I even throw some picky bits in the air fryer and put on some ambient music. But I soon realise that my small studio flat isn’t really set up for this, as we all squeeze on to my sofa, computers on our laps.I plan to get a handle on my finances: cancel subscriptions, study my outgoings and see how much I can save if I cut out all my frivolous spending. I make a good start, filling in a few columns of my spreadsheet but the close quarters setup soon becomes stifling. This, combined with the music, makes me feel as if I’m stuck in a cramped lift with no way out.Day 22View image in fullscreenA list is helpful when it comes to meal planning.Photograph: Tatiana Maksimova/Getty ImagesThings are firmly back on track. My notebook is getting well used and today is all about meal prep. Usually when I go shopping, I don’t have a list and grab whatever catches my eye. This results in some very haphazard meals that rarely hit the spot. No more, I say today, and go to the supermarket with a thought-out list accounting for protein, cost and taste. When I return home, I whip up an extra-meaty chilli, some spicy chicken noodles and, with my remaining mince, beef kofte and some bulgur.Would I have done this without my to-do (and shopping) list? No. Balanced nutrition is one of the last things I usually think about while trying to keep up with everything.Day 25Today doesn’t get off to a great start: I rush out of the door without jotting down my tasks. To be fair, I’mcoveringthe Clacton byelection and expecting a hectic day once I arrive in Essex. So when I have a moment, I do something that might sound pointless: I write down the tasks I’ve already done today – pack bag, buy train ticket, email XYZ – to take stock of everything I’ve accomplished so far. Reynal says some of her clients do the same: “You’re trying to tap a little bit further into that feeling of achievement.”The day drags on, and then the night. The result isn’t declared until about 5am. The lack of sleep must be making me hallucinate: an intergalactic bin came in second.Day 28A lot of the big tasks on my list are getting crossed out. My flat is getting decluttered, I’ve zoomed through a big pile of non-urgent work emails, and my financial and physical health has improved. A few hard tasks remain, though Reynal says ticking off the easiest things can “spark a virtuous cycle. It gives you a sense of confidence that you can achieve something.”But she advises against leaving the toughest stuff until the end, “when you’re depleted and your energy is at its lowest”. Her warning is ringing in my ears as I tackle two big cupboards I haven’t dug through properly in years. Aside from a few surprise items, including a pink minifridge, the expectation turns out to be worse than the reality. The bulk of the rubbish is empty appliance boxes. I speed through the clear-out, and proudly tick off this once daunting task.Day 31It’s the final day of my to-do list experiment. Has it changed my life? In some ways, yes. Not necessarily because of what I have thrown away, or replied to, or tidied up, but because of the sense of control it has given me. I had long assumed there was nothing I could do to battle my feeling of being overwhelmed. We are always accessible through our phones, subscriptions are king if you want to keep up with the cultural zeitgeist, and with contactless taps and takeaway apps the norm nowadays, it’s no wonder our finances and health can spin out of control.“As life becomes more chaotic and complex, it becomes increasingly difficult to hold everything in our minds. Our mental load is growing and, with it, so is the stress of holding it all together,” says Reynal. “Any tools that can help us hold it all in place are helpful and to-do lists are one of those tools.”Hear, hear. That gets a tick from me.Explore more on these topicsLife and styleHealth & wellbeingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Star Wars actor John Boyega on the day his 10-year-old school friend Damilola Taylor was killed: ‘It kept me up at night because I was just with the guy’ | Damilola Taylor | The Guardian
description: The star was just eight when his friend was stabbed. Decades on, he’s ready to talk about that day – how it shaped him, and how, as he becomes a father himself, it will shape him as a dad
Author: JN Benjamin
Headline: The star was just eight when his friend was stabbed. Decades on, he’s ready to talk about that day – how it shaped him, and how, as he becomes a father himself, it will shape him as a dad
Content: John Boyega:Photograph: Austin Hargrave/Austin Hargrave / AUGUSTView image in fullscreenJohn Boyega:Photograph: Austin Hargrave/Austin Hargrave / AUGUSTDamilola TaylorStar Wars actor John Boyega on the day his 10-year-old school friend Damilola Taylor was killed: ‘It kept me up at night because I was just with the guy’The star was just eight when his friend was stabbed. Decades on, he’s ready to talk about that day – how it shaped him, and how, as he becomes a father himself, it will shape him as a dadJN BenjaminSun 4 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 08.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“Ifeel a bit nervous,” confesses John Boyega, as he sits down in front of the camera. “Speaking about it could possibly help. I haven’t revisited this in a long time. Yeah, my heart is just beating.” The Attack the Block and Star Wars actor is talking in the opening scene of a new BBC Two documentary about the killing of 10-year-old schoolboyDamilola Taylor.On 27 November 2000, Damilola was stabbed in the leg with a broken bottle and left to die in a concrete stairwell, attacked as he walked home from an after-school club at Peckham library in south London. It took six years and three separate trials at the Old Bailey, costing a total of £16m, to secure a manslaughter conviction. His death shocked the nation not only because he was so young, but because all the suspects were also children. Boyega was one of the last people to see Damilola alive. The pair had enjoyed a close friendship since Damilola’s move to the UK from Nigeria in August of that year.View image in fullscreenDamilola Taylor, who was just 10 when he was killed.Photograph: PAWatching the film at a Bafta screening a few weeks before its premiere, it’s striking how young and vulnerable the 34-year-old actor looks as he talks about the death of his friend. Boyega is more often seen looking assured and confident, be that his impassioned, impromptu address to thousands of people at a Black Lives Matter protest in Hyde Park, posing for the Pirelli calendar, or portraying an African king in a Hollywood movie. Usually he stands tall, with broad shoulders supported by a proud stance. But in revisiting the memories of that day, it feels as if he has almost reverted to the eight-year-old child he was nearly 26 years ago when he found out his friend had died.A couple of hours later I reconvene with him at BBC New Broadcasting House to discuss the show. In person, Boyega is unassuming, with a calm demeanour and a welcoming smile. He has just returned from a trip to New York fashion week and looks surprisingly fresh-faced for somebody who has not long stepped off a transatlantic flight.Boyega is sitting comfortably with his father Samson, his mother Abigail and an older cousin. It’s a lively space – Boyega lives in Los Angeles now and I get the impression that everybody is excited to snatch a bit of time with him while he’s in London. We immediately get into a five-way conversation about the criminal proceedings around Damilola’s death. Everybody is talking at once.The first trial collapsed after the judge ruled that the prosecution’s key witness was unreliable and there was controversy about items of crucial evidence that were excluded from the proceedings. The family closely followed all three trials – in the second, the jury failed to reach a verdict for two of the three defendants on a charge of murder – and there is a sense of frustration at the opportunities missed when it came to bringing the killers to justice.“You would have thought the influence of the Stephen Lawrence case would have been way stronger, if they had actually learned something. It didn’t come across like that,” Boyega sighs. The police investigation was heavily criticised after it was found to have made a number of significant mistakes.The whole Boyega family knew Damilola; but the actor has previously said very little about him in public. Boyega has worked consistently since his 2011 debut in sci-fi cult classic Attack The Block, including a gamechanging role as a lead in Disney’s Star Wars franchise. His most recent projects, The Woman King (2022) and They Cloned Tyrone (2023), were both critically acclaimed. He has said that his professional success is in no small part due to being inspired by the way Damilola lived his short life.View image in fullscreenBoyega in 2011 film Attack the Block.Photograph: Optimum Releasing/ Sportsphoto/AllstarHe has been deeply involved in the documentary. “The first time I watched a rough cut I was in my living room and it was bright out. Since then, we’ve been watching daily edits, y’know, on a phone, on a laptop, on a little TV. But viewing it in the cinematic setup hits different – it was an emotional hill to get over, seeing the film like that. I feel really impacted by it.” Throughout the 75-minute screening, crying and sniffling could be heard around the room. “It’s one of those films I wouldn’t watch multiple times because of my personal relationship to it, but it’s definitely a film I will refer to – when my child comes of age I will show him this film. You need to know the realities of your lineage.”On Damilola Taylor’s first day at Oliver Goldsmith primary school in Peckham, shortly after his arrival in the UK, a teacher assigned Boyega’s sister Grace to be his chaperone. She says in the documentary: “My teacher was like, ‘Grace, there’s a new guy and he’s from Nigeria and obviously you’re Nigerian so you understand the language – you can show him around.’” They became a trio, because Boyega and his sister were inseparable at the time.“The only reason I was around him a lot was because I was always with my sister – I inherited Damilola,” Boyega tells me, laughing. “I stayed because I found him hilarious.”double quotation markThe psychological impact is something that definitely stayed with meView image in fullscreenBoyega in a still from the documentary about Damilola.Photograph: BBC/Optomen TVHis father chimes in with a poignant memory: “John don’t have many friends – at least not boys. John had girls surrounding him. And I remember asking, ‘John, why are you hanging around girls?’ and he said, ‘Dad, boys are dangerous – they’ll beat me up.’” At lunchtimes, the three of them would run around the playground together.Boyega describes the day Damilola died as a transformational moment for him. “The psychological impact is something that definitely stayed with me, but now it’s expressed through appreciation. Every time I wake up and I’m here, I appreciate it.” He smiles as he says of talking to his friends: “I’ll tell my boys, ‘Hey, a bullet don’t look at you and be like, “You’ve done movies before,” and swerve you!’” As a child, though, his thoughts were less positive. “When I would hear that anybody had been stabbed or whatever, it just felt like it was getting closer and closer and that awareness became part of day-to-day life. I was very scared of that.”Boyega was eight when Damilola was killed; he had previously thought that death “only happened to old people”. He was bewildered by it – “like when babies fall and everyone goes, ‘Oh my gosh!’ and then the baby [seeing the response] decides to cry? It was like that.” As the news sank in, he found it difficult to comprehend that bad things could happen to good people. “I was trying to compute what that meant. I thought about the practicality of it. The last breath. Does it hurt? I remember with Grace we would have conversations where I’d be like, ‘Do you think death is sleep?’ or, ‘Maybe they go for 20 years and then, they come back?’ It kept me up at night because I wasjustwith the guy, y’know?”In the aftermath of Damilola’s death, Boyega spent a lot of time at home in his bedroom. Sometimes friends would knock for him and he would tell his mother to relay the message that he didn’t want to go out. “The hand of death is influencing kids to kill kids. I’m like, ‘Damn, I’m a kid, let me stay where I feel the most safe.’ I had a home that granted extreme safety and my parents didn’t shy away from showing concern.”This played out in many ways, including their choice for his secondary school. Instead of the options in their home borough, he was sent to Westminster City School – almost an hour away by bus. Was getting out of the area a response to Damilola’s death? Boyega’s father answers: “Before John says anything, I went to his teacher when he was going to secondary school and he said to me, ‘Mr Boyega, why do you have to choose Westminster?’ And I never said to him what I saw: that the environment here will corrupt this guy,” he says, pointing at his son. “I saw what was coming, that in the future this environment is going to be very, very dangerous.” This was in 2003. By the end of the decade, 188 teenagers had been murdered on the streets of London.I direct the conversation back to Boyega. Did he have therapy back then? He lowers his chin and looks at me with a furrowed brow. What he appears to be conveying is there’s no such thing as therapy in an African household – especially not a 1990s African household. We both laugh. At this point I am conscious that my question could easily be construed as a criticism of his parents, who are sitting on the sofa opposite us in the suddenly quite claustrophobic room. We quickly move on.Over the years there have been numerous documentaries focusing on various aspects of Damilola’s killing, from a 2002 BBC Panorama special to most recently one fronted by broadcaster Yinka Bokinni to mark the 20th anniversary of Damilola’s death. This latest project focuses much of the narrative on the 24 hours leading up to his killing.We hear from a number of people who were critical to the investigation in its early stages, including the estate maintenance worker who first found Damilola as he lay bleeding in the stairwell. There were several months of discussions between Boyega and the director, Alex Thomas – who also directed the award-winning Sky Original documentary Bibaa and Nicole: Murder in the Park, about the 2020 killings of Bibaa Henry and Nicole Smallman. “It fell to me to decide who was coming from my world to sit down and talk,” says Boyega. “That’s when I decided that Grace would be more appropriate to discuss Damilola than me because that was her direct friend – they were around the same age. And I think her perspective on it was quite important.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThat was the easy part. More difficult was deciding how to address the ecosystem of bullying and fear on the streets of Peckham that led up to and ultimately underpinned Damilola’s killing. In the final edit, much of this element of the storytelling is omitted.It doesn’t go unnoticed. During a Q&A after the screening, a Bafta member in the audience queries the lack of backstory included about the lives of the two boys convicted of Damilola’s manslaughter. In August 2006, brothers Danny and Ricky Preddie were each sentenced to eight years in youth custody after the third trial. The questioner pointed out that the brothers appeared at the Old Bailey unattended by any family. “I’d love to know why you left that out,” they said, referring to the brothers’ troubled childhoods. It was well known that their single mother struggled immensely while raising them. The pair were eventually placed in a local authority children’s care home. “We did look at the option of interviewing the two brothers,”said Boyega, who explained a general concern within the team that it might be viewed as being too empathetic to the perpetrators. In the end, the decision was made not to approach them.But Boyega agrees that some elements of their backstory do have a place in the narrative, in particular when it comes to the debate about how to end youth violence. “Family. Discipline,” he says decisively. “The fact that you don’t have an adult at home that holds you accountable is a very important thing, especially for boys. Especially for boys.” He repeats the last sentence a little slower to emphasise its importance. “But y’know, you could have two parents at home and the child still goes out and does what they need to do, so there’s obviously a more nuanced conversation. Even in the sense that someone showed you that they loved you, that they cared about what you did or whether or not you made a mistake. What that person [in the screening Q&A] said made me think about what it meant – that they didn’t have that. Not even a social worker.”double quotation markI didn’t know I was poor until I was in year 7. When you’re super-young, you’re not really thinking about that. When you get to school, you start to see where you are in the food chain of lifeThere’s an extended silence when I ask Boyega what was difficult about making the documentary. “Poverty,” he replies, eventually. He means it brought back memories of the poverty he experienced as a child. Growing up, he lived in a small flat on Sceaux Gardens estate just off Peckham Road, with both his parents and his elder sisters – Grace, who appears in the documentary, and Blessing, who generally keeps a much lower profile. His mother was a care worker and his father a Pentecostal minister. “I didn’t know I was poor until I was in year 7. When you’re super-young, you’re not really thinking about that. And then when you get to school, you start to see where you are in the food chain of life, and that’s when you start to compare yourself with other children and other kids.” The process of filming the documentary brought that world back into focus.Boyega recalls being keen not to stand out for the wrong reasons in his first year at Westminster City School, and begging his mother to buy him a pair of Kickers. She took him to Barrie Howard, a shoe shop on East Street in Walworth – a strategic rite of passage for any south Londoner who hoped to survive the brutal transition from primary to secondary. But once he had the shoes he felt bad, because he could tell how much it cost her. “I never asked for Kickers from my mum again – I wore Clarks for the rest of school.” Recounting these memories, plus seeing the archive footage of Peckham and the burgundy Oliver Goldsmith school sweater, brought back the distinct feeling that he had so much less than many of his peers. “I did work hard to get out of that. In making this film I had to revisit who I used to be, and that bothered me.” The interviews took place while he was on location in the Isle of Skye making a supernatural horror movie,The Punishing, in which he stars alongside Cara Delevingne (it is currently in post-production). The surroundings served as a physical reminder of how far he’s come in life.View image in fullscreenBoyega with Oscar Isaac in Star Wars: The Force Awakens, 2015.Photograph: Disney/Lucasfilm/AllstarView image in fullscreen… and with his family at the London premiere of Star Wars: The Last Jedi, 2017.Photograph: PA Images/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.Boyega had some reservations about being involved in the project. His main concern was that he wanted to make sure that Damilola’s brother – Tunde Taylor, chair of the Damilola Taylor Trust – was happy with the way Damilola’s life is portrayed. “I’ve been in the public eye for a minute now and from my experience, you have to be very careful, because you don’t know which journalist is being stressed by an editor. You don’t know which person wants to grab a story and not use it with the right intentions. You don’t know if they’re gonna be respectful to the people who are really involved.” But he was reassured by meeting producer Nelson Adeosun, a childhood family friend, and fellow contributor Leroy Logan. Logan is the founder and former chairman of the Black Police Association, whom Boyega portrayed in the film Red, White and Blue, from Steve McQueen’s 2020 anthology series, Small Axe. The performance won him a Golden Globe award.Settling down thousands of miles away from Peckham has inevitably changed Boyega’s relationship with the place that made him who he is. “South is still familiar, but if I go now, people have to guide me … it’s so, so different,” he says, referring to the gentrification of the area. For him, though, the heart of the place is in the people who remember what it was like when he was growing up. We do a little reminiscing about which legendary hangouts have survived. He is pleased to note that Bagel King is on the list.Somebody pokes their head round the door to tell us we need to wrap up. Boyega’s on a tight schedule. I ask a final question. Tell me about your jewellery, I say, indicating towards his left hand. “Oh yeah, this is my wedding ring,” he says casually. “I’ve been married for coming up to two years now.” He doesn’t give any detail about his wife, but does say they had a small ceremony, joking that he got married the way Braveheart did, while miming the action of planting a sword in the ground. He continues by reaching to the deepest depth of his vocal range and bellowing, “Will you come with me?”His eldest sister has now joined us and the room has erupted into a chorus of unrestrained laughter. I note that the ring he is wearing is different from the one he wears in the documentary. “Yeah, this is our very sentimental ring,” he says of the two-toned band. “This is the one we decided to pick up spontaneously because I just wanted the ring on my finger, so we went to Walmart to get this. It was a lovely trip to Walmart. Shout out, Walmart Canoga Park!” he laughs. I am surprised to learn that he didn’t have a traditional Nigerian ceremony. “I would love to have a wedding celebration. We both like the idea of celebrating something established, rather than celebrating the entry. And by then, we’ll have to shut Nigeria down!”It occurs to me that the child he mentioned earlier in the conversation may not be hypothetical. Are you about to hard launch a baby, I inquire tentatively. “My baby’s on the way. We got a baby cooking.” And you said my son earlier – is that because you’re having a boy? He confirms this and that he also has a young stepson. “So, you know, my life is completely, completely fulfilled in terms of family. It’s been so nice with the timing.”Getting used to the new dynamic away from the public eye has obviously served him well – and perhaps this is why he is now ready to speak publicly about his friendship with Damilola. “I do think it’s important to reach back and tell people the grounded realities of your origins, because it wasn’t until I knew the grounded realities of other people’s origins that I decided to pursue something more.” When thinking about the kind of father he wants to be, it’s all still sinking in. “Us being parents is funny! I just want to make sure I’m present, I’m consistent and full of love.”These personal milestones explain why he’s been less visible in recent years. “I’ve tried to as much as possible – especially following periods when I’ve worked a lot – to de-centre my career. There have been certain moments when I’ve known that this is a time for family. Y’know, there’s stuff to do.” In this moment he’s clear that his purpose is to love his wife and sons and invest in the support system that he knows he is lucky to have had.Damilola: The Untold Story is on BBC Two and iPlayer from 5 OctoberExplore more on these topicsDamilola TaylorJohn BoyegaDocumentary filmsDeath and dyingChildrenFriendshipKnife crimefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: A cargo ship, 20 crew, and a huge stash of cocaine: the seafarer imprisoned for smuggling – on no evidence | Shipping industry | The Guardian
description: After Turkish police found drugs on board the Phoenician M, the ship’s chief mate, Ali Albokhari, was sentenced to 30 years in prison. His wife is still fighting to free him
Author: Will Coldwell
Headline: After Turkish police found drugs on board the Phoenician M, the ship’s chief mate, Ali Albokhari, was sentenced to 30 years in prison. His wife is still fighting to free him
Content: Elena Albokhari​ with the budgies bred for her in prison by her husband Ali.Photograph: Juuso Westerlund/The GuardianView image in fullscreenElena Albokhari​ with the budgies bred for her in prison by her husband Ali.Photograph: Juuso Westerlund/The GuardianShipping industryA cargo ship, 20 crew, and a huge stash of cocaine: the seafarer imprisoned for smuggling – on no evidenceAfter Turkish police found drugs on board the Phoenician M, the ship’s chief mate, Ali Albokhari, was sentenced to 30 years in prison. His wife is still fighting to free himWill ColdwellSun 4 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 10.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the early hours of 6 October 2023, Elena Albokhari was woken by a text message from her husband. Ali Albokhari, 42, a Finnish-Syrian with dark hair and cherubic features, was chief mate on a cargo ship named the Phoenician M and had been at sea since June. The 180-metre bulk carrier had docked at Ereğli in the Turkish Black Sea a few days earlier and Ali was due to return home to Helsinki soon, but instead of feeling excitement, Elena was growing increasingly worried about his welfare.She’d had a similar feeling of unease a month earlier, when the ship had arrived at Barranquilla,Colombia. Ali had called in a panic to report that drugs had been found; Armada Nacional officers had marched onboard and uncovered holdalls stuffed with 137kg cocaine. Labels on the packages – the crest of Turkish football club Kayserispor – hinted at their destination: Turkey was the next port of call. “I never want to work as a seaman again,” Ali told Elena. “We are having big problems.”For two days, the ship was held at the port. Elena, 39, a tour guide from Russia, was so anxious, she could barely sleep. Then she received a photo from Ali of the crew happily drinking beer in a restaurant – the drugs had been removed and, after a meeting with the harbourmaster, the ship cleared to depart. “So will you go on working as a seaman?” Elena asked. “Yeah,” Ali said. “Sometimes it happens … so it’s OK.”Yet when the Phoenician M arrived at Ereğli on 2 October, loaded with coal, it was targeted by Turkish narcotics officers. The ship’s captain, Marko Bekavac, 63, a steely Croatian with three decades’ experience as a seafarer, had already informed the ship’s management company about the incident in Colombia, and when Turkish authorities boarded, he immediately declared that drugs had previously been found on the ship. Despite this, officers delivered a statement: should anything be found onboard, he would be accountable.The 20 crew members, including citizens of Russia, Ukraine, Poland and the Philippines, were ordered to remain in the ship’s mess room as the police continued to investigate. Nothing was found in an initial search but days later, as the coal was unloaded, suspicious bags were reportedly found buried in the cargo hold. They were packed with more cocaine. The captain and other crew were escorted from the ship.Ali, who was second in command, remained onboard as unloading continued. He had managed to keep hold of his phone and was sending Elena updates. These had done little to allay her fears. Now, in the middle of the night, a text message confirmed the worst: “They are going to arrest us.”Unless we are related to a seafarer, or live near a major port, most of us don’t encounter the people who work in shipping. Yet without them our lives would grind to a halt. Oceanic trade routes are the thread that weaves the world together. Merchant shipping – often described as the “lifeblood of the global economy” – is responsible for the movement of 90% of trade; every year, 11bn tonnes of goods, from coffee to fuel to fashion, are transported by ship. The scale of the maritime infrastructure is staggering, but the 2.57 million seafarers who operate within it remain largely invisible, as do many of the challenges they face.Elena never thought of Ali’s work as inherently risky, and the life of a merchant seaman can seem mundane. Cargo ships travel at around 15 knots (17mph). A boat like the Phoenician M can take more than two weeks to traverse the Atlantic. The routine involves inspections, maintenance checks, paperwork and long stretches at sea. But seafarers have become vulnerable to rapidly shifting conflicts – from the Russian invasion of Ukraine to the battle around the strait of Hormuz – as well as poor regulatory oversight, abandonment by shipowners and abuse by port authorities. Seafarers’ rights are frequently neglected and they are too easily scapegoated for events outside their control. When an incident occurs, it is often far easier for authorities to pursue crew members than the shipping companies that employ them, who have an incentive to let the blame fall on individuals, and the P&I (protection and indemnity) clubs that insure them are there to serve the company, not individual crew members. The very nature of the job means voyaging to far-flung destinations, so if things do go wrong, seafarers can be forced to navigate unfamiliar judicial systems, with discretionary legal support, and face long periods of detention in a foreign country. Data on the scale of the problem is limited, but one 2018 survey by Nautilus International, the maritime professionals’ union, found that 90% of seafarers feared criminalisation above anything else. A recent survey by InterManager, the ship management association, has compiled 118 known cases over the past three decades, with a peak of 23 cases in 2023. Senior officers are most at risk; in 63% of cases, the captain was imprisoned.View image in fullscreenAli on a simulator vessel in Finland …Photograph: courtesy of Elena AlbokhariView image in fullscreen… and the Phoenician M, the ship he joined in June 2023.Photograph: courtesy of Bernard DelmontCases of seafarer criminalisation range from fuel smuggling allegations to collisions, but of particular concern is the global drug trade. Much like any other commodity, the vast majority of cocaine is transported by sea. Ports in Colombia are key export hubs. Cargo ships are up to 400 metres long and usually have just a couple of dozen crew; it’s not hard to find a place to hide something on them. In 2019, Capt Andrzej Lasota, a Polish seafarer, spent two years in prison in Mexico after 240kg of cocaine – planted on the ship at Barranquilla – was uncovered during unloading at Altamira. He was charged with “negligence” for failing to be aware of the drugs buried under coal in the cargo hold.The case was widely condemned, and resonates with that of the Phoenician M. Ali is now the only crew member who remains imprisoned, three years after his arrest. The International Maritime Organization has said the case “demonstrates how vulnerable seafarers are when they fall victim to organised international crime”. The International Transport Workers’ Federation (ITF), a union that represents seafarers, described it as a “gross abuse” of human rights.As a seafarer’s wife, Elena was used to spending time apart from her husband. But now Ali – whom she would speak to by phone or message almost daily – was no longer contactable, she felt truly alone. When she called the German crewing agency, Team Ship, desperate for answers, it was still unaware of the incident. A number she had for the company responsible for the crew and the ship, Iskenderun Ship Management, a Turkish operator, went unanswered. She waited for a call from some sort of official body, explaining what was going on, but none came.Elena frantically tried to make contact with anyone who might know what had happened. After she posted on online chat groups for seafarers, she was messaged by the wife of a crew member who had not been among those taken by the police. Only after calling him was she able to piece together what was happening. Ali, along with Bekavac and eight other crew members, had been arrested on suspicion of drug smuggling.Another week or so passed. Elena had another call with the crewing agency, which said lawyers would be provided by Iskenderun at no cost. “Don’t worry, they are in the police station, they are being questioned, then they will be released,” Elena recalls an agent telling her. “You just need to wait.” So she waited. But instead, the men were detained and charged. During those first days, Elena says, the crew had no legal representation.When shipping incidents occur, a lawyer is usually appointed by a local P&I club “correspondent”, an independent adviser who can act on behalf of the shipowner and the club. When a lawyer was appointed, the crew said they were encouraged to accept the charges and sign what they described as arrest warrants, written in Turkish. “So we did,” one told Human Rights at Sea International, an NGO. “We were detained.” UK P&I, the club that provided insurance for the Phoenician M, said all appointments in this case, “including legal representation and the P&I correspondent”, were made by the shipowner, not them. They added that while they were not bound to do so, they provided support for the crew’s “significant” defence costs.double quotation markI remember when he received the call about the job. He was so happyDays turned to weeks, then months. The men were moved from a local detention centre to a maximum security prison. Ali was one of many now isolated from their families, terrified about what would happen next. “Every day I was crying inside of that cell,” one Filipino crew member told me, adding that for a long time he didn’t know why he was being held. As for Elena, six months passed before she was finally able to speak with her husband. He put on a brave face, telling her he was OK, but asked her to send money: “If nobody sends you money in prison, you can’t buy food, you can’t buy anything.” Elena sent money and clothes, and waited for the men to stand trial. Another six months passed.Finally, on 16 September 2024, following a number of hearings at Karadeniz Ereğli high criminal court, a verdict was due. Elena was sure Ali would be released. While he sat in the courtroom, she spent the day at home, anxiously awaiting the outcome. Then she received a brief message from the Finnish embassy. “I’m so sorry ... ” it said. While the eight other crew members had been acquitted, Ali and Bekavac had been found guilty on the basis of “command responsibility” and sentenced to 30 years’ imprisonment. Elena was stunned. Eventually she replied, “What should I do now?”Ali and Elena’s home is a one-bedroom flat in a modern housing estate not far from Helsinki’s airport. When I visit in September, Elena, true to her profession as a tour guide, has laid out a spread of local treats: pancakes, blueberry juice, grilled cheese with cloudberry jam. Ali’s suitcase, which she was able to retrieve after his sentence, is still slumped near the balcony door. She tries to remain optimistic for his return. Every week, she buys fresh flowers. On the wall above it she has pinned a banner: “Welcome Home”.If the maritime industry is emblematic of the power of globalisation, Ali and Elena’s relationship is a story of what it means to live on its faultlines. Ali was born in Damascus, Syria. His mother raised him and his three siblings, together with his stepfather, who ran a shoe business. When Ali reached college age, his options for further education were limited – as were the countries he could travel to – so his family decided he should attend the maritime university in St Petersburg, Russia, which was the most affordable option. He graduated in 2011, just as Syria descended into civil war, meaning he could neither remain in Russia nor safely return home. He applied for asylum inFinlandand was accepted, continuing his studies at the Novia University in Turku. In 2017, Ali was granted full citizenship.Elena was born in Moscow. Her mother was a language teacher, her father an electrician. As she got older, she, too, was eager to build a life beyond her homeland and spent time as a student in Spain. She met Ali on a dating app in 2021. At the time, Elena, who had been working as a Spanish-language interpreter and tour guide in Russia, was hoping to continue her studies in Finland. If she managed to get accepted to a Finnish-language programme, the education would be free, and she was eager to practise with native speakers. When Ali struck up a conversation, she was intrigued by this Middle Eastern man who spoke her native Russian. He was at sea at the time, but they began speaking regularly over phone and video call. When Elena travelled to Finland to take her Finnish-language test, he met her at the airport. She passed her test and they married in January 2022. A month later, Russia invaded Ukraine.View image in fullscreenAli and Elena heading to their wedding in January 2022.Photograph: courtesy of Elena AlbokhariThey had all these plans, Elena says, but Ali struggled to find a job. For the past decade he had primarily worked on Russian ships; now Russia was at war and he struggled to find work with Finnish companies, which Elena believes was due to his Syrian heritage. Ali eventually secured a nine-month contract with a Russian shipping company, and Elena returned to Moscow to visit her mother. She was able to meet him briefly, when his ship stopped at Murmansk, but when Ali returned to Finland at the end of his contract, Elena became stranded in Russia for a further three months while she awaited the paperwork needed to leave. It was December 2022 when they finally reunited in Helsinki. For the first year of their marriage, they were like ships in the night.It took months for Ali to secure his next contract: not just a job but a promotion, too. “I remember when he received the call,” Elena says. “He was so happy.” In May 2023 he was packing his bags, preparing to head to London to join the existing crew as they finished their rotation. The ship he was heading for was the Clipper Palma. In June, under the new management of Iskenderun, it was renamed: the Phoenician M.Looking back, there were things about the job that seemed a bit off to Elena. Ali, who was appointed as the ship’s security officer, described the vessel as very old. He was also critical of the attitude of Iskenderun. When the crew made requests they would be unresponsive; some of these requests would prove critical to the case. When Bekavac noted Barranquilla was on the list of destinations, he requested additional security personnel, as well as cameras and locks for doors and hatches, due to the high risk of interference from drug cartels. Iskenderun did not respond.
