Elena says the lawyer appointed to Ali by Iskenderun visited him in prison rarely and did not seem to be prioritising his interests. “They were saying, ‘Don’t say a single word about the company … otherwise he will spend a long time there.’”Since Ali was sentenced, Elena has been lobbying for his release while trying to keep her own life afloat. When he was arrested, she was still a relative newcomer to Finland, with no support network and no job, as she was still studying. Sanctions on Russia meant their credit cards did not work: “I was left without money, without help.” Elena was dismayed by the lack of support from the Finnish government. While its consular service has visited Ali in prison a number of times since late 2024, statements on the case have been scarce, and it is notably absent from Finnish media. One reason may be that Finland andTurkeyhave not had the easiest relations in recent years. Ankara put up resistance to Finland’s application to join Nato in 2022; since then it has made a growing number of extradition requests for political dissidents, which Finland has largely rejected.View image in fullscreenAli (in red T-shirt) in court with fellow crew members.Photograph: courtesy of Elena AlbokhariFor Elena, the apparent indifference to Ali’s plight has been underlined by Bekavac’s experience. The Croatian prime minister and foreign minister spoke out against the verdict, and his then wife, Katja, received support to arrange prison visits without delay. When Elena went to Ankara, she attended the Palace of Justice with her lawyer and without consular assistance. It took all day to navigate the bureaucracy of the building and, after submitting documents and photos, she had to wait a further two weeks before a prison visit was approved. Katja, Elena says, was able to meet the captain without a barrier between them, but when she finally made it through the prison gates, after the humiliation of a strip-­search, she had to speak with Ali through a glass pane. “Psychologically, it was very difficult,” she says.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionDuring that first meeting, Elena was shocked by how much he had changed. “I have never seen my husband sad,” she says. “He’s always laughing, singing, dancing, but this time I didn’t recognise him. He was very thin, depressed and with grey hair.” The hardest thing was to contain her emotions: “When I’m alone here I can cry, I can tell my friends everything is very bad … but I can’t say such things to him. I have to support him.”She told him they had a new lawyer. That his mother was well. That they would be waiting for him. That they’d fight for him. After 40 minutes, their time was up.As Elena continued to battle for diplomatic support, travelling to Turkey to visit Ali every month, she became aware the Croatian authorities were working behind the scenes. In August 2025, Ali watched from his cell as Bekavac was collected from the prison by a Croatian diplomat and flown home. In Croatia, there has been speculation that his release was negotiated as part of a prisoner swap with Mustafa Yiğit Zeren, a Turkish billionaire and close friend of President Erdoğan who was wanted by the Russians over alleged embezzlement of €600m.When Elena heard the news she felt hopeful for Ali, but soon this turned to dismay. “I was absolutely sure that after that Finland would change their attitude … but nothing. Every time they say, ‘We don’t know what happened, we do not know why the captain was released.’” It was as if her husband did not exist.View image in fullscreenElena in front of Sincan prison in Ankara, Turkey, where Ali is being held.Photograph: courtesy of Elena AlbokhariWhen I spoke to Jussi Tanner, Finland’s director general for consular services, he told me he cannot comment on the details of the case but described it as “concerning and troubling”. Finland, he says, continues to engage with the Turkish authorities and, particularly since Bekavac’s release, has been seeking clarification regarding Ali’s prolonged detention. “Everything I know about the case seems to indicate that it makes no sense that he’s still in custody,” Tanner says.Elena says she spends all her spare time investigating the case herself, poring over the details as she grows increasingly suspicious of the motivations of all the parties involved. She pulls out a black folder of documents relating to Ali’s employment records. She also shows me her diary, a white book with a gold heart on the cover filled with neat handwriting. Its pages are full of memories, but from October 2023 they are blank.As the case of Phoenician M has lingered on, it has drawn attention to the protections afforded to seafarers and the need for these to be reaffirmed. There are numerous international agreements designed to protect their rights, such as the International Labour Organisation Guidelines on Fair Treatment of Seafarers and the Maritime Labour Convention – often described as the “seafarers’ bill of rights” – but in practice they are at the beck and call of whichever jurisdiction they happen to sail into. “It’s aspirational, but not very concrete,” is how James Turner KC, who specialises in shipping law, summarises it to me.Maritime organisations have also expressed growing concern at the extent to which supply chains are being exploited by organised crime. In 2019, MSC, the world’s largest ocean carrier, came under intense scrutiny after 20 tonnes of cocaine with a value of $1bn was discovered by US authorities on the MSC Gayane at Philadelphia. Large cocaine shipments were also found on three other MSC ships that year. Aninvestigation by Bloombergalleged the company had been infiltrated by members of a Balkan cartel. Eight Gayane crew members pleaded guilty of involvement in the drug-smuggling operation.Criminal actors clearly do exist in the industry, but innocent seafarers are also being caught in the net. Keith Svendsen, an executive at Danish group Maersk, told the Financial Times shipping companies were now dealing with “some of the most dangerous people in the world” and cited crew members coerced into helping smuggling gangs. Fabrizio Barcellona, a coordinator at the ITF, says the issue is not with countries taking a strong stance against drug trafficking, but that seafarers are being scapegoated. “It’s not good enough just to put them in jail without clear evidence,” he says.Over the past decade, Turkey has become a significant hub for the importation of cocaine to Europe, and there is growing pressure to address the issue. Erdoğan’s government has been accused of allowing organised crime to proliferate, and high-ranking political figures have been accused of involvement in drug trafficking. Imdat Öner, a former Turkish diplomat turned public policy analyst, told me that instead of effectively pursuing organised crime networks, the authorities are focusing on low-volume trafficking of the sort found on the Phoenician M. “It allows the government, the police, to save face internationally,” he says.View image in fullscreenThe banner Elena has ready for Ali’s return.Photograph: Juuso Westerlund/The GuardianDavid Hammond, a former military seafarer, qualified barrister and founder of Human Rights at Sea International, has published a review of Ali’s case which calls it a “grave miscarriage of justice” and questions the prosecution’s integrity and motivations. Court papers state that the investigation was triggered by intelligence from Kayseri province police narcotics department, and the conviction based on evidence gathered following the seizure. But according to Hammond, Turkish police failed to request documentation relating to the Colombian incident, key witnesses were not interviewed, and no forensic evidence linking crew members to the drugs was presented. It is unclear why, of 20 crew onboard, only 10 were arrested. The prosecution seems to have rested solely on the rank and responsibilities of the crew. The conviction, as Ali’s lawyer argued, “rests on speculation rather than proof”.There appears to be some awareness of these weaknesses within the Turkish judiciary. In April 2025, the chief public prosecutor referred the case to the supreme court of appeal, which in March 2026 upheld Ali’s conviction by a 3-2 majority. However, the opinions of the two dissenting judges pointed to many of the issues raised by Ali’s defence. They agreed the investigation was incomplete, there was not proper communication with the Colombian authorities, and police did not pursue an investigation in regard to the source intelligence that led them to the drugs on the ship in the first place. In July, Ali and Bekavac (who remains convicted as far as Turkish law is concerned) had their sentences increased to 33 years, due to a failure to pay a £3,000 fine that was part of their original sentence.Bekavac may now be at home with his family, but he remains incensed about the case and is outraged at the suggestion that he could have been involved in a drug-smuggling operation. He told me he was made aware of the destination list for the Phoenician M only three days before it arrived in Barranquilla and the responsibility for loading cargo fell on the stevedores working at the port. The cocaine reportedly found in Turkey was buried 5 metres deep within the coal, he adds, so could only have been concealed while the ship was being loaded in Barranquilla, not during the journey, as alleged by the prosecution. Bekavac, like the other crew, believed that, having been cleared by the Colombian harbourmaster, they would have no further issues.The captain also told me he documented his email correspondence relating to the incident on a USB drive. This was confiscated by Turkish police and not presented as evidence in the case. When it was returned to him, the drive had been wiped (he was later able to recover the data). In an interview with Slobodna Dalmacija, a Croatian newspaper, Bekavac said the lawyer provided to him by the company told him not to mention the stamps on the packages or talk about the company.Freshwater Five drug-smuggling convictions unsafe, court hearsRead moreAs Hammond sees it, there is evidence that gestures to serious organised crime – as well as the possible knowledge of state authorities – yet Turkish police appear not to have pursued lines of inquiry that might shed light on this. The cargo’s recipient, for example, does not seem to have been scrutinised, nor were any representatives from Iskenderun called as witnesses. If the crew can be held liable due to “command responsibility”, then the shipping company should, at the very least, have to answer as to whether it did all it could to address the risk of drug trafficking on its vessel.Hammond believes the case should be a wake-up call for everyone who has a moral duty to the welfare of seafarers – from P&I clubs to shipping companies to unions – and is appalled that a sector responsible for trillions of dollars of trade cannot guarantee the protection of its workers. Seafarers, he tells me, are simply treated as “disposable assets”.Iskenderun did not respond to requests for comment. However, the company appears to now be operating as Phoenician Shipping & Crewing, which has the same office address and is listed as the owner of the Phoenician M. Emails to Phoenician Shipping bounced, and the telephone number dialled to Orontes Shipping, another Turkish company established in 2024, which also lists the ship in its fleet. Emails and calls to this company also went unanswered. The Turkish Ministry of Justice did not respond to requests for comment.In January, Elena returned to Ankara to visit Ali. He always has presents for her, she says, holding up an intricately beaded cushion by way of illustration, but this time he told her there was a box waiting for her to take home. “The guards will give it to you,” he said. When she left, she collected it. Inside were two budgerigars. One boy, one girl. “A couple.”Ali has always loved birds, Elena says. There were budgies and parrots in the prison, and Ali began breeding them. Dozens of his fellow prisoners have a bird now and Ali wanted her to have some, too. Transferring them to Finland was not straightforward, though compared with the other challenges in her life, it was, at least, achievable. Panjo and Lucy now live in a cage above the kitchen counter, chirping loudly. Elena opens the cage and they flutter around the room before landing happily on her outstretched finger. Along with the cat, Koko, they join the list of those waiting for Ali to return home.Ali’s lawyer has petitioned the chief public prosecutor – who appears to believe there are questions over Ali’s conviction – to file an objection to the supreme court of appeal’s decision, which would prompt a further review of the case. While Elena awaited further news, she was distraught to receive a call from Ali telling her he was being moved to a unit for prisoners whose convictions are considered final. Then, in August, the prosecutor agreed to submit the objection to the court.No date for a decision has been set, so again Elena waits. She says Ali is coming under intense pressure from the Turkish authorities to accept a transfer to Finland, but to do so could disrupt attempts to overturn his conviction – and risk him remaining in prison on his return. For now, both their lives remain suspended. Elena takes care of the cat and birds, and continues to make a living as a guide in Helsinki. She avoids talking too much about herself to holidaymakers. To do so would probably tarnish the theme of the tour: “The happiest country in the world.”Explore more on these topicsShipping industryDrugs tradeTurkeyColombiaFinlandfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Thousands of child-on-child sexual offences reported at schools in England and Wales | Schools | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Average of nearly five sexual crimes a day against under-13s were reported to police between 2021 and 2025
Author: Carmen Aguilar García
Headline: Exclusive: Average of nearly five sexual crimes a day against under-13s were reported to police between 2021 and 2025
Content: Girls are more likely to be victims of sexual offences than boys, according to the analysis.Composite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenGirls are more likely to be victims of sexual offences than boys, according to the analysis.Composite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesSchoolsThousands of child-on-child sexual offences reported at schools in England and WalesExclusive: Average of nearly five sexual crimes a day against under-13s were reported to police between 2021 and 2025From unwanted touching to rape: the scale of child-on-child abuse in English and Welsh schoolsCarmen Aguilar García,Sally WealeandJohnny McDevittSun 4 Oct 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLawyers and campaigners have condemned the “horrifying” scale of child-on-child sexual abuse in schools after a Guardian investigation revealed thousands of sexual offences against under-13s, including multiple rapes, are reported to police every year.Close to five sexual crimes against children aged 12 and younger were recorded on average by police every day in primary and secondary schools in England and Wales, according to Guardian analysis of police data for 2021-25.The figures include reports of almost 2,000 rapes and attempted rapes, which is equivalent to an average of one allegation of rape at a school received by the police every single day. More than a third of the rape victims were children under 13.The new data showed at least 8,500 sexual offences against under-13s were recorded by police as having occurredon school premises or nearbybetween 2021 and 2025 – equivalent to 4.7 offences reported each day.From unwanted touching to rape: the scale of child-on-child abuse in English and Welsh schoolsRead moreWhile most of the police reports did not specify the age of the alleged perpetrator, they are likely to be fellow pupils, and in at least 1,890 of the offences reported as being committed against under-13s the offender was described as under 18.Girls are more likely to be victims of sexual offences than boys, according to the analysis, which found that close to two-thirds of reported crimes affecting under-13s where the sex of the victim was documented had involved female victims.Responding to the figures, the children’s commissioner for England, Dame Rachel de Souza, described peer-on-peer abuse in schools as “widespread, normalised and too often brushed under the carpet”.“We have taken important steps in the last few years,” she said. “But as these figures show we have a long way to go. This is not simply a school or college issue, it is a societal one.”The data, obtained via freedom of information requests, also includes reports of a further 6,140 crimes involving the possession, taking, making or distribution of indecent or prohibited images of children under 18.View image in fullscreenHeadteachers are hoping phone bans and social media restrictions will help to turn the tide.Composite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesThis has become a significant problem in schools, particularly with the introduction of AI and deepfakes, but headteachers are hopingphone bansand social media restrictions will help to turn the tide.Andrew Lord, a partner with Leigh Day solicitors who represents survivors of sexual abuse, said: “This new dataset evidences clearly the horrifying true scale of sexual abuse of children within schools.“Those in authority can no longer claim that they were not aware of how prevalent an issue this is. Parents deserve to know that their children are safe while undertaking their education, and anything short of concrete action to tackle this problem is simply not good enough.”The data also detailed reports of at least 2,300 sexual crimes against children aged 13 to 16 and a further 9,100 sexual crimes against those aged 13 or over recorded by police as having happened in or in the vicinity of schools between 2021 and 2025. Three-quarters of these involved a female victim.The true figure is likely to be significantly higher, since the analysis is based on data provided by 33 police forces that replied to FoI requests, out of a total of 43 in England and Wales. There may also be variation in the ways forces collect data.Janaya Walker, interim director of the End Violence Against Women (EVAW) campaign, said: “This data is shocking but sadly not surprising, and underlines the urgent need to protect children from sexual violence at school.“We’ve long raised the alarm about this national crisis in schools. However, despite what should have been numerous watershed moments, young people continue to be harmed en masse.”Excluding 2021, when schools were closed between January and March due to the Covid-19 pandemic, the rate of sexual offences increased by 4% outside London, with 26.6 offences per 100,000 children under 13 in 2022, rising to 27.6 in 2025.A government spokesperson described the figures as appalling. “No child should be unsafe at school, and no child should have to carry this alone. That is why schools’ duty to respond to sexual violence and harassment is now statutory, and why staff are trained to spot concerns early and support victims.“As part of our strategy to halve violence against women and girls, we have pledged to make sure all young people are taught about healthy relationships and consent from an early age – and we’ve forced tech companies to tackle harmful content and protect young people online through the Online Safety Act.”Acting chief constable Becky Riggs, who leads on child protection and abuse investigation for the National Police Chiefs’ Council, said the number of sexual offences reported in school settings was “deeply concerning”, but might also reflect growing awareness and greater confidence among child victims to come forward and report what has happened to them.“These findings underline the urgent need for a stronger focus on prevention through age-appropriate education, digital resilience, effective safeguarding measures and greater support for parents, schools and professionals to identify concerns early and intervene before harm occurs,” she said.“Tackling child sexual abuse requires a whole-system response, with policing, education, social care, health services, technology companies and communities working together to prevent harm, protect children and hold offenders to account.”Soma Sara is the chief executive and founder of the Everyone’s Invited campaign, which has played a key role in highlighting sexual violence in schools. She now runs education programmes for young people. “When we first launched [in 2020], people refused to even refer to rape culture,” she said.“It is now accepted as an issue both in wider society and within our schools. But we cannot expect schools to tackle it alone, particularly when the online world is changing so rapidly.“The proliferation of violent pornography and the increasing harms young people are exposed to online are creating challenges that are incredibly difficult for teachers to keep pace with.”Pepe Di’Iasio, general secretary of the Association of School and College Leaders, said: “The prevalence of these incidents is simply appalling and a source of great concern for everyone working in education.“We hope measures being taken by the government to better protect children online will improve matters but ministers must be prepared to go further in regulating online platforms.”Figures from some forces were taken from keyword searches of police summary notes, so may include cases that mentioned schools but happened outside school premises. Some other forces recorded schools as a location for crimes both on and nearby school premises.Explore more on these topicsSchoolsChildrenCrimeSexual harassmentViolence against women and girlsPrimary schoolsSecondary schoolsnewsShareReuse this content

title: US bombers pulled from RAF Fairford base after suspected terror plot | US military | The Guardian
description: Aircraft leave Gloucestershire base to return to US following arrest of dual British-Iranian national in central London
Author: Dan Sabbagh
Headline: Aircraft leave Gloucestershire base to return to US following arrest of dual British-Iranian national in central London
Content: A US Air Force Rockwell B-1 Lancer bomber seen at RAF Fairford on 29 September.Photograph: Ben Birchall/PAView image in fullscreenA US Air Force Rockwell B-1 Lancer bomber seen at RAF Fairford on 29 September.Photograph: Ben Birchall/PAUS militaryUS bombers pulled from RAF Fairford base after suspected terror plotAircraft leave Gloucestershire base to return to US following arrest of dual British-Iranian national in central LondonDan Sabbagh,Marina Dunbar,Charlie MoloneySun 4 Oct 2026 17.25 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe US Air Force has pulled its bombers from RAF Fairford following an investigation into an alleged planned terror attack at the base.The bombers were redeployed back to their home bases in the US, according to a Pentagon official who was not authorised to discuss sensitive military movements and spoke on Sunday on condition of anonymity.A Pentagon spokesperson said: “While ⁠operational security precluded us from confirming the movement of our ​assets and forces in ‌real time, we can acknowledge ‌now that all US bombers that were deployed to ‌RAF Fairford have redeployed to their home stations in the United States.”At least 10 B-1 bombers of 12 flew out of Fairford on Sunday, including some that arrived on rotation less than a week ago, underlining the haste of the departure and the apparent significance given by the US to the threat.There was no immediate comment from the UK Ministry of Defence, though the rapid pace of the withdrawal will heighten concerns in the area around the RAF base in Gloucestershire.According to reporting by US media, the withdrawal appears to be in response to fresh or renewed security concerns about safety on the base.A report in the New York Times said: “American officials on Sunday declined to specify the nature of the new information that prompted the rapid withdrawal of the Air Force bombers, some of which had just arrived in the past week as part of a normal rotation of forces.“One US official said the new information was part of the same threat warnings that surfaced three weeks ago, but specific details and a sense of urgency spiked in the past 24 hours, alarming commanders.”A dual British-Iranian national was arrested in central London last week on suspicion of plotting a terror attack, following a security incident at RAF Fairford in late September. In total, six people have been taken into custody and then released on bail during the investigation.Suspect in RAF Fairford case called police to report incidentRead moreBritish authorities have linked the incident to Tehran. Iran has denied involvement.RAF Fairford, located 100 miles (160km) west of London, has been used by American bombers during decades of conflicts in the Middle East.Its use in recent months came after then prime minister Keir Starmer granted Washington permission to use British bases for “defensive” strikes against Tehran.TheUS militarystill maintains a sizeable presence in the Middle East. On Thursday, a US official said the recently deployed USS Theodore Roosevelt aircraft carrier as well as the USS Makin Island amphibious readiness group – a group of ships that together carry more than 7,000 sailors and 2,000 Marines – were heading for the region. The official said the move could result in three carriers being in the region as early as the end of October.Explore more on these topicsUS militaryMilitaryRoyal Air ForcenewsShareReuse this content

title: Green party votes to adopt policy that equates Zionism with racism | Green party | The Guardian
description: Motion calling for single Palestinian state, which is opposed by most Green MPs and expected to be challenged, passes by 1,022 votes to 813
Author: Peter Walker
Headline: Motion calling for single Palestinian state, which is opposed by most Green MPs and expected to be challenged, passes by 1,022 votes to 813
Content: Israeli flags from a pro-Israel rally outside the Green party conference venue in Brighton on Sunday.Photograph: Gary Roberts/Sopa Images/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenIsraeli flags from a pro-Israel rally outside the Green party conference venue in Brighton on Sunday.Photograph: Gary Roberts/Sopa Images/ShutterstockGreen partyGreen party votes to adopt policy that equates Zionism with racismMotion calling for single Palestinian state, which is opposed by most Green MPs and expected to be challenged, passes by 1,022 votes to 813Peter WalkerSenior political correspondentSun 4 Oct 2026 13.40 EDTFirst published on Sun 4 Oct 2026 10.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Greens have formally adopted a policy that equates Zionism with racism and calls for Israel to be replaced by a single Palestinian state, a move opposed by the bulk of the party’s MPs and which is expected to face legal challenge.Zack Polanski, who heads the Greens in England and Wales and missed the vote at the party’s conference in Brighton to campaign in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection, has faced criticism for a perceived lack of leadership on a hugely divisive issue.There have also been concerns that the policy change was pushed largely by newcomers who have little interest in the rest of the party’s platform.Four of the party’s five MPs opposed the motion. Adrian Ramsay and Ellie Chowns said they were “deeply saddened” while Siân Berry and Carla Denyer said they would support any Jewish members who believed they were being targeted as a result of the policy change.The binding policy motion, passed by 1,022 votes to 813, saysZionism – the movement for a Jewish state– should be “treated as any other form of racism”. It calls for Israel to be replaced by a single Palestinian state “with equal rights for all”.Israel’s foreign ministry said the resolution “constitutes a clear antisemitic text according to the IHRA (International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance) definition, as it denies the Jewish people’s right to self-determination”.Foreign minister Gideon Sa’ar decided to declareGreen partyleader Zack Polanski barred from entering Israel, the ministry said, adding the decision had been coordinated with the relevant authorities.While opinion among Jewish Green members is split, some have expressed worry that this will mean they could face disciplinary action for belonging to Jewish organisations that officially support Zionism, even synagogues.After the vote, one backer of the motion, Salma Yaqoob, a former member of George Galloway’s Respect party who is now a Green, insisted this would not happen, saying: “Nobody will be removed, challenged, disciplined, suspended because they put forward or articulate their belief in Zionism.”However, an amendment put forward saying the motion should not be used to “pressure, proscribe or discipline members based on affiliation with Jewish community institutions” was voted down.It is understood that some Green members are consulting lawyers over whether the policy could be challenged for breaching equalities legislation.Adam Wagner KC, the barrister who led a casethat concludedJeremy Corbyn’s Labour broke equalities laws over antisemitism, said such a case would have a good chance of success.“I think there is a strong risk that the motion as passed contravenes the Equality Act 2010, which applies to political parties, as it will discriminate against and harass people who hold Zionist beliefs and Jewish people more generally,” he said.Zionism when defined in the broad sense of supporting a Jewish nation state “is likely to be a protected belief” under the act, he said.The motion argues that Zionism is necessarily racist as it “privileges one ethnic group on the basis of the subjugation of others”. It adds: “This motion is aimed at the political ideology and practice of Zionism, as defined, and not at the religious or ethnic background of those who may identify as Zionists. Not all Jews are Zionists and not all Zionists are Jews …“Zionism, as defined above, will be treated as any other form of racism, and this motion will be implemented by the anti-racism policy working group as appropriate and in accordance with its ordinary practice.”According to the Institute for Jewish Policy Research, about two-thirds of British Jews consider themselves Zionists.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhat is Zionism and why do some critics describe it as racist?Read moreDuring the lengthy debate, which was for members only, Chowns and Caroline Lucas, the former leader who was the Greens’ first MP, argued against the plan.The motion had been pushed by a group called Greens for Palestine,which encouragednon-party members to sign up to the party to make sure the policy was debated and adopted. After it was passed, supporters came to the front of the hall to hug and cheer.One member who opposed the motion said: “There are now two Green parties – the everyday members, and those who have joined for just one reason,Palestine, and who have no interest in anything else.”There is considerable disquiet among some senior Greens who feel that Polanski, who is Jewish, could have taken a stronger stance on the issue. The party leader has justified the motion’s broad argument by pointing to the death toll inGazaduring Israel’s assault on the territory.Asked on Saturday if he believed Zionism was racist, Polanski told the BBC: “Well, in the motion, it is defined as the displacement and genocide of the Palestinian people. I think that is clearly racism.”After the vote, the party’s five MPs, plus Polanski and his two co-deputy leaders, released a joint statement saying the party “will never tolerate any form of discrimination or harassment”, adding: “We know there is no conflict between supporting the rights of Palestinians and the rights of Jewish people.”However, Ramsay, Chowns, Berry and Denyer all posted this on social media with messages noting their opposition to the motion.The Movement for ProgressiveJudaism, one of the main Jewish denominations in the UK, condemned the vote, saying: “The motion is antisemitic in its formulation and intention. By adopting it, the Green party has made antisemitism party policy and become a racist party.“Jewish self-determination is a right. Declaring it racist is an attack on Jews. The Green party has chosen to brand Jews who hold this belief as racists and make their equal participation in the party conditional on renouncing it.”Adam Langleben, who coordinated complaints from the Jewish Labour Movement to the Equality and Human Rights Commission, said: “This is without doubt the most antisemitic and racist motion brought before a mainstream political party in my lifetime. It is Corbynism on steroids, and would seem even more open to legal challenge.”Explore more on these topicsGreen partyJudaismRaceGazaPalestineReligionZack PolanskinewsShareReuse this content

title: Nearly all women arriving on small boats have been raped, says Shabana Mahmood | Immigration and asylum | The Guardian
description: Home secretary warns people traffickers will exploit asylum seekers because they decide who comes to the UK
Author: Rajeev Syal
Headline: Home secretary warns people traffickers will exploit asylum seekers because they decide who comes to the UK
Content: The sifting of who gets on a migrant dinghy bound for the UK is in the hands of criminal gangs, according to Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary.Photograph: Yoan Valat/EPAView image in fullscreenThe sifting of who gets on a migrant dinghy bound for the UK is in the hands of criminal gangs, according to Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary.Photograph: Yoan Valat/EPAImmigration and asylumNearly all women arriving on small boats have been raped, says Shabana MahmoodHome secretary warns people traffickers will exploit asylum seekers because they decide who comes to the UKRajeev SyalHome affairs editorSun 4 Oct 2026 14.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 15.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNearly all women who try to reach the UK in small boats from northern France have been raped on their journey,Shabana Mahmoodhas claimed.In an interview with The Rest Is Politics podcast, the home secretary said far-right, balaclava-wearing activists would “kill” or “kick me out of my own country” if they took power.Speaking to the former Tory minister Rory Stewart and Tony Blair’s former close adviser Alastair Campbell, she said sexual abusers would exploit most asylum seekers as long as traffickers continued to decide who came to the UK.She said: “We’re not in control of this border. The sifting of the people that end up in the north of France and are about to get on a dinghy is done by criminal gangs who are also, by the way, people traffickers.“You can almost guarantee that every woman that’s in the north of France has probably been raped along the journey. Some of the men too, they’ve certainly been abused and threatened. That is not the model that should decide whether somebody gets to come to the UK, make this their place of sanctuary and ultimately become one of us.”View image in fullscreenShabana Mahmood said she was ‘very uncomfortable’ about the arrests of 82 people at the Labour conference for displaying articles in support of Palestine Action.Photograph: Martin Pope/Sopa Images/ShutterstockAsked by Campbell about balaclava-wearing protesters shutting down ports and praising her policies, she said they should “sod off”.She added: “They’re just troublemakers. You know, they’d kill me in a minute if they could, and they’d definitely kick me out of my own country. So let’s just be really clear about who and what they are. They don’t think I’m a true Brit and they hate the fact that I’m a Muslim.”Mahmood also said she considered herself “part of the pro-Palestinian cause” and felt “very uncomfortable” over the arrests of activists opposing the ban imposed on Palestine Action.Merseyside police arrested 82 people on Monday at theLabourparty conference on suspicion of wearing or carrying articles supporting a proscribed organisation.In a protest organised by Defend Our Juries, scores of people sat outside the conference centre in Liverpool, many holding handmade banners saying they supported Palestine Action.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenShabana Mahmood said far-right thugs ‘would kill me in a minute if they could’.Photograph: Peter Byrne/PAMahmood said: “For those of us who have been in the pro-Palestinian cause all of our lives, these are people – sometimes you’ll know who they are, you know, you’ve been on the marches with them – it feels very uncomfortable to see them falling foul of section 13 of the Terrorism Act.”However, she defended enforcing the ban, regardless of her views: “You’ve got to be able to apply your principles, even when it’s uncomfortable for you, because you’re going to really want to apply them when it’s something you, you know, with your whole heart, are feeling very passionately about.”Authorities were preparing on Sunday for the arrival of a migrant dinghy heading for the south coast. The boat was being shadowed by French coastguard and rescue vessels and moving toward the Channel boundary line, according to ship tracking data.It appeared to have set off from near the Utah Beach area of Normandy on Sunday morning.Caroline Dinenage, the Conservative MP for Gosport in Hampshire, said there was “nothing to suggest” the boat would land on the county’s coast but police were “making preparations should that situation change”.A government spokesperson said: “The Border Security Command works around the clock to monitor the Channel and protect our border. It is vital we continue to detain, check and process every small boat arrival.”Imran Hussain, a director at the Refugee Council, welcomed the home secretary’s acknowledgment of widespread sexual violence, but questioned why the government had closed safe and legal routes which could help asylum seekers avoid falling into the hands of predators.“We know from our services that women and girls fleeing war and persecution face sexual violence both in the conflicts they have escaped and on the journeys they are forced to make in search of safety,” he said.“That is why in welcoming the government’s announcement last week of new safe routes we called for them not to be limited to a few hundred people. Last year the government closed family reunion, the safe route for refugees which overwhelmingly benefits women and children.“It is entirely right to talk about the dangers women face on these journeys but we should not be closing the safe routes that could keep them out of harm’s way. Protecting women means more safe routes, not fewer.”Explore more on these topicsImmigration and asylumRefugeesViolence against women and girlsShabana MahmoodRape and sexual assaultLabournewsShareReuse this content

title: Strikes by North Sea oil workers could ‘severely disrupt’ UK fuel supplies | Oil | The Guardian
description: Union says staff left with no choice but industrial action after breakdown in pay talks with Texas oil firm Apache
Author: Kalyeena Makortoff
Headline: Union says staff left with no choice but industrial action after breakdown in pay talks with Texas oil firm Apache
Content: The Forties Bravo oil platform in the North Sea.Photograph: Allan Coutts/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe Forties Bravo oil platform in the North Sea.Photograph: Allan Coutts/AlamyOilStrikes by North Sea oil workers could ‘severely disrupt’ UK fuel suppliesUnion says staff left with no choice but industrial action after breakdown in pay talks with Texas oil firm ApacheKalyeena MakortoffSun 4 Oct 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA looming strike by oil workers in the North Sea could “severely disrupt” UK fuel supplies, theUniteunion has said, adding that staff were left with no choice after a breakdown in pay talks with the Texas oil company Apache.The union said Apache workers had “emphatically” backed strike action after being given what it said was an unacceptable pay offer that amounted to a real-terms pay cut for many employees, at a time when the company was “raking in eye-watering profits”.Unite said the operator had also set deadlines for reaching an agreement over back pay and indicated payments could be withheld, “leaving workers potentially thousands of pounds out of pocket”.Apache said it had “engaged constructively throughout the pay discussions” and added that it had offered a 4% pay increase for staff, “whose earnings already place them among the highest earners in the UK and whose offshore rota averages 153 working days a year”.Strike action could begin later this month, according to the union, and could involve more than 160 Apache offshore workers, including electrical experts, production technicians and radio operators.Any action would affect the Forties and Beryl oilfields, and could lead to one of the critical North Sea platforms, known as Charlie, “being brought to a standstill”, Unite said.That could ultimately result in the entire Forties pipeline system in the North Sea – which is said to handle almost a third of the UK’s oil and gas – “going down”, the union said, adding that the disruption could also ripple out and affect other large North Sea operators.Unite blamed the potential disruption on Apache’s failure to reach a pay deal, saying the company’s behaviour could have “far-reaching consequences for workers, operators and consumers”.Consumers have already beengrappling with rising fuel and gas pricesbecause of the US-Israel war on Iran, which has been disrupting supplies of crude and refined oil products from the Gulf.On Friday, British motorists were dealt a fresh blow when it emerged that the average price of diesel hadclimbed to a record £2 a litre.At the same time it was announced that leaders of G7 nations wouldrelease up to 100m barrelsof their emergency diesel and crude oil stockpiles after Donald Trump threatened to cut off supplies of US diesel.Commenting on the potential strike action, the Unite general secretary, Sharon Graham, said: “We will not tolerate unacceptable pay offers.”Stevie Davies, a Unite industrial officer, said any disruption to Apache’s platforms “would have a direct hit on the Forties pipeline and potentially severely affect the UK’s fuel supplies”.The Texas-based APA Corporation, which is the parent company behind Apache North Sea Production, reported $1.4bn (£1.1bn) in after-tax profits and $9.2bn in revenues for last year.“We believe our final offer to the union is fair and recognises the contribution of our offshore workforce, alongside the wider benefits in our total rewards package,” Apache said. “The proposed pay increase is also in line with that awarded to our non-unionised employees earlier this year.”Apache also said it had contingency plans in place, and that it did not expect any strike action to affect other producers and their ability to operate through the Forties pipeline system. The plans included keeping “experienced personnel” on key sites, and it said any reduction in pipeline pressure as a result of industrial action would be similar to what occurred during routine maintenance outages.“As a responsible operator, we are planning to maintain safe operations throughout any industrial action,” Apache added.Planned strikes by Neo Next offshore workers, organised by Unite,were called off this summerafter they secured a deal that the union said lifted the pay package by more than £4,000. The deal was reached days before workers were due to start a series of strikes from 22 July.Ineos, which operates the Forties pipeline system, was contacted for comment.Explore more on these topicsOilOil and gas companiesEnergy industryCommoditiesIndustrial actionTrade unionsUnitenewsShareReuse this content

title: Money stolen by scammers hijacking UK social media accounts rises 400% | Scams | The Guardian
description: Many cases involve criminals using other people’s identities to sell fake event tickets to friends and family
Author: Rupert Jones
Headline: Many cases involve criminals using other people’s identities to sell fake event tickets to friends and family
Content: The total reported amount stolen via email and social media account hacking reached £6.3m in the 2025-26 financial year, compared with £1.2m in 2024-25Photograph: Tim Goode/PAView image in fullscreenThe total reported amount stolen via email and social media account hacking reached £6.3m in the 2025-26 financial year, compared with £1.2m in 2024-25Photograph: Tim Goode/PAScamsMoney stolen by scammers hijacking UK social media accounts rises 400%Many cases involve criminals using other people’s identities to sell fake event tickets to friends and familyRupert JonesSun 4 Oct 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe total amount stolen by criminals who hack into people’s emails and social media accounts and then pretend to be them has risen by more than 400% in a year, official UK data shows.In many cases, the scammers are hijacking people’s accounts in order to use their identity to sell fake event tickets – such as to sold-out gigs – to unsuspecting friends and family.The total reported amount stolen via email and social media account hacking reached £6.3m in the 2025-26 financial year, compared with £1.2m in 2024-25, according to the Report Fraud service run by the City of London police, which holds national responsibility for economic crime.However, the true total may be much higher as many scam victims do not report the crime, often because they feel embarrassed, and sometimes because the individual amount of money involved was relatively small.The Guardianpreviously featured the caseof a music fan whose Instagram account was targeted by hackers, who used her identity to advertise tickets to an Oasis gig and stole £1,400 from her friends. She said the hackers impersonated her so well that her friends and family genuinely thought they were speaking to her.Others have been scammed by fraudulent WhatsApp and text messages in which a criminal pretends to be their child or a relative who is in an emergency situation and urgently needs cash. This has been dubbedthe “Hi mum” scam.Data from Santander has shown that among customers of the bank, fraudsters pretending to be someone’s son were the most successful at extracting cash, followed by daughters.Ch Supt Amanda Wolf, head of Report Fraud operations, said: “For most people, being hacked isn’t just a cyber issue – it’s personal. It can leave victims locked out of important accounts, worried about what information has been accessed, and concerned that criminals may use their identity to target others.”She added that what starts with one compromised account “can quickly impact family, friends and colleagues as fraudsters exploit trusted relationships to commit further fraud”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionReport Fraud is launching an awareness campaign urging the public to protect their online accounts from hackers by switching to passkeys where they are available. A passkeyuses an individual’s device and biometricsto authenticate them and cannot be hacked like a password.Explore more on these topicsScamsSocial mediaHackingConsumer affairsCrimenewsShareReuse this content

title: Tories to pledge to scrap Environment Agency and Natural England | Conservative conference 2026 | The Guardian
description: Shadow chancellor will also promise to scrap affordable homes regulations as part of strategy to refocus on growth
Author: Jessica Elgot
Headline: Shadow chancellor will also promise to scrap affordable homes regulations as part of strategy to refocus on growth
Content: The Conservatives will pledge measures they claim would cut the price of a new home by £50,000, including by scrapping net zero regulations on housebuilding.Photograph: Maureen McLean/Alamy Stock PhotoView image in fullscreenThe Conservatives will pledge measures they claim would cut the price of a new home by £50,000, including by scrapping net zero regulations on housebuilding.Photograph: Maureen McLean/Alamy Stock PhotoConservative conference 2026Tories to pledge to scrap Environment Agency and Natural EnglandShadow chancellor will also promise to scrap affordable homes regulations as part of strategy to refocus on growthJessica ElgotDeputy political editorSun 4 Oct 2026 17.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Conservatives will announce a bonfire of regulations including abolishing affordable homes and community funding rules as well as scrapping Natural England and theEnvironment Agency.The shadow chancellor, Andrew Griffith, will say the party intends to “streamline regulations” that protect nature and oblige developers to include affordable homes and community services such as GP surgeries, to speed up infrastructure and housebuilding.The announcements on Monday are a signal that the party intends to refocus on the economy, an area where it has made relatively little progress in the polls.View image in fullscreenAndrew Griffith arrives on the first day of the Conservative conference in Birmingham on Sunday. He will say the party intends to ‘streamline regulations’.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPATory strategists believe there is a major opening to make gains against Reform and Labour, given the limited focus on growth from Andy Burnham and the chancellor, John Healey, at the Labour conference last week.Return of the nasty party? Badenoch walks tightrope with ‘punch down’ policiesRead moreThe Conservative leader,Kemi Badenoch, published a new tract on Sunday called The Right Way, which she said would be the bedrock that underpinned the party’s policy development before the next election. Polls have the party still trailing third behind Labour and Reform UK.Introducing the document – inspired by Margaret Thatcher’sThe Right Approachfrom 1976 – Badenoch said the Conservatives still expected to win the next election and needed to “hit the ground running … We will need to be ready from day one, having already shown people what kind of government we are going to be.”“Keir Starmer didn’t have a plan. That’s why he’s gone,” she said. “Andy Burnham doesn’t have one either and that is why I know the announcements he is making will all come to naught. We have to be different, different from Labour, and different from the party we were two years ago.”In a slew of announcements at the Conservative party conference on Monday, the Tories will pledge measures that they claim would cut the price of a new home by £50,0000, including scrapping net zero regulations on housebuilding, such as the Future Homes Standard, which requires all new homes in England to be zero-carbon ready.The party will promise to replace section 106 agreements and the community infrastructure levy that oblige developers to build a proportion of affordable housing and support school and health service demands locally. Instead, there will be a “one stop” levy on developers, Griffith will say.The party has also pledged to abolishNatural Englandand the Environment Agency, “moving to a more streamlined regulatory landscape to protect our environment”.Griffith will say in his first speech as shadow chancellor that the Tories would continue to back the expansion of Heathrow airport and leave the Aarhus convention, which makes it easier for community groups to oppose developments.Conservative shadow Treasury ministers will be tasked with finding new ways of simplifying tax for individuals and businesses, Griffith will say, calling the tax code “a cat’s cradle of complexity”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBadenoch returns to Conservative conference much stronger than a year agoRead moreIn his speech, he will say: “No one else is coming to save our economy. Only we can inject reality, tell the hard truths and make this a country we are proud to hand on to the next generation.“Our task just got bigger. We face a prime minister that wants to return Britain to an imagined past. A socialist fever dream of the 1970s. Cheaper homes, lower taxes and less red tape. This will be the most ambitious deregulation project in a generation. We will be more prepared than ever before. We will set out our plans line by line. Every bill, every regulation, every chapter.”Griffith will say that the government must speed up the building of a Heathrow third runway in whatever way it can. “I refuse to accept for a single moment that the country of Brunel and Bazalgette, of the vaccine taskforce and theMulberry harbours, has to sit around waiting until the 2040s to get a third runway built,” he will say.Burnham has recentlyexpressed personal scepticismabout the Heathrow third runway, saying he would take differing views seriously.The Guardian view on the Conservative conference: a party still searching for a purpose | EditorialRead moreThe new shadow housing secretary, Katie Lam, will say the scrapping of housing regulations and of enforcement bodies would mean “anti-growth ideologues can never again hold our country hostage”.The party said Natural England and the Environment Agency were preventing too many homes being built and adding unnecessary costs to building. Both bodies would be scrapped, with their necessary functions brought directly into Defra.Explore more on these topicsConservative conference 2026Environment AgencyNatural EnglandPlanning policyHousingConservativesKemi BadenochnewsShareReuse this content

title: Children’s books with Black main characters down 8% in a year, study shows | Children and teenagers | The Guardian
description: Only 150 of 2,189 titles published in UK for young children last year focused on minority ethnic, disabled or neurodivergent characters
Author: Emma Loffhagen
Headline: Only 150 of 2,189 titles published in UK for young children last year focused on minority ethnic, disabled or neurodivergent characters
Content: Just 47 of the 2,189 books published for under-10s in 2025 featured a Black main character,Photograph: MBI/AlamyView image in fullscreenJust 47 of the 2,189 books published for under-10s in 2025 featured a Black main character,Photograph: MBI/AlamyChildren and teenagersChildren’s books with Black main characters down 8% in a year, study showsOnly 150 of 2,189 titles published in UK for young children last year focused on minority ethnic, disabled or neurodivergent charactersEmma LoffhagenSun 4 Oct 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 19.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe number of children’s books featuring Black main characters fell by almost 8% last year, according to research into diversity in UK publishing.Just 47 – or 2.1% – of the 2,189 books published for under-10s in 2025 featured a Black main character, a 7.8% fall from the previous year, according to Inclusive Books for Children. Black children make up about 8.5% of that age bracket in England and Wales.Representation of south Asian main characters fell by 14.3 percentage points to 1.4%, despite children of south Asian heritage making up about 12.4% of the population of under-10s. Just three books featured main characters of Middle Eastern and North African (MENA) heritage, down 50% from the previous year. This represented 0.1% of surveyed books, compared with the group’s 2.2% share of the population.The research by the literacy charity found that only 150 books – 6.9% of those surveyed – featured main characters from minority ethnic, disabled or neurodivergent backgrounds. Of these, 37.3% were written or illustrated by creators who did not share the background of their characters.View image in fullscreenThe author Sheena Patel says children need books ‘that reflect both the lives they live and the ones they don’t’.Photograph: Antonio Olmos/The ObserverThe author Sheena Patel said: “At an age when children are figuring out the world around them and where they fit in, it’s vital they have access to funny, inspiring, adventurous books that reflect both the lives they live and the ones they don’t. We must do better.”The report surveyed baby and toddler books, picture books and fiction for children aged up to nine. It found that representation of disabled characters in picture books fell sharply: the number with disabled main characters dropped by 60% in 2025, to just two titles. Neither was by a disabled creator.The survey also highlighted what it described as a lack of “incidental representation”: stories in which a main character’s identity does not explicitly drive the plot of the story.Dr Stella Louis, an early years consultant, trainer and author, pointed to this “continued reliance” on books where identity itself was the story. “Why can’t a child simply be south Asian, disabled, neurodivergent or bilingual and also be the hero of an ordinary story about friendship, adventure, loss or joy?” she said.The report found that all three books published in 2025 with MENA main characters were refugee narratives. The study authors said children of MENA heritage needed stories covering a broader range of themes and experiences.“As an Arab author, it is painful to see the number of children’s fiction books representing our region decline from six to only three in 2025,” said Nadine Kaadan. She said the fact that all three books published were focused on refugee experiences risked reinforcing a “single story” about the region, defining it through “war and displacement rather than our rich cultures and heritage”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThere were some signs of progress. Neurodivergent representation increased in picture books, from three titles in 2024 to 13 last year. In the baby and toddler category, the number of books with marginalised main characters rose by 29.4%.Jack Hope, a children’s book consultant, said: “When children’s enjoyment of reading is at a significant low, it’s more important than ever that the stories children encounter reflect their lives, identities, experiences and emotions.“These figures need to be more than mere statistics and a call to action for continued change and improvements.”Explore more on these topicsChildren and teenagersPublishingRaceBlack British culturenewsShareReuse this content

title: From unwanted touching to rape: the scale of child-on-child abuse in English and Welsh schools | Schools | The Guardian
description: Ten years after full extent of problem was revealed, Guardian investigation finds schools facing uphill battle amid rapid societal changes
Author: Sally Weale
Headline: Ten years after full extent of problem was revealed, Guardian investigation finds schools facing uphill battle amid rapid societal changes
Content: Interviews with experts, lawyers and campaigners suggest many cases never get reported. Photograph: Nick David/Getty ImagesTen years after full extent of problem was revealed, Guardian investigation finds schools facing uphill battle amid rapid societal changesThousands of child-on-child sexual offences reported at schools in England and WalesBySally WealeEducation correspondentSun 4 Oct 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 14.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt is 10 years since a report first revealed the epic scale of sexual bullying, harassment and abuse girls faced in England’s schools on a daily basis.Thereport, by MPs on the women and equalities committee, showed the horrifying normality of child-on-child abuse in schools. The need for government action was “overwhelming”, said the committee chair, Maria Miller. Ofsted duly investigated, recommendations were written, promises were made and a newsex educationcurriculum was rolled out.Thousands of child-on-child sexual offences reported at schools in England and WalesRead moreA decade later, and six years after theEveryone’s Invitedmovement began to collect anonymous testimonies from victims,a Guardian investigation has shownthe problem persists unabated at schools in England and Wales. In many ways it may be more pernicious as a result of the rise of social media, misogyny and the mass consumption of online pornography by teenage boys.The freedom of information investigation captures only the most serious incidents; those reported to and recorded by police. Interviews with experts, lawyers and campaigners suggest many more cases never get reported, often because the children involved are under the age of criminal responsibility and the assault is dismissed as “age-related exploration”.Andrew Lord, a partner with Leigh Day solicitors and a specialist in abuse claims, has dealt with cases of child-on-child sexual abuse in private and state schools, inner-city schools, rural schools, primary, secondary and boarding schools for more than a decade. He says the impact on victims can endure for years and many suffer from post-traumatic stress disorder.View image in fullscreenThe impact on victims can endure for years.Photograph: SolStock/Getty Images“From my own cases I can see it’s happening up and down the country to children of all ages,” he said. In many instances, however, schools were still struggling to deal with it appropriately. “If you have children in a physical fight, schools know exactly how to react. When you are talking about sexual assault, it’s a different matter.”Lord is currently representing a secondary school pupil who reported being subjected to a number of sexual and physical assaults by fellow pupils in a changing room. The family is seeking a claim for negligence and breach of human rights against the school for its failure to protect the child.“Schools do have a duty to ensure that both children [involved in an incident] receive their education, but I am aware of situations where the children continue at the same school and the victim has felt that they have not received adequate support to enable them to engage safely with their studies after disclosing incidents of sexual violence.“Victims can find themselves being ostracised, which may represent a breach of the Human Rights Act,” he added.Lord also represents a number of primary school children, including a boy who reported being seriously sexually assaulted by another child on school premises. He was scared he would be hit if he did not comply.View image in fullscreenThe mass consumption of online pornography by teenage boys was cited as one possible reason for the widespread child-on-child sexual abuse.Photograph: Matt Cardy/Getty Images“The biggest issue for me with primary-age cases, when children are below the age of criminal responsibility, is there is often no real statutory investigation and there’s an overreliance on ‘age-related exploration’.”What typically happens on primary school premises, Lord said, is that a child is taken to a more hidden area by fellow pupils – behind a shed, climbing frame or bushes – is forced to undress and is assaulted, often under threat of being excluded from play and friendship groups.While most victims of sexual abuse in schools are girls, boys are also targeted. Bethany’s* eight-year-old son was sexually abused on three occasions by a classmate during play dates at her home.She only discovered what had happened when he began crying at bedtime. She reported it to the school but claims it tried to dismiss what happened as relationship difficulties. “This was not a relationship difficulty. This was sexual assault,” she said. “No one was taking it seriously.”Her son was never interviewed. There was no proper investigation into what happened and no appropriate safety plan was drawn up to protect her son. “They wanted to sweep it all under the carpet, and that’s not good enough. It was like he was not believed.” In the end, he moved to another school. The other boy remained.“My son was never treated as a victim in any sense. They offered him no real support. What was worse than the incident itself was how the school dealt with it. It was just appalling. We both felt very, very let down,” said Bethany.View image in fullscreenSome of the abuse ‘will take place on school premises, some of it will be off-site’, one lawyer who deals with such cases said.Photograph: DGLimages/Getty Images/iStockphotoRichard Scorer is another lawyer who deals with civil claims arising from sexual abuse and receives regular approaches from parents, and in some cases teenagers who have suffered child-on-child sexual abuse of various kinds in school.“We see a lot more of it now than we would have done even a few years ago. As well as a greater awareness, it’s also possible there’s a greater underlying level of abuse and that may have something to do with the pervasiveness of online pornography, particularly in the lives of teenage boys.“It’s the full range of sexual assault, ranging from unwanted touching to rape. Some of that will take place on school premises, some of it will be off-site. Boys are overwhelmingly the perpetrators. There’s obviously all of the issues around revenge porn and the sharing of intimate photographs – that’s a big issue as well.‘Nowhere near enough’ being done to tackle misogyny among young boysRead more“My sense is that schools in some instances are struggling to know how to respond because of the extent of what’s going on and because safeguarding is quite resource intensive. Schools are forced into a bit of a social work role, picking up the pieces from things that are going wrong in society at large.”Tony Hartney, a school improvement consultant and former headteacher, said awareness around child-on-child sexual abuse was much better in schools and there was a greater willingness to tackle such issues, but they remained “tricky” to handle.“When there are allegations made like this, schools are very sensitive to the needs of both young people involved to try and make it as viable as possible for them to continue with their education in schools.“The difficulty of course is things take time. Whilst investigations are going on, you ideally want them to be in schools and to have as normal an education as they can. It’s tricky for schools to manage these situations.”When she became children’s commissioner for England in 2021, Rachel de Souza knew from her time as a headteacher about sexual harassment and abuse in schools.“But what I heard as I listened to young people shocked me.Childrenwere viewing violent pornography, it was changing behaviour and peer-on-peer abuse was widespread, normalised and too often brushed under the carpet.“We have taken important steps in the last few years – from work to bring highly skilled professionals together under one roof to care for child victims of abuse, to action to prevent children from accessing pornography, and a focus on evidence-based relationships education that addresses the realities of teenagers’ lives.“But as these figures show, we have a long way to go. This is not simply a school or college issue, it is a societal one. We need to address the causes – harmful sexual behaviours are increasingly shaped by the content and cultures that children are exposed to online.“And we need to urgently improve what happens when young victims of sexual assault speak out and their experience of the justice system, and make sure they get the support they need.”* Name has been changed for reasons of anonymityExplore more on these topicsSchoolsChildrenSexual harassmentViolence against women and girlsPrimary schoolsSecondary schoolsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘The violence is off the scale’: staff and passengers at risk as assaults on trains in Great Britain soar to record high | Public transport | The Guardian
description: Cases of abuse, spitting, head-butting and sexual harassment, have spiked as transport police numbers have dwindled
Author: Gwyn Topham
Headline: Cases of abuse, spitting, head-butting and sexual harassment, have spiked as transport police numbers have dwindled
Content: Rail staff feel increasingly under threat, with many wearing bodycams to log violence.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenRail staff feel increasingly under threat, with many wearing bodycams to log violence.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianPublic transport‘The violence is off the scale’: staff and passengers at risk as assaults on trains in Great Britain soar to record highCases of abuse, spitting, head-butting and sexual harassment, have spiked as transport police numbers have dwindledGwyn Topham,Stephen Morris,Nicola Slawson,Hannah Al-OthmanandEve LivingstonSun 4 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 12.49 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen a train was halted outside Exeter St Davids station on Monday, rail staff leapt to one conclusion: there had been a violent incident on board.“Someone will have kicked off,” one staff member said. “It happens all the time. My boss got head-butted recently.”On this occasion, they were wrong – but their assumption told a tale. Figures released late last month showed the number of reported assaults on Great Britain’s railways had risen by a fifth, to a record high of almost 25,000 incidents in a year.Staff in particular have felt increasingly under threat. While the total numbers reported by the Office of Rail and Road in 2025-26 covered threats, verbal abuse, and contact that might not have resulted in any injury, they included nearly 2,500 physical assaults on workers – an average of about seven every day.Reported assaults on Great Britain’s railways rise by fifth in a yearRead moreTheir unions said the numbers were horrendous, but unsurprising: the RMT and TSSA unions have campaigned for more staffed stations and policing, after the number of BritishTransportPolice (BTP) officers fell by more than 10% between 2024 and 2026.Many rail staff wear body cams to record and log incidents of violence. “I think it’s so sad that we have those,” said Dave*, a rail worker in south-westEngland. However, after 20 years in the job, he said: “The threats, the abuse, the violence we see is off the scale.”Drink and drugs play a part, he added. “We’re also seeing a lot more people with mental health issues. If you’re out on the street you can steer clear, but if you’re on a train or a platform you can’t. Our workplaces are becoming more and more dangerous.”‘Now it’s mostly bad days’Steve, a guard based in the north of England, was punched in the head by a passenger: “It was my last train of the night. I’ve had to look away to see the door controls and the next thing I know, I’m waking up on the platform.”Every guard gets verbally abused on a daily basis, he said, with behaviour worsening since the pandemic: “Now it’s mostly bad days, and you’re searching for good days, where nothing’s said, or nothing happens. The amount of times we’re getting threatened now with physical attacks, even when you walk through the train and say, ‘Tickets, please.’”View image in fullscreenEven a simple request for tickets can trigger abuse.Photograph: UK Stock Images Ltd/AlamyEven those working on the infrastructure can be on the receiving end. One rail contractor, Liam, based in Somerset, said: “We’re there working on the tracks and we sometimes get sworn at and even spat at. It’s just a minority, but somehow they think we’re responsible for slow journey times, cancelled trains. We’re in bright orange so we’re easy targets.”The railway is by no means unique: bus drivers have faced repeated abuse and threats, as the Unite union has highlighted. Transport for London staff working on roads are issued with “spit kits”, or forensic saliva collection tubes, so common is that form of assault.Violence against women and girls is of particular concern; at the Labour conference this week, the minister for buses and local transport, Simon Lightwood, described it as a “national emergency”.View image in fullscreenKim McGuinness said women need to know ‘that if you raise an alarm something is going to be done’.Photograph: DEW/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.Speaking alongside him, the mayor for the north-east, Kim McGuinness, said that as well as measures such as more staffing, lighting and CCTV, a crucial point for women was “knowing that if you raise an alarm something is going to be done. It’s a choice to use public transport or not … if you’re accepting 50% of the population don’t feel safe, that’s not good.”The rail industry and police say some of the sharp rise in recorded assaults on passengers – up 36% last year – is due to greater reporting, including using discreet text messaging to the BTP.But while many more incidents are now reported, plenty are not.‘Tearful, angry and scared’Emily, 24, was travelling home on a late-night train between Glasgow and Edinburgh last year when a stranger made a beeline for her. “He immediately tried to start a conversation and wouldn’t give up even when I showed no interest. He was asking what I’d been up to, whether I had a boyfriend, complimenting my outfit, and then it escalated really quickly.”The man began rubbing Emily’s upper thigh and asking her intrusive questions about her sex life. “I froze and didn’t know what to do. I looked around but everyone else was oblivious. I tried to move but I was on the inside seat and he just grabbed my leg harder and leaned in towards me,” she said.She managed to manoeuvre out of the seat and away from the man, who “shouted aggressively and called [her] a bitch”. Other passengers looked round but did not intervene. She moved to another carriage and arrived home shaken but decided not to report the incident.“I wanted to just move on,” Emily said. “But I never used to think twice about getting on a train by myself at night and now I’m much more nervous.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenPassengers are becoming more nervous about taking public transport.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianEdward, a trans man, was travelling home to Staffordshire with his partner, a trans woman, after a weekend inWales. On a packed train from Aberystwyth, a man began loudly making homophobic comments and became confrontational.“Normally in that situation I just walk on, but I physically couldn’t, we were so crammed,” Edward said. He finally yelled back, repeating: “You’re shouting homophobic abuse in front of your children.”A railway worker eventually intervened and told the assailant and his family to move to another carriage. Edward chose not to report the incident to police, dissatisfied with the response to previous incidents. He now tries to avoid public transport: “I felt tearful, angry and scared afterwards.”Tell us: have you recently been assaulted on Great Britain’s railways?Read more‘It’s put me off trains’A fraction of passenger reports end up with arrest or prosecution. Last year, Sam was travelling north from London on a train packed with football supporters. As she tried to reach her reserved seat, a drunken man confronted her and pushed her backward.She instinctively pushed him back. “Then I thought, what have you done?” she said. Other men began throwing beer cans while one held her by her rucksack. “I was being pushed and shoved … they were throwing punches as well.”Amid the assault, one man deliberately grabbed her breasts. “I realised: ‘Oh no, I’m trapped on here with them for the next two hours’,” she said. “There’s nowhere to go. There’s nowhere to get off.”Two BTP officers on the train got through to take a statement from Sam. The investigation was later dropped after police were unable to identify her assailant.The experience had a big impact, leaving her “not doing a lot of things I used to do. It’s put me off trains massively. I think if faced with a train like that, I would just not board it.”View image in fullscreenTransport police say offenders can expect a ‘robust response’.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianThe BTP assistant chief constable Ian Drummond-Smith said: “We will never tolerate violence or abuse directed at passengers or staff on the railway, and anyone committing these crimes can expect a robust response from us.”He noted that when staff had body-worn recording, police brought offenders to justice in about 85% of incidents. “Anyone who witnesses violence or abuse on the railway should report it to us by texting 61016, or call 999 in an emergency,” he said.The Department for Transport said the rise in assaults was “deeply concerning and unacceptable”. It has awarded a £63m increase in BTP funding by 2028-29, allowing more than 200 additional officers to be recruited, and investments in better CCTV and body-worn video. Dozens of new BTP officers will be specialised in tackling violence and intimidation against women and girls.* Names have been changedThe headline of this article was amended on 4 October 2026 to correctly refer to Great Britain rather than the UK.Explore more on these topicsPublic transportRail industryTransportRail transportPoliceCrimeEnglandfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Manhattan ‘mole’ mystery: rumors of lost gold spur clandestine excursions into New York sewers | New York | The Guardian
description: A recent arrest suggests that underground invaders of city’s sewer system are lured by the promise of lost valuables
Author: Adam Gabbatt
Headline: A recent arrest suggests that underground invaders of city’s sewer system are lured by the promise of lost valuables
