Content: Reports of mysterious gangs of sewer spelunkers have transfixed New Yorkers over the summer.Photograph: william87/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenReports of mysterious gangs of sewer spelunkers have transfixed New Yorkers over the summer.Photograph: william87/Getty ImagesNew YorkManhattan ‘mole’ mystery: rumors of lost gold spur clandestine excursions into New York sewersA recent arrest suggests that underground invaders of city’s sewer system are lured by the promise of lost valuablesAdam Gabbattin New YorkSun 4 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 08.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere’s been one thing in particular that has been intriguing New Yorkers this summer: the existence, and whereabouts, of so-called “mole people” – a mysterious group of individuals who spend at least some of their time wading about in the city’s sewers.New Yorkers learned a bit more about the phenomenon this week, when two men were caught red – or perhaps another color – handed, after allegedly emerging from a tunnel in Manhattan. Their arrests have shed some light on a slew of instances where people have been witnessed lifting manhole covers and clambering underground.Samuel Reveron and Kevin Rodriguez were apprehended in Queens after police tracked them down through video footage. The pair were allegedly spotted entering the sewers with four other people, who have yet to be identified.Three more people emerge from New York manhole, as UN general assembly ongoingRead moreBoth were charged with criminal trespassing, but it is the reason the men gave for their adventure that has proved particularly fascinating.“We go into the sewer and look for valuables that get stuck in the storm drains and sewers, gold, anything of value,” Reveron, 25, reportedly told police after his arrest.The gang’s quest fits an apparently misguided pattern of people thinking New York’s sewers are paved with gold. Last year, three men were arrested after they were allegedly seen emerging from a sewer in Brooklyn, one of themtelling police: “The reason we went down there is that people lose their gold down there. We got to get it and sell it to make money.”Despite that vaulting ambition, there is little evidence that sewer foraging is a lucrative trade. Steve Duncan, a former urban explorer who has spent a lot of time in New York’s sewers and subway tunnels,toldthe New York Times that in more than 100 sewer trips, the most valuable thing he found was an expired credit card.Still, the penchant for sewer exploration continues. In May this year there were three separate reported incidents of people climbing down into sewers, two of whichwere captured on video. In footage of the first incident, three people, wearing dungaree-style hip waders and carrying flashlights, walk into the middle of the road in Astoria, Queens. They haul a circular man cover aside, and descend into the darkness of the sewer.“Three random guys walking around in a strange suit. Open the sewer, go in like the Ninja Turtles,” eyewitness Aki Jakupovic told NBC New York at the time.Jakupovic isn’t the first to make the comparison to the Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles, a fictional group of human-turtle hybrids who, across a comic book, cartoon TV show and feature film, are depicted as living in the sewers. Per canon, the turtles mutated into humanoids after being exposed to a toxic green goo. They are subsequently trained in martial arts by a large rat.The turtles, who are brothers, fight crime, frequently crossing paths with a man called Shredder and his accomplices Bebop, who is a mutant warthog, and Rocksteady, who is a sort of rhino. They also encounter Krang, an alien blob-thing who lives in a robot.While there appears to have been an increase in sewer incidents this year, this isn’t a new phenomenon. In 2015, a trainee at the New York department of environmental protection was arrested after being caught in the sewers, and last year three men were arrested after entering the sewer system in Brooklyn, allegedly in an attempt to find gold.“God knows what they were looking for. I know for damn sure I wouldn’t be crawling through the sewers of New York, but these three were evidently looking for something,” the then New York police commissioner, Bill Bratton, told journalists at the time.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Around 2-3 times a daySign up toBreaking News USGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionReveron and Rodriguez’s September sojourn might have been written off as a bit of a hoot, but police were seemingly extra interested because it coincided with world leaders gathering at the UN, some of them staying at swanky hotels close to where the two men went underground.Brian Kennedy, an attorney for Reveron, dismissed those concerns when hespoke to NBC News.“It seems like not much of a case,” Kennedy told NBC News. “I understand that it is strange that it’s alleged he went [into the sewer]. But there’s no connection to the UN or the appearance of Netanyahu or any other kind of nefarious scheme.”It’s both strangeanddangerous, Rob Wolejsza, a spokesperson for New York’s department of environmental protection,previously told the Guardian. Wolejsza said it was “both illegal and extremely dangerous” to go into the sewers, adding: “Sewers can contain numerous hazards, including noxious and potentially deadly gases, unstable surfaces, flooding risks and confined spaces. For these reasons, members of the public should never enter a pipe, drain, catch basin, manhole or outfall.”Whether people will listen remains to be seen. On the same day Reveron and Rodriguez were arrested, another three men were spotted climbing out of a sewer at 4.30am in Bensonhurst, south Brooklyn.ABC7NYreportedthat police found a shovel in the sewer, but the men got away.Explore more on these topicsNew YorkGoldUS crimeInfrastructurefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The Reluctant Vampire review – Lenny Rush’s absolute joy of a comedy is perfectly cast | Lenny Rush | The Guardian
description: This gag-packed adaptation of Eric Morecambe’s children’s books – by the writing team behind Alan Partridge – is full of stunning comic talent. Bill Bailey, Ross Noble, Tom Davies, Sian Clifford and Asim Chaudhry are all brilliant
Author: Lucy Mangan
Headline: This gag-packed adaptation of Eric Morecambe’s children’s books – by the writing team behind Alan Partridge – is full of stunning comic talent. Bill Bailey, Ross Noble, Tom Davies, Sian Clifford and Asim Chaudhry are all brilliant
Content: Astonishing talent … 17-year-old Lenny Rush in The Reluctant Vampire.Photograph: BBC/Boffola PicturesView image in fullscreenAstonishing talent … 17-year-old Lenny Rush in The Reluctant Vampire.Photograph: BBC/Boffola PicturesTV reviewLenny RushReviewThe Reluctant Vampire review – Lenny Rush’s absolute joy of a comedy is perfectly castThis gag-packed adaptation of Eric Morecambe’s children’s books – by the writing team behind Alan Partridge – is full of stunning comic talent. Bill Bailey, Ross Noble, Tom Davies, Sian Clifford and Asim Chaudhry are all brilliantLucy ManganSun 4 Oct 2026 14.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOh my goodness; how long has it been since we all had a lovely teatime treat? Too long, that’s how long! But now joy is at hand, courtesy ofNeil and Rob Gibbons(the pair behind the most recent incarnations of Alan Partridge) and The Reluctant Vampire. It is their adaptation of Eric Morecambe’s 1982 children’s book of the same name and its 1983 sequel, The Vampire’s Revenge. They have kept the books’ warmth and daftness and added their own talents to the six-part series for youngsters. There are jokes for parents in there too, but the brothers have wisely kept the exquisite cruelty with which they craft Alan’s misadventures safely stowed away.Here is the tale of an undead royal-ish family (temporarily usurped a few generations back when the paterfamilias choked on a scab), living a traditional vampiric life in their traditionally gothic castle. There is proud patriarch Victor (Tom Davis), who revels in the hunting and draining of the humans he despises (“I see,” he says, looking round the overdecorated bedroom of his latest about-to-be-victim, “you have a keen eye for tat”). He is married to Valeeta (Sian Clifford) – they share a hot-to-trot vibe with Gomez and Morticia of The Addams Family films – and they have two children. Vernon (an absolutely wonderful turn from Gabriel Nagy in his first major screen role) is a chip off the old block, loving the vampire life and able to identify blood vintages with a single sip (“Poor circulation … lavender … the neck of a Flemish merchant?”).View image in fullscreenAddams Family vibes … (from left) Sian Clifford, Lenny Rush, Gabriel Nagy and Tom Davis in The Reluctant Vampire.Photograph: James Pardon/BBC/Buffola PicturesBut he is the second son and so the spare to the heir, Valentine (Lenny Rush, who counts as a veteran actor by experience but is still only 17 and whose age only highlights his astonishing talents). And Valentine, alas, is not a very good vampire. His fangs still haven’t come in, he’s not a fan of blood and he can’t fly or turn into a bat. A very late developer, his family all sigh and agree. Eventually, however, Valeeta is forced to admit the truth to her boy – that he is not a vampire at all, but a human baby she rescued from a fire while Victor was away in Carpathia and raised as her own. “You were going to eat me, weren’t you?” sighs Valentine. “Maybe a little bit, at first,” she agrees. But then she fell in love with him and thought he would pick up their vampire ways. But alas, he has not. Possibly because, as Val notes: “It’s not conversational French.”Soon a series of misunderstandings lead Victor to believe Val is at last ready for his initiation ceremony and the struggle to conceal the truth from him and an increasingly suspicious Vernon is on. Underneath runs a gently developing friendship and maybe more between Val and Gertie (Dodger’s Ellie-May Sheridan, in another great performance), whom he meets while on the run from a horde of villagers – led by a man who turns out to be her father (Charlie Cooper), which adds another complication to life.Around the family is gathered a perfectly cast collection of supporting characters. There is Bill Bailey and Ross Noble as gargoyles Guy and Gary, not just siphons for rainwater (“A common misconception”) but effectively the castle’s CCTV cameras, if CCTV cameras were easily distracted and no use at surveillance at all. There isAsim Chaudhryas Igon (he wears an eyepatch over the missing one because when Eric Morecambe writes that joke, it stays in the act), and there is Joe Wilkinson as Wilf the werewolf, a perfect send-up of a certain type of man, as he leans heavily over an anxious-looking maid telling her that he “totally gets the female experience, because in a way I have a monthly cycle too”. He is keen that people shouldn’t let the monster define the man. “No one ever talks about the yeti’s love of literature or his wonderful baritone!” he cries. And Jekyll, he says, “in the daytime, is a bloody good GP”. The Reluctant Vampire is full of these little flourishes as well as the more straightforward gags coming thick and fast. And I really must insist that you stick around until at least the second episode in order to catch the ham-sandwich-based homage to Morecambe’s finest hour (courtesy of the late, great Eddie Braben, of course).The Reluctant Vampire has a stacked cast, a gag-packed script and the ineffable air of a labour of love – of Eric, of the tradition he worked in, of comedy itself as something for all and not just for snarky adults – with nobody phoning anything in. Fang-tastic.The Reluctant Vampire aired on BBC One and is available on BBC iPlayerExplore more on these topicsLenny RushTV reviewNeil and Rob GibbonsTelevisionBill BaileyRoss NobleAsim ChaudhryreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Digger may lose $150m after Tom Cruise film bombs at the box office | Tom Cruise | The Guardian
description: Alejandro G Iñárritu’s critically panned satire took just $20m globally in its opening weekend, against a reported $150m production budget and $100m marketing spend
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Alejandro G Iñárritu’s critically panned satire took just $20m globally in its opening weekend, against a reported $150m production budget and $100m marketing spend
Content: Tom Cruise as Digger Rockwell and Riz Ahmed as Dr Nirav Ganesh in Digger.Photograph: Warner Bros Entertainment Inc/PAView image in fullscreenTom Cruise as Digger Rockwell and Riz Ahmed as Dr Nirav Ganesh in Digger.Photograph: Warner Bros Entertainment Inc/PATom CruiseDigger may lose $150m after Tom Cruise film bombs at the box officeAlejandro G Iñárritu’s critically panned satire took just $20m globally in its opening weekend, against a reported $150m production budget and $100m marketing spendAssociated PressSun 4 Oct 2026 19.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDigger has flopped in its opening weekend with a $20m global box office, handingTom Cruiseone of the worst debuts of his career and serving as a bitter final note for Warner Bros as a standalone studio.Alejandro G Iñárritu’s critically panned satire grossed a paltry $8m at the North American box office. Cruise is typically a big draw overseas, but international sales – $12m from 74 markets – were also weak.Digger review – Tom Cruise’s loudmouth oil tycoon goes hard in Alejandro G Iñárritu’s eco-satireRead moreIt is a rough start for a movie that cost at least $125m to make. Reports have pegged the production budget closer to $150m, while the marketing spend is estimated at another $100m. After reviews so bad that Warner Brosopted to run “decide for yourself” ads, estimates for Digger had been revised down over the past week.No 1 in North American theaters instead went to Amazon MGM’sVerity, which debued with $32.6m, extending the streak for Colleen Hoover adaptations at the box office. The Michael Showalter-directed film stars Dakota Johnson as a writer hired to ghostwrite a book series by an incapacitated author, played by Anne Hathaway.Digger had been positioned as a potential awards-season heavyweight, dated almost exactly the same as Warner Bros’ One Battle After Another was last year. The Tom Cruise film is a similarly politically charged release that handed a large budget to a top film-maker working from an original story – but One Battle After Another grossed $213.2m worldwide and, more importantly, won best picture at the Academy Awards.The disappointing opening comes as Paramount Skydance completes its acquisition of Warner Bros Discovery after approval from the US district court for the $110bn deal was received last Wednesday. Paramount said it would close the merger on Tuesday and mass layoffs are anticipated to follow.In a flush year for Hollywood, Warner Bros has failed to get one film to $100m in the US, though its December release, Dune: Part III, will easily cross that.“Digger collapsed this weekend and the new management of the combined Paramount and Warner Bros, David Ellison and Josh Greenstein and Dana Goldberg, will soon decide what kind of movies they want from WB,” wrote David A Gross, a film consultant who publishes a newsletter on box office figures. “Paramount does not have a recent history of making big, auteur-driven films like this – that strategy appears to be over and out.”Critics have mostly slammed Digger as a strained climate change farce, though Cruise’s over-the-top performance was received more warmly. Audiences agreed, giving it a “C+” CinemaScore.Cruise has spent most of the last decade starring in Mission: Impossible movies and Top Gun: Maverick, franchises that have allowed him to remain a top action hero into his 60s. The 64-year-old’s last major box-office disappointment was 2017’sThe Mummy remake, which grossed $409.2m worldwide on a $195m budget.Last weekend’s top film, Avengers Endgame: Encore, slid to seventh place with $4.4m domestically and $14.4m overseas. But the Marvel rerelease’s second week allowed Endgame to nudge ahead of Avatar to reclaim the title of highest grossing film ever, not accounting for inflation. The two films have traded spots in recent years with rereleases: Endgame now tallies $2.9255bn, while Avatar is at $2.9237bn.Explore more on these topicsTom CruiseAlejandro González IñárritunewsShareReuse this content

title: This is how we do it: ‘My mistress has complete control over me and makes me so happy’ | Life and style | The Guardian
description: LD is the submissive to Lady Alice’s dominatrix and it’s been a revelation for them both
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: LD is the submissive to Lady Alice’s dominatrix and it’s been a revelation for them both
Content: Illustration: Ryan Gillett/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Ryan Gillett/The GuardianThis is how we do itLife and styleThis is how we do it: ‘My mistress has complete control over me and makes me so happy’LD is the submissive to Lady Alice’s dominatrix – and it has been a revelation for them bothHow do you do it? Share the story of your sex life, anonymouslySun 4 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLD, 43double quotation markI have cerebral palsy and live with my parents. Lady Alice is a delicious secretI met Lady Alice on X. We aren’t lovers or friends. She is my mistress and has complete control over me. I am hers to use however she pleases and she expects nothing less than absolute obedience. I don’t pay Lady Alice a fee, though I might pay for a service she needs such as a pedicure. These payments are “tributes”, tokens of respect and devotion.I am 43 and use a wheelchair because I have cerebral palsy. I live with my elderly parents; they cut up my food and wash me. Lady Alice is a precious secret.I never felt in control and hated my body. I had sexual impulses, but because I have ornamental hips that I can’t thrust and erectile dysfunction, I’m not equipped for sex in the conventional sense. I had a “friend with benefits” 20 years ago. We had two – admittedly fun – meetings that unfortunately lacked any real penetration.double quotation markWhy do I do this when I already experience enough humiliation? With her, I don’t feel disabledIn our sessions she makes me feel like there’s nothing wrong with me, as though I was simply born to kneel and be her “stress toy”. I need help cutting up food due to limited control over my fingers, but I am able to crawl and get down on my knees for Lady Alice.Most of our sessions happen online, but recently, I flew over 400 miles to kneel at Lady Alice’s feet. My father took me on the journey because I can’t travel alone, but he didn’t know who I was meeting. He thought he was dropping me off at a friend’s house.The setting for my ordeal wasn’t a dark, oppressive dungeon filled with chains, but a light and comfortable living room. Many might wonder why I’d want to be dominated when I must already experience enough pain and humiliation being disabled. But when I’m in a session, I don’t feel disabled. I feel human, happy.Put it this way: would you rather feel as though your life was ruled by brain damage or a beautiful woman who enjoys playing with your flawed body and appreciates your devotion?Share your experienceIf you’re keen to talk to us about your sex lives you can get in touch by filling in the form below. It is very important that both sexual partners are happy to participate.Please share your story if you are 18 or over, anonymously if you wish. For more information please see ourterms of serviceandprivacy policy.Tell us hereYour responses, which can be anonymous, are secure as the form is encrypted and only the Guardian has access to your contributions. We will only use the data you provide us for the purpose of the feature and we will delete any personal data when we no longer require it for this purpose. For alternative ways to get in touch securely please see ourtips guide.First name of partner oneFirst name of partner twoLength of relationshipContact number or email address of partner onePlease include your country's area code if outside of the UK.Contact number or email address of partner twoPlease include your country's area code if outside of the UK.Do both parties agree to being contacted by a journalist from the Guardian?YesBy submitting your response, you are agreeing to share your details with us for this feature.SubmitShow moreLady Alice, 53double quotation markAfter years of sexual apathy, I became something of a carnally incontinent alley catMost of my sessions with LD happen via video call. He kneels for me, wearing his collar, and I tell him erotic stories or make him masturbate. I know the phrases that send him into a blissful state of submissiveness. This is my ultimate goal – in the BDSM community, this is called subspace. For submissive people, this feeling is more sought after than an orgasm.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionLD is unbelievably respectful. Many so-called submissive men can’t truly surrender and really only wish to serve themselves. LD puts me first, always.double quotation markI got requests from men describing themselves as ‘pay pigs’I discovered that I had an aptitude for consensual humiliation three years ago, rather unexpectedly. I started hormone replacement therapy and the transformation was almost instant: after years of sexual apathy, I became a carnally incontinent alley cat.This is how we do it: ‘As carers, we have to be responsible. During sex, we relinquish control to each other’Read moreI got on the apps, and alongside the conventional profiles were some rather strange ones: requests from men describing themselves as “pay pigs” wishing to be “financially drained”; others wanted me to tell them they were sexually inadequate; and there are an ungodly number of boys begging to be “pegged”. A self-professed “financial domination” addict in Dundee became my unlikely mentor. I grilled him on specifics: how to present myself online; how to monetise it; what to share; what to withhold?LD and I have only met once in person, but more important to both of us is our daily relationship. I’ve seen him bloom. Having life restricted due to limited mobility is so frustrating and unpleasant. I want so much more for LD than he currently has. He’s a fiercely intelligent, creative man. Through being “owned” by me, he has another lens to view himself. This inspires him. Before we met, I don’t think LD had much of an outlet for his sexuality. I know how energising discovering this side of yourself can be.Names have been changedExplore more on these topicsLife and styleThis is how we do itSexRelationshipsDisabilityOnline datingSexualityBody imagefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The perfect everyday coffee machine: De’Longhi Magnifica Start review | Coffee | The Guardian
description: This automatic bean-to-cup machine will be ideal for many: a single button press serves up espresso, black coffee and cappuccinos – and it’s affordable, too
Author: Sasha Muller
Headline: This automatic bean-to-cup machine will be ideal for many: a single button press serves up espresso, black coffee and cappuccinos – and it’s affordable, too
Content: A fresh Start: this De’Longhi is ‘simple to use, sensibly designed and makes really good coffee’.Photograph: Sasha Muller/The GuardianView image in fullscreenA fresh Start: this De’Longhi is ‘simple to use, sensibly designed and makes really good coffee’.Photograph: Sasha Muller/The GuardianGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterCoffeeReviewThe perfect everyday coffee machine: De’Longhi Magnifica Start reviewThis automatic bean-to-cup machine will be ideal for many: a single button press serves up espresso, black coffee and cappuccinos – and it’s affordable, tooThe best coffee machines for every homeSasha MullerSun 4 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYou don’t need to spend big money to get a good coffee machine. Strictly speaking, you don’t need acoffee machineat all – anice cafetièrewill do just fine. If you do crave a lower-effort solution that doesn’t cost a fortune, then a fully automatic bean-to-cup machine, such as the De’Longhi Magnifica Start ECAM220.60, is a good place to, um, start.It makes espresso. It makes black coffee. It makes cappuccino. It produces hot water on demand. Fill the hopper with good coffee beans, top up the water and fill the little milk carafe (if you want milk, that is), and all you need to do is plonk a cup on the drip tray and prod the corresponding button. Whirr, hum, splutter. Your cup is now full of coffee. Nice coffee, too.View at De’LonghiView at ArgosHow I testedView image in fullscreenGood cup of Joe? The De’Longhi can make espresso, long black and cappuccino.Photograph: Sasha Muller/The GuardianAs with every coffee machine I test, I put the Magnifica Start ECAM220.60 through its paces in my home for several weeks. I used the full range of its drink settings and assessed how easy it was to set up, use and maintain.I’ve tested more than 30 coffee machines for the Filter, so not only do I know a good cup of Joe when I taste one, but I also have a sense of where this machine sits in an overwhelmingly crowded market.What you need to knowView image in fullscreenAutomatic for the people: a fuss-free model for those who want to keep things simple.Photograph: Sasha Muller/The GuardianView at De’LonghiView at ArgosThe Magnifica Start is one of De’Longhi’s most affordable fully automatic models. It’s simple to use, well designed and if you time it right you can sometimes find it on sale from about £300.At this price you can expect to forgo features such as touchscreens or LCD panels, but many people will find the Start’s fuss-free controls more user-friendly.Before you rush out and buy one, be aware that – as with many of De’Longhi’s machines – the Magnifica Start comes in an array of models – four on the brand’s website, and a few retailer-specific options. Cheaper ones swap the milk carafe for a simple wand, which you can use to steam and froth milk manually. They share the same grinder, brew group and general design, though, so will make an equally pleasant espresso or longer black coffee. They’ll still make a decent milk-based coffee, but you’ll need to hone your barista skills to manually steam milk using the steam wand. If you develop a knack for it, this can help with the lack of adjustability you’ll find with fully automatic models, but there’s a learning curve. If you like the sound of manual milk steaming, look for a model with a lower number at the end of its part code, such as ECAM220.22. These are usually cheaper.If you prefer your bean-to-cup machines to be fully automated – and I think most people do – then make sure you’re buying a Magnifica Start with a 6 in its part code, such as the ECAM220.60 I have here. This will create frothy coffees poured into a cup at the touch of a button.De’Longhi Magnifica Start ECAM220.60 specificationsType: assisted espresso machineDimensions: 24 x 44 x 35cm (WDH)Water tank: 1.8l removableReplaceable water filter: yesAccessories supplied: water hardness test strip, measuring scoop, milk carafe, descaler, water filterTime to heat up: 40 secondsGrinder included: yes, 13 settingsNoise: grind 75dB, brew 55dB, steam 60dBWeight: 8.8kgWarranty: two yearsWhat we loveView image in fullscreenWash and brush up: the De’Longhi’s parts separate for cleaning.Photograph: Sasha Muller/The GuardianDespite all the fancy – and pricier – coffee machines at my disposal, the Magnifica Start has kept its place in my kitchen over the past few months. That’s because it makes a decent coffee at the touch of a button, and it’s simple to use. All the buttons are easily accessible on the front panel, meaning choosing drinks and adjusting the strength of each is straightforward. The buttons are touch-sensitive rather than old-school clicky ones, but I had no trouble with accidental presses or prods not registering.The drinks menu is small, but it’ll suffice for most people. You can choose between espresso, long black coffee, cappuccino or hot water. I found the default amounts on the small side – 45ml espresso, 150ml cappuccino and 200ml of black coffee. Thankfully, it’s easy to adjust each drink if you want a longer coffee. For cappuccino, you can adjust the volume of coffee and milk individually to get the strength and consistency you want – and that means you make it more of a flat white, or a latte, depending on what settings you choose. Just hold the corresponding drinks button for a few seconds, then tap it once you’re happy with the amounts of coffee or milk in your cup.The Start’s milk carafe is smaller than on pricier models, but it clips on and off easily and opens the door to one-touch cappuccinos. It does a cracking job of producing a reasonably fine, creamy foam, too. It’s not as silky as the best bean-to-cup machines, but it’s not a million miles away.double quotation markA dial gives you 13 steps of grind adjustment, which is plenty enough to suit most coffee beansThere’s no ability to adjust the amount of froth, however: if you want hot, unfrothed milk, then you’ll need to either make it yourself in the microwave or on the hob, or upgrade to one of De’Longhi’s machines with more adjustability, such as the rather excellentRivelia, which starts at £599.Black coffee and tea drinkers can press the quick-release button on the carafe’s side, slot the water spout into place, and the little LED light under the hot water button illuminates. This allows you to top up a black coffee or turn an espresso into an americano. Or even just make a cup of tea if you don’t want to boil the kettle, although puritans should be warned that the water is hot, not boiling.The rest of the design is similarly sensible. Lift off the plastic lid on top of the machine, and you can fill the bean hopper with up to 250g of coffee beans. A dial in the middle gives you 13 steps of grind adjustment, which is plenty enough to suit most coffee beans. In its centre, a flap hides the ground coffee chute – if you run out of beans or you want to switch to decaf, you can add a dose of preground coffee with the supplied plastic scoop.The 1.8-litre water tank slots in on the right-hand side and is made from clear plastic so you can see how much is remaining. A water filter comes in the box, and this lasts for about two months under normal usage. Replacements cost about £15 at full price from De’Longhi, but if you shop around you can get theprice down to about £7.The drip tray has a decent capacity, so it doesn’t need emptying too often. Slide it out, and you’ll discover that it’s attached to the grounds bin, which is large enough to contain at least a few days of coffee grounds, depending on your dose settings and caffeine consumption. The various parts separate for easy cleaning – and are dishwasher safe aside from the grounds bin – but normally a quick rinse and wipe down to remove coffee and milk residue and clean coffee grounds out of the bin is all that’s required.Once the water tank is out, you can quickly pull out the coffee infuser, also known as the brewing head, where the ground coffee sits during brewing. This is very welcome. These kinds of machines can get mucky inside, so being able to pull out the infuser and give it a thorough rinse is definitely a good thing.What we don’t loveView image in fullscreenThe white stuff: a dedicated hot milk button would be a huge improvement.Photograph: Sasha Muller/The GuardianOne minor irk is that, at 75dB, the Start’s grinder is noisier than any coffee machine I’ve tested. That’s 12dB louder than the otherwise comparablePhilips LatteGo 5500. This is mostly because the thin plastic lid doesn’t have a tight seal, so it doesn’t muffle the noise as much as other designs.My main complaint, though, is that the milk carafe could – and should – be bigger. Its 220ml capacity is much smaller than on De’Longhi’s pricier models – such as theRivelia, which is more than double the size. You’ll get a couple of small, default-sized cappuccinos out of it, but if you increase the preset volume of milk, you’ll need to refill the carafe after every drink.Also, unlike De’Longhi’s pricier machines, there’s no dial to adjust the milk froth – you get a fixed amount, and that’s it. Yes, it produces a fine, creamy foam without too many big bubbles, but it’s a shame you can’t adjust it to your preference, especially if you’re a fan of a flat white, which tends to have less frothy milk than a cappuccino.That said, my review model did occasionally produce barely frothed hot milk. It turned out, however, that this wasn’t a hidden setting. It was because I hadn’t cleaned one crucial part of the carafe. The button on the side of the carafe doesn’t just allow you to remove it from the machine, it also releases the light-coloured plastic connector for cleaning. Fail to rinse this regularly, and even small amounts of residue will block the air hole and prevent optimal frothing. Lesson learned.Although not exclusive to the Magnifica Start ECAM220.60, a downside of any coffee machine with a removable milk carafe is that you need to be diligent when it comes to cleaning – forget, and the milk residue may mature overnight. Milk has a tendency to taint plastics when it goes off, so once it’s got into the rubber tubes and plastic parts, you’ll need to buy milk cleaning tablets to soak it off – or potentially replace them. Washing-up liquid does not suffice. My advice is to dismantle and clean it after every use, either by hand or in the dishwasher if you’re feeling lazy. And if there is milk left in it, then pop the carafe in the fridge overnight to prevent the milk from spoiling. Some users may find this fiddly – if you’re at risk of forgetting to clean the frother, you might want to consider a manual steam wand instead.View image in fullscreenGrinding my gears? The coffee preset caused some annoyance, leaving long blacks tasting overly bitter.Photograph: Sasha Muller/The GuardianAnd if all this talk of spoiled milk hasn’t put you off your babyccino, then you’ll be disappointed to hear that there is no dedicated hot milk button with the Magnifica Start. To get the Start to froth milk without making a coffee, it’s necessary to use a trick: namely, to select the cappuccino option and set the strength setting to use ground coffee. Do this without adding any ground coffee to the chute, and the Start will froth hot milk into your cup. Once it detects that there’s no coffee, it abandons the brewing cycle. I’d prefer a button, but as workarounds go, it’s not hard.The only other criticism is one I could level at most bean-to-cup machines that come through my door: the coffee preset – the long black – tends to taste bitter. This is because the machine uses the same dosage and grind size of coffee as it does for an espresso, but pulls more water through the grounds to brew a longer drink. This is drinkable at default settings, but noticeably more bitter than espresso. Adjust it to pour a longer coffee, however, and bitterness overwhelms.This can be fixed. One option is to grind coarser, but then you’ll find that your espresso will become weak, watery and under-extracted. My advice with this – and most bean-to-cup machines – is to make an americano instead. Get the espresso tasting good by adjusting the grind size (normally a little finer than default) and reducing the volume slightly. Then simply top this up with hot water to make an americano. You can add milk if you like. Yes, it’s a bit more of a faff, but it tastes way better.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe FilterGet the best shopping advice from the Filter team straight to your inbox. The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWarranty and repairabilityView image in fullscreenGood coffee, guaranteed … with a two-year warranty, plus care and repair options.Photograph: Sasha Muller/The GuardianYou get a standard two-year warranty from De’Longhi, covering the usual faults, and the brand will attempt free repairs in that period. If not, you’ll get a replacement, which may be new or a refurbished model – at De’Longhi’s discretion.Once you’re out of warranty, De’Longhi still offers servicing for a flat fee. With its £99 Essential Service, De’Longhi will pick up the machine from your home, identify any show-stopping or potential issues, descale the machine, change seals and advise of any repairs. If there are issues to be fixed, you can either upgrade to the £150 Comprehensive Service, or else pay that fee upfront if you’re specifically sending it to repair a problem. Bear in mind, though, that parts will cost extra – depending on the scope of the repairs required, it may cost significantly more.An alternative is to use an independent coffee repair engineer. I spoke to our go-to coffee whisperer, Radu Bria, and his experience with these machines is that repairs are viable. Replacement parts can be sourced from approved parts resellers such as4DeLonghi. If you’re a dab hand at fixing things yourself, you can always buy the replacement parts direct and give it a go, although bear in mind that you’re very likely to void your warranty in the process.De’Longhi Magnifica Start ECAM220.60: should I buy it?View image in fullscreenEasy does it: ‘makes good coffee with little faff’.Photograph: Sasha Muller/The GuardianIf you’re concerned that you should be spending more than this machine costs, then don’t be. When it comes to fully automatic machines, the differences in coffee quality between a really good £400 model and a £1,000 rival aren’t that pronounced. The upgrades are more drink choices, bigger milk carafes and more adjustability to suit a wider range of coffee beans.So, if you’re looking for an affordable fully automatic bean-to-cup coffee machine, then the Magnifica Start lives up to its name. It’s simple to use, sensibly designed and makes good coffee with little faff. For everyday coffee drinkers, it’s a great buy.View at De’LonghiView at ArgosDe’Longhi Magnifica Start ECAM220.60 vs …De’Longhi RiveliaView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sasha Muller/The Guardian£749.99 at De’LonghiWondering what a more upmarket bean-to-cup machine can offer? There are several reasons to upgrade to De’Longhi’s Rivelia. The key one is better coffee; another is choice.The Rivelia offers a wide menu of coffee drinks – 16 one-touch drinks for starters – and each recipe can be saved to one of the four user profiles, with adjustments for strength, drink size and temperature. The amount of milk foam is adjustable, too, and there are two interchangeable bean hoppers in the box, so you can swap to decaf or different beans without having to empty the hopper.The Rivelia’s Bean Adapt technology is the standout feature, though. This helps you fine-tune the brewing process to eke out the most refined flavours from light, medium or dark roast coffee beans. The touchscreen runs you through the process, and after a few test shots, uses your feedback to change the brew settings and dial in the perfect grind size. It really works, too.Nespresso Vertuo LattissimaView image in fullscreen£199 at John Lewis£199 at AmazonSometimes, even an automatic bean-to-cup machine can be too much faff – and this is where a capsule machine may be a better choice. For instance, because De’Longhi manufactures a number of Nespresso machines under licence, the Nespresso Vertuo Lattissima upgrades one of the brand’s standard Vertuo machines with the same De’Longhi LatteCrema technology found on the Magnifica Start. The result? A relatively compact machine that brews pretty much everything from espresso to long black coffees through to cappuccinos and indulgently long, creamy latte macchiatos at the touch of a button.The library of Vertuo capsules is vast, and all are tailored to a specific length of drink. These capsules can brew anything from 25ml to 80ml shots of espresso, through to 150ml to 355ml black coffees – or even a 535ml jug. Opt for a milk-based coffee, however, and the machine will automatically tailor the recipe to create the tastiest drink possible. All that’s left is for you to slot in a capsule, fill up the milk carafe, and find a suitably giant cup.De’Longhi Stilosa EC230View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sasha Muller/The Guardian£89.99 at De’Longhi£79 at AmazonEspresso is the bedrock of great coffee. All the machines here will create a tasty shot, but none can compete with an attentively brewed cup from a manual espresso machine. This is where the Stilosa saunters in: if you’re willing to grind your own beans, steam every jug of milk by hand and perfect your own brews, this budget manual machine will leave its automatic brethren in the dust.For good results, it’s essential to budget for a small set of scales and a grinder, but with about £300 in your pocket – or even a little less – you can put together a capable package. For instance, buy aKingrinder K6 hand grinder, and you’ve got a pairing that, with a little elbow grease, can soon see you rivalling your local coffee shops. And if you prefer an electric grinder, something such as theBaratza Encore ESPis a great pick. The kicker? You can spend the money you’ve saved on great coffee beans and start practising.For more:The best coffee machines for every home and budgetThe best espresso machines, testedSage Oracle Jet espresso machine reviewNinja Luxe Cafe reviewSasha Muller is a tech and consumer journalist, avid coffee drinker and craft beer enthusiast with more than two decades of experience in testing products and avoiding deadlines. If he’s not exploring the local woods with his kids, boring people talking about mountain bike tyres or spending ill-advised amounts on classic drum’n’bass vinyl, he’s probably to be found somewhere swearing at an inanimate objectExplore more on these topicsCoffeeThe FilterKitchen essentialsHomesGadgetsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Let’s stop doubting Thomas Tuchel: England are impressive and Euro 2028 is the target | England | The Guardian
description: Coming third in the World Cup was really not a disaster, and Saturday’s rout of Croatia and building the team around Jude Bellingham are good signs
Author: Barney Ronay
Headline: Coming third in the World Cup was really not a disaster, and Saturday’s rout of Croatia and building the team around Jude Bellingham are good signs
Content: Thomas Tuchel celebrates after England’s 7-0 Nations League win over Croatia in Rijeka on Saturday.Photograph: Paul Childs/Action Images/ReutersView image in fullscreenThomas Tuchel celebrates after England’s 7-0 Nations League win over Croatia in Rijeka on Saturday.Photograph: Paul Childs/Action Images/ReutersEnglandLet’s stop doubting Thomas Tuchel: England are impressive and Euro 2028 is the targetBarney Ronayin RijekaComing third in the World Cup was really not a disaster, and Saturday’s rout of Croatia and building the team around Jude Bellingham are good signsSun 4 Oct 2026 17.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 21.30 EDTShareMove fast and fix things. It has been a fine week so far forThomas Tuchelas he attempts the cyclical task of soldering together not just an England team, but a way of looking like one, all the while being battered by the to-and-fro conflicting winds of England managerdom.There is nothing new here. This is a job that involves not just picking the right players and making high-stakes calculations over your second-half substitutions, but carrying out these basic duties while wrestling with aggrieved members of the Thuggee cult on a collapsing rope bridge outside the Temple of Doom, and simultaneously having your heart ripped out.No other nation makes quite the same twin-track demands. Manage the games. Yeah, do that obviously. But also tell us who we are and how we should play. This is why the job will always take its pound of mince meat, why these people end up drained and hollowed out, an empty tracksuit resigning in the Wembley toilets, Roy Hodgson in Nice looking like a desiccated vampire, saying “I don’t know why I’m here”.Bellingham stands out for high-grade England but Uefa sends out wrong message on racism | Barney RonayRead moreIt is also why it was heartening in Rijeka to see Tuchel gripped with the familiar energies, still whirling about on the touchline in penitent black shoes and black trousers, looking as ever like a famine-ridden earl out taking the hounds for a walk, while simultaneously cracking the Enigma code in his hunting shed.It feels absurd to say that Tuchel is now safe in the job, if only because the idea he wouldn’t be is so hysterical. Tuchel was never realistically in any trouble. But such is the nature of a role where you’re only ever a few rapid-fire defeats away from the incredible twin feat of a greatest-ever overseas World Cup and a near-instant heaving from the job.We should of course keep a sense of scale over a couple of Nations League wins against underpowered opponents. The7-0 steamrollering of Croatiawas always a strange affair. From the moment the doors opened the whole occasion felt like a youth club association sports day, where everyone gets a medal at the end and the teachers do a disco dance routine.It was an atmosphere that seemed to communicate itself to theCroatiaplayers even as they were warming up in a notably fun and jokey way, cheered by shrill groups of junior ultras, and blasted by the Croatian version of We Didn’t Start the Fire through the ear-shredding speaker system.Croatia played from the first minute like a team recovering from a dose of herbal sleeping tablets. Luka Modric’s every touch was met with the kind of noise more usually associated with an appearance by a Korean boyband at an Apple Store launch event, but one of the great players of the age was simply run over by England’s youthful and hungry midfield.View image in fullscreenJude Bellingham was superb in the win over Croatia, as he was during the World Cup.Photograph: Igor Soban/Pixsell/MB Media/Getty ImagesThese are also the teams you play, however. Croatia were decent enough at the World Cup. Mainly, though this came at an absolutely vital moment in the age of Tuchelism. The next 20 months are basically it, the engine room, the space where Tuchel gets to decide how good his team can be, leading in to a tournament England will never have a better chance of winning.The only questions that really matter right now are: is there vision of a team and a way to play? And do we have forward progress? The answers to both of which are yes.England were good in an interesting way in Croatia. We’re used to England teams that seem powerful but also flawed. In Rijeka they looked likea World Cup semi-finalistthat has used that experience to improve, strong in every area, physically, technically and in its basic balance.At times in the current era England have brought to mind the Gareth Southgate team of 2019 into 2020, when some key new players entered a blooming environment, and suddenly they were blowing away mid-range opponents. The Covid break would complicate that arc. An unprovable counter-factual: nudge those first Southgate Euros forward a year and England might have had themomentum to overpower Italyin the final.There are two aspects to Tuchel’s England this time around. First, the reckoning up with the mistakes of the recent past. Why, oh why didn’t he take Cole Palmer? Well, maybe for the same reason Palmer’s not here now. Well, why of why, then, didn’t he take Phil Foden? This has also answered itself. The same goes for not selecting the back-up striker who is now, it turns out, playing in Saudi Arabia. It is entirely legitimate to still disagree with all these things. But it feels clearer that there was logic and reasoning here.The past can re-litigate itself. The second key element is the sense of progress. This was always likely to be the case. It takes time to get to know your players. Tuchel had never been to an international tournament before. He was never the knockout specialist some seemed to assume. Just take a look at his record. He’s a process guy. And we are now right in the middle of that process.View image in fullscreenLewis Hall has enjoyed a fine international break and looks to be first choice for England at left-back.Photograph: Darko Bandić/APSo what has changed? Most obviously makingJude Bellinghamthe hub of this team is an excellent idea, and not just because of his astonishing talent. Rallying around Bellingham is Tuchel’s version of Southgate’s inflatable unicorns, the talk about Spitfires, the away-days with the SAS crawling through an assault course made entirely from Cheddar cheese and Eccles cakes.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHow do you make players want to play for England? Here’s a short cut. Give them aura, brand power, magnetism. Put the big guy right at the centre. Everyone’s turning up if Jude is loving it, and you have a chance for two weeks to exist in his forcefield.Then there’s the way England have played. There is always talk about “a Premier League style”, which has never been a single thing. But these players are definitely best suited to high-intensity, hard-running, duel-winning football. This wasn’t only there in successfully outmuscling an ageing Mateo Kovacic, who even in his pomp had the air of a frail Victorian child masquerading as an elite modern midfielder, shorts hiked up, skinny legs gamely covering the turf.England also played like this for half an hour against the world champions, andnarrowly lost a gamewhere they went 1-0 down after a minute and missed a late penalty. This felt like an evolved version of the “packet-ball” intensity that blew Croatia away at the World Cup for 20 minutes then could never quite click into gear again. The next Euros are in England. Cancel the heatwave, and they can play like this for longer.Then there is the issue of balance. Lewis Hall: yes, a proper left-back with a left foot. Jarell Quansah makes lots of sense now, offering something of the Kyle Walker-style recovery athleticism. Alex Scott looked really good in Rijeka, a genuinely smart, head-up, surging midfield presence.Tuchel is right. He can’t roll into a tournament with two first-choice midfielders. Scott offered something different in the exact area England lose these high-stakes, high-intensity games. He even knows who his back-up centre-forward is now, and it is of course Jude. Ask any question right now. The answer is likely to be the same.Lamine Yamal stars again as Spain see off Czechia and maintain perfect startRead moreHere is another unprovable counter-factual. England would have beaten that Argentina team in Atlanta with this team in Rijeka. This should not be a source of why-oh-why frustration. It’s forward momentum, learning new patterns, adding new tricks. Stick Bellingham up front in the second half, pack Scott into a three-man midfield, and they’ve got a far better chance of seeing that game out.The process is also far from done. England need competition on the right wing. Bukayo Saka is an excellent footballer. But he’s not a weapon other teams will fear. Add an England-issue Michael Olise, for example, and this team looks entirely different in its threat levels. Max Dowman is still just a very nice idea at this point. But there’s time. And he doesn’t need to be perfect.Finally, and back to the key figure in this cycle, there is the total weaponising of Bellingham, whose role in the team is now beautifully clarified. Station him in forward areas and he will still press and harry and add a defensive function. But turning, running, breaking in transitions, making risky creative passes, he is just a supreme footballer. Not to mention a one-man mission statement of the way this team wants to play.Tournaments aren’t won with a 7-0 win on the Adriatic coast in front of 6,000 over-caffeinated schoolchildren. But there is progress here. And that time will pass in a wink.Explore more on these topicsEnglandCroatiaNations LeagueThomas TuchelJude BellinghamcommentShareReuse this content

title: Hallgrímsson calls on Uefa to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future after bad-tempered draw | Nations League | The Guardian
description: Troy Parrott’s first-half penalty for Ireland was cancelled out by Israel’s Dor Peretz in a 1-1 draw but tensions spilled over between the sides at various points
Author: Guardian sport
Headline: Troy Parrott’s first-half penalty for Ireland was cancelled out by Israel’s Dor Peretz in a 1-1 draw but tensions spilled over between the sides at various points
Content: Ireland’s Jayson Molumby and Jason Knight argue with Eli Dasa and Oscar Gloukh, of Israel, as tensions spilled over.Photograph: Stephen McCarthy/Sportsfile/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenIreland’s Jayson Molumby and Jason Knight argue with Eli Dasa and Oscar Gloukh, of Israel, as tensions spilled over.Photograph: Stephen McCarthy/Sportsfile/Getty ImagesNations LeagueHallgrímsson calls on Uefa to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future after bad-tempered drawGuardian sportand agenciesSun 4 Oct 2026 17.13 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Republic of Ireland’s manager Heimir Hallgrímsson has called on Uefa to keep his side away from Israel in future draws after a pair of fixtures he admitted “has been tough on us all”. Ireland were pegged back to a draw in another tetchy encounter, this time played without fans at TSC Arena in Backa Topola, Serbia.Hallgrímsson did not want to comment on a half-time confrontation, after which it is understood a member of his backroom staff alleged he was spat at by an Israeli player – something the Icelandic manager said was better left to a disciplinary committee.“We need now some time to reflect and go forward,” he said. “It’s also the best time to find your enemies when you’re lying on the ground and people are kicking you. It’s easy to see who was trying to kick you.”Denmark sink Wales as Rasmus Højlund makes Danny Ward pay for blunderRead moreAsked on RTE whether the two sides should be playing in the future, he said: “No, they shouldn’t. That’s not ours to decide, that’s Uefa. I wouldn’t want or wish any national team to go through what we have gone through these two weeks. Uefa needs to step in and do something.’Troy Parrott’s first-half ­penalty was cancelled out after the break in the Group B3 game. Parrott, who has now scored 10 times in his past seven competitive internationals, fired the Republic in front from the spot in the 39th minute before Dor Peretz drew the sides level two ­minutes after the restart.Ireland players again wore black armbands and bowed their heads ­during the Israeli national anthem before the teams’ secondNations Leaguemeeting on Sunday. The Israeli players also wore black armbands in memory of the people killed in the Hamas-led attacks on Israel on 7 October 2023.Ireland goalkeeper Caoimhín Kelleher stepped in as captain for Dara O’Shea – who was excused to be with his wife for the birth of their child – and he pointedly avoided shaking hands with the Israel captain Peretz, despite completing the usual pre-match formality with the referee and one of his assistants.Kelleher repeated O’Shea’s actions before the first match in Debrecen, Hungary last week, when O’Shea declined to shake the Israel captain Manor Solomon’s hand. Ireland went on towin that game 3-0 through three first-half goals. Solomon was dropped to the bench for Sunday’s match. The Israel forward Sayed Abu Farchi was back in the squad after serving a suspension for getting sent off following his goal celebration during Israel’s 3-1 defeat to Austria last month.Finn Azaz, whose mother has Israeli heritage, was among the Irish substitutes after playing from the start against Austria on Thursday.View image in fullscreenThe Ireland goalkeeper Caoimhín Kelleher avoids shaking hands with the Israel captain Dor Peretz before the game.Photograph: Andrej Čukić/EPAIreland had started to find some fluidity when Dunne won a penalty. The Israel goalkeeper Assaf Tzur scrambled to smother the ball, and Jimmy Dunne was brought down under the challenge, with the spot-kick confirmed after a lengthy VAR check.Peretz levelled the scoring two minutes after the restart. An Oscar Gloukh effort took a favourable deflection off Liam Scales and into the path of the acting captain, who gave ­Kelleher no chance with a low finish.YesterSunday’s game was initially supposed to be played in Dublin, but the Football Association of Ireland moved the game to a neutral venue for “operational reasons” in June following widespread calls for a boycott in protest of Israel’s actions in Gaza. The FAI said the game would be played with no fans present.It followed the FAI’s own motion the previous November calling on Uefa to ban Israel from club and international competitions.The difficult atmosphere between the sides spilled over during a clash as the sides entered the tunnel at half-time. Officials then broke up a second altercation in three minutes of added time, and there were more heated words exchanged after the final whistle.Explore more on these topicsNations LeagueRepublic of IrelandIsraelmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Jonathan Taylor’s double earns Colts win against Commanders in London | NFL | The Guardian
description: The running back scored touchdowns either side of half-time to give Indianapolis a 30-13 win against Washington at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium
Author: Graham Searles
Headline: The running back scored touchdowns either side of half-time to give Indianapolis a 30-13 win against Washington at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium
Content: Jonathan Taylor ran for 95 yards and scored two touchdowns at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium.Photograph: Hugo Philpott/UPI/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenJonathan Taylor ran for 95 yards and scored two touchdowns at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium.Photograph: Hugo Philpott/UPI/ShutterstockNFLJonathan Taylor’s double earns Colts win against Commanders in LondonIndianapolis 30-13 WashingtonTreylon Burks scores 47-yard TD for WashingtonGraham Searlesat the Tottenham Hotspur StadiumSun 4 Oct 2026 14.28 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“Welcome to the NFL’s home away from home,” was the rallying cry from former running back and current in-stadium hype man Ronde Barber before the league’s 19th year holidaying in the UK began. And welcome Washington’s injury bug which must have stowed away on the flight to London. The mighty Commanders defense that overwhelmed the Colts at times could not overcome having another quarterback knocked out of commission. Indianapolis capitalised on the misfortune with crafty running back Jonathan Taylor carrying them to a 30-13 victory.The Commanders were already missing starting quarterback Jayden Daniels with an elbow injury and their pesky interloper wasn’t satisfied that Washington had endured enough torment. The game-defining moment came early as a knee injury forced backup passer Marcus Mariota out of the contest after a strong start. Rookie third-stringer Athan Kaliakmanis replaced him and though he delivered the play of the game with an incredible showcase of vision and accuracy on a 47-yard touchdown throw, it was too much, too soon for the 23-year-old.Watson and Browns hold off Steelers’ fightback on last-gasp 56-yard field goalRead moreWashington’s brutal defense, fresh fromtoppling the Super Bowl championslast week, burst out of the traps as defensive tackle Odafe Oweh drove his opposite number Bernhard Raimann straight into Colts quarterback Daniel Jones. The stunned signal caller fell backwards while coughing the ball up to the Commanders who had a turnover after two plays and three points after a 31-yard field goal from Drew Stevens.From then on it mattered little that Jones continued to struggle in the face of Washington’s ferocious front seven. The Colts passer would finish with 19 completions from 34 attempts for 143 yards, no touchdowns and an interception. Lucky for Indianapolis that they have the capable legs of Taylor who picked up the quarterback’s slack with 95 yards on the ground and a pair of touchdowns either side of half-time. His game-winning efforts sandwiched a 48-yard Spencer Shrader boot that put the Colts 17-6 up at the break and out of sight.Meanwhile Kaliakmanis was dealing with the pressure of being thrust into his first professional game. The crowd noticeably quietened at defeat looming far too early as veteran running back Austin Ekeler edged the Commanders to midfield. Those in burgundy and gold had accepted their fate after the unknown QB had started the second half with an ominous interception that set up Taylor’s second score.The backup’s backup quickly restored some faith though with a breathtaking throw. Kaliakmanis saw Treylon Burks breaking down the left sideline and drove the arcing pass just ahead of the sprinting receiver’s path. Burks made the grab in stride for the touchdown. The crowd could not believe it. Neither could Kaliakmanis as he grinned from ear to ear after giving his team a fleeting spark to sit 17-13 behind.View image in fullscreenTreylon Burks runs into the endzone after a throw from Washington Commanders quarterback Athan Kaliakmanis.Photograph: Mickael Chavet/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockThe rookie continued to receive help from his impressive defense as Indianapolis favoured conservative play calling to avoid any more costly turnovers as they added a field goal from Shrader. Alarm bells from the early fumble and interception had been silenced with Taylor taking care of the ball.Then for a few seconds it looked as if Kaliakmanis could be delivering a quarterback debut for the history books as his receiver Antonio Williams raced 80 yards for another touchdown that would have levelled the scores. To the crowd’s deafening ire it was not to be due to an illegal shift penalty.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |FortnightlySign up toThe HotspotA new fortnightly newsletter covering the intersection of sport and the climate crisisEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAs the final quarter began it was the reliable Taylor again at the controls. Two 12-yard rushes moved the Colts to the goalline. A faked handoff to their linchpin then allowed Jones to tuck and run for a score to add some much-needed positivity after his arm wilted under Washington pressure.Indianapolis will be glad to escape London with a 2-2 record and realistic ambitions of making the playoffs after the rockiest of starts. Washington will lick their wounds hoping Daniels is back soon to revive their season.Explore more on these topicsNFLIndianapolis ColtsWashington CommandersUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Insane’: F1 drivers unite over engine regulations after chaotic Bahrain GP | Formula One 2026 | The Guardian
description: Kimi Antonelli and Lewis Hamilton led the criticism for Sunday’s Bahrain GP after the race was delayed for 53 minutes because of software problems in the wet conditions
Author: Giles Richards
Headline: Kimi Antonelli and Lewis Hamilton led the criticism for Sunday’s Bahrain GP after the race was delayed for 53 minutes because of software problems in the wet conditions
Content: Kimi Antonelli joined Lewis Hamilton in criticising the FIA after farcical scenes in Sepang.Photograph: Antoine Lapeyre/Reveries Agency/ABACA/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenKimi Antonelli joined Lewis Hamilton in criticising the FIA after farcical scenes in Sepang.Photograph: Antoine Lapeyre/Reveries Agency/ABACA/ShutterstockFormula One 2026‘Insane’: F1 drivers unite over engine regulations after chaotic Bahrain GPAntonelli and Hamilton led the criticism in SepangRace delayed after software problems in wet conditionsGiles RichardsSun 4 Oct 2026 11.30 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 19.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFormula One drivers issued a damning condemnation of the sport’s current engine regulations that caused the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia to open with farcical scenes of cars stopping on track and unable to accelerate because of software problems in the electronics that control the engines.Red Bull’sMax Verstappen won in Sepangbut only after F1 suffered the embarrassment of a host of cars barely able to complete two ­formation laps in the wet as they were making their way to the grid.Max Verstappen wins chaotic F1 Bahrain GP in Malaysia amid farcical scenesRead more“It was insane,” said the championship leader Kimi Antonelli of Mercedes. “At some point we were five-wide in the straight, because we couldn’t understand what was going on.”Lewis Hamilton was one of the field who ground to a halt. “I had to stop on-track, stop the car, the engine, and restart it. I’ve never done that before,” he said, while Verstappen reiterated his previous criticism of the engine regulations. “What can you say? It’s not what you want for the sport. I hope there is a lesson learned,” he said.The issue was caused by software designed to control the engine but which had been insufficiently tested in low-grip, wet conditions which led to what the sport’s governing body the FIA called “an unintended loss of power”.The start had to be aborted and the field returned to the pit lane to have the software updated in a delay that lasted 53 minutes, leading to a ­chorus of disapproval from the drivers who were already dissatisfied with the current engine formula.The defending world champion, Lando Norris, who finished ninth for McLaren and is one of many who have been critical of the engine regulations, described it as “just ­horrible” and noted once more that it demonstrated the sport had taken a wrong turn, adding: “We shouldn’t have any of that stuff, the electronic side.”The formula, an almost 50-50 split between electronic and combustion power, will not be changed this ­season with a minor adjustment next year and more serious change in 2028, but the issue had once more raised the question of how the sport reached this point.View image in fullscreenThe safety car leads Max Verstappen in a wet formation lap.Photograph: Clive Mason/Getty Images“[F1] needs to have a hard look at themselves and see how we ended up in this situation,” said Williams’ Carlos Sainz. “It is clear the regs are extremely complicated for the drivers, for the teams, for the power units, for the manufacturers. It is too complicated. Again, my only question mark is who five years ago decided that this was the direction to go?”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe FIA did act swiftly to ­rectify the problem with the software update but their single-seater director Nikolas Tombazis admitted the regulations and the “software bug” had caught the governing body out.“We didn’t manage to test the software as extensively as we would have liked because there’s been very little wet running this year and there was a bit of a combination of circumstances which caused this bug to kick in,” he said.“Basically, the formation lap, some cars went very slowly, almost came to a standstill. There was a bit of a ­concertina effect between cars, and some cars almost stopped completely. That bug prevented the power to be redeployed and for the cars to start again. I think if we had a bit more testing, we probably would have managed to catch it in time and not to have such a situation.”Explore more on these topicsFormula One 2026Formula OneMotor sportnewsShareReuse this content

title: Shaw seals thrilling win over Arsenal to extend Manchester City’s 100% WSL start | Women's Super League | The Guardian
description: Manchester City came from behind twice to win a six-goal thriller against Arsenal and continue their 100% start to the WSL season
Author: Tom Garry
Headline: Manchester City came from behind twice to win a six-goal thriller against Arsenal and continue their 100% start to the WSL season
Content: Manchester City's Bunny Shaw scores the fourth goal to seal victory over Arsenal and top spot in the WSL.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PAView image in fullscreenManchester City's Bunny Shaw scores the fourth goal to seal victory over Arsenal and top spot in the WSL.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PAWomen's Super LeagueShaw seals thrilling win over Arsenal to extend Manchester City’s 100% WSL startTom Garryat the Etihad StadiumSun 4 Oct 2026 14.07 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleArsenal’s under-pressure head coach Renée Slegers still believes they will turn their form around, despite falling 10 points behind Manchester City with Sunday’s defeat in an absorbing six-goal thriller against the defending champions.Arsenal were last season’s runners-up in the Women’s Super League and had high hopes of mounting a strong challenge this term but their chances of lifting a first WSL title since 2019 now appear to be hanging by a thread after five rounds of fixtures, while City maintained their 100% start by coming from behind twice to beat Slegers’ struggling side.Manchester City 4-2 Arsenal: Women’s Super League – liveRead moreThe 37-year-old Dutchwoman, who in January signed a new contract until the summer of 2029, said on Friday that she felt the full support of the club. Asked, after this pivotal 4-2 defeat, whether she would be the one in charge after this month’s international break, she replied: “All I know so far is that the last couple of days we’ve been together as a club, as a team, with support, aligning on the direction. Of course, this result is disappointing, but I’m here, I’m full of energy and I care a lot for the club.”Slegers added she feels the international break will come at a good time to change environments and that there will be a “big review of our season so far” during the break. She continued: “We see solutions and we see the closeness. It’s not that we’re totally off it. It’s been consistently about margins – when we get them on our side, I think we’re going to be really good.”The match was the first to be played at the Etihad Stadium since the Premier League published the guilty verdict against Manchester City and there was something of a subdued atmosphere outside the stadium in the buildup to kick-off. That quickly changed once the game started, and was wholly different in the second half as the hosts began to take control and their supporters were thoroughly enjoying themselves.City had frequently insisted their women’s team were treating this as “business as usual”before their draw with Real Madridon Thursday. There were very few references to the ongoing saga here on Sunday, aside from some Arsenal fans chanting “same old City, always cheating” during the first half, and one City fan – sitting just in front of the media seats – who defiantly shouted about which part of the anatomy people could “stick your 115 charges”, but nobody else joined in. Matters on the pitch were more interesting.City will have felt aggrieved about the nature of Arsenal’s opener, as replays showed that Lisa Baum appeared to be offside when Lotte Wubben-Moy headed goalwards. Baum was the quickest to get to the rebound after Ayaka Yamashita’s save and poked home. The visitors could not hold on until the break, however, as Lauren Hemp’s deflected strike found its way into the far corner.Arsenal went back in front shortly after half-time when Yui Hasegawa lost the ball inside her own area and Alessia Russo pounced, curling a terrific finish into the far corner. It was her first league goal of the campaign. Arsenal appeared to be in control until a triple substitution from Andrée Jeglertz, including the introduction of Kerstin Casparij, changed things.View image in fullscreenAlessia Russo pounces to make it 2-1 to Arsenal at Manchester City.Photograph: Ed Sykes/Action Images/ReutersThe 26-year-old, playing as an inverted full-back, latched on to a loose ball and curled in a delightful strike to equalise and soon afterwards Hemp tucked a tidy finish through Anneke Borbe’s legs to make it 3-2. Suddenly Arsenal’s body language changed and City were on top. They added a clinical fourth when Shaw latched on to Aoba Fujino’s excellent through-ball and her low finish was superb.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMoving the GoalpostsNo topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionJeglertz was full of praise for Casparij and his centre-back pairing of Jade Rose and Alex Greenwood. Asked about Arsenal’s woes, he said he still expects them to have a strong campaign, saying: “They have great football players - I’m pretty sure that when we are coming into spring that they will definitely be one of the teams battling.”Arsenal’s problems were exacerbated by their midfielder Mariona Caldentey going off with a suspected hamstring injury. The Arsenal defender Wubben-Moy said there was unity as she told Sky Sports the players “fought for ourselves, for Renée and for the fans - but ultimately the result didn’t do that justice”, adding: “This is an unprecedented position for Arsenal to be in. It’s up to us to get ourselves out of it.”Her words may offer some solace to Slegers. So will the sight of the 2,000 travelling fans applauding her after the game. The upcoming “review” will determine whether or not that was a farewell.Explore more on these topicsWomen's Super LeagueManchester City WomenArsenal WomenWomen's footballmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Committed Sale beat non-vintage Saracens despite Vermeulen red card | Prem Rugby | The Guardian
description: Nathan Jibulu, Tom O’Flaherty and Ben Bamber were Sale’s try scorers in their 21-17 victory at Saracens
Author: Robert Kitson
Headline: Nathan Jibulu, Tom O’Flaherty and Ben Bamber were Sale’s try scorers in their 21-17 victory at Saracens
Content: Tom O'Flaherty breaks a tackle from Saracens' Fergus Burke on his way to scoring a try.Photograph: Andrew Matthews/PAView image in fullscreenTom O'Flaherty breaks a tackle from Saracens' Fergus Burke on his way to scoring a try.Photograph: Andrew Matthews/PAPrem RugbyCommitted Sale beat non-vintage Saracens despite Vermeulen red cardSaracens 17-21 SaleJibulu, O’Flaherty and Bamber score Sale’s triesRobert Kitsonat the StoneX StadiumSun 4 Oct 2026 12.37 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt doesn’t always require a qualified ‘wine consultant’ to identify a non-vintage performance. Brendan Venter, whose ever-changing job title atSaracenshas been a subject of debate all week, will certainly not be cracking open the special reserve when he rewatches this game, ultimately most notable for Sale’s perseverance, physicality and resilience after being reduced to 13 players at one stage in the first quarter.Committed and cussed from start to finish,Saledeserved this unexpected success over hosts who seldom made it beyond second gear despite having a liberal sprinkling of England internationals in their pack. Tries for Nathan Jibulu, Tom O’Flaherty and Ben Bamber, underpinned by the experience of George Ford, Tom Curry and Courtney Lawes, represented a major upgrade on their opening weekend home loss to Bristol.Newcastle have wings clipped by Leicester but look to play long gameRead moreTo compound Sarries’ pain, their England duo of Theo Dan and Elliot Daly departed prematurely in the second half while Alfie Barbeary lasted only 40 minutes. Jamie George is back in training but this was a timely day for a young English hooker like Jibulu to prosper. The former Harlequin was given the man-of-the-match award and was singled out for special praise by his director of rugby, Alex Sanderson.“It shows he’s of international class,” said Sanderson. “He nailed his lineouts and was a wrecking-ball runner. It could be the year where he explodes onto the international scene. There’s been a lot of rotation for England after Luke Cowan-Dickie or Jamie. There’s not really one person standing up and taking that No 2 shirt. This could be a good opportunity for him.”The contrast with last season, when Sale leaked 150 points in their two fixtures against Saracens, could scarcely have been more pronounced. It certainly seemed to help the Sharks that the high-flying Noah Calouri was not involved here, with Sarries often struggling for consistent rhythm despite the presence of England forwards like Maro Itoje, Ben Earl and George Martin.A nicely worked try scored by Charlie Bracken following a compelling surge from his brother Jack, did narrow the gap to 21-17 entering the closing stages but Sale, motivated and physical, had enough in reserve physically to silence a home crowd previously encouraged by last week’s win at Leicester.At least it was a lovely sunny afternoon in north London, mellow enough to start pondering what ­Saracens’ ‘wine consultant’ might have served up had he still be in position. Unfortunately Venter – or ‘Brendan Vintner’ as he has been dubbed – now goes by the less snappy title of ‘head of culture and technical director’ with corkscrews no longer required. Speaking to the written media, regardless, is not top of his priority list, with head coach Joe Shaw again wheeled out for post-match duties instead.View image in fullscreenBen Bamber scores Sale’s third try against Saracens.Photograph: Colorsport/Ashley Western/ShutterstockIt is a shame on multiple fronts, partly because the ex-Springbok is good value on numerous topics and, perhaps more pertinently, because English club rugby currently needs all the publicity it can muster. Speaking to TNT Sport before the game, Venter even suggested he is not in charge of picking the team, which is a bit like arguing the prime minister is not wholly responsible for his government’s policies. Instead he says it is a collegiate enterprise which, this week, lasted five hours and involved selecting teams for the season’s first eight weeks. The ‘wine’ analogy arose from a pre-season theme about the importance of finding the right blend.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe BreakdownThe latest rugby union news and analysis, plus all the week's action reviewedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMake of that what you like but it is on-field performances that will ultimately do the talking. Saracens took far too long to get going on Sunday and were kept scoreless until the 33rd minute, when Eroni Mawi finally ploughed over from close range.
