Given Sale were two men down for a large chunk of the opening half hour, Jacques Vermeulen having received a 20-minute red card for a high challenge on Tomos Williams after Alex Lozowski had been binned previously, the hosts’ lethargy was even stranger.To say the first half was messy would be overselling it, particularly given the talent on the pitch. There was even a split second when it seemed Sale might be reduced to 12 but, fortunately for them, an attempted knock-down of a Fergus Burke chip by Lawes flew backwards rather than forwards. Saracens, though, had a potential score by Nick Tompkins belatedly scrubbed out for obstruction at a preceding lineout and the crowd fell increasingly silent. It was hard to see much in the way of patterns or consistency until Mawi’s plunge provided much-needed relief.The second half, thankfully, was more absorbing. After O’Flaherty’s solo intervention, reacting quickest as everyone else waited for a mishit high punt to descend, Saracens badly needed something having replaced Barbeary, Hugh Tizard and both starting props at half-time. The reshuffle was duly rewarded when centre Sione Va’enuku exploited a narrow visiting defence but Bamber’s last-quarter charge, set up by Ford’s cute offload, proved to be the killer blow.Explore more on these topicsPrem RugbySaracensSaleRugby unionmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Daryz makes history with back-to-back Arc de Triomphe triumphs | Prix de l'Arc de Triomphe | The Guardian
description: Daryz became the first colt for 48 years to win the Prix de l’Arc de Triomphe in successive seasons with a brilliant victory at Longchamp
Author: Greg Wood
Headline: Daryz became the first colt for 48 years to win the Prix de l’Arc de Triomphe in successive seasons with a brilliant victory at Longchamp
Content: Mickaël Barzalona riding Daryz to win the Prix de l'Arc de Triomphe.Photograph: Alan Crowhurst/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMickaël Barzalona riding Daryz to win the Prix de l'Arc de Triomphe.Photograph: Alan Crowhurst/Getty ImagesPrix de l'Arc de TriompheDaryz makes history with back-to-back Arc de Triomphe triumphsWinning rider Barzalona hails ‘exceptional horse’Stud beckons over bid for unprecedented third winGreg Woodat LongchampSun 4 Oct 2026 12.47 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt was a very different, distinctly brutalist Longchamp that last saw a colt go back-to-back in the Arc, and 48 years on from Alleged’s second victory in 1978 with Lester Piggott holding the reins, the uber-modernist new grandstand rose to acclaim its first legend here on Sunday as Daryz produced the same overwhelming turn of finishing speed down the straight that had carried him to victory in the Prix de l’Arc de Triomphe 12 months ago.Daryz and Mickaël Barzalona did not hit the front until inside the final furlong, but they had been closing on Bay City Roller, who had disputed the lead for much of the way, to such effect from well over a furlong out that the result was in no real doubt.Daryz wins back-to-back Prix de l’Arc de Triomphes at Longchamp – as it happenedRead moreOisin Murphy had worked wonders to get Bay City Roller into contention from stall 15, and likewise Christophe Soumillon, on Aidan O’Brien’s Diamond Necklace, who finished strongly into third from the widest draw of all. But unlike some recent runnings of the Arc – Enable’s narrow defeat of Sea Of Class in 2018, for instance – there was no sense that swapping the draws might have changed the result. Daryz, quite simply, proved himself a class apart.“To win this kind of race twice proves that Daryz is an exceptional horse,” Barzalona said. “It was a really tough race, it didn’t go as we expected but he showed his talent and that made the difference in the end.“The pace was not strong, it was a rough race and nothing went to plan, but the horse deserved to win again and he’s proved all season he is the best one.”For Francis-Henri Graffard, Daryz’s trainer, the win set the seal on another remarkable, championship-winning season in which he has won more than twice as much prize money as the runner-up, André Fabre.“He’s a champion,” Graffard said. “It’s rare I’m confident before a race as it is so hard in a race like this, but I knew things were going right and he’d be very hard to beat. I was confident but I was putting so much pressure on myself [before the race] and you can make yourself look a fool, so it is easier not to speak and not say anything.“We kept losing position early, we were too far back, but we were lucky Daryz has good acceleration.”The only real disappointment on an otherwise perfect, sun-drenched afternoon at Longchamp was a clear hint afterwards that becoming only the sixth colt in Arc history to record back-to-back wins is as much ­history as Daryz will be able to make. No horse has ever won the Arc three times and Daryz seems sure to be completing his first season as a stallion with the Aga Khan Studs when the racing clans gather again in Paris next year.View image in fullscreenBarzalona celebrates after victory on board Daryz in the Prix de l’Arc de Triomphe.Photograph: Frank Sorge/racingfotos.com/Shutterstock“We’re breeders,” Princess Zahra Aga Khan, who has taken over the running of Aga Khan Studs since the death of her father in 2025, said afterwards. “You get to the point where you’re taking a risk every time you run the horse. He’s improved with age, that’s true, and the dam [Daryakana] did, but would we want him to train on for another year? I’m not sure. I think he has other things to do.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn the likely absence of Daryz, it will be up to the beaten horses in Sunday’s race to represent the form in 12 months’ time, and George Scott’s Bay City Roller seems sure to be back next October after his fine run into second from out wide, on ground that was quicker than ideal.Quick GuideGreg Wood's Monday tipsShowYarmouth1.15 Eightthreeone 1.50 Awwjaan 2.25 Zhuri 3.00 Chaise Longue 3.35 Evening Call 4.05 Lucky Hero 4.40 Media Legend (nb)Pontefract1.30 Narrjoo 2.05 Floral Maid 2.40 Fiscal Policy 3.15 American Gulf 3.50 Physique 4.21 Selection 4.56 Noble Grace 5.33 Jojo RabbitStratford-On-Avon1.41 No More Bolero 2.16 Arcturus Flame 2.51 Stellarmasterpiece 3.26 Another Folly 4.00 Pescatorius 4.35 TurbogeistKempton4.10 Shareek 4.45 Footstepinthewoods 5.15 Pursuit Of Love 5.45 Sax Avoidance 6.15 Moving Force 6.45 Buccabay 7.15 Ararat 7.45 Ridger 8.15 Super HitWolverhampton4.26 Solar Swing 5.00 Dreams Galore (nap) 5.30 Iron Dome 6.00 Lady Branksome 6.30 Apex Star 7.00 Faeberon 7.30 Kaaranah 8.00 Alkaios 8.30 Alfa WhiteburdWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.“I could see Daryz coming, but it was an incredible run,” Scott, who saddled a Group-race double on ­Saturday’s card here, said afterwards. “What an amazing racehorse he is and what an amazing ride. He wears his heart on his sleeve, and he’s got all the talent and ability to go with it. Second in the Arc, but we need to go one better.”By then, Daryz will likely be ­completing his first covering ­season at stud, but if Sunday’s race was indeed his final flourish on the track, the sight of his first foals ­setting foot on a racecourse in 2030 will at least summon up memories of an ­outstanding colt and a special afternoon at Longchamp.Explore more on these topicsPrix de l'Arc de TriompheHorse racingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Wakefield’s wondrous Super League fairytale a victory for loyalty and logic | Super League | The Guardian
description: The owner has put in £10m but seven victorious players at Old Trafford were in the Championship two years ago and stayed at Trinity
Author: Aaron Bower
Headline: The owner has put in £10m but seven victorious players at Old Trafford were in the Championship two years ago and stayed at Trinity
Content: Fans line the streets on Sunday as Wakefield Trinity players celebrate their first Super League Grand Final win.Photograph: Asadour GuzelianView image in fullscreenFans line the streets on Sunday as Wakefield Trinity players celebrate their first Super League Grand Final win.Photograph: Asadour GuzelianSuper LeagueAnalysisWakefield’s wondrous Super League fairytale a victory for loyalty and logicAaron BowerOwner has put in £10m but seven victorious players at Old Trafford were in the Championship two years ago and stayed at TrinitySun 4 Oct 2026 11.51 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 21.30 EDTShareIt may seem quite obvious to suggest there is plenty Super League can learn from its newest champions but as Wakefield Trinity’s dreams came true afterbeating Warrington 23-10at Old Trafford on Saturday evening, it was easy to ponder just how transformational a moment this is for not only them, but so many others, too.This fairytale has captured the national attention and punctured the mainstream unlike few otherSuper Leaguestories in recent times. A second-tier club just two years ago, Wakefield are now champions of England and have a possible showdown with the NRL champions, Sydney Roosters, to contemplate early next year in the World Club Challenge.Wakefield dominate Warrington in Grand Final to claim fairytale Super League titleRead moreA city which has languished in the rugby league pecking order for generations has now been awoken in vivid Technicolor, epitomised by the scenes in Wakefield on Sunday as tens of thousands of supporters lined the streets to welcome home their heroes. Trinity, champions of Super League: it is a statement that still defies belief.But there are lessons in here for everyone. This is all happening at an intriguing time, with a Super League-NRL partnership set to be signed off in the coming weeks and potentially opening the door for more opportunity for growth for the English game, in a year when more than two million supporters attended matches for the first time.Wakefield’s rise from cellar-dwelling afterthought to champions of Super League is inspirational to so many, but it is how they have done it which warrants further attention. Firstly, the loyalty they have shown to their players. The headlines have all been about owner Matt Ellis’s investment and how that has been the catalyst for this remarkable turnaround.That, of course, is true. But the fact that seven of the 17 who lifted the trophy at Old Trafford were playing for Wakefield in the Championship two years ago is proof loyalty matters, and some can tell this story with first-hand experience.View image in fullscreenOwner Matt Ellis holds the Super League trophy aloft at Old Trafford.Photograph: Anna Gowthorpe/ShutterstockMax Jowitt has spent his entire career with Wakefield, and remembers the days where Trinity were training at amateur-standard facilities, playing in a crumbling Belle Vue, pre-Ellis, and fighting for survival on an annual basis. He still recalls sitting on the pitch at Leigh in 2023 in front of a couple of hundred supporters when Wakefield were relegated.On Sunday afternoon he was sitting down again: this time on an open-top bus that ran through the city centre with the Super League trophy for company. “I’ve seen it at its lowest low and now its highest high,” the full-back, who will end a career-long association with the club to join York in 2027, says.“It’s an unbelievable story for the game. To be part of the worst time in Wakefield’s history being relegated and then the best, winning the title, within three years is beyond my wildest dreams. What a ride.” A fine lesson in loyalty paying off.There is another lesson for clubs now chasing Wakefield too; sensible, logical recruitment. Trinity’s rise to the top has been underpinned by a “moneyball” strategy of plucking players from Australia’s lower grades and making them stars. The likes of Caleb Hamlin-Uele and Caius Faatili, now Wakefield legends, moved to England on a pittance: less than the average man on the street.They just wanted an opportunity to shine, and Hamlin-Uele would have been in England’s World Cup squad on Monday had he not opted to correct a knee issue. While others have splurged big money on big names, Wakefield have been meticulous. “It’s unbelievable, I can’t put into words what a dream come true this is. I owe Wakefield everything,” Hamlin-Uele said.Wakey-Wakey: Trinity’s rapid rise and Grand Final run shocks fans from long slumberRead moreThen, of course, there is Ellis. Ridiculed in 2023 when he said Wakefield would win a trophy within five years just as they were heading for the Championship and he had purchased a club on its knees on and off the pitch, his only inaccuracy was that it took just three, not five. This third and final lesson from this story is one which stretches beyondWakefield Trinity, though.Ellis estimates it has cost him £10m to make this dream, one he harboured since he stood on the Belle Vue terraces as a boy, come true. That includes renovating the stadium and putting together the squad that has just won the league title for the first time since 1968.With NRL investment coming over the hill, you wonder if there are others considering purchasing Super League clubs who feel they could make a similar vision a reality. In comparison to the money spent in other sports, £10m is small change to reach the very pinnacle; Ellis and Wakefield have shown dreams can become a reality if you go about it the right way.Wakefield Trinity made their supporters believe again for the first time in generations. If they can do it, why can’t everyone else?Explore more on these topicsSuper LeagueWakefield TrinityWarringtonRugby leagueanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Evans ends Britain’s wait for world rally title after Solberg crashes two corners from glory | Rallying | The Guardian
description: Welshman Elfyn Evans is the first British winner of the title since Richard Burns in 2001, emerging victorious after Oliver Solberg careered down a bank
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Welshman Elfyn Evans is the first British winner of the title since Richard Burns in 2001, emerging victorious after Oliver Solberg careered down a bank
Content: Elfyn Evans speeds towards a dramatic first World Rally Championship title on Sunday – he had been runner-up five times in the last six years.Photograph: Nikos Katikis/DPPI/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenElfyn Evans speeds towards a dramatic first World Rally Championship title on Sunday – he had been runner-up five times in the last six years.Photograph: Nikos Katikis/DPPI/ShutterstockRallyingEvans ends Britain’s wait for world rally title after Solberg crashes two corners from gloryElfyn Evans becomes first British winner since 2001Oliver Solberg’s hopes shattered by tumble down bankReutersSun 4 Oct 2026 14.14 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 15.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google⁠Elfyn Evans ended years of heartache, and a quarter-of-a-century wait for Britain, by winning the World Rally Championship title with Toyota after a dramatic season ⁠finale in Sardinia on Sunday.The ⁠Welshman had been ​championship runner-up five times in the last six years but emerged triumphant after a final Powerstage duel with teammate Oliver Solberg ended with the charging Swede crashing ⁠out two corners from the finish while on course to take the crown.‘Insane’: F1 drivers unite over engine regulations after chaotic Bahrain GPRead moreSolberg, 25, ran wide and careered down a bank before getting the car back on the road. ⁠He still won the rally but lost the crucial bonus points on offer for the top five in the ​final stage.Evans, with co-driver Scott Martin at his side, ‌became the first British world ‌rally champion since Englishman Richard Burns in 2001 and only the third since Scottish driver Colin McRae became ‌the first in 1995.Sweden’s Solberg, son of Norway’s 2003 champion Petter, ended the season as runner-up. The final standings left Evans on 243 points, Solberg on 238 and Sami Pajari on 237 in what was also the end of an era for the sport with new regulations in force next year.View image in fullscreenOliver Solberg is consoled by his co-driver Eliott Edmondson after his title dreams evaporated.Photograph: Nikos Katikis/DPPI/ShutterstockEvans said: “It hasn’t sunk in. I was sure it was over. I didn’t drive the best ‌stage but threw everything at it but it wasn’t clean. I feel for Oliver. He had an incredible weekend.” The Welshman completed his final run first and had to ​watch and wait to see whether he had done enough to take the title.“I don’t really know what my reaction is, it’s surreal with how it happened. It’s a relief. It wouldn’t be my proudest way of winning it, but it’s job done,” added the 37-year-old, who finished fifth in the gravel rally.Evans had started the rally – the ⁠final round after Saudi Arabia’s finale was cancelled due to conflict in the region – ​17 points clear of Finland’s Pajari, ​also in a Toyota, and 21 clear ​of Solberg.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenElfyn Evans (right) sprays spectators alongside his co-driver Martin Scott after sealing the title.Photograph: Nikos Katikis/DPPI/ShutterstockThe Swede took control of the rally on Saturday, knowing he had nothing ​to lose and all to ‌gain, and started ​the final day 33.6 seconds ​clear of the field and the momentum swinging his way.That feeling was reinforced when Evans lost time changing a wheel on Sunday’s penultimate stage, leaving the championship outcome hanging on the short final stage and the title going to which of the pair finished ahead of the other.Toyota had already won the manufacturers’ championship.Explore more on these topicsRallyingMotor sportnewsShareReuse this content

title: Own a mobile phone? Then you’re paying the ‘app tax’. It’s a racket and it’s time the UK faced Apple and Google down | Chi Onwurah | The Guardian
description: A deep-seated duopoly allows the tech giants to exploit the public and developers. But the regulator has powers to stop this abuse – it should use them, says Labour MP Chi Onwurah
Author: Chi Onwurah
Headline: A deep-seated duopoly allows the tech giants to exploit the public and developers. But the regulator has powers to stop this abuse – it should use them, says Labour MP Chi Onwurah
Content: With no alternative platforms, app developers simply have to accept the terms set by Silicon Valley.Photograph: Yui Mok/PAView image in fullscreenWith no alternative platforms, app developers simply have to accept the terms set by Silicon Valley.Photograph: Yui Mok/PAOpinionSmartphonesOwn a mobile phone? Then you’re paying the ‘app tax’. It’s a racket and it’s time the UK faced Apple and Google downChi OnwurahA deep-seated duopoly allows the tech giants to exploit the public and developers. But the regulator has powers to stop this abuse – it should use themChi Onwurah is the Labour MP for Newcastle upon Tyne Central and West and chair of the parliamentary science, innovation and technology committeeSun 4 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 15.28 EDTShareDebates around big tech and digital regulation can sometimes feel distant from the everyday concerns of voters. But the power that a small number of global tech companies hold over our lives goes far beyond what most people realise.As chair of the parliamentary science, innovation and technology committee, I have spent years raising concerns about this: from the data they harvest and the digital “twins” they build of us, to the algorithms that decide what our children see.But there’s a much less visible example of this imbalance of power sitting in the pocket of almost every smartphone user in Britain: the app tax. Apple and Google control the two app stores through which almost every mobile app in this country reaches its customers, and that position lets them set terms for app developers that most businesses would never accept from a supplier. Sell a subscription, game or piece of software through either app store and both companies now charge a commission of up to30% on purchases made inside apps, regardless of what the product is or what it costs to make. With no alternative platforms, developers simply have to accept the terms set by Silicon Valley.Leave big tech behind! How to replace Amazon, Google, X, Meta, Apple – and moreRead moreDevelopers are also prevented from telling users that a cheaper option exists elsewhere, known as “steering”. That restriction is enforced by Apple andGoogleto protect their own profits. For small British developers who might struggle to absorb the cost, that could be the difference between hiring their next engineer or not, investing in a new product or shelving it, or growing their business here or uprooting and building overseas instead.Consumers pay the price, too. Research commissioned by the Coalition for App Fairness, asreportedin the Daily Mail, indicated that British consumers pay approximately £700m per yearto Apple and Google, a full £232m more than the companies paid in UK corporation tax last year combined. This is equivalent to around £55 annually for a household with four smartphone users. It is a cost built into the price of the product, invisible on any receipt, that has far more to do with market control and bolstering profits than anything the companies actually did to earn it.My last job before coming into parliament was with Ofcom, the regulator for communications markets. I was responsible for assessing the competitiveness of markets, because it is through competition that consumers get choice. The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) has found thatAppleand Google’s mobile platforms hold an effective duopoly, with at least 90% of UK mobile devices running on their mobile platforms. App developers have no choice but to distribute their product through the Apple App Store or the Google Play Store. If a developer happened to dislike Apple’s terms and another app store existed, they would take their app, and their customers, elsewhere, and the price would fall. But there is no alternative app store on an iPhone, and no practical route for Android users outside Google Play either. Apple and Google set the rules unchallenged.Parliament anticipated this problem when, in 2024, it passed theDigital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act(DMCCA) with cross-party support, giving the CMA genuine powers to force dominant platforms to change their behaviour. But, so far, the CMA has resorted to weak, voluntary commitments from Apple and Google rather than requirements it is actually obliged to enforce.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionStop shaming people for using AI. Start organizing to prevent our obsolescence | Garrison LovelyRead moreIts consultation on “steering”, which would finally let developers point users to cheaper options elsewhere, has now closed and a decision is due soon. Many are rightly nervous that this could end up with another voluntary gesture, rather than a binding rule, deemed acceptable.But this moment also represents an opportunity. It will be one of the first serious decisions this government makes on big tech, and will likely determine the direction it takes on this issue. The prime minister has been clear, both before and since entering Downing Street, that tech sovereignty means reducing our dependence on a handful of overseas platforms. I want to see that instinct applied to decisions such as this.This is not about being anti-technology or anti-growth. It is about whether British consumers, British developers and British regulators are able to shape the terms on which technology operates in our own market and influences our society. I urge the CMA to use the powers we gave it, and I urge my colleagues in government to back it in doing so.Chi Onwurah is the Labour MP for Newcastle upon Tyne Central and West and chair of the parliamentary science, innovation and technology committeeExplore more on these topicsSmartphonesOpinionAppsGoogleAppleMobile phonescommentShareReuse this content

title: Can teaching schoolchildren about Britain’s role in the transatlantic slave trade remain optional? | National curriculum | The Guardian
description: Mounting evidence about how slavery shaped Britain shows that teaching about its history cannot be a matter of choice
Author: Morgan Ofori
Headline: Mounting evidence about how slavery shaped Britain shows that teaching about its history cannot be a matter of choice
Content: Britain’s transatlantic enslavement of Africans and much of its imperial history sits as non-statutory content in the national curriculum in England.Photograph: Kath VialaView image in fullscreenBritain’s transatlantic enslavement of Africans and much of its imperial history sits as non-statutory content in the national curriculum in England.Photograph: Kath VialaCotton Capital: ongoing seriesNational curriculumCan teaching schoolchildren about Britain’s role in the transatlantic slave trade remain optional?Morgan OforiMounting evidence about how slavery shaped Britain shows that teaching about its history cannot be a matter of choiceSun 4 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 07.02 EDTShareIoften think back to my years as a secondary school history teacher, and to what I was and wasn’t able to teach. History is a foundational subject inEngland, taught to children from the age of five to 14 to build critical thinking, weigh evidence and help pupils understand the world they’ve inherited.Thekey stage 3 national curriculum, covering ages 11 to 14, states that pupils should understand how “Britain has influenced and been influenced by the wider world”, including a historically grounded understanding of empire.That standard was on my mind as I trawled through the recently publishedRegister of British Slave Traders, read thenames commemoratedin the Great Hall atBarts hospital, and followed our seriesEnslaving Nationas it traced connections to enslavement across thechurch, themonarchyand thebanking system.Soon after, the Former British Colonies Enslavement Registers made the records of 4 million enslaved people across 20 former coloniessearchable to the publicfor the first time, a searing record of how enslavement irreversibly altered lives across the former empire.Britain’s transatlantic trafficking of Africans and much of its imperial history sits as non-statutory content in the current national curriculum, included to preserve choice. But the evidence keeps mounting that enslavement was so embedded in British society that choice is the wrong framework. In my experience, non-statutory becomes optional within a term, and optional is quickly recoded as sacrifice-worthy. Teachers end up teaching the history they can defend, not the history that matters.Monarchs, MPs and merchants: the register laying bare Britain’s slave-trading pastRead moreIn November 2025, the government’scurriculum and assessment reviewwas published. It recommended clarifying what counts as statutory and non-statutory, so teachers understand exactly how much optionality they’re working with, before a new national curriculum due next spring. The government’s response promises to “strengthen” the teaching of the country’s history, and to let teachers reflect Britain’s Black history within it.Take, for example, Elizabeth I’s resistance to the Spanish Armada in 1588, a mainstay of English history. Two decades earlier, the same monarch had funded John Hawkins’s voyages along the west African coast, among the earliest English expeditions into the slave trade. Teach the armada without Hawkins and you keep the crown’s ambition, but you lose where a bulk of its money came from.A teacher trying to build a class of intellectually curious students who are keen to learn about enslavement and its legacies has to find the lesson time, build the resources, and defend every hour spent on it. The government’s own responseconcedes the pressure, citing curriculum overload as grounds to loosen what’s compulsory. The Holocaust remains the only topic children in England must study between the ages of 11 and 14. In Wales, by contrast, learning about Black, Asian and minority ethnic histories has beenmandatory sincethe current curriculum was introduced in 2022.Black History Month in some settings exists precisely because of this gap, an annual fix for a curriculum that doesn’t otherwise make room. TheBlack Curriculum, founded in 2019 to get British Black history taught year-round, provided a wake-up call regarding the knowledge gaps around the lives of Black people on these isles.Those initiatives have not always been popular in political circles. In 2021, the then schools minister Nick Gibbdefendedthe government’s decision not to make lessons on empire and the slavery compulsory, triggering criticism. The leader of the Conservative party, Kemi Badenoch,continues to sayBritain ultimately led the fight to end the slave trade and that’s where the focus should be. A month, or a bolt-on curriculum, however well meant, risks treating this history as an addition to the national story rather than part of it. The fix for optionality can’t itself be optional.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |MonthlySign up toCotton CapitalStarting with the Guardian’s own history, Guardian journalists explore the legacies of enslavement and reparative justice around the worldEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe history survives in today’s context where an individual teacher is stubborn enough to protect it. I read scheme after scheme of work marking whole periods “optional” or “if time allows”. If you hail or have heritage from a Commonwealth country, you have probably encountered scholarship that adequately contextualises and foregrounds how imperial history is central to British history – that cannot be omitted. The Guyanese historian Walter Rodney argued that Europe didn’t simply fail to develop Africa, it drained it. Howard W French, the US journalist and author, argues that Africa and its people were central to the making of the modern world, not marginal to it. And in addition to these foundations, undeniable feats of research are adding intellectual weight to arguments around what should be covered.None of it changes the basic fact: enslavement is a load-bearing wall in Britain’s story. Remove it and the country becomes unexplainable – the wealth of its ports, the reach of its empire, the shape of its economy. To make that history elective is to make the explanation itself optional.No wonder critics would rather toast the abolitionists than audit the traders who came before them. I rarely got to choose. The curriculum did that for me.Explore more on these topicsNational curriculumCotton Capital: ongoing seriesCurriculumsSchoolsEducation policyBlack History MonthSlaveryEnglandcommentShareReuse this content

title: Are my gen X peers the influencers the world has been waiting for? | Emma Beddington | The Guardian
description: Their careers are peaking, they’re rich in money and time – and young people think they’re cool. But maybe it’s not as simple as that, writes Emma Beddington
Author: Emma Beddington
Headline: Their careers are peaking, they’re rich in money and time – and young people think they’re cool. But maybe it’s not as simple as that, writes Emma Beddington
Content: Three cheers for competent older women!Photograph: RealPeopleGroup/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThree cheers for competent older women!Photograph: RealPeopleGroup/Getty ImagesOpinionMiddle ageAre my gen X peers the influencers the world has been waiting for?Emma BeddingtonTheir careers are peaking, they’re rich in money and time – and young people think they’re cool. But maybe it’s not as simple as thatSun 4 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 16.27 EDTShare‘Stop sleeping on gen X.” I heard this on TikTok recently. I misinterpreted it, with a guilty start, as: “Stop sleeping, gen X,” because I am 51 (peak X), so always tired; while not sleeping at the time, I may have been resting my eyes. In fact,Joel Marlinarson, a marketing guru, was suggesting my generation have become a powerful, if underrated, force online.Aged between 46 and 61, gen Xers with proper jobs are peaking, career-wise (although it’s a different story for those out of work, as a report last month onthe struggles of over-50s jobseekersmade plain). We’remore likely to own homesthan thefollowing generations; we’re emerging from the trenches of childrearing and, the argument goes, ready to indulge in some me-time. “If gen X were a country, it would be the world’s second-largest consumer market,” theWorld Economic Forum reported last year, with gen X women in particular influencing 70% to 80% of all consumer spending.That makes us great customers – witness the tidal wave ofmenopause-washed wellness guff(Which? reported last month that many pricey supplements wereno better than a cheap multivitamin) and beauty brands for peoplesuddenly horrified by their necks. But does it give us content-creating clout? We’re supposed to be (or at leastmeme lore presents us as) the forgotten generation, low-key, countercultural slackers on the sidelines in the grudge match between millennials and boomers; aspiration and self-promotion aren’t really part of our brand.Sure, kids are scrambling for Oasis tickets andrediscovering zines;US Voguecalled us “the cool ones” and theNew York Timeswent further with “the greatest generation”. I get the argument that it’s our time to shine. But real gen Xers have a lot on their plate and it doesn’t necessarily lend itself to fun, aspirational content.Being peak career means peak responsibility: our parents are faltering (I’m writing this as my mother-in-law is moving into sheltered accommodation) and our kids are facing awful geopolitical and economic prospects that undermine their mental health and chances of independence. We’re falling apart physically: for women, the sorting hat of perimenopause doles out a set of grim symptoms, while men are wondering what will fell them next – heart, stomach, back or knees? Who wants to hear about that? And who can be arsed to make perky TikToks?I’ll tell you who:Kathryn Turner. I was introduced to Turner, M&S Food’s director of product development, by Marlinarson, for whom she is evidence that over-50s employees are “the next biggest influencers”. Turner, a cheery woman in smart trousers who exudes quiet competence, has worked for M&S since 1995. She launched her account in May, but her TikToks already garner up to 2m views and her nearly 250,000 fans are devoted: “Would follow that woman into war,”commented one. “Why did we give Andy Burnham the job over her,”asked another. “I love you Kathryn turner[sic],” wrote an account claiming to be the Heartstopper actorJoe Locke. I love her, too: Turner’s calm sunniness, as she talks viewers through innovations in the picky bits space, is a balm in a fractious world.Turner isn’t Kate Moss,Miranda Julyor any of the other impossibly glamorous gen X figureheads – she seems like a normal, middle-aged woman who knows her stuff and does it well. I love that she’s popping up on TikTok and I get it – I’m projecting, but I bet Turner’s great in a crisis, her desk drawer and handbag well stocked with protein-rich treats, blister plasters and ibuprofen.Maybe this is our online USP. Could watching grownups quietly bossing their busy, complex lives be the next ASMR? Because, mostly, gen X aren’t the “cool ones”: they’re the knackered ones, dealing with life, death, work and frozen shoulders. I don’t know any Mosses or Chloë Sevignys, but I know lots of Turners and I, too, would follow them into war, or at least get a dopamine hit from watching them be extremely competent in short-form videos. No one would want to watch me staring at a screen then breaking to fold some pants, obviously, but I’d love to see more of my capable peers ditch the self-deprecation (very gen X) and shine online.Emma Beddington is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The demands of Welsh devolution are simple: just give us what Scotland has | Will Hayward | The Guardian
description: Andy Burnham is a Westminster leader whom Welsh nationalists could finally work with - but only if he stands up to the devo-sceptics in UK Labour, says Guardian columnist Will Hayward
Author: Will Hayward
Headline: Andy Burnham is a Westminster leader whom Welsh nationalists could finally work with - but only if he stands up to the devo-sceptics in UK Labour, says Guardian columnist Will Hayward
Content: Rhun ap Iorwerth at Plaid Cymru’s annual conference in Llandudno, 2 October 2026.Photograph: Peter Byrne/PAView image in fullscreenRhun ap Iorwerth at Plaid Cymru’s annual conference in Llandudno, 2 October 2026.Photograph: Peter Byrne/PAOpinionWelsh politicsThe demands of Welsh devolution are simple: just give us what Scotland hasWill HaywardAndy Burnham is a Westminster leader whom Welsh nationalists could finally work with - but only if he stands up to the devo-sceptics in UK LabourSun 4 Oct 2026 08.21 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 11.22 EDTShareAs I sat in the firstPlaid Cymru conferencesince the party won the Welsh election and started leading the Welsh government, I heard things I had never heard before. I have been to a lot of Plaid conferences and not once have I heard people being really positive about a UK Labour leader. But there was no mistaking it: the Welsh nationalist party feels that Andy Burnham is a man it can work with.When I interviewed Welsh first ministerRhun ap Iorwerth, he indicated he was hopeful – in a way he never was under Keir Starmer – that there was a prime minister who had a genuine desire to give Wales meaningful concessions when it comes to additional powers.Inhis speech in Llandudno,the first minister saidthat the prime minister had“looked me in the eyes and promised he would not [bypass the Senedd]”. He said he had written to Burnham with a “formal ask” for “a new deal for Wales”.There were five demands from the Welsh government to Westminster: powers over policing and justice, powers over rail infrastructure, control overthe crown estate, “fiscal fairness” and control of welfare. Seems like a pretty long shopping list, right? Well, it can actually be summarised in just five words: “Give us what Scotland has.”The Scots have control of the crown estate, a better funding settlement, with moremoney through the Barnett formula,heavy rail is devolved, and the Scottish government controls policing and justice, as well as havingpartial control of welfare spending.Slowly then all at once: this emboldened Celtic alliance could spell the end of the UK | Simon JenkinsRead moreWhen you look at it from that perspective, it’s not as if the Welsh government is asking for something unprecedented. The UK government only has to look north to see the precedent.You don’t have to be a Welsh nationalist to think it’s unfair that Wales’s government is equipped with fewer tools than its Scottish counterparts to meaningfully tackle Wales’s challenges. Wales has lessborrowing capacity than a local counciland, as mayor of Greater Manchester,Burnham had more power over policingin his area than the first minister of Wales does.The stars are aligning forWalesto get more parity with Scotland. If Burnham follows his own devolution logic – that decisions should be taken closer to the people they impact –then how could he defend a region of England getting more autonomy than a nation?Though figures within Plaid clearly believe that Burnham is genuinely open to giving Wales more powers, they have real concerns that the more devo-sceptic figures within both the UK Labour party and the civil service will hinder their attempts. These fears are not unfounded. A leaked memo from Starmer revealed thathe warned his cabinetagainst being “overly deferential” to devolved governments. In December 2025,11 Labour Senedd members wroteto the then PM accusing him of “rolling back” devolution.View image in fullscreenRhun ap Iorwerth meets Andy Burnham for bilateral talks in Glasgow, 23 July 2026.Photograph: Alastair Grant/Pool AP/APThis fear led to one of the better lines in ap Iorwerth’s speech, where he said that if Burnham fails to give Cymru concessions:“Wales will know again that our best interests will never be served by Westminster, and that it matters little whether who lives in No 10 Downing Street is an Evertonian or an Old Etonian.”With all the talk of “the Burnham bounce”, one thing that I think is being missed in the wider media is the total collapse of Labour’s status in Wales. Before the Senedd election in May, Welsh Labour was themost successful democratic partyin history, having been the largest party in Wales at every general and Senedd electionsince 1922.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhen Labour was struggling in England and Scotland against the Tories, led by both David Cameron and Boris Johnson, Welsh Labour was winning election after election. But now Labour’s dominance in Wales is over. In a 96-seat Welsh parliament,Labour now has just nine seats.AtLabourconference in Liverpool, speaking to people on both the Welsh and UK sides of the party, it was clear to me that they were facing very different trajectories. UK Labour members were full of hope, optimism and excitement for what is to come: the conference was like an engagement party, to celebrate a union with their new partner.Meanwhile, Welsh Labour members had just broken up with their partner of 27 yearsand were totally cut up about the divorce. They were at the engagement party, trying to keep a stiff upper lip while nursing a can of strong lagerand wondering how they were going to afford to furnish their new one-bed flat.But this is a very bad time for Welsh Labour to have an identity crisis. All of the demands made by Plaid to Burnham arelongstanding Welsh Labour policies. For so long, Welsh Labour and devolution were synonymous with each other, but now the mood music is very different. Welsh Labour’s new leader,Ken Skates, has actively criticised Plaidfor pursuing the very policies Labour previously sought around more devolution.There is a chance for the people of Wales to get more direct tools to improve their own prosperity, but to do so they need all their representatives to understand the value of devolution and be united in their fight for it, regardless of the party they represent.Will Hayward is a Guardian columnist. He publishes aregular newsletteron Welsh politicsExplore more on these topicsWelsh politicsOpinionDevolutionWalesRhun ap IorwerthPlaid CymruLabourAndy BurnhamcommentShareReuse this content

title: Does the word ‘Dumbass’ flash up when your husband calls your phone? | Polly Hudson | The Guardian
description: From ‘Sharon London Sex’ to ‘Trashy Anne’, the names saved in our phones are tiny records of how relationships began, writes Polly Hudson. Why erase the evidence?
Author: Polly Hudson
Headline: From ‘Sharon London Sex’ to ‘Trashy Anne’, the names saved in our phones are tiny records of how relationships began, writes Polly Hudson. Why erase the evidence?
Content: ‘The comfort we get from a reminder of these origin stories may be more important than it seems.’Photograph: Westend61/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘The comfort we get from a reminder of these origin stories may be more important than it seems.’Photograph: Westend61/Getty ImagesOpinionRelationshipsDoes the word ‘Dumbass’ flash up when your husband calls your phone?Polly HudsonFrom ‘Sharon London Sex’ to ‘Trashy Anne’, the names saved in our phones are tiny records of how relationships began. Why erase the evidence?Sun 4 Oct 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 11.10 EDTShareAt first glance, it’s such a simple, reasonable ask. A Threads user went vaguely viral last week, witha post announcing: “In other news, my wife of 11 years is respectfully requesting that I take ‘(hinge)’ out of her contact name on my phone.” A lively discussion then followed, which included the pertinent note that Rob in the Channel 4 comedyCatastrophe“has the mother of his children in his phone as ‘Sharon London Sex’”. Somebody else reported a husband of more than a decade saved as “Feyonce”, but this makes perfect sense, because if you thought of a pun that good, of course you’d be reluctant to let it go.Personally, I’ve never got over noticing – on their reality show rather than while lunching – that Kim Kardashian has her mother saved as Kris Jenner instead of, say, Mom. It felt like an extremely revealing detail from the queen of the genre.Is your kid off to a sleepover? Don’t forget the secret codeword | Polly HudsonRead moreThe Threads debate raised an interesting question, though: should your contact list be amended and updated, or preserved as a historical artefact? Perhaps the poster is underestimating the warm glow to the heart and soul he subconsciously receives whenever his wife’s name pops up and he’s transported back to the beginning of their unlikely love story. Living app-ily ever after is rare, after all.Other replies echoed the notion that contacts provoke memories. “I’m coming up on the 10th anniversary of ‘Trashy Anne’ … who I got to know volunteering as bin collectors at a local festival,” said one. Another confided: “My best friend and I met through a mutual friend almost 15 years ago. I’m still ‘Ayannah (Gabby’s friend)’.” The comfort we get from a reminder of these origin stories may be more important than it seems.There are exceptions, though, particularly when you edit in haste. As this repenter-at-leisure explained: “When I was still dating my husband, I got mad and I changed his contact to ‘dumbass’. It was like that for about seven years, lol.”Polly Hudson is a freelance writerDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: It’s never been so easy to find answers. But sitting with uncertainty can ultimately bring wisdom | Muhammad Abdulsater | The Guardian
description: Even the greatest prophets had questions but they learned to wait to see the full picture
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Even the greatest prophets had questions but they learned to wait to see the full picture
Content: ‘We interpret delays as failures and endings as defeats. We rarely consider that we may simply lack the vantage point from which the full picture can be seen.’Composite: Getty images/Guardian DesignView image in fullscreen‘We interpret delays as failures and endings as defeats. We rarely consider that we may simply lack the vantage point from which the full picture can be seen.’Composite: Getty images/Guardian DesignMaking sense of itReligionIt’s never been so easy to find answers. But sitting with uncertainty can ultimately bring wisdomMuhammad AbdulsaterEven the greatest prophets had questions but they learned to wait to see the full pictureSun 4 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 16.50 EDTShareWe live in an age that has become profoundly uncomfortable with not knowing.A delayed email reply becomes a source of anxiety. A medical symptom is immediately searched online. We refresh news feeds, ask AI for instant explanations, and expect the answers to life’s biggest questions to arrive at the same speed as food deliveries.Modernity has conditioned us to believe that uncertainty is a dilemma to be solved.Perhaps that is why one of the Qur’an’s most remarkable stories, involving Prophet Moses and al-Khidr, feels so unexpectedly relevant today.In the story, Prophet Moses embarks on a journey to learn from a mysterious servant of God known as al-Khidr, otherwise known as the “Green One” or “Green Man” . Before the journey even begins, al-Khidr warns him: “You will never be able to remain patient with me.” It is a curious statement. Moses is one of the greatest prophets, a man of extraordinary faith and wisdom. If anyone should possess patience, surely it is him.My dad’s determination to choose life despite his cruel illness has taught me gratitude | Nomi KaltmannRead moreBut the lesson is not about Moses’s character. It is about the limits of human understanding. As they travel together, Moses witnesses some deeply troubling events. Among them, al-Khidr deliberately damages a boat belonging to poor fishers. He repairs a crumbling wall for a town whose people had refused them hospitality, without asking for any payment.Each time, Moses objects. Each time, he judges what he sees according to justice, compassion and reason. Each time, he is gently reminded that he does not yet possess understanding of the whole story.Only at the end of this story are the hidden reasons revealed. The damaged boat was saved from confiscation by a tyrannical king. The wall protected an inheritance belonging to orphaned children.The story is not asking us to suspend thinking or rational inquiry. Rather, the narrative exposes something far more subtle: our tendency to mistake partial knowledge for complete understanding.That tendency feels particularly familiar today.Our lives are increasingly shaped by technologies that promise certainty. Artificial intelligence summarises complex subjects instantly. We have become accustomed to immediate explanations, immediate diagnoses and immediate conclusions.The great paradox of our age is that although information has become ubiquitous, our tolerance for uncertainty has never been lower. We increasingly expect life itself to function like a search engine with immediate output in response to our input.The Quranic story of Prophet Moses and al-Khidr gently suggests that reality does not work that way.One of the most overlooked aspects of this story is that understanding arrives only after patience. The explanations are deliberately delayed. Had al-Khidr explained each event before it occurred, there would have been no lesson at all. The transformation lies precisely in learning to remain faithful before understanding appears.This challenges one of modernity’s deepest assumptions, that peace comes from having all the answers.The Islamic spiritual tradition proposes something different. Peace is not born from eliminating uncertainty but from learning how to inhabit it without despair.This is not an invitation to passive resignation or to explain away suffering. What the story offers is humility about the limits of our own knowledge and perspective.Most of us are living somewhere in the middle of our own stories. We judge our lives from chapter three without knowing chapter 20. We interpret delays as failures and endings as defeats. We rarely consider that we may simply lack the vantage point from which the full picture can be seen.That is why the story continues to resonate across centuries. It reminds us that there is a profound difference between something that is meaningless and something whose meaning has not yet become apparent.In a culture that rewards instant opinions and relentless certainty, perhaps one of the most radical spiritual practices is learning to say: “I do not yet understand.”Not because reason has failed. But because wisdom sometimes arrives more slowly than information.And perhaps faith begins, not when every question has been answered, but when we discover the courage to keep walking before the explanation arrives.Dr Muhammad Abdulsater holds a PhD from the school of law and business at the University of Notre Dame Australia where he is a sessional academic. He is also a student of Islamic sciences at the eHawza international school of Islamic theologyExplore more on these topicsReligionMaking sense of itPhilosophycommentShareReuse this content

title: Trump wants control of South America. If Bolsonaro Jr wins in Brazil, that could become a reality | Steve Bloomfield | The Guardian
description: The US president has taken credit for far-right victories across Latin America, but those wins have had more to do with fears of gang crime than his meddling, says journalist Steve Bloomfield
Author: Steve Bloomfield
Headline: The US president has taken credit for far-right victories across Latin America, but those wins have had more to do with fears of gang crime than his meddling, says journalist Steve Bloomfield
Content: Flavio Bolsonaro at a rally in Campo Grande, Rio de Janeiro state, Brazil, 3 October 2026.Photograph: Bruna Prado/APView image in fullscreenFlavio Bolsonaro at a rally in Campo Grande, Rio de Janeiro state, Brazil, 3 October 2026.Photograph: Bruna Prado/APOpinionBrazilTrump wants control of South America. If Bolsonaro Jr wins in Brazil, that could become a realitySteve BloomfieldThe US president has taken credit for far-right victories across Latin America, but those wins have had more to do with fears of gang crime than his meddlingSun 4 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 16.29 EDTShareDonald Trump has enjoyed very few foreign policy victories since returning to power. From failed wars to failed peace processes, his second term in office has been marked by one costly blunder on the world stage after another. In Latin America, though, the US president has a different story to tell.His administration’s national security strategy outlined how the US wanted to “restore American preeminence in the Western Hemisphere”. It was a brazen document, laying out how his government would interfere in the political life of countries it considered part of its sphere of influence, rewarding governments and movements that are “broadly aligned with our principles and strategy”.To this end, Trump bailed out Argentina to the tune of $40bn and threatened to withdraw the funding if President Javier Milei’s party lost the midterm elections. In Colombia, he repeatedly bullied and threatened the leftwing president, Gustavo Petro, hitting him with personal sanctions and accusing him of being an “illegal drug leader”. And most dramatically, he invaded Venezuela and kidnapped its president. The day after Nicolás Maduro was brought to the US, the state department posted a picture of Trump above the slogan “This is OUR hemisphere”.Over the past 18 months, seven rightwing or far-right candidates have won presidential elections across Latin America. In most of them, Trump openly backed the winning candidate. “We’re doing very well in South America,” Trump said last month. “Lots of people that I got elected.”This weekend, he will be hoping to add the greatest prize of all: Brazil, South America’s biggest country and its largest economy. Flávio Bolsonaro, son of the former far-right president Jair Bolsonaro, is neck and neck with the leftwing incumbent,Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. If he wins, Trump wins – and the hemisphere really will be his.View image in fullscreenFlávio Bolsonaro, centre, on the campaign trail in São Paulo last week.Photograph: Allison Sales/APThe White House has not simply been watching the election from afar. Since Trump returned to power in January 2025, administration officials and Maga-world allies have been doing what they can to damage Lula and boost the Bolsonaros. Initially, the aim of the support was to keepJair Bolsonaroout of jail. Like Trump, he had not accepted defeat at the ballot box when he lost in the 2022 general election. Like Trump, his supporters stormed government buildings. But there were two crucial differences in Brazil – the seriousness of Bolsonaro’s attempt to hold on to power, and the determination of Brazilians that he should be held to account.Investigators uncovered asprawling conspiracyled by Bolsonaro and seven of his closest allies to keep him in power. It included an astonishing plot to kill Lula and his running mate, as well as a supreme court judge. A draft decree had been written that would overturn the result. The military would step in and ensure Bolosnaro returned to power. But the plot failed and Bolsonaro and allies, including his defence minister and the navy chief, were arrested and put on trial.In response,Trump threatenedin July 2025 to impose a 50% tariff on all imports from Brazil, arguing the case against Bolsonaro was a “witch hunt”. This blatant attempt at interfering in the judicial procedure of another country backfired. Lula made clear he wouldn’t bow to US pressure, the trial went ahead and Bolsonaro was found guilty and sentenced to 27 years in prison. Lula also received a bump in the polls after standing up to Trump.In July, as the election campaign was kicking into gear, Trump tried his tariff trick again, imposing a new 25% rate on some Brazilian goods. The state department then tried to dispatch two officials toBrazilto investigate “electoral integrity” – Brazil denied them visas, accusing the officials of coming to “meddle in Brazil’s elections”.In the final weeks of the campaign, Lula has leaned into those accusations. A recent advert accused Flávio Bolsonaro of being “Trump’s candidate” and said the US president wants “to colonise Brazil, take our riches, steal our future and leave us in the dust”. What remains unclear is whether the White House’s strategy in Brazil is working. “Some in Brazil joke that Lula’s most effective surrogate is Trump,” Brian Winter, editor in chief of Americas Quarterly, told me.Indeed, while Latin American countries have undoubtedly moved to the right in the past 18 months, US interference, despite Trump’s boasts, has arguably had little direct impact. In Peru and Chile, the Trump-aligned candidates were careful not to seek his endorsement for fear it would cause more trouble than it was worth. In Bolivia, the leftwing Mas government wasresponsible for its own downfall, winning just 3.16% in last year’s election after 20 years of increasingly chaotic rule.3:43How Trump is meddling in Brazil’s election – explainerThe biggest reason countries have moved to the right has nothing to do with the US and everything to do with safety and security at home. Organised crime gangs, many of them linked to drug trafficking, are increasing in power. AsCrisis Group put it in a report last year, while drug-related organised crime has been a problem across the continent for decades, “never has it spread so wide, and rarely has it penetrated so deeply into states and communities”. The failure of leftwing governments to deal with the problem has hurt them more than Trump’s attempts at interference.If there is a foreign president whose policies are having an influence on Latin America, it’s El Salvador’s Nayib Bukele. His authoritarian clampdown, which has involved arresting tens of thousands of people, mostly without legal process, has become a model for other rightwing leaders in countries beset by gang and drug cartel-related violence.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionDemocracy has been eroded andhuman rights trampled upon, but Bukele claims that his strategy – best described as “security populism” – has turned one of the most violent countries in the world into one of the safest. Other rightwing populists have found success in vowing to emulate him.In Brazil, Flávio Bolsonaro has made a crackdown on drug cartels and organised crime gangs the centrepiece of his campaign. “We’re going to give the streets back to the Brazilian people,” he said at a recent campaign stop, vowing to chemically castrate rapists and reduce the age of criminal responsibility.The Guardian view on Lula v the Bolsonaros: the decision of Brazilian voters will affect us all | EditorialRead moreOn this issue, Trump may have an influence. The US decision in May to designate two criminal organisations – the Red Command and First Capital Command (PCC) – asterrorist organisationshas put Lula on the back foot. Bolsonaro has campaigned relentlessly on the issue, accusing Lula of weakness. Lula has talked about targeting the crime boss “who lives in a penthouse”, but has been more comfortable campaigning on improvements he wants to make in education and health. Bolsonaro Jr, should he win, will almost certainly sign Brazil up to Trump’s Shield of the Americas, a coalition of 18 rightwing Latin American and Caribbean heads of state that promises to use “lethal military force to destroy the sinister cartels and terrorist networks”.Trump arguably paved the way for this new generation of Latin American political leader. His first victory in 2016 showed that posing as an outsider, using coarse language and embracing authoritarianism could be popular. Jair Bolsonaro was the first to emulate him, embracing the “Trump of the Tropics” tag. If Flávio Bolsonaro wins this month – either on Sunday or in the probable second round on 25 October – Trump’s ideology will dominate the continent.It is likely to outlast the man himself. The rise of organised crime has spread fear across the continent and, at the moment, the security populists are the only ones who voters believe have the answer. As long as that remains, the right’s grip on Latin America will only get stronger, regardless of who is in the White House.Steve Bloomfield is the former international editor of the ObserverExplore more on these topicsBrazilOpinionDonald TrumpUS foreign policyAmericasLuiz Inácio Lula da SilvaJair BolsonaroDrugs tradecommentShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on trapped leaseholders: Labour must keep its promise to set them free | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: The government pledged to end an unfair system. Ministers must give homeowners power over costs, rather than another place to complain
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: The government pledged to end an unfair system. Ministers must give homeowners power over costs, rather than another place to complain
Content: ‘It is remarkable that while legislation banning new leasehold properties is expected before the next election, it is unlikely to come into force until after it’: Angela Rayner at Labour conference.Photograph: Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreen‘It is remarkable that while legislation banning new leasehold properties is expected before the next election, it is unlikely to come into force until after it’: Angela Rayner at Labour conference.Photograph: Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockOpinionLeaseholdThe Guardian view on trapped leaseholders: Labour must keep its promise to set them freeEditorialThe government pledged to end an unfair system. Ministers must give homeowners power over costs, rather than another place to complainSun 4 Oct 2026 12.30 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 14.19 EDTShare“To the millions of leaseholders across the country, you have my word. The days of you being squeezed for every penny are coming to an end,”Andy Burnham told the Labour party conference. Only a few hours earlier, his housing secretary, Angela Rayner, had announced that the government wouldlegislate for a new independent regulatorand launch a consultation to cap “rip off” administrative fees. While these are undoubtedly steps in the right direction, they are miles away from Labour’smanifesto promiseto “finally bring the feudal leasehold system to an end”.In itsmodern form, leasehold in England and Wales turns homes into income streams for freeholders. It should be abolished. There are powerful vested interests –billionaires,aristocratsandbig businesses– that would oppose this move. But the system of service charges is crippling the housing market because its exorbitant cost puts off prospective buyers. The average annual service charge for a flat in England and Wales is now£2,405, up 32.6% since 2020 and 55.6% over a decade. Owners of flats in high-rise blocks in London are paying service charges of more than£7,000a year. Little wonder that first-time buyers areincreasingly bypassing flats.The current system sees homeowners enter into long-term leases in which they must pay sums annually to freeholders. These can rise quickly to very high levels. The government proposes a£250 annual capon ground rents for existing residential leases andlimits on fees for requestssuch as keeping a pet. Ministers are consulting over whether residents could pay less tobuy out freeholds. But there is no sign of action on annual service charges for maintenance costs determined by distant firms. Last year, 37% of flats across England and Wales had a service charge that exceeded 1% of their value – making them hard to mortgage and sell. Surely homeowners should not have to buy their freedom at an outrageous price while being charged for years by a management system they cannot realistically change?View image in fullscreenZack Polanski.Photograph: Andy Rain/EPAThe issue of leasehold has become a campaign flashpoint in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection.Six out of seven homessold in the constituency last year were sold as leasehold. The Green leader, Zack Polanski, who is standing to be the MP, has made the issue aconcrete test of Labour’s credibility. The Greens have paired leasehold abolition with rent controls and affordable housing as part of their claim to end “rip-off Britain”, accusing Labour of favouring developers. Labour denies this, but ministers know that housing is a political powder keg that has already exploded inBerlinand acrossSpain.It isremarkablethat while legislation banning new leasehold properties is expected before the next election, it is unlikely to come into force until after it. Ministers are said to be afraid of being taken to court by freeholders. But government has alreadywon against them in the courtswhen defending Michael Gove’s housing bill. The question for the government is whether the proposed reforms give the owners of theexisting 5m leaseholdhomes a credible route out of their dependency – or just regulate their continued subservience. Ministers must show how a leaseholder trapped today will in the future take back control – by obtaining the right to manage property, being able to buy the freehold or converting to commonhold. If ministers offer just another complaints mechanism, they will have broken their promise to end an injustice.Explore more on these topicsLeaseholdOpinionLabourHousingLabour conference 2026PropertyWaleseditorialsShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on nurseries: some things are going right for under-fives | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: England’s strong results in an early learning study are a Sure Start legacy that ministers must build on
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: England’s strong results in an early learning study are a Sure Start legacy that ministers must build on
Content: ‘It is heartening that England’s five-year‑olds were found to be thriving.’Photograph: Stuart Boulton/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘It is heartening that England’s five-year‑olds were found to be thriving.’Photograph: Stuart Boulton/AlamyOpinionEarly years educationThe Guardian view on nurseries: some things are going right for under-fivesEditorialEngland’s strong results in an early learning study are a Sure Start legacy that ministers must build onSun 4 Oct 2026 12.25 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 14.14 EDTShareRecognition of the importance of babyhood and early childhood continues to grow. It is widely understood by many ordinary people, as well as experts, that what happens to us when we are very small, and ourbrains are at their most malleable, has lasting effects. As the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) put it in astudy of early years education, “the first five years of a child’s life represent a window of opportunity, but also of vulnerability”.New Labour’s grasp of this underpinned its pioneering Sure Start programme. Much of this was dismantled under the Tory-Liberal Democrat austerity programme. But despite that loss,England’s resultsin this year’s OECD Early Learning and Child Well‑being Study were strong. This study does not have the high profile of the programme for international student assessment (Pisa) comparing the academic performance of 15-year-olds. It is newer and relies on a far smaller sample size. But while its findings should not be treated as gospel, it is heartening that England’s five-year‑olds were found to be thriving. On a social-emotional development measure, they came out on top.Concerns aboutschool readiness, with a rising number of children in England arriving in reception classes without basic skills such as climbing stairs, must continue to be taken seriously. So must the attainment gap between economically disadvantaged children and those from wealthier backgrounds. The recent announcement by the health secretary, Yvette Cooper, that theHealthy Babies programme will be extendedto more family hubs should be warmly welcomed as one means of tackling these problems.But as well as addressing the inequalities that restrict children’s chances, ministers should focus on the early years sector’s strengths – which are a legacy of Sure Start and all the investment that went in. While less often discussed than the national curriculum, England’s early years framework is admired internationally.Early years funding hasexpanded massively, with eligible working parents entitled to 30 hours’ childcare weekly for children from nine months until school age. The Tories now propose removing the £100,000 earnings ceiling: a£700m policythat rewards richer families. The model sees public money follows working parental demand rather than building universal provision. Families without working parents remain less well supported, while private providers gravitate towards wealthier areas, where extra hours and charges are more affordable.The Competition and Markets Authority found that private providers were makingexcess profitsin the children’s social care market. Astudy into their role as childcare providersrequested by the former education secretary Bridget Phillipson should establish whether something similar is going on in nurseries, and assist ministers in finding ways to target low-income areas. Alan Milburn’s review of young people and work is expected to highlight therole of early yearsin getting toddlers on track for school.The OECD was right to acknowledge the vulnerability, as well as the potential, of the youngest children. The horrific abuse of toddlers byVincent Chanat a nursery in London was a grim reminder of what can go wrong. Safeguarding must continue to be strengthened; the switch to more frequent inspections by Ofsted was a good move. But as well as facing up to failures, ministers should embrace past successes – and work out how they can be built on.Explore more on these topicsEarly years educationOpinionEducation policyChildrenEnglandOECDChildcareLaboureditorialsShareReuse this content

title: Good palliative care and assisted dying can go hand in hand | Death and dying | The Guardian
description: Letters: Readers respond to an article on the urgent need for palliative care reform
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Readers respond to an article on the urgent need for palliative care reform
Content: ‘Some pain cannot be controlled quickly, and some suffering cannot be treated at all.’Photograph: Getty/iStockphotoView image in fullscreen‘Some pain cannot be controlled quickly, and some suffering cannot be treated at all.’Photograph: Getty/iStockphotoDeath and dyingLettersGood palliative care and assisted dying can go hand in handReaders respond to an article on the urgent need for palliative care reformSun 4 Oct 2026 13.06 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 14.33 EDTShareJane Turner is right that end-of‑life care needs fixing (MPs, you told us clearly that end-of-life care in the UK is broken. So now we need you to fix it, 28 September), and I argue that it needs fixing on two fronts at once. My husband, John, died in March aged 43 after nearly six years of bowel cancer treatment. He endured more than 70 rounds of chemotherapy, determined to watch our children grow up. He spent his last three months in a hospice, receiving the best palliative care on offer. Even so, he suffered terribly.Some pain cannot be controlled quickly, and some suffering cannot be treated at all. One evening he screamed in agony while stranded in a bath, unable to move, for nearly an hour before relief took effect. As the cancer swelled his torso, he slowly suffocated – and no drug could prevent it. He was fully aware throughout, and told me repeatedly that he could not go on. In his last hours, I wore earplugs to bear the sound of his gasping.Most hospices are charities that receive very little state funding – that must change. Better palliative care will spare many people needless suffering. But it cannot spare everyone, and no amount of funding would have given John what he wanted: the chance to face the inevitable on his own terms.Improving palliative care and legalising assisted dying are not rivals. Doing both would also free hospice beds for those who want them; John occupied one for three months.John was always going to die from his cancer, but the trauma of his final months, for him and for our children, was preventable. MPs should not choose between fixing care and offering choice. They must do both.Liz WilsonCoventryJane Turner is absolutely right that we need to invest in palliative and end-of life care. She is also correct that the greatest unmet needs are seen in NHS hospitals, and that it is here where investment is most urgent. That all sounds very expensive, but if we look at the headline financial figures, we see that actually it might cost very little in terms of new money. The Nuffield Trust tells us that the UK spends£6.6bn on emergency hospital carein the last year of life. This contrasts with only£1.1bn to run all 204 UK hospices, including the 24 NHS hospices.I was a consultant physician at one of these units for 20 years, and I am told that it now costs around £5m annually to provide a comprehensive specialist palliative care service to a population of 250,000, delivered across all settings, including hospital wards. This implies a total cost of around £1.4bn to provide thisNHSservice across the UK population of 70 million people. The NHS has complete access to the patient activity and financial figures of these 24 units, so these figures can easily be confirmed.One of the strengths of specialist palliative care services is that they always try to help patients and their families to plan for the future: when you get more poorly, where would you want to be cared for? If this planning enabled us to avert only 10% of emergency admissions in the last year of life, the money saved would more than fill the funding gap. If emergency admissions fell by more than 10%, it would, overall, save the nation money.Stephen KirkhamLytchett Minster, DorsetJane Turner is absolutely right that palliative and end-of-life care must be properly funded and available to everyone who needs it. Those of us who campaigned for assisted dying have never argued otherwise. Better palliative care and greater choice at the end of life should not be competing ambitions.But there is an important question that cannot be lost now the parliamentary vote is over: what happens to the people whose suffering even excellent palliative care cannot adequately relieve?I am living with incurable secondary breast cancer. I love my life and want to be here for my daughter for as long as possible. But I also know from painful personal experience that I am allergic to opioid painkillers. After the birth of my daughter, when I needed multiple operations, my pain could not be properly controlled. It was frightening. So when I am told that better palliative care will remove the need for assisted dying, I have a very simple question: what if it cannot?Jane is right that even with the best quality care, some deaths can still be difficult. Those people matter too. Since the fall of the terminally ill adults (end of life) bill, terminally ill people have not suddenly become less frightened about what lies ahead. Our diagnoses have not changed, and neither have the limits of medicine.So yes: fix palliative care. End the postcode lottery. Make sure nobody reaches the end of their life without the support, expertise and compassion they deserve. But we should be able to hold two thoughts at once. Excellent palliative care can transform many deaths. It cannot guarantee that every dying person’s suffering can be relieved.The question for those who opposed assisted dying therefore remains: what is the answer for those people?Sophie BlakeHove, East SussexHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today?
