title: White House defends new press aide who posed with rifle in ‘Fuck Joe Biden’ shirt | Trump administration | The Guardian
description: Beni Rae Harmony, 24, has been ‘a trusted voice for the MAGA movement as a White House correspondent’, White House says
Author: Robert Mackey
Headline: Beni Rae Harmony, 24, has been ‘a trusted voice for the MAGA movement as a White House correspondent’, White House says
Content: Donald Trump takes questions from members of the media, including Beni Rae Harmony, on Air Force One after a two-day visit to Ireland, on 13 September.Photograph: Kylie Cooper/ReutersView image in fullscreenDonald Trump takes questions from members of the media, including Beni Rae Harmony, on Air Force One after a two-day visit to Ireland, on 13 September.Photograph: Kylie Cooper/ReutersTrump administrationWhite House defends new press aide who posed with rifle in ‘Fuck Joe Biden’ shirtBeni Rae Harmony, 24, has been ‘a trusted voice for the MAGA movement as a White House correspondent’, White House saysRobert MackeySun 4 Oct 2026 19.38 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 19.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe White House has defended a newly hired press aide who posed for a holiday photograph in 2021wearing a “Fuck Joe Biden” T-shirtand holding a rifle.Beni Rae Harmony, the new assistant White House press secretary,revealedon Friday that she was going to work for Donald Trump just days after covering him as a correspondent for Real America’s Voice, a partisan rightwing outletoriginally createdas a video podcast platform for the president’s former adviser Steve Bannon.According toa LinkedIn profile, Harmony, 24, previously worked asa producerfor the far-right Turning Point USA host Jack Posobiec – and as a press aide “focusing on crisis management” for two far-right Republicans: congressman Paul Gosar of Arizona and former congressman Matt Gaetz of Florida.In 2021, whenGosar was censuredby the US House for posting an animated video that depicted him killing Democratic congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and attacking Joe Biden, Harmony recordedan outraged defense of her bossfor his YouTube channel.The photograph of Harmony and an older man posing with rifles in matching anti-Biden shirts, in front of Christmas decorations, was reportedly posted on Instagram in November 2021 by a far-right Republican House candidate, Jarome Bell, who mounted a failed campaign for Congress in 2022.A screenshot of that post,published by the Daily Mirror, shows that it included the caption: “My campaign Public Affairs Director @beniraeharmony is a beast. This is how we roll.”Harmony appeared to verify the authenticity of the photograph in December 2021, when it wasshared on social mediaby an anti-Maga outlet, PatriotTakes, which alsoidentified heras an aide to Gosar.The next day, Harmonyrepliedto the PatriotTakes post of the image with another image of herself, wearing the same shirt in the same location and grinning into the camera. When another social media user posted a sarcastic question about the relationship between the older man and the young woman seen in the image, asking: “Daughter or date?”,Harmony repliedwith a one-word answer: “Uncle.”Biden at the time was serving his lone term in the Oval Office, and Trump supporters chanting “Fuck Joe Biden” at a Nascar race that autumn inspireda viral memefeaturing a variation of the slogan.Harmony did not reply to requests to comment on the photograph. But the White House press office responded with a statement from a deputy press secretary, Anna Kelly, who praised the new hire for her advocacy of Trump’s Make America Great Again movement, while ostensibly covering the president as a journalist.“Beni Rae Harmony has been a trusted voice for the MAGA movement as a White House correspondent,” Kelly wrote. “She will be an outstanding addition to President Trump’s communications team as an Assistant Press Secretary – we look forward to having her on board!”Harmony joins a White House press office that has taken unprecedented steps to ensure that the president is surrounded at all times by correspondents from partisan outlets who shower him with praise, and limit or deny access to reporters from nonpartisan outlets who challenge him.Trump hastried to ban CNN, Politico and MS Nowfrom the White House entirely, for what he considers overly negative coverage, and his aides now select which outlets are in place to ask him questions, with frequent slots reserved for correspondents who openly support him.Harmony became the White House correspondent for Real America’s Voice after her predecessor, Brian Glenn, fell out of favor with Trump when his partner, Marjorie Taylor Greene, broke with the president and accused him of betraying the Maga movement.Glenn had previously worked hard to advance Trump’s political agenda when invited by the president to ask questions. In 2025, for instance, Glennpointedly askedUkraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, why he refused to wear a suit in the Oval Office, a question that inflamed an already volatile encounter.Duringa press availability on Air Force Onelast month, Trump approached reporters with a sheaf of papers in his left hand. Harmony asked Trumpa series of friendly questionsthat seemed designed to help him score political points. AsTMZ reportedon Friday,Associated Press photographstaken during that exchange showed that Harmony’s name was at the top of the first page in the president’s hand, suggesting that he might have been holding her résumé as he took her questions.Harmony achieved a measure of celebrity in the rightwing media in 2025, when she left her job as an on-air host at a local TV station in Springfield, Illinois, after deliveringan on-air tributeto the late Charlie Kirk, describing him as her first boss and mentor.The station’s news directordeniedthat Harmony had been suspended over the tribute, as she claimed, and clarified that she had never been a member of its news team, and instead hosted a program run by the channel’s sales department that featured clients who paid to be interviewed on television.Explore more on these topicsTrump administrationUS politicsUS press and publishingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Nigel Farage questioned by standards commissioner over £5m gift | Nigel Farage | The Guardian
description: Reform UK leader was interviewed for half an hour last month over money from crypto billionaire
Author: Rowena Mason
Headline: Reform UK leader was interviewed for half an hour last month over money from crypto billionaire
Content: Nigel Farage insists the £5m gift was for his personal security.Photograph: Scott Heppell/ReutersView image in fullscreenNigel Farage insists the £5m gift was for his personal security.Photograph: Scott Heppell/ReutersNigel FarageNigel Farage questioned by standards commissioner over £5m giftReform UK leader was interviewed for half an hour last month over money from crypto billionaireRowena MasonWhitehall editorSun 4 Oct 2026 11.04 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNigel Farage has been interviewed by the standards commissioner for an investigation into whether he should have declared a £5m gift from the crypto billionaireChristopher Harborne.TheReform UKleader spent about half an hour being questioned over the money, the Sunday Times reported. Farage maintains the gift was for his personal security.The interview conducted last month is a sign the process is nearing a conclusion, although Reform UK is not believed to have been informed that the report is finished.An MP under investigation is usually notified before the conclusion of the process. If the commissioner finds that there has been a serious breach of the rules, the matter is passed to the standards committee of MPs and lay members, which can ask for further evidence.The committee can recommend a sanction or override the report.If it suggests more than a 10-day suspension from the Commons – and parliament agrees – the Reform UK leader could find himself facing a recall petition and second byelection in his Clacton constituency.Farage has been under investigation over the gift since shortly afterthe Guardian revealed in Maythat Harborne had given him £5m just before the last election in 2024.The Reform leader has said itwas a personal matter, not political, and the money did not need to be declared. The rules state that financial support related to an MP’s job needs to be registered if given in the 12 months before they enter parliament.After a slide in the polls over the summer, Reform is about to embark on a major reorganisation at its headquarters to try to revive its fortunes.Insiders said it would involve a big shake-up of staffing, in addition to the suspensions of James Orr, the party’s head of policy, and Dan Jukes, Farage’s close aide. The pair are facing an internal investigation into whether they encouraged illegal foreign donations during an undercover investigation by reporters from Verbatim.1:15Footage from the Channel 4 News and Verbatim undercover investigation into Reform finances – videoThe inquiry is being carried out by lawyers who are expected to reach their conclusions soon. The matter is also the subject of a police inquiry.The party is working out how to spend £72m in donations from Harborne and another crypto billionaire, Ben Delo. The huge sums have prompted calls from political rivals for a donation cap.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWelcome to the new Reform roadshow. Same as the last but more desperate | John CraceRead moreA possible use of the money is the relaunch of a TV channel that produces Reform-related video coverage and a show fronted by Farage.Farage told the Sunday Times he thought the reaction to the donations would be “far worse” but had produced “some grudging respect – the fact that I managed to pull off a coup of that magnitude, I think people were quite impressed”.It is not clear whether the donations fall within the rules because the government is putting forward legislation toban overseas donorsfrom giving more than £100,000 in a calendar year – backdated to March this year.Harborne joined the UK electoral register only this summer and Delo has been largely based in Hong Kong, although on the register for some years.If the donations are ruled impermissible, Reform could have to hand them back, a prospect that is likely to lead to court action.Explore more on these topicsNigel FarageChristopher HarborneReform UKCryptocurrenciesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Woman in Cornell rape allegations case targeted with threats, her lawyer says | US universities | The Guardian
description: Attorney says people have threatened to silence or harm ‘Jane Doe’ if she does not withdraw civil lawsuit
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Attorney says people have threatened to silence or harm ‘Jane Doe’ if she does not withdraw civil lawsuit
Content: Cornell University’s Chi Phi fraternity house in Ithaca, New York.Photograph: Lauren Petracca/ReutersView image in fullscreenCornell University’s Chi Phi fraternity house in Ithaca, New York.Photograph: Lauren Petracca/ReutersUS universitiesWoman in Cornell rape allegations case targeted with threats, her lawyer saysAttorney says people have threatened to silence or harm ‘Jane Doe’ if she does not withdraw civil lawsuitReutersSun 4 Oct 2026 12.15 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 13.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe woman who has alleged that ⁠she was drugged ⁠and raped ​by Cornell University studentshas been the target of threats, her lawyer said on Sunday.Cornell University to take ‘serious look’ at fraternities after rape allegationsRead moreThomas Giuffra, who represents the ⁠woman identified as “Jane Doe”, told CNN that people have threatened to silence or harm her if she does not withdraw her civil lawsuit ⁠alleging that several members of a Cornell fraternity drugged and raped her in 2024.“She’s ​received multiple threats,” Giuffra said on ‌CNN’s State of the Union.Giuffra ‌said he had also been threatened.“I’m not afraid of these people,” he ‌said. “But the threats, the abuse to protect what’s going on, the status quo – these guys are disgusting. They should stay in their mother’s basement and stay out of the world.“The Cornell University president, Michael Kotlikoff,saidin a video message on Saturday that the university will examine the role of fraternities and sororities on ‌campus after the outcry over the school’s handling of the rape allegations.“At their best, these organizations can provide students with friendship, belonging, ​mentorship and a powerful sense of community,” he said. “But being part of a group can never diminish individual responsibility.”Since the lawsuit was filed in September, prosecutors in Tompkins county, New York – where Cornell is – have been criticized for their initial handling of the allegations in 2024. ⁠The New York governor, Kathy Hochul, on Thursdaynamedstate attorney general ​Letitia James as special prosecutor ​to look into the case.Donald Trump, a critic of James for years, lambasted ​the decision to ‌appoint her. “And I ​feel badly for whoever ​she’s looking at because they won’t get a fair shake,” the president told reporters on Friday.Asked about Trump’s comment, Giuffra said the case shouldn’t be politicized. “It has nothing to do with politics,” Giuffra said.Information and support for anyone affected by rape or sexual abuse issues is available from the following organizations. In the US,Rainnoffers support on 800-656-4673. In the UK,Rape Crisisoffers support on 0808 500 2222. In Australia, support is available at1800Respect(1800 737 732). Other international helplines can be found atibiblio.org/rcip/internl.htmlExplore more on these topicsUS universitiesNew YorkUS justice systemUS crimeFraternities and sororitiesLaw (US)newsShareReuse this content

title: Revealed: Government quietly dropped plan to prepare England for wildfires | Wildfires | The Guardian
description: FOI request shows wildfire risk scheme scrapped, as data highlights many fire services lack proper protective gear
Author: Pippa Neill
Headline: FOI request shows wildfire risk scheme scrapped, as data highlights many fire services lack proper protective gear
Content: A wildfire in Suffolk in July as the UK experienced a record-breaking number of fires.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAView image in fullscreenA wildfire in Suffolk in July as the UK experienced a record-breaking number of fires.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAWildfiresRevealed: Government quietly dropped plan to prepare England for wildfiresFOI request shows wildfire risk scheme scrapped, as survey highlights many fire services lack proper protective gearPippa NeillEnvironment reporterSun 4 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 07.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe government quietly scrapped plans to prepare the countryside inEnglandfor wildfires, it has been revealed. This was despite new data showing fire crews do not have the proper protective gear to tackle them.This summer has been a potent reminder of the scale of the threat posed by the climate crisis, with the UK experiencing record-breaking wildfires after punishingly hot and dry weather turned large parts of the countryside into a tinderbox.In the third national climate adaptation programme, published in July 2023, the Conservative government, then headed byRishi Sunak, said it would run a wildfire risk programme in England from 2023 to 2027 so land management would be adapted for the risk.However, it has now emerged the programme was never implemented, with the current government stating the commitment “was made by the previous government but was not brought into effect”.The environmental campaigner and author Guy Shrubsole, who obtained the information via a freedom of information request, said it was “appalling” the government “couldn’t be bothered to pay attention to wildfire risks until jolted into doing so by Britain burning this summer”.After a wildfire spread across an areaincluding several homes in Stourbridge in the West Midlandsin August, the prime minister, Andy Burnham, convened an emergency Cobra meeting and issued atemporary ban on the sale of disposable barbecues, criticised as being too little too late.View image in fullscreenHomes in Stourbridge in the West Midlands were destroyed by wildfires in August.Photograph: Alex Dodd/EPA“Successive governments have been asleep at the wheel in preparing us for the impacts of the climate crisis,” Shrubsole said.Alistair Carmichael, a Scottish Liberal Democrat MP and the chair of the Commons environment food and rural affairs committee, said it was alarming that ministers had not prioritised work to adapt land for wildfire risk. “It begs further serious questions about whether this summer’s wildfires could have looked different with more resources on the ground,” he added.Shrubsole said the government must agree a plan to re-wet the UK’s peat bogs, restore lost ponds in farmers’ fields, and stop grouse moor owners setting fire to moorland.New data obtained by the Country Land and Business Association has also revealed that more than half of the 29 fire services that responded to requests for information had no wildfire personal protective equipment (PPE).They included the Suffolk fire and rescue service, which had to deal with an “apocalyptic” wildfire earlier this summer that burned close to theSizewell B nuclear power stationand destroyed vast areas ofa protected nature reserve.Standard particle-filtering respirators do not protect against dangerous gases such as carbon monoxide, which are heavily present in wildfire smoke.Standard PPE can also be too hot and heavy for wildfire conditions. This can cause crews to overheat, or remove their PPE altogether, exposing them to greater danger from heat, smoke and radiation.View image in fullscreenA firefighter attempts to control a fire on moorland in the Bannau Brycheiniog, formerly known as the Brecon Beacons, in south Wales.Photograph: Jeff Morgan 03/AlamyThe data also revealed that training for wildfires was limited. For example, in Cleveland just five staff (1.2%) were qualified to give tactical advice or command wildfires, and in Cheshire just 8.62% of employees were trained to undertake wildfire operations.In response to these findings, the Fire Brigades Union is calling for correct PPE to be provided to all members combating wildfires, alongside adequate training programmes.The UK wildfire investigators: ‘If someone has used a match, chances are you’ll find it’Read moreSteve Wright, the union’s general secretary, said: “It is vital for our country’s wildfire resilience to have better land management, stronger public awareness campaigns and long-term prevention measures. Only by proper investment and a wildfire strategy can we make the country more resilient.”A government spokesperson said: “We have made wildfire preparedness a government priority and, following incidents this summer, we are convening a summit with fire and rescue service partners to make sure we are as resilient as possible. This includes making sure services have the right equipment and resources, building on the £100m we previously gave to upgrade our national resilience assets.“Land management and landscape adaptation play an important part in this, and we work closely with land managers and experts to support the restoration of peatlands, the creation of firebreaks and other adaptations that help to prevent fires from starting or from spreading as quickly during incidents.”Get in touchContact us about this storyThe best public interest journalism relies on first-hand accounts from people in the know. If you have something to share on this subject, you can contact us confidentially using the following methods:Secure Messaging in the Guardian appThe Guardian app has a tool to send tips about stories. Messages are end to end encrypted and concealed within the routine activity that every Guardian mobile app performs. This prevents an observer from knowing that you are communicating with us at all, let alone what is being said.If you don’t already have the Guardian app, download it (iOS/Android) and go to the menu. Select ‘Secure Messaging’.SecureDropIf you can safely use the tor network without being observed or monitored you can send messages and documents to the Guardian via ourSecureDrop platform.Our guide attheguardian.com/tipslists several ways to contact us securely, and discusses the pros and cons of each.Show moreExplore more on these topicsWildfiresClimate crisisFirefightersEmergency planningEmergency servicesExtreme heatRishi SunaknewsShareReuse this content

title: Oat of this world: cooks descend on Scotland for ultimate porridge making contest | Scotland | The Guardian
description: Technical mishaps and plenty of whisky as competitors from as far afield as US and Australia vie for Golden Spurtle
Author: Eve Livingston
Headline: Technical mishaps and plenty of whisky as competitors from as far afield as US and Australia vie for Golden Spurtle
Content: Competitors were tasked with producing a traditional porridge – made only from untreated oatmeal, water and salt – and a speciality dish where additional ingredients and flourishes were permitted.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenCompetitors were tasked with producing a traditional porridge – made only from untreated oatmeal, water and salt – and a speciality dish where additional ingredients and flourishes were permitted.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianScotlandOat of this world: cooks descend on Scotland for ultimate porridge making contestTechnical mishaps and plenty of whisky as competitors from as far afield as US and Australia vie for Golden SpurtleEve LivingstonSun 4 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 14.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere are many varieties of spurtle. The traditional Scottish cooking implement, designed for stirring porridge without forming lumps, comes in a range of sizes, can be formed from cherry wood, beech, or maple, and might be topped with a decorative finial or smoothed out at its end for a more modern finish. But on Saturday in Carrbridge, in the Scottish Highlands, only one spurtle mattered: the Golden Spurtle, awarded annually to the winner of the WorldPorridgeMaking championship, which have been hosted here since 1994.View image in fullscreenThe day began with a pipe band parade through Carrbridge and a toast to the porridge at the village hall.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianThe sun shone on the picturesque village as almost 40 competitors lined up in the village hall for six heats across the day. Tasked with producing a traditional porridge – made only from untreated oatmeal, water and salt – and a speciality dish where additional ingredients and flourishes were permitted, entrants had travelled from acrossScotlandand as far afield as Australia and the US for a shot at the Golden Spurtle.View image in fullscreenJosh Kettleson from the US, who reached the finals.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianAs the first heat kicked off, technical difficulties beset some contestants when the provided induction hobs, new this year after a long tradition of gas, failed to heat. But the reigning champion, Norway’s Sven Seljom, was unaffected, serenely stirring Norwegian mutton into oats and filtered water he had brought with him especially for the competition. He had planned to bring Norwegian cheese, too, he said, but import rules meant he had to make do with something more local. A sizeable entourage watched on in traditional Scandinavian dress as he measured, stirred and tasted, boisterous chants of “SVEN, SVEN, SVEN” breaking out at each mention of his name.View image in fullscreenSupporters of the Norwegian defending champion, Sven Seljom.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianThe first of the day’s many whisky breaks came 10 minutes into proceedings at 10.40am, with shots of a lowland malt distributed throughout the exuberant crowd as competitors did well to retain their focus. The drams’ effects meant nobody seemed to mind too much when the crucial timer was accidentally reset just moments from the heat’s tense final countdown.View image in fullscreenThe judges blind-tasted each batch, assessing primarily for taste, texture and colour.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianAny initial teething problems were quickly ironed out as the day settled into a well-oiled rhythm. In a separate “judging chamber”, a trio of judges from Scotland’s culinary scene blind-tasted each batch, assessing primarily for taste, texture and colour. Among the speciality porridges on offer throughout the day were a “Granola Espanola”, a porridge cannoli from the Australian national champion,Robert Reid, and a recipe featuring soft-boiled quail eggs.View image in fullscreenThere were some initial issues with the induction hobs, but contests soon got going.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The Guardian“The first thing I did was burn my oats,” lamented Switzerland’s Jeremy McTeague after a heat that didn’t quite go to plan. But he remained upbeat: “It gave them a distinctive toastiness – maybe the judges will like it.”View image in fullscreenDoug Mackay’s speciality porridge featured langoustines.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianHundreds of spectators showed up for the day’s spectacle, from Carrbridge residents who turn out each year to support the community-powered event, to tourists such as Joe, 43, and Tina, 39, who were visiting from England and had overheard a conversation about the championship in a local pub the previous night.“We looked it up and decided straight away we’d be here,” said Joe. “It’s Scotland, it’s porridge, someone said there would be whisky … it was a no-brainer.” The pair said they were making a beeline for the tasting room to sample the produce left over from judging.View image in fullscreenThe Australian national champion, Rob Reid, gets going.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianThe event proved so popular that the village hall had to operate a one-in, one-out policy. Those who couldn’t fit inside were decanted into a merch tent bursting with oats, spurtles and “always stir clockwise” tote bags, while local cafes and tourist centres screened a live stream of the competition. There was plenty of action to be found around the village, from competitors spotted calming their nerves with pints in the local hotel, to an American visitor who accidentally caused controversy by dressing as a box of Scott’s Porage Oats – rolled oats of the kind not allowed in competition, and a rival to the event’s sponsors, Hamlyns.View image in fullscreenThere were whispers of a ‘porridge war’ after an American visitor arrived dressed as a carton of oats from the rival brand to the sponsors.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianBy the afternoon, the hall was full of cooking aromas and the crowd full of whisky and porridge as they took their seats once more to see who would walk away victorious. There was a minor upset when the reigning champion, Seljom, missed out on the final, but a surprise win for McTeague saw him through to the cook-off despite his earlier woes.Once the top six had taken to the hob one last time, though, it was the Netherlands national champion, Gina Saarberg, who emerged victorious in the traditional competition, with the speciality prize going to Reid for his cannoli.View image in fullscreenGina Saarberg, the Netherlands national champion, receives her prize.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The Guardian“I’m at a loss for words,” Saarberg said as she clutched her Golden Spurtle. “To be here was already such a win in the first place. This is a beautiful community, so of course I’m very happy I won, but it’s also just a pleasure to be here.”Explore more on these topicsScotlandPorridgeFoodHeritagefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: UK justice secretary unable to say how many early release prisoners have been tagged | Prisons and probation | The Guardian
description: Alex Norris says ‘too soon’ to say how many released this week from jails in England and Wales have monitoring devices
Author: Rajeev Syal
Headline: Alex Norris says ‘too soon’ to say how many released this week from jails in England and Wales have monitoring devices
Content: Alex Norris: ‘We don’t have that number. But you know, we’re very candid about who’s leaving prison and when they do.’Photograph: Jeff Overs/BBC/PAView image in fullscreenAlex Norris: ‘We don’t have that number. But you know, we’re very candid about who’s leaving prison and when they do.’Photograph: Jeff Overs/BBC/PAPrisons and probationUK justice secretary unable to say how many early release prisoners have been taggedAlex Norris says ‘too soon’ to say how many released this week from jails in England and Wales have monitoring devicesUK politics live – latest updatesRajeev SyalSun 4 Oct 2026 12.53 EDTFirst published on Sun 4 Oct 2026 10.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAlex Norris has been unable to say how many prisoners freed early from jail this week have been tagged, despite previous reassurances from the justice department.In an interview on Sunday, the justice secretary said it was “too soon” to say how many of the roughly 700 male prisoners let out on Thursday had been fitted with monitoring devices.The government has introduced a “presumption of electronic tagging” for offenders released early from prisons inEnglandand Wales to help manage severe overcrowding.Prisoners thank Andy Burnham as they leave jail in first wave of early releasesRead moreThe first wave of releases began on Thursday, with nearly 5,000 prisoners due to be freed in stages over the next year as the Sentencing Act 2026 comes into force.Asked how many of those released so far had been tagged, Norris told the BBC’s Sunday With Laura Kuenssberg programme: “I don’t have that figure today, it only happened on Thursday. You know, there can be a bit of a lag.“We don’t have that number. But you know, we’re very candid about who’s leaving prison and when they do.”Asked if he knew if released domestic abusers have been tagged or not, he said: “It would be too soon to know that, as it was only on Thursday. We’ve been talking to every victim to offer them the chance to say what controls they’d like to see over that individual.“I’m well aware of the past in tagging. Over the last year, performance has increased significantly.”Several prisoners released last week told the Guardian that they had not been tagged.Michael Bogle, a former bus driver who left HMP Wandsworth on Thursday having served 78 days in prison after breaching a 32-week suspended sentence for shoplifting, said he had no idea when he was going to be tagged. “I have an appointment with probation officers on Thursday, but as far I know it could take months before I actually get given a tag,” he said.Bogle, who is taking anti-psychotic drugs and has more than 100 convictions including for common assault and drug possession, was told in prison that he would be housed in a bail hostel and had been promised a place in south-east London. However, he said he had instead been housed in a bed and breakfast facility in north-west London.“I am running out of money, and if I have to shoplift a sandwich to stop being hungry, I will just have to do it,” he said. “I won’t have a choice. But I really do not want to go back to prison – it is a pigeon-infested, rat-infested place and people are dying in the conditions there.”Prisoners thanked the prime minister as they celebrated walking free from jail on Thursday. One told the press as he left HMP Durham: “Justice system, what justice system? Thank you,Andy Burnham.”A prisoner released from HMP Cardiff after being jailed for burglary said he would “probably be back in the next month or two”.Ministers intervened to exclude rapists and the most serious child sexual offenders from early release, after criticism of the policy over the summer.The rules will also not apply to those guilty of manslaughter, such as the killers of PC Andrew Harper, who died in the line of duty in 2019.Almost half of electronic tags used to track offenders’ movements are not fitted on time, with significant delays putting victims in England andWalesat risk, a report found last month.HM Inspectorate of Probation said some criminals waited up to five months to be fitted with a tag, leading to repeated breaches of court and prison orders.Explore more on these topicsPrisons and probationAlex NorrisUK criminal justiceEnglandWalesLabourAndy BurnhamShareReuse this content

title: Court quashes block on mothers and children in Gaza joining families in UK | Immigration and asylum | The Guardian
description: Immigration court judge finds ‘unsafe journeys’ policy was applied unlawfully to two families
Author: Diane Taylor
Headline: Immigration court judge finds ‘unsafe journeys’ policy was applied unlawfully to two families
Content: The government has taken a strict approach to people in Gaza who hope to reunite with family members in the UK.Photograph: Ramadan Abed/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe government has taken a strict approach to people in Gaza who hope to reunite with family members in the UK.Photograph: Ramadan Abed/ReutersImmigration and asylumCourt quashes block on mothers and children in Gaza joining families in UKImmigration court judge finds ‘unsafe journeys’ policy was applied unlawfully to two familiesDiane TaylorSun 4 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 15.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA decision by theHome Officeto block mothers and children in Gaza from joining their families in the UK has been quashed by a court.Families abroad who have had their applications approved to reunite with loved ones in the UK usually have to undergo biometric checks, including fingerprinting and facial images at a visa application centre. But the VAC inGazahas been closed since October 2023 and it is difficult to get out of the territory.The government has anunsafe journeys policythat offers some flexibility in this kind of situation, but has taken a more strict approach to families – often mothers with very young children – in Gaza who are hoping to reunite with husbands and fathers granted refugee status in the UK.A judge in the immigration court known as the upper tribunal has found the home secretary acted unlawfully in the way the policy was applied to two families and has quashed the decision to block them.Both are young mothers with five children between them aged seven and under, hoping to reunite with their husbands who have been granted refugee status in the UK. Both families are living in dire straits in tents in Gaza with insufficient food, no access to clean water, rodents, mosquitoes, bedbugs and the risk of snipers.The Home Office says it is looking to appeal against the decision.An estimated 250-300 people in Gaza who want to reunite with immediate family members who have been granted refugee status in the UK aresimilarly stranded. The Home Office says biometrics should be obtained before families travel. The Foreign Office has said it is willing to evacuate some of these families from Gaza so they can obtain biometrics in Jordan.In her judgment, the judge, Fiona Lindsley, said the families were living in vulnerable structures in a war zone, malnourished, unwell and struggling psychologically with anxiety from their husbands and fathers in the UK that they would not survive much longer if they remained in Gaza.“The best interests of these children should be the primary consideration, and it cannot be in their best interests to be afraid, undernourished and suffering from diseases of poverty and insanitary conditions without their fathers and no end in sight to that separation,” she said.Decla Palmer, a solicitor at Greater Manchester Immigration Aid Unit who represents the families, said: “The Home Office is doing everything possible to delay and to defend its unlawful decisions, taking a policy position that blocks people in Gaza who are eligible to come to the UK from being able to do so.“These families are completely broken – it is difficult to put into words the trauma they have faced and continue to endure. The mothers and children, trapped in Gaza, are suffering each and every day.The fathers, in the UK, are facing the prospect that they may never hold their children again. The Home Office is actively keeping these families apart, leaving them stranded in Gaza in grave danger.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOn Monday,the Home Office announced refugee resettlement routesincluding for Palestinian refugees and women from Afghanistan. However, this scheme processes only a few hundred applications each year. It is not known when the much larger refugee family reunion scheme will restart, after it was suspended in September 2025. The Refugee Council estimates that since then approximately 20,000 people have been denied family reunion. Initially, the government indicated that new refugee family reunion rules would be introduced in the spring of 2025, but the scheme remains suspended. Home Office sources have indicated that no further details will be announced about this safe and legal lifeline for refugees to reach the UK until 2027.A Home Office spokesperson said: “We will be looking to appeal this decision. Biometrics, including fingerprints and facial images, are a core part of the UK’s immigration system, and their enrolment at a UK overseas visa application centre is a standard requirement when making a visa application to come to the UK.“The enrolment of biometrics enables comprehensive checks against UK and international immigration and criminal records to identify individuals who may pose a threat to national security, public safety or immigration controls, or who are likely to breach UK laws if admitted.”Explore more on these topicsImmigration and asylumHome OfficeShabana MahmoodGazaPalestineIsrael-Gaza warnewsShareReuse this content

title: Bosnian Serb nationalist Dodik declares party victory in Bosnia election | Bosnia and Herzegovina | The Guardian
description: Staunchly pro-Russia politician has dominated campaign and inflamed divisions despite not appearing on ballot
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Staunchly pro-Russia politician has dominated campaign and inflamed divisions despite not appearing on ballot
Content: Formerly the president of the country’s Serb-majority entity of Republika Srpska, Dodik has been banned from holding public office.Photograph: Marko Đurica/ReutersView image in fullscreenFormerly the president of the country’s Serb-majority entity of Republika Srpska, Dodik has been banned from holding public office.Photograph: Marko Đurica/ReutersBosnia and HerzegovinaBosnian Serb nationalist Dodik declares party victory in Bosnia electionStaunchly pro-Russia politician has dominated campaign and inflamed divisions despite not appearing on ballotAssociated PressSun 4 Oct 2026 16.42 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 16.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBosnian Serb nationalist politician Milorad Dodik has declared victory for his party in an election in Bosnia shaped by economic pressures, the prospect of the Balkan nation joining the European Union and ethnic tensions that have divided the country since its brutal 1992-95 war.Dodik is a staunchly pro-Russia politician who, despite not appearing on the ballot, has dominated the campaign and inflamed divisions with separatist rhetoric that has sparked fears of renewed instability in Bosnia.Formerly the president of the country’s Serb-majority entity of Republika Srpska, Dodik was banned from holding public office after being convicted last year of defying decisions by the international envoy overseeing the 1995 peace agreement that ended the war.With nearly 90% of votes counted, Dodik’s ally Željka Cvijanovićof the rightwing Alliance of Independent Social Democrats had more than 55% of the votes to take one of the three seats in the country’s tripartite presidency, leading her nearest opponent by about 30 percentage points.Speaking at a news conference late on Sunday, Dodik said his nationalist party would also hold a “vast majority” in Republika Srpska’s assembly, and credited US president Donald Trump’s “magnificent victory” in 2024 and Russian president Vladimir Putin’s support for the election win.“No one should ask us to change our politics,” Dodik said. “We will not give up, but continue for our people … I cannot believe that we smashed it like this.”About 3.4 million voters were eligible to choose the three members of the country’s multi-ethnic presidency, lawmakers for the national parliament and heads of institutions for the country’s two entities: the Muslim-majority Federation ofBosnia and Herzegovinaand Republika Srpska, which is dominated by ethnic Serbs.With more than 94% of votes counted on Sunday, Darijana Filipović of the nationalist Croatian Democratic Union of Bosnia and Herzegovina held a commanding lead for the Croat seat on the presidency, while the incumbent Bosniak member of the presidency, Denis Bećirović of the Social Democratic party, led his nearest opponent, Bakir Izetbegović, by fewer than three percentage points.Can anything politicians say at Sunday’s election stop young people from leaving Bosnia?Read moreBoth Filipović and Bećirović declared victory in their races late on Sunday before all votes were counted.Bosnia’s central election commission said that 1,432,269 votes were cast in total, a turnout of 42% that was down by about 8% from Bosnia’s last election in 2022.Bosnia has a complex web of governing institutions that were created by a US-brokered peace agreement in 1995 in an effort to manage the ethnic divisions between Muslim Bosniaks, Orthodox Serbs and Catholic Croats that gave rise to the war.Yet Dodik has consistently tested those limits, openly defying Bosnia’s national government in the capital Sarajevo and making moves for Republika Srpska to separate from the country.At his party’s final election rally on Friday night in Banja Luka, Republika Srpska’s administrative capital, Dodik told supporters that Bosnia “is dead”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“It is an impossible country. It doesn’t make any sense,” Dodik said at the rally, which was also attended by Russian ambassador Igor Khalabukov.Such political and ethnic divisions – in which the country’s Bosniaks, Serbs and Croats largely vote along ethnic lines – have blocked Bosnia’s progress toward joining the EU despite the bloc’s efforts to encourage the country’s divided leaders to work together for reform.Dragan Bursać, an analyst, said that despite Dodik not appearing on the ballot for the first time in nearly 30 years, he “is still in command. He is everywhere.”“It is obvious that these measures to ban him from political life are not working, and he is using them,” Bursać said.One of the poorest countries in Europe, Bosnia is still struggling to recover decades on from the war, which started in 1992 after the country declared independence from the Serb-led former Yugoslavia and ethnic Serbs took up arms to carve out their own state and join Serbia. The conflict killed more than 100,000 people and displaced millions.Bosnia’s wartime wounds were recently revived by a public homage in Serbia and among Bosnian Serbs to the wartime army commander Ratko Mladić, who died in late August while serving a life sentence for genocide and other war crimes.Explore more on these topicsBosnia and HerzegovinaEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: More than 400 schools in France to be closed on Monday as more protests planned | France | The Guardian
description: Education minister says 24 schools have been burnt or ransacked and 78 staff members injured since student unrest began last month
Author: Rory Carroll
Headline: Education minister says 24 schools have been burnt or ransacked and 78 staff members injured since student unrest began last month
Content: High-school students protesting in France.Photograph: Nacho Doce/ReutersView image in fullscreenHigh-school students protesting in France.Photograph: Nacho Doce/ReutersFranceMore than 400 schools in France to be closed on Monday as more protests plannedEducation minister says 24 schools have been burnt or ransacked and 78 staff members injured since student unrest began last monthEurope live – latest updatesRory CarrollSun 4 Oct 2026 11.08 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 15.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMore than 400 schools inFrancewill be closed or partly closed on Monday as authorities brace for another week of student protests.Lessons will be totally or partly suspended in 400 to 500 schools because security conditions “have not been fulfilled”, the education minister, Édouard Geffray, said on Sunday.The minister said 24 schools had been burnt or ransacked and 78 education staff members injured. The number of school closures on Monday would be comparable to Friday’s but the government envisaged a “partial, progressive return to lessons”, said Geffray.Thousands of teenagers staged widespread demonstrations anderected barricades last weekto protest against what they said was underfunding and neglect of the education system.View image in fullscreenStudents block the entrance to Ampere high school in Lyon.Photograph: Konrad K/Sipa/ShutterstockClashes with riot police left hundreds of people injured, led to more than 5,000 arrests, mostly of minors, and jolted President Emmanuel Macron’s centrist administration.There was a lull at the weekend, but protest organisers called for renewed demonstrations on Tuesday because the government had failed to produce “concrete measures”.Authorities say political agitators have infiltrated the protest, which started at a Paris school on 17 September and spread across the capital and the rest of France.“There are activists – particularly from the far left – who have infiltrated the high school student movement, hijacked it from the students themselves, and engaged in extreme violence,” said Geffray. “Clearly, this poses a risk to both our staff and our students.”The injured education staff members were deliberately targeted, “something we have never seen before”, said Geffray.The protestscaught the government by surpriseand confronted Macron with his worst crisis in months. Images of burning barricades and police using teargas, batons and other methods to disperse protests have dominated TV news.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenSecurity forces are stationed at Place de la Nation in Paris on Friday during the student protests.Photograph: Giulia Morici/NurPhoto/ShutterstockStudent grievances include overcrowded classes of up to 40 children in crumbling buildings, poor teacher pay, staff absences and an unequal system in which social background determined success. Other factors are an opaque and difficult online system for university applications as well as the sweltering temperatures in classrooms duringheatwaves.Protesters have accused the state of disengaging from secondary education and cited difficult conditions such as leaks, cockroaches, collapsed ceilings and decayed buildings. Others have complained about excessively long school days and a lack of teaching staff.The government said the grievances were legitimate but condemned what it called “urban violence”. On Sunday, police detained a 16-year-old in relation to an assault of a teacher in La Ciotat, a town on the southern coast between Marseille and Toulon. The teacher, 59, was doused with gasoline and struck during a protest on Friday.The government is also under pressure from trade unions that called a day ofstrikes last weekto compel the new prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, to rethink budget cuts and consider a form of wealth tax on the super-rich. The CGT trade union exhorted workers to sustain the pressure with demonstrations this week.Explore more on these topicsFranceProtestEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Russia strikes Kyiv bridge as German chancellor visits Ukraine in show of support | Kyiv | The Guardian
description: Attack shortly after Friedrich Merz arrived on unannounced visit intended to underline Germany’s backing
Author: Pjotr Sauer
Headline: Attack shortly after Friedrich Merz arrived on unannounced visit intended to underline Germany’s backing
Content: Soldiers inspect the damage from a Russian drone strike on the Northern Bridge in Kyiv.Photograph: Mykola Tymchenko/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSoldiers inspect the damage from a Russian drone strike on the Northern Bridge in Kyiv.Photograph: Mykola Tymchenko/AFP/Getty ImagesKyivRussia strikes Kyiv bridge as German chancellor visits Ukraine in show of supportAttack shortly after Friedrich Merz arrived on unannounced visit intended to underline Germany’s backingPjotr Sauerin KyivSun 4 Oct 2026 12.12 EDTFirst published on Sun 4 Oct 2026 07.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRussia has struck another major bridge in Kyiv as the German chancellor,Friedrich Merz, arrived in the capital in a show of support for Ukraine.A Russian drone hit Kyiv’s key Northern Bridge over the Dnipro River, marking the fourth consecutive day thatRussiahas targeted bridges used by tens of thousands of residents commuting between the city’s two banks. Video footage showed cars driving across the bridge as the drone plunged into the roadway and exploded in a burst of fire. Two people were injured in the strike, said Kyiv’s mayor, Vitali Klitschko.The attack came shortly after Merz arrived in the city on an unannounced visit intended to underline Germany’s backing of Ukraine, as the country enters one of the most precarious periods since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022.Germany has become Ukraine’s biggest provider of military aid since Merz entered office in May 2025, surpassing the US as American support has declined.Russian drone strikes North Bridge in Kyiv, UkraineKyiv has comeunder near-constant attackfrom Russia’s new jet-powered drones in recent weeks, as an intensifying strike campaign increasingly disrupts everyday life in the capital and threatens to leave the city without power this winter.On his visit, Merz announced that Germany would fund the joint production of drones designed to intercept Russia’s jet-powered drones, adding that “significant technical breakthroughs” in recent weeks were speeding up production.“This will quickly and tangibly strengthen Ukraine’s air defence,” he said. “And this strengthening is urgently needed.”The German leader got a taste of the new reality of daily life in the Ukrainian capital. Air-raid sirens sounded repeatedly during his visit, including as Volodymyr Zelenskyy showed him the badly damaged National Academy of Sciences building, wherea Russian drone strike killed two people last week.The Ukrainian president told Merz that people inKyivwere suffering “terrible nights and days” from the relentless attacks, and called Ukraine’s Russian adversaries “absolute barbarians”.“We can see the entire pointlessness of this war at this place,” said Merz, adding as he arrived that Ukraine “needs all our support in the coming weeks”. “If Russia is not stopped, its war machine will sooner or later turn against us,” he said.View image in fullscreenVolodymyr Zelenskyy (left) and Friedrich Merz in Kyiv on Sunday.Photograph: dts News Agency Germany Bundesregierung/Tobias Koch/ShutterstockRussia had already damaged Kyiv’s Northern Bridge and repeatedly struck its Southern Bridge. Although the crossings remain standing, repeated attacks and the threat of further strikes have prompted the city’s authorities to restrict or suspend traffic on five of the city’s six road bridges over the Dnipro, causing temporary closures and large traffic jams.If Moscow succeeds in seriously damaging Kyiv’s bridges, it could create a logistical nightmare for the city of 3 million people, whose crossings over the Dnipro were last destroyed on a large scale as Nazi German forces retreated in 1943. More than a third of residents live on the left bank while much of the city’s employment and infrastructure is concentrated on the right.View image in fullscreenA Russian jet-powered drone strikes a bridge in Kyiv on 2 October.Photograph: Valentyn Ogirenko/ReutersThe attacks form part of a broader Russian campaign against civilian and industrial infrastructure inside Ukraine. In recent weeks, strikes have hit logistics hubs, railway lines, datacentres, medical storage facilities and steel plants, alongside a sustained assault on the country’s energy system that is expected to intensify over the winter.“He [Putin] is counting on constant escalation. He wants this very much,” Zelenskyy said at a press conference alongside Merz. “This is an answer to everyone – to those who believe that all you have to do is simply ask Putin and he will end the war for real. It won’t happen, simply.”Russia’s foreign ministry on Saturday warned foreign nationals and diplomatic staff against remaining in or travelling to Ukraine. “Responsibility for any possible adverse consequences lies entirely with those who choose to disregard this warning,” the ministry said.mapA number of foreign ambassadors, including Germany’s, responded on social media that they intended to remain in Kyiv.“The EU delegation is staying,” the European Union ambassador, Katarína Mathernová, wrote on X on Sunday. “Threatening us will not stop Europe’s support for Ukraine. It only reminds us why that support matters.”In Moscow, some pro-war commenters noted with glee that the Russian strikes had continued despite Merz’s arrival. “Russia used to pause strikes on Kyiv during visits by European politicians. Not any more,” wrote Sergei Markov, a prominent pro-war commentator.The trip is Merz’s second to Ukraine since becoming chancellor. He has been among Kyiv’s most outspoken supporters in Europe and a leading voice warning about Russia’s hybrid campaign against other nations.Incinerated novels and destroyed warehouses: Russia’s war on Ukrainian booksRead moreLast month, Germany formally accused Moscowof being behind a suspected plot targeting Leipzig/Halle airport, a key logistics hub for western military aid to Ukraine. But Merz is also facinggrowing discontentat home over his support for Ukraine, as his approval ratings fall.Germany’s far left and far right are sceptical of support for Ukraine and want Berlin to scale back aid. The pressure has intensified as the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD)has made big electoral gains.Alice Weidel, the AfD’s co-leader, wrote in a social media post: “Merz is travelling to Ukraine on Germany’s national holiday and promising further billions in German taxpayer money that is missing from the pension and health insurance funds, while Germany is mired in its worst energy crisis.”Explore more on these topicsKyivUkraineRussiaGermanyFriedrich MerzEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Egyptian journalist faces terrorism charges after entire newsroom detained | Egypt | The Guardian
description: Calls for release of six Matsadaash staff after one is charged, while whereabouts of other five remain unknown
Author: William Christou
Headline: Calls for release of six Matsadaash staff after one is charged, while whereabouts of other five remain unknown
Content: Clockwise from top left: Mohamed Ashraf, Omar Helal, Islam Barakat, Mohamed Adel, Mohamed Mahmoud and Abdallah Qadri.Photograph: Matsadaash/APView image in fullscreenClockwise from top left: Mohamed Ashraf, Omar Helal, Islam Barakat, Mohamed Adel, Mohamed Mahmoud and Abdallah Qadri.Photograph: Matsadaash/APEgyptEgyptian journalist faces terrorism charges after entire newsroom detainedCalls for release of six Matsadaash staff after one is charged, while whereabouts of other five remain unknownWilliam Christouin JerusalemSun 4 Oct 2026 11.16 EDTFirst published on Sun 4 Oct 2026 11.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn Egyptian journalist has been charged with joining a terrorist group, days after an entire newsroom was detained in what rights groups have said is a crackdown on press freedoms.Last week, authorities arrested six journalists from the independent fact-checking and investigative platform Matsadaash – literally meaning “don’t believe” – accusing them in a statement of being unlicensed and publishing false news on behalf of the outlawedMuslim Brotherhood.The outlet’s six journalists, Abdallah Qadri, Mohamed Ashraf, Mohamed Adel, Islam Barakat, Mohamed Mahmoud and Omar Helal, were arrested by security forces over the course of two days.On Sunday, Egyptian authorities charged Ashraf with joining a terrorist group and spreading false news, according to a statement by the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights, a NGO. The charges came after an interrogation that lasted from 10pm to 8am and focused exclusively on material published by Matsadaash, the rights group said.Ashraf was to be held for 15 days, pending investigation, while the whereabouts of the other five journalists were still unknown.View image in fullscreenEgyptian authorities have charged the journalist Mohamed Ashraf with joining a terrorist group and spreading fake news.Photograph: Matsadaash/APAbdelrahman Mansour, the co-founder of the platform, denied having any association with the Muslim Brotherhood, a transnational movement that was designated a terrorist organisation by Egypt in 2013 after the former president Mohamed Morsi, a senior Brotherhood figure, was ousted in a coup. Mansour called the arrests “one of the gravest attacks on journalism in Egypt’s modern history”.“My colleagues were doing what journalists should do: asking difficult questions, uncovering facts, and reporting on issues that affect people’s lives. They deserve recognition for their work. Instead, their homes were raided, and all six were taken away,” he said. “The government must answer this question: why have you arrested six journalists? What have they done beyond doing their jobs?”The Guardian contacted the Egyptian State Information Service for a comment but did not receive a reply by the time of publishing.Dozens of journalists staged a sit-in outside the Egyptian Journalists Syndicate (EJS) in Cairo on Saturday, demanding the release of the Matsadaash staff. Members said they would keep the sit-in open ended until the journalists were released, and the EJS said it would convene an emergency meeting on Monday.The EJS had filed a request with the ministry of interior and public prosecutor for the release of the journalists, as well as for information on their whereabouts.More than 80 rights groups, including Human Rights Watch and the Committee to Protect Journalists, condemned the arrests as a violation of freedoms, and demanded the immediate release of the Matsadaash staff.The arrests came little over a week after the US government waived its human rights conditions on $320m (£242m) in military aid to Egypt, citing Cairo’s “helpful role” to US national security after the US-Iran war.The US gives about $1.3bn in aid to Egypt annually, but a portion is contingent upon the Egyptian government meeting certain human rights and democracy-related requirements. The US has withheld portions of aid several times since the 2013 coup owing to Egypt’s poor human rights record, but has largely kept funds flowing.This year, Washington waived the human rights requirement in total, as doing so was “essential for the US-Egypt relationship and US national security priorities”, according to a state department memo revealed by Reuters.While saying that he was unsure whether the arrests were linked to the recent waiver, Mansour said: “The use of the national security waiver on human rights conditions by the US by many years, a willingness by other states to look the other way on Egypt’s human rights record … certainly enables violations like this to occur more easily.”Cairo has for years faced criticism for its human rights abuses, with the rights monitor Freedom House saying Egyptian security forces “engage in human rights abuses and extrajudicial killing with impunity”.Since the Egyptian president Abdel Fatah al-Sisi took power in the coup that ousted Morsi, civil liberties have been curbed and domestic political opposition has been violently crushed.Egypt ranks 169th out of 180 countries on the Reporters Without BordersPress freedomindex. Freedom of the press is tightly restricted in the country and independent platforms such as Matsadaash are rare. About 26 journalists are held in Egyptian prisons, according to the EJS.Explore more on these topicsEgyptPress freedomMuslim BrotherhoodMiddle East and north AfricaAfricaNewspapersNewspapers & magazinesnewsShareReuse this content

title: UK car industry faces ‘difficult trade-off’ between Chinese and EU markets | Automotive industry | The Guardian
description: Britain under pressure to put tariffs on cheap Chinese vehicle imports ahead of protectionist trade measures
Author: Alex Daniel
Headline: Britain under pressure to put tariffs on cheap Chinese vehicle imports ahead of protectionist trade measures
Content: Chinese EVs wait to be shipped for export at Yantai Port in Yantai City, Shandong Province, China.Photograph: Costfoto/NurPhoto/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenChinese EVs wait to be shipped for export at Yantai Port in Yantai City, Shandong Province, China.Photograph: Costfoto/NurPhoto/ShutterstockAutomotive industryUK car industry faces ‘difficult trade-off’ between Chinese and EU marketsBritain under pressure to put tariffs on cheap Chinese vehicle imports ahead of protectionist trade measuresAlex DanielSun 4 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 14.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBritain’s car industry is grappling with a “difficult trade-off” between China andEurope, as manufacturers struggle to balance the benefits of both markets ahead of looming trade measures that could restrict UK exports to the EU.The UK is an outlier in choosing not to put import taxes on Chinese vehicles, even as the US hasshut them out almost entirely, and the EU imposesduties of up to 45%.EU officials reportedly warned Andy Burnham last month that the UK must put tariffs on cheap Chinese vehicles otherwise Brussels would impose protectionist“made in Europe” barrierson British exports to the bloc, hitting British carmakers in their largest market.Ministers have so far resisted such calls, with Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary, arguing any levies would “probably be reciprocated” – costing UK manufacturers sales inChina.Tariffs would also raise prices for British drivers, who haveflocked to cheaper Chinese models, and could deter brands such as Chery, which isin talks to build cars at Nissan’s Sunderland plant, from investing further in the UK.“There is a difficult trade-off,” said Emily Sawicz, of the consultancy RSM UK, adding that the UK “cannot afford to drift between the two indefinitely”. Chinese investment could be a “lifeline” for carmakers, while access to Europe would also be “crucial” for smaller manufacturers.“Being excluded risks UK suppliers becoming increasingly shut out of those European opportunities,” she added. “Manufacturers need clarity on which direction the government intends to take so they can make long-term investment decisions.”Ian Plummer, commercial director at Autotrader, said competition from Chinese brands had made cars more affordable and “is encouraging more people to go and buy a new car”.Brands such as BYD, Omoda and Jaecoo more than tripled their share of the UK new car market in the first eight months of 2026, reaching 12% of sales, according to industry figures.Figures released on Friday showed that British new car ⁠registrations rose 12% in the year to September, the best month for annual growth since 2017. The preliminary data from the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders (SMMT) showed the boom was powered by a demand for electric vehicles and Chinese brands, with the Jaecoo 7 and BYD’s ​Sealion ‌7 among the top sellers.The trade body said on Wednesday that the European Commission’s made in Europe rules, which restrict subsidies, tax breaks and public procurement contracts to vehicles built within the EU, pose an existential threat to British car production. The EU accounted for 58% of UK car exports in the first half of the year, compared with about 4% for China.Mike Hawes, the SMMT’s chief executive, said: “The UK and EU automotive industries are deeply integrated, so effectively excluding British-produced vehicles from their largest market would assure mutual damage.”.Massimiliano Messina, Nissan’s chair in Europe, said last month: “Europe cannot have a Trojan horse where the Chinese are going to flood the market through the UK.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionVictor Zhang, the deputy UK chief of Chery, which owns the Jaecoo and Omoda brands, rejected that claim, saying: “Most of what we sell are super-hybrids, not the cars that those tariffs are about, and the cars we sell here stay here.”He added: “Tariffs can come and go, but we won’t change our ongoing investment in the UK.”Brussels raised its own tariffs on Chinese EVs in 2024, triggering a decline in what was then an accelerating sales trajectory. It is now facing calls for fresh barriers to be imposed on importing hybrid electric vehicles, potentially quotas or price floors.Imports of plug-in and battery hybrid carsrocketed after the EU tariffs were imposedon EVs, underlining China’s ability to pivot its export efforts when hit by trade barriers.Others in the industry believe tariffs could help protect the UK’s manufacturers, whose market share in Britain continues to be eroded Chinese firms.Tim Tozer, a former chair of Vauxhall, said that tariffs were “vital” to stop Britain’s car sector “atrophying”. He said: “We are at last knockings now, trying to save the industry.”He added that Reynolds was “whistling in the wind” with hopes of continuing to export to China en masse, arguing the market had become “fiercely nationalistic,” with buyers increasingly loyal to domestic brands “because they’re bloody good”.Explore more on these topicsAutomotive industryEuropean UnionChinaTrade policyManufacturing sectorAsia PacificEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: OpenAI safety leader quits, warning AI company’s culture is ‘broken’ | OpenAI | The Guardian
description: David Robinson joins other insiders in urging industry to take more care over rapidly developing technology
Author: Dan Milmo
Headline: David Robinson joins other insiders in urging industry to take more care over rapidly developing technology
Content: David Robinson said AI firms were not ‘being nearly careful enough’ about developing the technology.Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersView image in fullscreenDavid Robinson said AI firms were not ‘being nearly careful enough’ about developing the technology.Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersOpenAIOpenAI safety leader quits, warning AI company’s culture is ‘broken’David Robinson joins other insiders in urging industry to take more care over rapidly developing technologyDan MilmoGlobal technology editorSun 4 Oct 2026 03.48 EDTFirst published on Sat 3 Oct 2026 15.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA safety leader atOpenAIhas quit the company, warning that its culture was broken and that AI firms were not “being nearly careful enough” about developing the technology.David Robinson, who led the writing of safety reports that accompanied the ChatGPT developer’s product releases, explained his resignation in an essay headlined: “I quit OpenAI because its culture is broken.”Robinson wrote that a cultural overhaul was needed at cutting-edge AI firms and incidents such as a “swarm” of OpenAI agents – AI programmes operating autonomously without human oversight –attacking the AI startup Hugging Facewere “typical of the industry, given the speed and flexibility with which people operate”.Writing inthe Atlantic magazine, Robinson wrote: “I agree with other recently departed staff that the companies building this technology aren’t being nearly careful enough. But I believe that we need to look deeper than specific rules or new laws. We need to talk about culture.”Referring to OpenAI’s pace of development, he wrote: “As the company sprints from one launch to the next, it is failing to achieve the level of care that I believe is needed.”OpenAI has shown signs of caution in recent weeks, after the Hugging Face incident and the revelation that it has notified more than 100 organisations about rogue agent activity. This week it announced it wasscrapping the release of a next-generation ⁠AI modelafter researchers raised safety concerns ⁠during internal testing. OpenAI hasalso paused trainingof its most advanced models.Geoffrey Irving, who worked at OpenAI and was chief scientist at the UK government’s AI Safety Institute before joining the AI safety researchcompany Resolution, also issued a warning on AI on Saturday.Writingin Time, he said: “Recent warnings about the potential destructive power of AI are understating the severity of the situation. I believe there’s about a 50% chance we all die because of the development of smarter-than-human AI systems, and that our actions over the next two to 10 years will determine the outcome.”The warnings follow the resignation of Jacob Coxon, a researcher at the OpenAI rival Anthropic, who quit the Claude chatbot developer last month. He said he believed AI “could kill us all by the end of the decade” – and wasbacked up by an Anthropic employee warningthere was a more than 10% chance AI would wipe out humanity within the next decade. Critics of such warnings have cautioned, however, thatthey are unscientificbecause they cannot be verified or falsified.Robinson wrote that Silicon Valley lacked an awareness of “how to handle dangerous technology” and “what it means to care for people”. Warning that OpenAI had “unimpeded optimism” about solving problems as they arose, he wrote that this internal culture meant safety failures would only grow as systems became more capable.“Imagine ‘rogue’ agents that work like teams of hackers (for example, holding hospital computer systems for ransom) but never need to sleep,” wrote Robinson.Robinson called for two safety changes: that AI firms rely on safety expertise in other fields such as nuclear and aviation, and that they develop “new science” that ensures powerful systems in the future are capable of being reined in when they are operating autonomously.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Given today’s risks, frontier labs need to run like nuclear power plants or busy airports, with layers of redundancy and careful, time-consuming planning, so that the occasional and inevitable human error does not open a door to disaster,” he wrote.An OpenAI spokesperson said the company was continuing to “strengthen our safety and security practices to address the risks we see today”, while working on dealing with the risks that might be created by future AI breakthroughs.“We’re making sure our models don’t become more capable than we can safely manage and secure, and we pause training or hold back models when we need to slow down,” said the spokesperson.Get in touchContact us about this storyThe best public interest journalism relies on first-hand accounts from people in the know.
