title: Once Upon A Time In Sokoto review – exuberant history lesson on intra-African slavery | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Inua Ellams displays a Stoppardian or Fraynian relish in turning complex topics into enjoyable theatre in his latest play
Author: Mark Lawson
Headline: Inua Ellams displays a Stoppardian or Fraynian relish in turning complex topics into enjoyable theatre in his latest play
Content: Expansive narrative … Will Atiomo, Adeola Yemitan and Antonia Layiwola in Once Upon A Time In Sokoto.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianView image in fullscreenExpansive narrative … Will Atiomo, Adeola Yemitan and Antonia Layiwola in Once Upon A Time In Sokoto.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianTheatreReviewOnce Upon A Time In Sokoto review – exuberant history lesson on intra-African slaveryRoyal and Derngate, NorthamptonInua Ellams displays a Stoppardian or Fraynian relish in turning complex topics into enjoyable theatre in his latest playMark LawsonSun 4 Oct 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 11.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOver the last decade, Inua Ellams has written inventive and educational plays centred on modern Nigeria, starting withBarber Shop Chroniclesin which hair care allowed cutting commentary on masculinity and politics.AlthoughThe Half God of Rainfallhad a detour to Mount Olympus, typical of Ellams’s structural fun, the focus was postcolonial Nigeria, his superb relocation of Chekhov’sThree Sistersto 1960s Africa showing ructions resulting from British imperial ruler Lord Lugard coercing the playwright’s birth nation from multiple cultures.Across 24 scenes set from 1865 to 1903, when Lugard crushed local resistance, Ellams’s new play, Once Upon A Time In Sokoto, maps pre-colonial history, mainly around the many emirates of the Sokoto Caliphate in West Africa but with diversions to Libya and Egypt.Using aspects of traditional storytelling – the audience learns a call-and-response chant in the Hausa language – the expansive narrative is anchored to Zinari (Antonia Layiwola), a matriarchal upper-class entrepreneur, and Nafisa (Adeola Yemitan), her former slave who fights for more agency. Suggesting a precocious feminism in the culture, Ellams also illustrates its limits. When Zinari chooses to be childless, her husband, Hadiru, (Bayo Gbadamosi) cites religious law to take Nafisa as a second, fecund wife.For many, the play will be a history lesson, though more exuberant and engaging than most schools. Ellams’s international curriculum, though, teaches much deeper.View image in fullscreenTragedy and comedy … Atiomo and Layiwola  in Once Upon A Time In Sokoto.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianMoral horror about slavery, in this case intra-African, incorporates a cold-eyed account of its economics: “Nafisa’s value has quadrupled 433% to one million, one hundred and forty thousand.” The currency is cowries, sea snail shells, showing how this economy – including literal shell companies– develops competition, taxation, inflation and a catastrophic crash when international predators – represented by the British-schooled Yusufu (Will Atiomo) – flood the market with imported cowries. This felt to me more fiscally astute than James Graham’s JM Keynes play,The Standard Of Living.Another subject tackled is philology, developing languages shown through clashes over rival alphabets and the colonisers’ import of exotic metaphors: “Many ways to skin a cat” alarms pro-feline Egypt. We learn the meaning of “Boko Haram”, later claimed by a Nigerian jihadist group.The fabular note in the title Once Upon A Time In Sokoto also often inflects the text. Anticipating modern advertising, Zinari adlibs an “ancient” legend to raise sales of her indigo cloth. Later, she and Nafisa conduct a late-19th-century poetry slam in a market square, the former’s Koranic verse trumped by the latter’s more populist quasi-rap.Scattering incidental but engaging data – the introduction of the lip kiss to a forehead-rubbing culture, the colonial significance of Millwall FC shorts – Ellams shows a Stoppardian or Fraynian relish in enjoyably compressing complex topics. His cast adept at tragedy and comedy, director Roy Alexander Weise brings characteristic grace and pace, a domestic conversation transitioning within seconds to a funeral.At theRoyal and Derngate, Northampton, until 10 October,then touring.Explore more on these topicsTheatreInua EllamsNigeriaBritish empireSlaveryreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I can’t listen to Pink Floyd - I find their music dreary’: Elvis Costello’s honest playlist | Elvis Costello | The Guardian
description: The singer-songwriter owes a lot to Georgie Fame and likes the romantic side of Jimi Hendrix – but which ringtone song can put him in a bad mood?
Author: Rich Pelley
Headline: The singer-songwriter owes a lot to Georgie Fame and likes the romantic side of Jimi Hendrix – but which ringtone song can put him in a bad mood?
Content: ‘Karaoke? Certainly not. I do this for a living’ … Elvis Costello.Photograph: Mark SeligerView image in fullscreen‘Karaoke? Certainly not. I do this for a living’ … Elvis Costello.Photograph: Mark SeligerHonest playlistElvis Costello‘I can’t listen to Pink Floyd - I find their music dreary’: Elvis Costello’s honest playlistThe singer-songwriter owes a lot to Georgie Fame and likes the romantic side of Jimi Hendrix – but which ringtone song can put him in a bad mood?As told toRich PelleySun 4 Oct 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe first song I fell in love withThe Wind Cries Mary by Jimi Hendrix, which came out in 1967 when I was 12. Hendrix was known for outgoing music, but I was a romantic soul, so the emotional side of his music led to that strain in my own writing.The song I do at karaokeKaraoke? Certainly not. I do this for a living. Would you have made my great-grandfather dig ditches for fun? I prefer to live vicariously through Bill Murray singing (What’s So Funny ’Bout) Peace, Love and Understanding in Lost in Translation.The song I inexplicably know every lyric to’Cross the Green Mountain by Bob Dylan is a bit hidden away, but in the very top tier of his songwriting. It’s full of images from the American civil war: conflict, overwhelming love, officers being shot, mothers receiving terrible news. It’s poignant and involving.The first single I boughtI saved my pocket money to buy the Fame at Last EP by Georgie Fame from Potter’s Music Shop in Richmond. He introduced me to Gerry Goffin and Carole King, Louis Jordan, Ray Charles, Big Joe Turner, Mose Allison, Willie Dixon and Lambert, Hendricks & Ross – which was a lot of education for an 11-year-old who didn’t play an instrument.The song I can no longer listen toAnything by Pink Floyd. Never could, never will. I find their music dreary. I love the imagination and playfulness of See Emily Play, but after Syd Barrett left they just never appealed to me.The best song to have sex toHow impertinent.The song I secretly like, but tell everyone I hateI’ve written a few songs that I secretly hate, but I can’t think of anything I secretly like apart from Milkshake by Kelis – and I don’t think that’s a secret.The best song to play at a partyI haven’t been to a party since I was 15. Then it would have been Double Barrel by Dave & Ansel Collins.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe song that changed my lifeMy mother claimed I’d request I’ve Got You Under My Skin by Frank Sinatra before I could form sentences. I can still visualise the record player we had in our basement flat near Olympia, which had a red eye on the front and looked a bit like a robot.The song that gets me up in the morningArmagideon Time by the Clash. I found having Good Morning from Singin’ in the Rain as my ringtone put me in a bad mood.The song I want played at my funeralKeepin’ Out of Mischief Now by Louis Armstrong.My Aim Is True (49th Anniversary Edition) is out now.Explore more on these topicsElvis CostelloHonest playlistPop and rockJazzReggaefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: A Statement review – outstanding climate change dramedy about a 1980 meeting | New York film festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Paul Rudd, Paul Giamatti and Tatiana Maslany lead an excellent ensemble in this dramatization of a failed 1980 conference on climate change
Author: Adrian Horton
Headline: Paul Rudd, Paul Giamatti and Tatiana Maslany lead an excellent ensemble in this dramatization of a failed 1980 conference on climate change
Content: A still from A Statement.Photograph: Sabrina Lantos/Sony Picture Classics/AllstarView image in fullscreenA still from A Statement.Photograph: Sabrina Lantos/Sony Picture Classics/AllstarFirst look reviewNew York film festival 2026ReviewA Statement review – outstanding climate change dramedy about a 1980 meetingNew York film festival:Paul Rudd, Paul Giamatti and Tatiana Maslany lead an excellent ensemble in this dramatization of a failed conference on climate changeAdrian HortonSat 3 Oct 2026 20.15 EDTLast modified on Sat 3 Oct 2026 20.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn late October 1980, days before the election ofRonald Reagan, Congress summoned 20 experts in various fields to a beachfront hotel in Florida. Their mandate was simple: figure out how to address the dire threat posed to the climate by fossil fuel emissions, then deliver their recommendations to Congress in the form of a statement.Every word said during four marathon sessions over the next 36 hours – every disagreement or digression, tirade or truce – was recorded by a stenographer for posterity into a single document, hundreds of pages long, that stands as an artifact from a time when expertise was trusted, before corporate greed and political expediency mired “debate” about rising levels of CO2 in the atmosphere in a haze of misinformation and inaction. The fact that this meeting took place at all – that experts in climate, energy, law, philosophy, politics and more agreed on the fundamental facts, yet struggled to reach consensus on what to do about them – is fascinating, if perhaps not the most natural fit for a movie. This was, after all, a conference room of specialists sharing evidence via overhead projector.Behemoth! review - Pedro Pascal classical music drama hits all the wrong notesRead moreNevertheless, A Statement, a new film fromSpotlightdirector Tom McCarthy that dramatizes the landmark conference, bets on the inherent sparks of watching fractious personalities forced together, as outlined in a 10-page section within Nathaniel Rich’s 2019 book Losing Earth. McCarthy and fellow screenwriters Noé Debré and Thomas Bidegain have embarked on an admirable act of faith: every word said within the conference room walls – roughly half of the movie – is pulled verbatim from the stenographer’s document. That is no mere fun fact within the press notes; though occasional text overlays from the actual transcript suggest some level of verisimilitude, it is in fact helpful to one’s appreciation of the movie, which dives headlong into the weeds and spins out in circular debates, to know that every tedious discussion of semantics, every frustrating spiral of potentials, was not in fact a writerly decision, but a real event – the natural and instructive result of 20 individual humans, each with their own personal feelings and professional responsibilities, confronting an existential problem of global scale.View image in fullscreenPaul Rudd and Amy Ryan at a press conference for A Statement at the New York film festival on 3 October.Photograph: Roy Rochlin/Getty Images for FLCMcCarthy, of course, is the writer/director of one of the great so-called competency porn movies of our time; the thrill of Spotlight is in both the successful reveal of a corrupted institution, and the frisson of watching people be unflappably good at their jobs. A Statement puts a misty-eyed spin on that pleasure: its people may be failing their objective – it’s a 46-year-old spoiler to say that no consensus was ever reached, nor a statement ever issued – but they’re at least trying their best, generally respecting each other’s views and, in the speculative bits outside the conference room that thankfully make the movie a treatise on the interminable condition of being human, actually befriending and learning from each other. If there is competency porn to be found, it is in McCarthy’s proficient, no-frills filmmaking, gracefully condensing 36 hours of collective tedium and personal reckonings into a tight 104 minutes.You Can See Everything review – Nathan Fielder’s Elizabeth Holmes doc is a modern masterpiece of deceitRead moreThat, as well as a stacked cast of character actors demonstrating their mastery of type.Paul Ruddis awkwardly charming as the conference moderator who just wants everyone to get along.Paul Giamattiis never less than commanding as the curmudgeonly stick-in-the-mud from the Department of Energy with wisdom to spare, should you wait for it.John Turturroprovides comic relief as an endearingly serious oddball scientist who has stared down the void. Evan Peters, playing “the Paul Revere of climate change”, can still do boyish live wire while pushing 40, as the film’s moral conscience.Tatiana Maslanydisappears so fully into her role as a law professor, nervously holding the room hostage in legalese, that I did not clock her until the credits. The film’s ensemble – including Amy Ryan,Silicon Valley’s Zach Woods andSomebody Somewhere’s Mary Catherine Garrison, among others – are uniformly excellent and calibrated, no one performer running away with things (though Giamatti, perhaps unsurprisingly, has the best go at it, in a fictionalized nighttime scene that satisfyingly pits his hardbitten pragmatism against Peters’s fiery idealism).That is the gristle of the work, the difficult collaborations required to even have a shot of getting out of our human-made bind. For all its commendable historical accuracy – and there is a thrill in seeing, exactly, how we once thought about modernity’s most pressing and intractable problem – it’s the additional stuff, the late nights and vulnerable phone calls, dishy drinks and bruised egos, that makes A Statement a much more effective film about climate change than, say, a smug satire likeDon’t Look Up. If we’ve learned anything in the decades since that beachside conference, it’s that the science can say what it will, but emotion will rule the day. The conference may have been a failure, but there is a satisfaction in watching them naively try.A Statement is playing at the New York film festival with a US release later this year and UK and Australian releases to be announcedExplore more on these topicsNew York film festival 2026First look reviewPaul GiamattiPaul RuddJohn TurturroTom McCarthyDrama filmsPeriod and historical filmsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: TV tonight: Eric Morecambe’s children’s book comes to life | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: The Reluctant Vampire is a fun story starring Lenny Rush. Plus: secrets are spilled in juicy divorce drama The Split Up. Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Hollie Richardson
Headline: The Reluctant Vampire is a fun story starring Lenny Rush. Plus: secrets are spilled in juicy divorce drama The Split Up. Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: No biting … The Reluctant Vampire on BBC One.Photograph: BBCView image in fullscreenNo biting … The Reluctant Vampire on BBC One.Photograph: BBCTV tonightTelevision & radioTV tonight: Eric Morecambe’s children’s book comes to lifeThe Reluctant Vampire is a fun story starring Lenny Rush. Plus: secrets are spilled in juicy divorce drama The Split Up. Here’s what to watch this eveningHollie Richardson,Priya Elan,Phil Harrison,Graeme VirtueandSimon WardellSun 4 Oct 2026 01.15 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 01.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Reluctant Vampire6.40pm, BBC OneFifteen-year-old Valentine (Lenny Rush) grew up thinking he was a really rubbish vampire. But his mother (Sian Clifford) is about to tell him the reason why he doesn’t have bloodlust: he’s actually a human. She asks him not to tell his loving but despairing father (Tom Davis) – the vampire king! Can poor Valentine pull off being the heir to the vampire throne? Neil and Rob Gibbons – the team behind Alan Partridge – have done a fun job of adapting Eric Morecambe’s much-loved children’s book.Hollie RichardsonWagging Rights8pm, U&WHalfway through the competition and we’re into the freestyle challenge. It’s a fully choreographed routine or, as Rhod Gilbert explains, “It’s like Strictly Come Dancing, but with a human and a dog.” With the judges wanting clarity as well as a full spin, will Sara Pascoe and Mouse manage to retain their, erm, lead?Priya ElanThe Split Up9pm, BBC OneView image in fullscreenWedding woes … The Split Up on BBC One.Photograph: BBC/Sister PicturesThe penultimate episode of Ursula Rani Sarma’s family law firm drama arrives, and it’s the morning after the eventful night of spilled secrets before. Aria wakes up in Luke’s bed – and the day ahead involves them working hard on a meaty divorce case with Aria’s husband-to-be. Concludes on Monday.HRThe Blame9pm, ITV1It’s notable how many cop shows currently involve internal malfeasance. Ahead of the return of Line of Duty, this generic but sturdy drama continues to intrigue. This time, Michelle Keegan’s implacable DI Crane finds a suspect slipping through her fingers. But this strengthens her conviction that the real problem lurks within Wakestead station.Phil HarrisonStar Trek: Strange New Worlds10.15pm, ITV1In the year of Star Trek’s 60th anniversary, it’s pleasing that this vibrant streaming hit – a direct prequel to the original series – is getting beamed down to terrestrial TV. Season two begins with Spock (Ethan Peck) behaving in a very Kirk-like fashion by stealing the USS Enterprise to save a crewmate.Graeme VirtueThree Women11pm, Channel 4In a series based on Lisa Taddeo’s nonfiction book, Shailene Woodley plays a writer who follows three women who “had the audacity to believe that they deserved more”. They are homemaker Lina, who starts an affair, Sloane, who is in an open marriage, and Maggie, who had a sexual relationship with her high-school teacher.HRFilm choiceThe Deb,6.15am, 5.45pm, Sky Cinema PremiereView image in fullscreenBrush up! … The Deb on Sky Cinema Premiere.Photograph: Vertigo ReleasingRebel Wilson’s directorial debut is the subject of long-running legal disputes but you wouldn’t know it from watching this sweet, simple musical comedy. It’s set up as a city v country clash: rebellious Sydney teenager Maeve (Charlotte MacInnes) is banished to the bush to stay with farming cousin Taylah (Natalie Abbott) in “the town where feminism has come to die” – and where the debutante ball is still a thing. Issues of body positivity and stifled ambition are showcased in songs with a certain Aussie pep (the first one is titled Fuck My Life).Simon WardellThe Order,10pm, BBC TwoJude Law adds to his recent run of interesting character choices (Putin, Henry VIII, a Star Wars villain) in Justin Kurzel’s gripping fact-based crime thriller. He plays FBI agent Terry Husk, whose new posting to rural Idaho comes with an Aryan Nation splinter group, led by Nicholas Hoult’s charismatic Robert Jay Mathews, who are progressing from counterfeiting and bank robbery to something much bigger. Law’s Husk is a convincingly raddled near has-been but he’s a dog with a bone when he gets a sniff of Mathews’s racist plot.SWThe Crime Is Mine, 12.50am, BBC TwoProlific French director François Ozon is the master of many genres, and the comic melodrama – of which this is his latest – is his most effortlessly enjoyable. In 1935 Paris, struggling actor Madeleine (Nadia Tereszkiewicz) is falsely accused of killing a famous theatre producer. However, aided by her flatmate, lawyer Pauline (Rebecca Marder), she plans to confess to “legitimate defence”, hoping the publicity will be good for both their careers. That is, until Isabelle Huppert’s wrecking ball of a silent film star pops up.SWLive sportWomen’s Super League Football: West Ham v Chelsea, 1.30pm, Sky Sports Main EventMan City v Arsenal is at 4.15pm.Uefa Nations League Football: Wales v Denmark, 7.30pm, BBC TwoAt Cardiff City Stadium.Explore more on these topicsTelevision & radioTV tonightfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Scottish Ensemble review – singular sounds from an ever-adventurous string orchestra | Classical music | The Guardian
description: A contemporary piece by David Fennessy is framed by JS Bach and Arvo Pärt in a show characterised by uncanny sounds and ghostly chorales
Author: Alexandra Coghlan
Headline: A contemporary piece by David Fennessy is framed by JS Bach and Arvo Pärt in a show characterised by uncanny sounds and ghostly chorales
Content: Disarming directness … the Scottish Ensemble.Photograph: Ed Maitland Smith/Ed Maitland Smith/BarbicanView image in fullscreenDisarming directness … the Scottish Ensemble.Photograph: Ed Maitland Smith/Ed Maitland Smith/BarbicanClassical musicReviewScottish Ensemble review – singular sounds from an ever-adventurous string orchestraMilton Court, LondonA contemporary piece by David Fennessy is framed by JS Bach and Arvo Pärt in a show characterised by uncanny sounds and ghostly choralesAlexandra CoghlanSun 4 Oct 2026 09.45 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 13.49 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt’s not every day a concert promises “Bach & Blood”, nor delivers it so thoroughly. There were no massacres from the Scottish Ensemble, mercifully, just a characteristically singular bit of programming from this ever-adventurous string orchestra that framed Irish composer David Fennessy’s 2024 Blood with music by Bach and Arvo Pärt.On 7 July 1720, while JS Bach was away in Carlsbad, his wife Maria Barbara died suddenly, buried before he could return. She was just 35. “Sei solo” – you are alone – the composer wrote at the top of his collection of Sonatas and Partitas for Solo Violin completed soon after. A slip of pen, misspelling “Sei Soli” (six solos), or a deliberate play on words? The intensity of the works – particularly the monumental 15-minute D minor Chaconne, with its weeping chromatic theme – suggest the latter.How touching, then, to hear it (performed with disarming directness by Jonathan Morton) haloed by ghostly chorales, the violin no longer solo but one half of an other-worldly duet. Helga Thoene’s arrangement extrapolates these hymns from fragments within the piece, and the effect is uncanny. The nine talented voices of the Chamber Choir of the National Youth Choir of Scotland (directed by Christopher Bell) weren’t helped by an imbalance among parts, remaining a delicate but distant presence.Voices are just a memory in Pärt’s Greater Antiphons – the composer’s own arrangement of his Sieben Magnificat-Antiphonen for string orchestra. In the absence of counterpoint all emphasis is on texture and gesture, and the Scottish Ensemble mined every relationship between bow and string – percussive, bell-like, husky and half-breathed – to characterise these tiny prayers.View image in fullscreenFrom intense to delicate … the Scottish Ensemble.Photograph: Ed Maitland Smith/Ed Maitland Smith/BarbicanIn many ways the Pärt was the musical dock, leading us gently forward before we were pushed out to sea by the Fennessy. There’s no sight of land to orient the ear in this not-concerto for solo violin, strings and voices, whose seven movements take a Hildegard of Bingen chant “O ruby blood” as their starting point. Morton was a fierce soloist, refusing to tame the composer’s “hard-earned virtuosity”, sending out little pulses of musical electricity that sparked around the ensemble. But for all the work’s prickly complexity, it shares Pärt’s urge towards a single unison pitch – a quest never quite fulfilled, but tantalisingly close in the smudgy echoes of violin and voices that bring Blood to its whispered close.Explore more on these topicsClassical musicreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Undertones review – silver-haired fans get Teenage Kicks once more | Punk | The Guardian
description: Derry’s answer to the Ramones play 30 songs in a breakneck and breathless ride through the punk humour and new-wave surrealism of their repertoire
Author: Katie Hawthorne
Headline: Derry’s answer to the Ramones play 30 songs in a breakneck and breathless ride through the punk humour and new-wave surrealism of their repertoire
Content: Far from sentimental … Paul McLoone and Michael Bradley in the Undertones.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenFar from sentimental … Paul McLoone and Michael Bradley in the Undertones.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianPunkReviewThe Undertones review – silver-haired fans get Teenage Kicks once moreCorn Exchange, EdinburghDerry’s answer to the Ramones play 30 songs in a breakneck and breathless ride through the punk humour and new-wave surrealism of their repertoireKatie HawthorneSun 4 Oct 2026 08.09 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 08.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“This is the first record we ever made. Still sounds good to me,” smiles bassist Mickey Bradley, deliberately downplaying the song released in 1978 that secured the Undertones’ legacy for almost 50 years and counting. Played hard and unceremoniously tonight, Teenage Kicks still sounds lonely, horny, thrilling: it’s the stuff of raw teen spirit, but has also aged poignantly with the Derry band and their now silver-haired audience, with something moving to say about the weight of nostalgia.When brothers John and Damian O’Neill’s guitars crash to a halt, many in the crowd are hugging – but the Undertones are already on to the next. This anniversary tour is far from sentimental: ripping through 30 songs in 90 minutes, it’s a breakneck ride through the punk humour, new-wave surrealism and open vulnerability of their first two albums.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSleeve NotesGet music news, bold reviews and unexpected extras. Every genre, every era, every weekEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenCrashing guitars … lead guitarist Damian O’Neill, whose brother John plays rhythm.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianYou’ve Got My Number (Why Don’t You Use It!), with its bouncing, fidgety frustration, remains an all-timer about waiting by the phone, while Male Model rages against a penny-pinched fashion crisis with a tongue-in-cheek, Ramones-y chorus. There’s surfy guitar and barbershop harmonies on (She’s a) Runaround, mixed with slice-of-life commentary about a girl dithering her life away, and the quiet tragedy of Jimmy Jimmy buried beneath that earworm melody. All the while drummer Billy Doherty is flying, holding the band to a breathless pace.The first incarnation of the Undertones lasted just eight years, and when they returned in 1999 it was without quivery-voiced frontman,Feargal Sharkey. Singer Paul McLoone was a savvy recruitment – he pulls off the shaky, brittle vocals that some of their classics demand, but is otherwise an entirely distinct performer. Tonight he’s flamboyant, cutting flamenco shapes with his arms twisted in the air, and his richer voice brings out the hip-shaking, even glam, qualities of rock’n’roll tracks such as Get Over You and (relatively) newer cut 2003’s Thrill Me.Despite its morbid title, unreleased newbie Time is Terminal accelerates faster still – as if the band are playing to outrun that teenage legacy, rather than indulge it. Are teenage dreams so hard to beat? Bus-pass punk feels just as essential. Here’s to the next 50 years.The Undertonesare touring the UK and Ireland.Explore more on these topicsPunkPop and rockreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘We have been dispossessed’: Nick Hayes on land rights and a peaceful revolution at the real Toad Hall | Books | The Guardian
description: The co-founder of the Right to Roam campaign and author of The Book of Trespass discusses the Oxfordshire riverside community he calls home and how Hardwick Hall has been taken back by the people
Author: Patrick Barkham
Headline: The co-founder of the Right to Roam campaign and author of The Book of Trespass discusses the Oxfordshire riverside community he calls home and how Hardwick Hall has been taken back by the people
Content: Nick Hayes at the Hardwick Estate.Photograph: Megan Eagles/The GuardianView image in fullscreenNick Hayes at the Hardwick Estate.Photograph: Megan Eagles/The GuardianBooksInterview‘We have been dispossessed’: Nick Hayes on land rights and a peaceful revolution at the real Toad HallPatrick BarkhamThe co-founder of the Right to Roam campaign and author of The Book of Trespass discusses the Oxfordshire riverside community he calls home and how Hardwick Hall has been taken back by the peopleSun 4 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn the banks of the Thames in South Oxfordshire, the Hardwick estate has been owned by the Rose family for generations. When Sir Charles Rose, a banker, sportsman, yachtsman and aviator, sped through the lanes in his Rolls-Royce in the early days of motoring, heinspired Kenneth Grahameto create Mr Toad in The Wind in the Willows. Grahame’s character became a symbol of decadent aristocracy whose foolishness leads to the temporary loss of a fine house to weasel-socialists.Now Toad Hall has been taken over for good and Nick Hayes, artist, writer and co-founder of the Right to Roam campaign, has had a riverside view of this striking turn of events. When Hayes, who lives on a beautiful wide-beamed barge on the Thames, became the Hardwick estate’s artist-in-residence, he discovered that Rose’s heirs are, in effect, disinheriting themselves. The estate is gradually being turned into a charity which will be run by the tenants and the alternative community that has grown up in its shelter.The story of this peaceful revolution unfolds in his new book, The Medicine Tree, a sweeping alternative history of England that reaches across the globe for examples of colonial oppression and Indigenous enlightenment. Hayes poses some big questions. Why do English people lack a culture of connection with their land? And how might we forge a new one?Indigenous societies have stories, songs, philosophies and religions that bind them to their terrain. Such sacred traditions are still alive in many countries and can encourage modern societies to live sustainably, resist pollution and extraction, or create assertive legal rights for nature, as established on New Zealand’s Whanganui River. It is “an act of extreme exceptionalism to suppose that we were the only country on Earth not to have had a spiritual, mythopoetic relationship with the land,” Hayes writes.“If we were to look at English history through a colonial prism, we’d start to see ourselves as people that have been dispossessed as well,” he says, as we talk inside his cosy boat, swallows dipping over the water. “Community and ecology are the two big losses. England is in desperate need of repair in terms of epidemics of loneliness, in terms of one in six species going extinct.”There was no one moment when England’s land culture was lost, Hayes argues, but “a very steady letting of England’s veins” over 2,000 years: Christianity took away animism, while myth and folklore was lost with enclosure and the agricultural and industrial revolutions. The Medicine Tree is his attempt to plot a recreation of a useful English land culture: not nationalistic, not nostalgic and not off-the-peg folklore as invented by, say, Robert Graves in The White Goddess.Hayes was inspired by poet and storyteller Hugh Lupton’s idea of “restorying the landscape” to take one local tree, his “medicine tree”, as a symbol of his story. This soaring tree, beside the busy Thames path, turns out to be a hybrid of a (native) black poplar and an eastern cottonwood, brought to Europe from North America by French colonists. It invites a comparison between disparate cultures, not least because in both Indigenous and old European societies the poplar stood for community.Hayes grew up near here in the 80s and 90s. When we meet he is wearing a grubby pink vest adorned with an image of the Cerne Abbas giant and has just watched two boys jump into the water from the pretty, white-painted bridge that dinks over the river at Pangbourne. The elder boy led the way with a back-flip; his nervous younger brother eventually following with a maiden jump. “Did you see that?” he says. “It was so beautiful.”It is an idyllic scene but it is also bittersweet. The Thames has sewage discharged into it by privatised water companies and the bridge, nicknamed “the troll bridge” by locals, is an anachronistic privately owned toll bridge, which causes traffic jams every morning as motorists queue to pay 60p to cross the Thames. The bridge belongs to a company owned by a family who can trace their ancestry to one of William the Conqueror’s barons. Hayes estimates this local waster of everyone’s time enriches the company by more than £1m each year.View image in fullscreen‘I wanted to lean into the whole story as a fairytale, a folktale’ … Nick Hayes.Photograph: Megan Eagles/The GuardianThe English mostly accept such states of affairs as normal, natural and possibly even desirable. When Hayes was young, he couldn’t wait to escape this “affluent, middle-class” suburban environment and assumed he would never return. He had no real connection with the land, or nature, until university, where he was taught by Robert Macfarlane. After reading Macfarlane’s book The Wild Places, he cycled from Cambridge to wild-camp on the Gog Magog hills outside the city. “I felt like a weirdo bedding down, had a joint because I didn’t know if I’d sleep, and woke up having had a gorgeous night. The membrane burst in my head,” he says. He began camping with friends in fields and forests, trespassing, and learning more about the land.In 2020, he and Guy Shrubsole founded the Right to Roam campaign, seeking a responsible right of access to the 92% of land in England and Wales we are now excluded from. Hayes put his vision inThe Book of Trespass, a strikingly original, bullishly well-written declaration of the benefits and responsibilities that could flow from people being granted more access to private land. In the years since, Right to Roam has held more than 15 peaceful mass trespasses and defended attempts to restrict access by major landowners, including a court battle by a hedge fund manager seeking to curb wild camping rights on Dartmoor.double quotation markWhen people come to the country, it doesn’t take them long to shed their need for a mobile phone, to shed their post-industrial mindThe Medicine Tree follows Hayes’s journey home, living on his boat (because no artist could afford a house in this London commuter belt), and discovery of Hardwick, where an alternative community of around 90 tenants renting on the estate has slowly coalesced over several decades. On learning how their family wealth was ultimately derived from colonial extraction and exploitation in North America, the sibling heirs to the land have decided to turn it into a charity, andEngland’s first community-owned estate.In The Medicine Tree, the members of this community are named only after their occupations: the Dyer, the Head Grower, the Heiress. “I wanted to lean into the whole story as a fairytale, a folk-tale,” says Hayes. Unlike much contemporary nonfiction, Hayes does not fill the book with himself but instead directs his rage at the “taxidermied corpse” of English heritage, with its country houses that are “decorative manhole covers on a system of sewerage that drained, and still drains, the wealth of England and the world”.Hayes strikes me as a natural rebel, but he bristles at this for the same reason he doesn’t like being described as “a campaigner”: he thinks it diminishes taking a rational stand against an issue by suggesting it is a personality trait. That said, he read Christopher Hitchens’s Letters to a Young Contrarian “about 15 times”. He has always opposed “unfair or pointless rules. The big thing for me is orthodoxies so deep-set that they don’t even seem to be rules any more.” He points to a “Danger! Adders in this area” sign, one of many trophies that ornament his boat. “The purpose of that sign is to keep people out of their land, not warn people of adders. I would suggest that most adders are unsigned. All of these things can embed in our operating system.”What’s also embedded in England’s exclusionary, profit-making system of land ownership are landowners’ rights. Hayes tells of his community’s (daring, futile) attempts to stop the no-fault, short-notice eviction of the Carver and his family from their home on a neighbouring estate. “Losing a family who have done nothing but contribute to this valley for 26 years made me realise that eviction is not just an action against one family but an action against a community. The thing that makes me contrarian is that we just accept it. There doesn’t have to be a society where eviction is seen as the landowner’s right.”How do we reforge a culture of connection with the land? More land rights would help, says Hayes, but so would more time on the land. “I’m not suggesting that everyone needs to be a basket weaver, but when people come to the country from the town, it does not take them long to shed their need for a mobile phone, to shed their post-industrial mind.”As night falls, people from all over Hardwick emerge from the darkness to gather in a circle on the banks of the Thames beside Hayes’s boat. They bring guitars and accordions and even a saxophone. Songs are played and stories are told.“I’m wondering if land culture just grows like weeds,” says Hayes. “This English obsession with ancient heritage is tripping us up. Put people together with a certain amount of freedom, rights and responsibilities – work, duties, stuff to do on the land. People are going to start talking. People are going to start singing.”The Medicine Tree: Repairing the Rotten Roots of England by Nick Hayes is published by Allen Lane. To support the Guardian order your copy atguardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.Explore more on these topicsBooksScience and nature booksfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Antigone Exits review – emotions run high in experimental reworking of Greek tragedy | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Nina Segal’s revisiting of the Sophoclean story is pleasingly experimental – but not all the ideas work in Jeff James’s fourth-wall breaking production
Author: Holly O'Mahony
Headline: Nina Segal’s revisiting of the Sophoclean story is pleasingly experimental – but not all the ideas work in Jeff James’s fourth-wall breaking production
Content: Blurred boundaries … Max-Bennett as Creon in Antigone Exits.Photograph: Andy ParadiseView image in fullscreenBlurred boundaries … Max-Bennett as Creon in Antigone Exits.Photograph: Andy ParadiseTheatreReviewAntigone Exits review – emotions run high in experimental reworking of Greek tragedyMinerva theatre, ChichesterNina Segal’s revisiting of the Sophoclean story is pleasingly experimental – but not all the ideas work in Jeff James’s fourth-wall breaking productionHolly O'MahonySun 4 Oct 2026 06.43 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLibations were typically poured to appease the gods and honour the dead in Ancient Greece, but as a black, tar-like substance is dribbled here, forming a runny circle on a bright yellow stage, the image conjures danger. It’s befitting for the court of this particular King Creon (Max Bennett), whose condemnation of his niece Antigone (Nina Cassells) after she defies him in retrieving her brother’s body for burial, is framed as an inability to even question let alone reconsider his own laws. The tar circle becomes a dividing line, separating the hypothetically welcome from the unwelcome in Thebes. The line is eventually crossed in more ways than one, and the oily substance spreads, smearing those irrevocably affected by the mess.Nina Segal’s revisiting of the Sophoclean tragedy is keen to explore the far-reaching consequences of our actions and their trickle-down effects. It’s pleasingly experimental, but not all ideas coalesce in Jeff James’s production, in which a combination of fourth wall breaking and direct address sees the boundaries blur further. Cast members break away from their Greek characters to relay anecdotes that could well be their own. Reaching for a mic that hangs suspended above the stage, one tells of watching a fox decompose, another of a husband dying and another of his teenage daughter’s suicide. The stories are moving, even if links to Antigone’s own plight are somewhat tenuous.View image in fullscreenTimeless appeal … Alex Lowde’s set.Photograph: Andy ParadiseAn emphasis is placed on emotions over actions, but having each key player describe their anger, fear or sadness, rather than showing us, has a distancing effect that prevents this production from striking the chords it might. Watching them mine seemingly personal memories in order to find a connection to these centuries-old characters is a little like watching a workshop in method acting.There’s a timeless appeal to Alex Lowde’s set, which features a giant hollowed-out eggshell structure, out of which the cast emerges one by one to take up their positions, as if born into the play. Later it becomes the cave through which Antigone vanishes, and as the rest look on, we’re reminded again of what lingers – physically and emotionally – after death.Antigone Exitsruns at the Minerva theatre, Chichester, until 17 October.Explore more on these topicsTheatreSophoclesChichester Festival theatrereviewsShareReuse this content

title: Wakaliga Uganda review – a blistering superhero movie with hardboiled cops and a nefarious ‘girl with a voluminous bum’ | Art and design | The Guardian
description: A young man possessed by the spirit of a mythical Buganda warrior leads the film-making collective’s explosive new diatribe against the theft of cultural artefacts – with the help of a ‘video joker’
Author: Ben Eastham
Headline: A young man possessed by the spirit of a mythical Buganda warrior leads the film-making collective’s explosive new diatribe against the theft of cultural artefacts – with the help of a ‘video joker’
Content: A message without jeopardising the entertainment … Wakaliga Uganda: Kibuuka Omumbaale.Photograph: Courtesy of the artistView image in fullscreenA message without jeopardising the entertainment … Wakaliga Uganda: Kibuuka Omumbaale.Photograph: Courtesy of the artistArt and designReviewWakaliga Uganda review – a blistering superhero movie with hardboiled cops and a nefarious ‘girl with a voluminous bum’Chisenhale Gallery, LondonA young man possessed by the spirit of a mythical Buganda warrior leads the film-making collective’s explosive new diatribe against the theft of cultural artefacts – with the help of a ‘video joker’Ben EasthamSun 4 Oct 2026 03.04 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 03.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWakaliga Uganda makes action movies with a cast from the Kampala streets, props built out of scrap, desktop special effects and a bucketload of wit. The studio’s breakout hit,Who Killed Captain Alex?, followed a martial arts master on a mission for revenge against the mafiosi who killed his brother, a Ugandan military officer sent to clean up the capital’s slums. Featuring helicopter gunships, shootouts and kung fu showdowns, and reportedly made for a few hundred dollars, this blockbuster bears little relation to the films you might expect to find in an art gallery (setting aside the shoestring budgets). Which is to say, it is very good fun to watch.Founded by Harriet Nakasujja and Isaac Nabwana, the film studio also known as Wakaliwood came to the attention of the wider art world in 2017 when it was included in the German art festivalDocumenta. That influential show was part of a general turn towards the culture being made by independent collectives outside Europe and North America, especially those that pioneer unconventional ways to fund their activities (indicatively, the studio used the money to install fibre-optic cables in its neighbourhood). Its entry on to the international art circuit brought higher production value and – if the new commission now showing at the Chisenhale is any guide – a subtle shift in direction and purpose.View image in fullscreenDesigned to provoke emotions … Kibuuka OmumbaaleBecause while its previous films addressed the residents of the Wakaliga neighbourhood,Kibuuka Omumbaalespeaks to an international – and specifically British – audience. The 40-minute film is named after a mythical warrior of the Buganda kingdom (now a region in Uganda that includes Kampala) whose relics were removed by an Anglican missionary to Cambridge University in 1906. The remains were returned to Uganda the year before its independence in 1962, setting a precedent for the restitution of looted objects that UK museums have proved notoriously reluctant to follow.Clearly, there is the material here for a lecture on the evils of colonial expropriation and the ethical imperatives of restitution. Yet Wakaliwood has produced something considerably more complex and persuasive, designed to provoke its audience’s emotions as well as prick their consciences. In practice, this means telling the story as a blistering superhero movie featuring hardboiled detectives, courageous women, corrupt politicians, a nefarious “girl with a voluminous bum” and much else besides. It begins when a young man visiting the remains of Kibuuka Omumbaale is possessed with the warrior’s spirit. There is an important precedent for this: in the 1950s, a Ugandan truck driver had the same experience and became a key figure in the anticolonial resistance.View image in fullscreenReady for a showdown … Kibuuka OmumbaaleHis possession enables him to fly around the city and, according to a liberal reinterpretation of the warrior’s powers, zap death rays from his fingers. Unfortunately, the negative aspects of Kibuuka have been incarnated in another young man, a doppelganger bent on evil. Concerned journalists look to local folklorists and museum curators for answers, allowing the film-makers to embed some history lessons without jeopardising the entertainment. As the president calls in the helicopter gunships, it becomes clear that the disaster can be averted only by reconciling good and bad aspects of the past – by means of an explosive showdown.Essential to the film’s appeal and meaning (as in all good art, they are inseparable) is that it comes with two soundtracks. Over the conventional mix of dialogue, sound effects and music plays a disembodied voice that tells jokes, makes asides, casts aspersions and offers a running interpretation of what’s happening. This device derives from the tradition of screening films in Kampala to the live accompaniment of “video jokers” (VJs), whose entirely free translations of foreign-language films make them local celebrities.View image in fullscreenThey seize control of the narrative … Kibuuka OmumbaaleIn earlier Wakaliwood productions, the VJ might, for example, play for laughs by suggesting that a torture victim is being punished for the unforgivable crime “of watching Nigerian films”. On this occasion, Kampala’s first English-language VJ (most speak Luganda) mixes very funny interjections with repeated reminders that “this is how we watch films in Uganda!”. Shown without frills on a screen before painted bleachers, it is nonetheless hard to avoid the sense that this new work lacks some of the anarchic local energy of the original films. But this is something of which the film-makers are acutely aware: there is a history, after all, of the British removing cultural artefacts from the country to exoticise them.So they seize control of the narrative, and the opportunity to speak back. Yet rather than simply railing against the theft of a cultural artefact, they draw on everything from Cantonese kung fu to Hollywood popcorn movies to bring that heritage back into the cosmopolitan present. In the process they reclaim a local hero from the mausoleum of the colonial museum and put him back into the service of the Wakaliga community (battling corruption, femicide, inequality) without shying away from the ethical conflicts of precolonial history. As 20th-century art movements from cubism to expressionism were invigorated by indigenous traditions, so artists in Kampala and elsewhere are transforming the moribund cultures of the west into something richer, stranger and better fitted to the historical moment. Wakaliga Uganda is the model of a thriving culture: fearless, hybrid, irreverent and popular.AtChisenhale Gallery, London, until 6 DecemberExplore more on these topicsArt and designUgandaColonialismMuseumsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Dining across the divide: ‘Without being patronising, I think as he grows older he’ll tune in to the damage “free speech” can do’ | Life and style | The Guardian
description: Did a Tory voter who opposes all censorship offend a leftwinger concerned about how people treat one another?
Author: Zoe Williams
Headline: Did a Tory voter who opposes all censorship offend a leftwinger concerned about how people treat one another?
Content: Ted and Nicky. All photographs: Alicia Canter/The GuardianView image in fullscreenTed and Nicky. All photographs: Alicia Canter/The GuardianDining across the divideLife and styleDining across the divide: ‘Without being patronising, I think as he grows older he’ll tune in to the damage “free speech” can do’Did a Tory voter who opposes all censorship offend a leftwinger concerned about how people treat one another?Want to meet someone from across the divide? Clickhereto find out howZoe WilliamsSun 4 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleView image in fullscreenTed, 24, LondonOccupationWorks for a thinktankVoting recordConservativeAmuse boucheTed does am dram with Loughborough’s Festival Players – probably his biggest part was in The Railway Children in 2019View image in fullscreenNicky, 58, EssexOccupationExecutive coachVoting recordMostly Labour; will vote tactically for Lib Dem, but after Nick Clegg really has to think about itAmuse boucheNicky’s mum and dad met at a Louis Armstrong concert in Malawi. He was helping with independence and her grandparents ran a hostel on the top of Zomba mountainFor startersNickyHe was a really lovely, warm, enthusiastic human being. Obviously considerably younger than me.TedShe was basically what I expected. It was a very pleasant evening.NickyBecause I knew it was Italian, I was homing in on the tiramisu.TedI had a sirloin steak.View image in fullscreenThe big beefTedI am a free speech absolutist – I don’t believe in any restrictions whatsoever. Things such as the Communications Act 2003 and the Online Safety Act 2023 are resulting in huge numbers of arrests for speech offences. You start by criminalising things most of us would agree were abhorrent, but it’s the thin end of the wedge. You end up seeing people arrested for perfectly valid points of view, things that are relatively tame.NickyI challenged him on a lot of things, and he did have caveats. For instance, he had quite strong views on abortion, but he didn’t necessarily believe people making that difficult decision should be hounded. When you pushed him on detail, on the moral implications, on the silent mental damage of unchecked free speech, he did say there’s a time and a place for saying what you think. Without sounding patronising, I think as he grows older he will tune into the damage you can do.TedShe raised the point of people in her family who would be caused serious mental harm if others were allowed to express their opinions freely to them. I think being able to take offence is not a right, or certainly more important is the right to say what you want. I want to know who holds abhorrent views, rather than it be pushed underground. I want to look my enemy in the face.NickyIf you stand in front of somebody and diminish them, and do that enough, the toll that takes means there will be suicides and anguish that you will never see the numbers on. Do I believe the government should tell us everything we need to do and say? No. We are in a democracy. But we should also treat others as we’d wish to be treated ourselves.View image in fullscreenSharing plateNickyOn healthcare, he was spouting the example of Norwegian and other countries’ semi-insurance policies, and I said: “This just drives us to the US position.” I’m a base-level healthcare believer: there’s a duty of care and any emergency should be dealt with. And he agreed with that.TedI expressed my desire to abolish the NHS and replace it with a social insurance model. This would still have provision for free treatment at the point of need, but people would pay through insurance systems, and they would choose the level of cover they’ve got. Those models deliver far better outcomes for patients.View image in fullscreenFor aftersNickyHe loves the monarchy. Look, given the chance, I’d probably vote “no” to keeping them. But I do respect the fact they bring in huge amounts of tourism and I don’t really resent state payments, so long as it’s for work. I haven’t got an issue with the security cost, either. But do I think people should be born into privilege and power? No. He did say, at one point, “When is enough? For these ultra-rich people, what will be enough?” That showed a sensitive side, and I really warmed to him.TedIt’s not the people, it’s the institution that I love. I think it’s fundamental to the system of governance of this country, which led to us being so strong. Not just the monarchy, but the constitution as a whole and a parliament that is sovereign. It’s worked for 1,000 years.View image in fullscreenTakeawaysTedWe both said it had been a really interesting and fun evening and we were glad we’d done it.NickyHe was a lovely human being. I think he’ll evolve – he’s one to watch!View image in fullscreenAdditional reporting: Kitty DrakeNicky and Ted ate atAlfiin London, E1Want to meet someone from across the divide?Find out how to take partExplore more on these topicsLife and styleDining across the divideSocial trendsHealthMonarchyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: John Cooper Clarke looks back: ‘Getting older sucks – it’s marginally better than being dead’ | Family | The Guardian
description: The punk poet on his heroin years, dressing like Ronnie Wood, and achieving his boyhood ambition
Author: Harriet Gibsone
Headline: The punk poet on his heroin years, dressing like Ronnie Wood, and achieving his boyhood ambition
Content: FlashbackFamilyJohn Cooper Clarke looks back: ‘Getting older sucks – it’s marginally better than being dead’The punk poet on his heroin years, dressing like Ronnie Wood, and achieving his boyhood ambitionHarriet GibsoneSun 4 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJohn Cooper Clarke in 1957, wearing a cowboy hat and shirt, and holding a toy gun, and recreating the picture in 2026,John Cooper Clarke in 1957 and 2026. Later photograph: Pål Hansen. Styling: Andie Redman. Grooming: Alice Theobald at Arlington Artists. Archive photograph: courtesy of John Cooper ClarkeBorn in Salford in 1949,John Cooper Clarkeis a poet and author. He cut his teeth in the clubs of Manchester before signing to Epic Records in 1978. He performed alongside the Sex Pistols, Joy Division, the Buzzcocks and Elvis Costello, scoring a UK Top 40 hit with Gimmix! Play Loud in 1979. His poem Evidently Chickentown was later used in The Sopranos, introducing him to a whole new generation, and his work is now on the GCSE English syllabus. As well as three poetry collections he published a memoir, I Wanna Be Yours, in 2020. His new poetry collection, Have It, is out now and he is touring the UK until 27 November.This is me dressed up as a cowboywith a hat and six-shooter.Not the full schmear with the chaps and all the rest, but the best I could do. I was crazy about westerns. Still am, actually. My uncle Dennis was the only camera-owning relative at the time, so he would have taken the photo in our apartment above a chemist’s shop in Salford, located on a busy traffic intersection.My childhood is an ever-fading mystery to me, but somewhere around this time I know I got diagnosed with tuberculosis. Something serious like that takes you out of the world, but once I stopped coughing up arterial blood and scar tissue it wasn’t a problem. I stopped going to school, which was great, and not before I’d learned the rudiments of literacy. Really it happened at an opportune moment in that all that I had any energy to do was read.Once I had recovered, life went back to normal, and I went back to hating every minute of school. Apart from when I was in the company of my teacher, Mr Malone. He was the one who introduced me to poetry as a phonetic medium. He didn’t single me out as a boy genius or anything like that, but he did convey to the entire class a love of poetry. He read it out loud and we had to learn it off by heart. I would have to stand up and reiterate whatever verse he requested.I was a mod in my teenage years– dissatisfied with everything all the time, aside from music, girls and clothes.Poetry, too. One day we had these career officers in, asking us what we wanted to do. I didn’t get any encouragement when I said that I wanted to be a professional poet. They said: “You can’t make a living out of poetry, blah, blah, blah.” When I told my dad, he replied: “Name one poet that’s ever made a living.” The way he saw it, every poet was just swinging the lead. “Get a job,” was his advice. “Keep poetry as a hobby.” But I was determined I could somehow make a living in the entertainment industry.I knew I had to apply for grants from governmental bodies, but as someone who isn’t very good at filling in forms, close to phobic, I didn’t fancy that route. In any case, I didn’t think I would be very successful, as I had already sent my stuff to publishers, with a view to them putting my poems in some kind of anthology of modern verse. Of course, it didn’t happen, because who was I? I realised the best way was to declaim my poetry in public at various places of entertainment. That’s been my MO ever since. For most of my career, I’ve been a club act.double quotation markThe boy in the picture would be thrilled to know he was making a living while not actually having a jobFrom the very start I’ve known that presentation is important– especially because I’m taking poetry into the world of showbusiness. A place where people don’t think it should exist. I went to see the Birds in 1965. Ronnie Wood had spiky, unruly hair, and a big beak nose like me. I figured: he looks good, I’ll go for that. I’ve been dressing vaguely like him ever since.Bernard Manning gave me my first ever paid gig. He tried to put me off at first, though. I went into the Embassy Club in Manchester in the afternoon knowing that he’d be free. He said, “What is it you do?” I told him it was poetry. He said, “They don’t like poetry here, kid. Half of them can’t fucking read.” Still, he gave me 15 minutes, and I was met with the poet’s worst enemy: indifference. Nobody shouted anything rude out, nobody threw anything. I was faced with an audience of people who were not interested and conversed with each other instead. That’s about as bad as it gets.By the time I went to the cabaret joints in the centre of Manchester in the mid-70s I was prepared for anything. It wasn’t until I met Howard Devoto, who was then the singer with the Buzzcocks, who said, “What are you doing pottering around in these cheesy cabaret joints, Jonny? You should be working with us in the world of punk rock.” After that, I started moving around with the Buzzcocks and the Fall, and went from strength to strength. The punk world held no terrors after the Embassy Club.The 80s were my wilderness years. Punk rock only lasted for two years, then it lost its fun and style. The 80s was about conspicuous consumption, expensive promotional videos and new romanticism. Nothing wrong with any of those things, but when it got sleek, I realised anything punk was a non-starter. I suffered for that, but I never stopped working. I had to work to get money, to get dope. Most people avoided heroin because they didn’t like the idea of injecting themselves. But I was straight in with the hypodermic. I preferred the sterility of the intravenous. Looking back, it is almost as though somebody else did all that – and I’ve got nothing but regrets. Heroin was a stupid thing to do.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionActor and writer Paterson Joseph: ‘Tilda Swinton asked me a question that changed everything that came next’Read moreEverything changed in the 1990s.I met Evie, the woman who would go on to be my wife, but I was still using junk, so it was the longest engagement ever. Eventually I went to rehab, and then we had our daughter Stella. I was used to erratic hours anyway, so having a baby didn’t bother me, and it was a lot of fun having a kid. The next thing was my poem Evidently Chickentown being used for the credits of The Sopranos. The new wave of people discovering my poems felt sensational. Later on Arctic Monkeys adapted my poem I Wanna Be Yours. I also started going to America again, which I hadn’t done for 30 years, due to convictions of one kind or another. All of which improved my life completely.I still love writing poetry, but getting older sucks. It’s marginally better than being dead. I’m totally computer illiterate. I’m not a modern guy, in any sense of the word. But I remain quite a careful dresser. I’ve got standards. I don’t know why people sit down at a particular age and think: “I’d better stop looking like that.” Not me. I’ve got to maintain my front so I can keep making my game.On the plus side, I get to perform at large theatres now. And TV’s never been better. Bangers and Cash, Wheeler Dealers. Portillo’s Railway Journeys is what I like. He takes us to those places too distant for the bike.The boy in the picture would be thrilled to know he was making a living while not actually having to have a job. That was always my ambition: remunerative idleness. Idleness where people pay you for the results of your idle hours. So I got what I wanted.Explore more on these topicsFamilyFlashbackJohn Cooper ClarkePoetryPhotographyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: How to make the perfect zuppa di cozze – recipe | Shellfish | The Guardian
description: A tomatoey, southern Italian alternative to moules marinière – but who makes the definitive version?
Author: Felicity Cloake
Headline: A tomatoey, southern Italian alternative to moules marinière – but who makes the definitive version?
Content: Felicity Cloake’s perfectzuppa di cozze.Photograph: Dan Jones/The Guardian. Food styling: Stevie Taylor.View image in fullscreenFelicity Cloake’s perfectzuppa di cozze.Photograph: Dan Jones/The Guardian. Food styling: Stevie Taylor.How to cook the perfect ...ShellfishHow to make the perfect zuppa di cozze – recipeA tomatoey, southern Italian alternative to moules marinière – but who makes the definitive version?Felicity CloakeSun 4 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 08.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAbundant, good value and ready in minutes, mussels are one of my favourite seafoods, but when it comes to preparing them, I rarely look farther than northern France. Italians, of course, also eat mussels, and this tomato-rich recipe is a particular favourite in the south –Neapolitans traditionally tuck intozuppa di cozzeon Maundy Thursday but it’s found on menus all year round. With its bold flavours and oily, garlicky sauce, it’s a great alternative to creamymoules marinières, and similarly needs no accompaniment but a hunk of bread to make a meal, though chips, of course, are rarely unwelcome.The musselsView image in fullscreen‘Specifically Neapolitan’: Giallo Zafferano’s zuppa di cozze. All thumbnail photographs byFelicity Cloake.There’s not much to say about the main ingredient, except to bemoan the increasing difficulty in getting hold of live mussels due to the disappearance of so many fresh fish vendors, and the subsequent closure of supermarket fish counters (another rant for another day). Any remaining fishmongers should have British mussels, orthey can easily be bought online. Don’t wash them until you’re ready to cook, when you should dump them in the sink and sort through them, discarding any with broken shells or that don’t close when you give them a sharp tap. Rinse with cold water; most mussels on the market are farmed, and rope-grown, so should be pretty clean, and I’ve never seen the point of scrubbing away at barnacles for hours when you’re not going to be eating the shells anyway (though please do enlighten me as to why I should bother). Remove any remaining trailing beards, though – I do have some standards!The Silver Spoondry-fries the mussels, then shells them to add to the soup later, while theGiallo Zafferano websitesteams them in garlicky oil and a little white wine, then removes them from the pot to be returned to the finished soup. It makes more sense to me to eat them as freshly cooked as possible – asElizabeth Davidcautions in Italian Food, these “final operations must be carried out only immediately before serving”. Not only does this leave less chance of the shellfish overcooking, but necessarily ensures that every last drop of that delicious mussel liquor makes it into the sauce; tipping it back and forth, as in the Zafferano recipe, risks sacrificing a little, and when there’s not a lot to start with, that’s a gamble I’m not prepared to take.View image in fullscreenFor her zuppa di cozze, Elizabeth David insists that the steaming of the mussels ‘must be carried out only immediately before serving’.Zafferano, whose recipe is specifically Neapolitan, includes octopus, squid and prawns alongside the mussels. Delicious as all those things are, we find the squid and prawns are overcooked and rubbery once they’ve been fried and then simmered in tomato sauce for 15 minutes. If you’d like to include them, I’d fry them briefly first, then return them to the pan right at the end (and buy the octopus ready-cooked, if you can).The baseDavid and the Silver Spoon are the only ones to use onions as the base of their dishes, with the former also including celery. More common is garlic in more or less generous amounts – Zafferano simply uses it to flavour the oil, whileMarcella Hazan, perhaps reflecting the more Italian-American milieu in which she was writing The Essentials of Classic Italian Cuisine, sticks in a whole teaspoon and a half of the stuff, finely minced. I like the fiery flavour, especially alongside the chilli she also includes, plus this feels like a dish that should pack a punch.View image in fullscreenBenedetta Rossi’s zuppa di cozze uses cherry tomatoes but is ‘a bit light on sauce’.And that also applies when it comes to the tomatoes. Hazan uses tinned, and reduces them to a jammy, oily sauce before adding the bivalves, a similar approach to David, but the latter’s more watery fresh fruit (and seeded summer san marzano plum tomatoes are about as far from watery as you’re likely to get) yields a lighter, fresher flavour. My favourites, however, are the cherry tomatoes suggested byBenedetta Rossiof the Fatto di Casa da Benedetta website, because they strike a good balance between the intensity of the tinned variety and the zingy acidity of plum tomatoes. My recipe uses a few more than Rossi’s, though, because we find her version a bit light on sauce, and cooks them for a little longer, in homage to Hazan.The Silver Spoon flavours the base with saffron, Hazan chilli and parsley (Rossi adds the stalks, reserving the leaves as a garnish), and David suggests fresh marjoram, thyme or basil. I really like the echoes of Mediterranean French fish soups that the saffron brings with it, but my testers are ambivalent as to its merits, so I’ll leave that one up to you. Herbs, I think, are better used on top; not only do they look pretty against the glossy black shells and vivid sauce, but the peppery flavour of the parsley gets lost in the heat.The liquidView image in fullscreenSilver Spoon’s zuppa di cozze is more of a soup that’s garnished with mussels.Not all recipes add extra liquid – the mussels give off enough to make a sauce, but it’s fairly scanty, so it makes sense to dilute it a little so everyone gets a decent spoonful alongside the shells. Wine is popular, used by David (who also adds a little water), Zafferano andEdinburgh’s Contini, while the Silver Spoon, whose recipe is more of a mussel soup garnished with a few actual bivalves than a pot of mussels, goes for fish stock. If you don’t drink, then this, with a spritz of lemon juice, is a decent substitute, but the zesty acidity of a crisp white is the ideal, not least because you can then drink it as an accompaniment.Serving suggestionView image in fullscreenFelicity Cloake’s perfect zuppa di cozze.Peppery parsley looks good, and tastes great, according to those who like it better than I do (if you share my aversion, you might like to experiment with mint, thyme or basil), and the garlicky toasts that pop up in the Silver Spoon, Hazan and Zafferano’s recipes are the perfect accompaniment, whether you want to spoon the mussels on top, so the bread soaks up their liquid, or serve it on the side to mop up the end of the sauce.Perfect zuppa di cozzePrep10 minCook15 minServes22 garlic cloves500g cherry tomatoes3 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil, plus extra to serve1 pinch dried chilli flakes(optional)1 pinch saffron(optional)Salt800g live mussels2 tbsp white wine, or dry vermouth or fish stock2 thick slices crusty bread1 small bunch flat-leaf parsley, to serveFinely chop one and a half cloves of garlic. Cut the tomatoes in half. Heat the oil on a medium flame in a saucepan large enough eventually to hold all the mussels, then fry the garlic and chilli, if using, until pale golden.View image in fullscreenFelicity Cloake’s perfect zuppa di cozzePhotograph: Felicity Cloake/The GuardianStir in the tomatoes, saffron, if using, and a pinch of salt, then turn down the heat a little and cook until soft and pulpy. You can prepare the dish ahead up to this point if needed.For this recipe, I’m assuming you’ve bought your mussels; should you have gathered them yourself, however, you’ll need to purge them in salt water overnight first, to get rid of any grit (havea look online for specific instructions).View image in fullscreenEither way, just before cooking, tip the mussels into a large colander and give them a good rinse with cold water. Sort through them, discarding any with broken shells or that don’t close when given a sharp tap (unless you can see the creature moving within). Scrub off any dirty patches (and barnacles, if you wish), and give any trailing beards (the weedy bits hanging out of the side of the shell) a sharp tug to pull them off.View image in fullscreenAdd the wine to the pan, turn up the heat, then tip in the mussels. Cover and leave to cook, shaking the pan occasionally, for five to eight minutes, until most of them have opened (discard any that do not).View image in fullscreenMeanwhile, grill or toast the bread, then rub it with the remaining half-clove of raw garlic and drizzle with oil. Finely chop the parsley.View image in fullscreenDivide the bread between serving bowls, then use a slotted spoon to scoop out the mussels and arrange on top (or serve the bread on the side). Bring the liquid back to a simmer, reduce slightly, taste for seasoning and ladle on top of the mussels. Sprinkle with parsley and devour immediately.Zuppa di cozze – how do you like yours, and can anyone explain the many regional variations that surely exist on Italy’s extensive coastline? And which other mussel recipes would you recommend to anyone wanting an alternative to marinières?The Guardian aims to publish recipes for sustainable seafood.
