title: Dante Mayfair, Claridge’s, London W1: ‘Are chips ever worth £11? Probably not’ – restaurant review | Food | The Guardian
description: The whole point of going to Claridge’s in the first place is to sweep in through the grand main hotel entrance
Author: Grace Dent
Headline: The whole point of going to Claridge’s in the first place is to sweep in through the grand main hotel entrance
Content: Dante Mayfair, London W1: ‘You could invite anyone here, at any time.’Photograph: Beca B Jones/The GuardianView image in fullscreenDante Mayfair, London W1: ‘You could invite anyone here, at any time.’Photograph: Beca B Jones/The GuardianGrace Dent on restaurantsFoodReviewDante Mayfair, Claridge’s, London W1: ‘Are chips ever worth £11? Probably not’ – restaurant reviewThe whole point of going to Claridge’s in the first place is to sweep in through the grand main hotel entranceGrace DentSun 4 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 11.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDante Mayfair, inside Claridge’s on Brook Street in London, has been created, the hotel’s management says, to become “the living room of Mayfair”. It’s a charming idea: pop in, have a cuppa or a bowl of pappardelle bolognese, or lie about on the fancy sofas wearing elasticated tracksuit bottoms and slurping soft-serve with s’mores. No, sorry, I’ve gone too far: it’s nowhere nearthatinformal.Still, like many well-used living rooms, this one has been rearranged, redecorated and repurposed many times over the years. I’ve eaten fancy-schmancySimon Rogan dinners here when it was Fera, as well as his table experience at Aulis during which venture capitalist “foodies” bored the pants off me over a 12-course meal in the kitchen itself. I’ve stared unmoved atDaniel Humm’s New York-style pomp at the short-lived Davies and Brook, and have visited several times since Claridge’s took matters in-house in the shape of a rather anonymous ye olde British brasserie.View image in fullscreenTuna tartare at Dante Mayfair, where ‘service is warm, slick, effusive and casual’.Now I’m here for Dante, and we’re back in New York again, this time in the hands of Linden Pride and Nathalie Hudson, with no named chef at all, although there’s absolutely definitely a man plinky-plonking his way throughJohn Legend’s Ordinary Peopleon the piano. Pride and Hudson are a husband-and-wife team from Sydney, Australia, who met at college, moved to New York and in 2015 boughtCaffe Dante, an institution of a Greenwich Village coffee house that’s been open since 1915.By 2019, the place had been named the world’s best bar. The couple’s new space on Brook Street is a restaurant site in need of stability and comprehensible finery, as well as of caviar tarts with champagne pearls, shrimp cocktails and lobster linguine, and of caviar martinis and vintage or chocolate negronis.If you like, you can enter via a small side door on Davies Street, but ignore that. The whole point of going to Claridge’s in the first place is to sweep in through the grand main hotel entrance past the men in top hats – you need to feel like Paddington, a little bear in a big city just making it on your own. Take a right turn, hand in your coat at the beautiful little cloakroom, then quickly powder your nose in the vintage loos where nice ladies polish the sinks. Order a marmalade sandwich … sorry, I mean dover sole meunière or veal milanese. For this part of Mayfair, the prices are weirdly reasonable – a bowl of fazzoletti with pesto may be £27, but you should see how much they charge for pasta atBacchanaliajust down the road – and a mini martini is a tenner between 3pm and 5pm.View image in fullscreen‘The sauce lacked depth and the pasta was a touch overcooked’: Dante’spappardelle al ragu, or house bolognese.Dante is useful for client lunches or intimate tête-à-têtes when you want to be heard perfectly and don’t want to be constantly interrupted by the waiting staff. After all, no one needs a tomato and peach salad with marinated feta and freekeh explained to them, even though this one is very fresh, very nicely arranged and whispers more of California than of Italy. A large plate of San Daniele prosciutto comes with baked mozzarella, and the iceberg salad features very neatly dressed lettuce wedges. Thepappardelle al ragu, or house bolognese, lacks depth and the pasta is a touch overcooked, but chickenalla diavolawith green goddess dressing is earthy and fresh. Are chips ever worth £11? Probably not, but then this is Claridge’s, not Clacton seafront.I do wonder, however, whether Dante’s most noteworthy offering is its “dessert cocktail” list, which is aimed squarely at that moment after the main course when customers wrinkle their noses at shelling out on “something sweet” but will happily carry on drinking. That’s when the rounds of honey bees (tequila, coffee liqueur, amontillado, raspberry, salted honey cream) are ordered. And wait, what? It comes with my own face printed on top of it!?! Dante has a piece of kit that stamps photographs on to the foam in edible ink, and I defyanyonenot to be exhilarated by that – or to think that it’s not perfectly sensible to have a nonna’s alexander or a grasshopper afterwards. We wanted pudding, too, though, and the waiter asked if we fancied the sticky toffee doughnut with whisky flambé. Yes. Yes, please. Yes, I would like you to set fire to things. It goes up like a firework and is a sweet, sticky mess.View image in fullscreenDante Mayfair’s sticky toffee doughnut with whisky flambé ‘goes up like a firework’.On this Tuesday lunchtime, Dante was probably the quietest place in Mayfair. A small, elegant wedding had taken over the side room, while a few hotel residents were eating burgers in the main room. Service was warm, slick, effusive and casual, and completely on it. The issue with a semi-casual restaurant inside Claridge’s is that the very name scares off the general public. But you could invite anyone here, and at any time; I’d use it for breakfasts and meet-ups. Dante is not a destination dinner, but it is, as promised, a living room. It won’t win prizes for its food, but it is friendly and handy as hell, which in Mayfair these days is exceptionally rare.Dante MayfairClaridge’s, Brook Street, London W1, 020-7629 8860. Open all week, noon-9.30pm (10.30pm Thurs-Sat); breakfast 8-11am. From about £60 a head à la carte, plus drinks and serviceExplore more on these topicsFoodGrace Dent on restaurantsRestaurantsAmerican food and drinkBritish food and drinkfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: My friends are spouting conspiracy theories – what should I say? | Friendship | The Guardian
description: You can be curious about others’ beliefs without compromising your own
Author: Annalisa Barbieri
Headline: You can be curious about others’ beliefs without compromising your own
Content: Illustration: Alex Mellon/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Alex Mellon/The GuardianAsk Annalisa BarbieriFriendshipMy friends are spouting conspiracy theories – what should I say?You can be curious about others’ beliefs without compromising your ownAnnalisa BarbieriSun 4 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 12.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRecently, I had a conversation with a friend who explained that her ill health was down to reasons I would describe as dubious. Taking certain supplements and changing her diethavesignificantly improvedher health. Good for her. However, she was disappointedand a little annoyedthat I didn’t share her outrage and wasn’t going to follow her views.I’ve got another friend whothinks cholesterol is a lie and that we should live largely on meat (and supplements). Another went through a sugar causes cancer phase. And another is sceptical of vaccines.Each of them may be right. They might not. We are learning moreabout the human body every day.But I was raised by scientists and I want to see a large-scale trial before Iget outraged and change the way I live. Equally, I’m not convinced that a lightly regulated for-profit industry (supplements) isautomaticallymore trustworthy than a highly regulated for-profitone (pharma).I wantto be respectful of their choicesand the research they have done into their specific conditions,but for them to respectmybeliefs too. The feeling I get is that they thinkthey have the keys to the real intel andI’m being duped by the medical establishment. Or that I’m not a good friend because I don’t believe them.I’mnot sure how to have a respectful conversation about that. I’dprefer to avoid it, but it comes up often. I find myself making non-committal comments such as “how interesting”. But I know, and they know,I’msceptical.But isn’t it OK for your scepticism to still be there? Isn’t this how so many of us get along, skirting over differing views of politics, religion and science? You’re not going to convince them any more than they’ll persuade you, so you need to find common ground.I went to psychotherapist Ryan Bennett-Clarke, who said: “Healthy relationships don’t need collusion to survive. In fact, healthy discourse can strengthen and invigorate relationships, so long as people are able to listen to each other and demonstrate a desire to hear what the other person is saying. We can be curious and compassionate without having to commit ourselves to something that doesn’t align with our own beliefs and experiences.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMy partner’s sister has published a family memoir that's unfair to him. Should we cut ties? | Ask Annalisa BarbieriRead moredouble quotation markThe more you dig in with your beliefs the more likely your friends will try to convince you of theirsOf course, there are some beliefs that may be harmful for others to hold, but even then you can’t force someone to listen. What I have found often works best is something gentle such as “That’s really interesting, I used to think that until I read XYZ”, and leave it at that. No one is receptive if they are forced into a defensive position. You could even say “Oh really, tell me more”, without having their beliefs tattooed on to you. But if all you have between you are these differences, then a friendship gets harder to sustain. And yes it is difficult to listen to some theories.Bennett-Clarke thought it was important to remember that “we can retain our right to have our own minds while thinking about the experiences and beliefs of others. Wanting to be understood and similar to others can help us feel less alone in the world. But we can stay in relational contact with someone, even if we don’t share their experiences or beliefs.”The truth is that the more you dig in with your beliefs the more likely your friends will be to try to convince you of theirs, so be mindful of this. You might also find useful a podcast I made on conflict with resolution expert Gabrielle Rifkind,How to Agree to Disagree. It’s all about how to turn conflict into connection and looks at why being seen to be right isn’t always necessary – even if we are, indeed, right.Every week, Annalisa Barbieri addresses a personal problem sent in by a reader. If you would like advice from Annalisa, please send your problem toask.annalisa@theguardian.com. Annalisa regrets she cannot enter into personal correspondence. title: ‘They call every week’: the phishing attacks targeting past victims | Scams | The Guardian
description: Scammers reuse personal details harvested from fake Esta websites – and texts and calls can keep arriving for months
Author: Shane Hickey
Headline: Scammers reuse personal details harvested from fake Esta websites – and texts and calls can keep arriving for months
Content: After using a fake website to apply for an Esta travel document one victim’s details have been reused by other scammers.Photograph: NetPhotos/AlamyView image in fullscreenAfter using a fake website to apply for an Esta travel document one victim’s details have been reused by other scammers.Photograph: NetPhotos/AlamyScam watchScams‘They call every week’: the phishing attacks targeting past victimsScammers reuse personal details harvested from fake Esta websites – and texts and calls can keep arriving for monthsShane HickeySun 4 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 02.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen the British actor Lisa Riley was preparing to travel to the US last year, she applied online for an Esta so she would not need a visa. After finding the site through a Google search she filled in her passport, bank and personal details and waited for the confirmation, which normally takes just under an hour.When it failed to arrive, she emailed an address from the site where she had paid and got back a message unlike any she had seen before, with a link to a website that displayed a jumble of words and letters.It was then she realised she had been scammed. But that was just the start of her problems, which persist to this day. She has been repeatedly targeted by criminals, receiving text messages and calls many times every week.Riley was the victim of a fraud where criminals create websites similar to the legitimate one run by US Customs and Border Protection (CBP). After fooling unsuspecting applicants they pocket a fee and use the personal details of victims for later scams.View image in fullscreenLisa Riley, pictured with other Emmerdale characters, was scammed on an Esta application and her personal details harvested to sell to other criminals.Photograph: ITV/ShutterstockRiley lost £16 – the cost of an Esta back then – but says there has been a huge increase in the number of scam calls and texts she has received in the 17 months since the fraud happened.Often the person claims to be from her bank with queries about a money transfer. “Calls areonce a week, easy – sometimes twice a week,” she says. “And the texts even more often.”Research from Nationwide building society suggests that 15% of people have given personal information to something who later turned out not to be genuine, leaving them open to future frauds.“Criminals do sadly retarget people after an initial scam,” says Annya Burskys, head of fraud operations at Nationwide. “They take the personal information they have gained and either sell it on to other scammers or use them to make follow-upbank impersonation calls, texts and emails appear more convincing.”What it looks likeThe fake Esta site that stole Riley’s personal details looked very similar to the official one and showed up high in search results, she says.“The webpage was absolutely identical so there was nothing that would remotely make me fearful up until [I realised],” she says.View image in fullscreenCriminals retarget people after an initial scam, says Annya Burskys, head of fraud operations at Nationwide.Photograph: Michael Kemp/AlamyCriminals can use AI to recreate legitimate government sites and will frequently use key words such as “Esta”, in the domain name to try to portray legitimacy.A spokesperson for the US CBP says some sites may demand action by the applicant quickly, a common tactic by criminals to try to get people to act without thinking something through.What to doOnly use the official Esta website, which has a .gov address, or the mobile app.“Applicants should protect their Esta confirmation number and payment details, retain application records, and review financial statements for unauthorised charges,” says the CBP spokesperson.View image in fullscreenNationwide advises customers not to feel pressured to act. ‘A genuine call or message from your bank will never ask you to move money, never ask you to share codes.’Photograph: Liubomyr Vorona/Alamy“Suspected fraud should be documented and reported promptly to the applicant’s financial institution and appropriate local government reporting channels.”In the UK that means telling your bank andReport Fraud.If you have inadvertently handed over your personal details you are at risk of future scams, so be alert to unexpected calls, texts or emails, says Burskys.“Don’t feel pressured to act. A genuine call or message from your bank will never ask you to move money, never ask you to share codes, and will never tell you what to say to your bank or friends, family,” she says.“Take a moment to verify who you’re speaking to and contact your bank directly using trusted contact information from your bank card or search for the official website if you’re unsure.”Explore more on these topicsScamsScam watchCrimeConsumer affairsIdentity fraudNuisance callsCybercrimeInternetfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Miu Miu turns ‘real clothes’ into high fashion with sportswear style | Miu Miu | The Guardian
description: Brand’s signature desire to subvert the ordinary brings blazers with track pants and crop tops under blazers to Paris fashion week
Author: Chloe Mac Donnell
Headline: Brand’s signature desire to subvert the ordinary brings blazers with track pants and crop tops under blazers to Paris fashion week
Content: Olivia Colman wore a cracked suede skirt suit on the catwalk in Paris.Photograph: Giovanni Giannoni/WWD/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenOlivia Colman wore a cracked suede skirt suit on the catwalk in Paris.Photograph: Giovanni Giannoni/WWD/Getty ImagesMiu MiuMiu Miu turns ‘real clothes’ into high fashion with sportswear styleBrand’s signature desire to subvert the ordinary brings blazers with track pants and crop tops under blazers to Paris fashion weekChloe Mac DonnellSun 4 Oct 2026 12.45 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 15.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSpeaking backstage at Miu Miu’s show on Sunday atParis fashion week, Miuccia Prada said she had been thinking about “real clothes”. The clothes people wear on the street for running errands rather than posing on social media. Her findings? Succinct. “The reality of clothing today is this mix – sportswear, casual, normal,” she said. Her challenge? To make them “more interesting, more rich”. To achieve this, she outlined how she had decided to focus on mixing “elements of sports with sophistication”.The collection opened with a series of five neatly pleated checked skirts. The first was worn with an equally neat checked blazer but rather than a smart shoe, such as a pump or loafers, there were brightly coloured trainers. The second featured a crop top under the blazer, the trainers swapped for spiky high heels. The other looks ditched the blazer and clipped the tops so they sat just under the bust line.View image in fullscreenCropped tops were worn with tailored skirts.Photograph: Giovanni Giannoni/WWD/Getty ImagesLater came the type of track pants usually made for mooching around in; here they were paired with smart knitwear and tailored jackets. Gym knickers were given the same upgraded styling treatment, while sports bras were reimagined as sparkly tops, more party than pilates; some were worn solo, others over clingy jersey tops. Jeans, a collaboration with Wrangler to rework its vintage denim, hung low below hips. Instead of buttons, zips or even belts, there were fastenings that riffed on shoelaces.Stella McCartney makes waves with ‘sea life, not sea food’ theme in zero-wool Paris showRead morePrada described the approach as “nonconformist dialogues exploring a form of friction and tension”. This method of clashing clothing genres and subverting the ordinary has turnedMiu Miuinto a near-billion-euro brand.It was originally launched in 1993 and seen as a sort of younger sister to Prada (Miu Miu was Miuccia’s childhood nickname). Since then it has made everything fromembellished pantstoplastersand aprons desirable. On the Lyst index, a quarterly report that ranks brands on demand, Miu Miu currently sits at No 2, just below Chanel. In July sales were up 3% to more than €700m.View image in fullscreenBlazers were paired with track pants.Photograph: Giovanni Giannoni/WWD/Getty ImagesIn a challenging luxury market, part of what has buoyed Miu Miu’s success has been a clear understanding of what it refers to as its “Miu Miu girls”. A clear archetype, the person who wears Miu Miu or aspires to wear it, likes a look that is a bit odd, a bit messy and perversely sexy. Miu Miu girls are not limited to a fixed youthful age or even gender. Sunday’s cast included the actor Emma Corrin, who wore white knickers paired with a croc jacket; Olivia Colman in a cracked suede skirt suit; and Jamie Bell in low-rise Prince of Wales checked trousers and a two-tone vest top.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFashion StatementStyle, with substance: what's really trending this week, a roundup of the best fashion journalism and your wardrobe dilemmas solvedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSport is an area Miu Miu is delving into beyond the catwalk. Earlier this year, it partnered with New Balance on a collection of performance wear for Coco Gauff. The tennis star wore it for the first time during the Italian Open in May and later on Centre Court at Wimbledon.The move reflects a wider strategy by Miu Miu to maintain hype around the brand through cultural links. The brand has a popular literary club that has explored the works of Simone de Beauvoir and Ama Ata Aidoo and for the past 15 years has been commissioning female-directed films including projects by Mona Fastvold and Miranda July.Explore more on these topicsMiu MiuParis fashion weekWomen's sportswearFashion weeksnewsShareReuse this content

title: Alone with the stars, lynx and wolves in ‘Empty Spain’ | Spain holidays | The Guardian
description: A world away from the tourist hotspots of the coast, Extremadura and Castile and León offer unpolluted skies, lower prices – and hope for the future of vulnerable wildlife
Author: Stephen Phelan
Headline: A world away from the tourist hotspots of the coast, Extremadura and Castile and León offer unpolluted skies, lower prices – and hope for the future of vulnerable wildlife
Content: Extremadura’s astrotourism initiative is called Buenas Noches.Photograph: Extremadura, Buenas NochesView image in fullscreenExtremadura’s astrotourism initiative is called Buenas Noches.Photograph: Extremadura, Buenas NochesSpain holidaysAlone with the stars, lynx and wolves in ‘Empty Spain’A world away from the tourist hotspots of the coast, Extremadura and Castile and León offer unpolluted skies, lower prices – and hope for the future of vulnerable wildlifeStephen PhelanSun 4 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 11.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs photographed at night from a satellite, or the International Space Station (ISS), the Iberian peninsula looks encrusted with lights along its coastal edges. Madrid forms a big pulsing cluster near the centre, while surrounding hinterlands appear as something of a void. Ever fewer people live out in Castile and León and Extremadura, adjoining regions that cover much of what is known asLa España Vacía, or “Empty Spain”.Not many visit either, or at least not compared with Barcelona and other glowing nodes of the tourist circuit. So, while the big ports and resorts struggle to manage surplus holidaymakers, there is room for plenty more out west, toward the Portuguese border. Some have been following the stars that way lately, under the auspices of an astrotourism initiative calledExtremadura Buenas Noches.View image in fullscreenA route map plotted point-to-point between optimal stargazing sites leads to distant outposts likeLa Siberia(so-called because it felt that remote to workers who laid down the first roads and railways in these parts) and the Corral de los Lobos, an ancient stone enclosure on a hilltop, built to trap wolves when they outnumbered the farmers and shepherds around here.Corral de los Lobos also lies in one of the rainier reaches of the Spanish interior, and the weather has mostly closed over the night sky when I go up to look. But even through breaks in the clouds, I can see the ISS pass in its elliptical orbit. Beyond that, Jupiter. And, much farther out, the Milky Way.View image in fullscreenThe Iberian lynx population is increasing in Monfragüe national park, in Extremadura.Photograph: imagebroker.com/Alamy“Big region, small population, almost no light pollution,” says forestry engineer and nature guide Alberto Garzón Fernández the next day, on a misty hike throughGarganta de los Infiernos, a nature reserve named for the fearsome sound of water through its gorges.There are no other forms of pollution either, it seems. We look down into gigantic cauldrons of granite known asmarmitas, where the River Jerte swirls like soup in a pot around eroded rock smooth as brushed steel. The lichen across the wet surface is a luminous green, “a bioindicator of clean air”.double quotation markThe Iberian lynx population is climbing steadily from dangerous lows of a few decades ago in Monfragüe national park“Extremadura is, no doubt, the most natural and healthy place to live,” Garzón says. His claim extends to non-human natives, not least the birds, and he points skyward to the ghostly profiles of honey buzzards and griffon vultures floating in the vapour off the peaks above. Thanks to “sound management”, as he puts it, the Spanish imperial eagle is now seen in much healthier numbers up there.The Iberian lynx population, meanwhile, is climbing steadily from dangerous lows of a few decades ago in neighbouring Monfragüe national park, where Garzón was born and raised. And the Iberian wolf – hunted and displaced almost to extinction before recent, belated protections – has been making a comeback over the flanking Gredos mountains.That’s close enough for their howls to be heard again from the Corral de los Lobos, on those same clear nights when “the stars look so close you could touch them”, says Garzón. The return of these signature species gives him hope for our own. “To me, they represent our capacity to do things right, but we so often wait until the last minute.”View image in fullscreenIn the River Jerte’s giant cauldrons of granite, water swirls like soup in a pot.Photograph: Manoli Perez/AlamyIf this region has felt the benefit of a minimal human presence lately, it’s hardly untouched by the increasing hazards of our time. The heatwave-borne wildfires of 2025 burned through nearly 20,000 hectares (49,400 acres) of the Jerte valley’s famous cherry orchards. All that damage is bound to affect the harvests to follow – one of the few events to draw a crowd to this area. “It will still be beautiful,” says Sara Cudero Morcuende at Alimentación Sara, a grocery store in the nearby mountain town of Valverde de la Vera.Her shop is so well stocked with local delicacies that the place would make a killing if transplanted to, say, east London: figs and olives from surrounding groves, sweet and hot paprika dried over open fires, all sorts of cherry jams and liqueurs. But her town, like many in the region, has lost thousands of residents in recent years.double quotation markYou can often eat and drink better and cheaper in ‘Empty Spain’ than in the country’s busier quartersThere’s a gothic-romantic hush to the cobbled streets below Valverde de la Vera’s ruined and overgrown castle. The quietude, the quasi-abandonment, may yet enhance the appeal to those passing through, though it can’t be good for business. “A few more customers would be nice,” says Cudero, but otherwise the town has only a couple of tapas bars, a few guesthouses, and no hotel.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFor my part, I make use of Spain’s state-ownedparadornetwork, which tends to offer surprisingly affordable rooms in converted convents and palaces, mostly within the medieval walls of the nearest comparatively big cities. The provincial capital, Cáceres; Trujillo, with its dreamlike hilltop fortress; and Plasencia, with its two half-cathedrals (one never fully demolished, the other forever unfinished), make good, solid bases.Fun fact: there are more pigs than people in these regions, including the black, acorn-fed pigs of thedehesaforest, whose meat becomes the world-renownedjamón ibérico.Including, too, the very chunky fellow I encounter in La Alberca, enjoying a siesta in a sty that is also a kind of shrine. Custom dictates that a single fat pig be allowed to wander and eat at its leisure for seven months of each year, until it’s raffled off for the feast of San Antón in January. In the past, that porker was invariably eaten, but some recent winners have apparently kept them as pets.View image in fullscreenThe city of Trujillo makes a good base for exploring  rural areas.Photograph: Ventura Carmona/Getty ImagesLa Alberca is also known for its gorgeous three-storey houses with half-timber facades, the legacy of Christian settlers from Burgundy, who came to occupy territory reconquered from the Moors 1,000 years ago. The encircling mountains are called the Sierra de Francia for that reason, their slopes thick with oak forests that yield many fine species of mushroom.“You can eat them all,” says biologist and guide Marino Esteban (La Albercavisitor centreoperates hikes into the forest), on a walk through woods that look more like French or even English countryside. “But some you can only eat once.” This is his way of saying that certain types are toxic. This is also to say that a massive meal at Meson de San Martín – a stonebuilt tavern that seems the only place open in nearby village San Martín del Castañar – is not all about the ham.‘So big and so close’: spotting endangered bears on a trip to northern SpainRead moreThere’s plenty of that, but also plenty of the freshly picked penny bun mushrooms grilled with garlic salt and olive oil, not to mention the chestnuts, cheeses, tomatoes and potatoes of surrounding farmlands, and the red wine made from native rufete grapes – as good as anything I’ve tried from more domineering production regions such as La Rioja and Ribera del Duero.And here’s the big secret I learn on this little road trip: you can often eat and drink better and cheaper in “Empty Spain” than in most of the busier quarters. This was one of the great lunches of my life, I tell the cheery chef, Alfonso Buenaventura Calvo. His wife and co-owner Belén answers for him: “Of course it was.”The trip was provided by theSpanishtouristoffice,Turismo ExtremaduraandTurismo Castilla Y León. Accommodation provided byParadores). title: Do humans really have a ‘lizard brain’ lurking beneath our rational minds? | Neuroscience | The Guardian
description: It’s a powerful analogy that captured the popular imagination, but the biological reality is quite different
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: It’s a powerful analogy that captured the popular imagination, but the biological reality is quite different
Content: Illustration: Elia Barbieri/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Elia Barbieri/The GuardianThe big ideaNeuroscienceDo humans really have a ‘lizard brain’ lurking beneath our rational minds?It’s a powerful analogy that captured the popular imagination, but the biological reality is quite differentHannah CritchlowSun 4 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 07.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHumans have a cognitive quirk for the number three. Think of the many stories that use it, from The Three Little Pigs to Goldilocks and the Three Bears and The Three Musketeers. Public information and political campaigns use it for impact and ease of recall (“Stop, look and listen”; “See it. Say it. Sorted”; “Reduce, reuse, recycle”). And then there are psychological or philosophical frameworks: Freud with his id, ego and superego; Plato’s three parts of the human soul; the Holy Trinity.Well, it turns out neuroscience isn’t immune from tri-mania. In 1959 Paul D MacLean set out a new way of thinking about the evolution and function of the brain, which he christened the “triune” – three-in-one – model. It quickly became one of best known and most enduring concepts in human biology. His idea was that a trio of distinct brains are layered inside our skulls, one on top of the other, all fighting to generate our feelings and thoughts.Deep inside, at the centre, lurks the primitive lizard brain, retained from an ancestor we share with reptiles. This contains ancient regions responsible for survival, helping us to hunt and forage, and driving our sexual impulses so that we reproduce. A second layer sits wrapped around the first, the so-called mammalian brain. It contains the limbic system, deemed to be the seat of our emotions. It enabled mammals to play, care for and nurse their young and communicate in some crude way.The third and final layer, sheathing all of this and making humans in particular a cut above, is the “neomammalian” brain: the eminently rational cortex. This, it was proposed, provides us with our superior intellect, capacity for language and ability to reason. According to MacLean, it helped to keep in check our primitive, lizard-like impulses and rudimentary emotional reactions.double quotation markThe analogy – of an onion-like brain made up of different strata – is now considered deeply misleading by neurobiologistsHuman behaviour was thought to be a result of interactions between all three layers of the triune brain. Frayed tempers, impulsive acts and short termism were signs of the lizard brain winning out. The notion of reptilian impulses “breaking through” proved so popular it found its way into the worlds of pop psychology, business and self-help, and has proved remarkably tenacious. A mini-industry of books, talks and training grew up around the idea that you could draw on the power of the neomammalian brain to keep basic, unhelpful or destructive emotions in check.The underpinning analogy – of an onion-like brain made up of different strata – is now considered deeply misleading by neurobiologists. It’s easy to grasp, sure, and tells a compelling story. But evolution just doesn’t bolt-on neatly divisible mental capacities in this way.MacLean conducted dissections of living creatures to try to prove his theory, but the results, and his interpretations of them, have since been largely discredited. For example, it’s now accepted that many reptiles do actually possess the “mammalian” limbic system, while all mammals exhibit “neomammalian” features previously thought to be unique to “higher” ones like us. Alongside these anatomical observations, there’s the behavioural data too, with many “lower” animals good at problem solving, responding and learning via emotion, and communicating in complex ways.As Guy Leschziner, consultant neurologist at London’s Guy’s and St Thomas’ hospital put it to me: “the concept of different parts of the brain having different functions is extremely well established. However, to portray humans as having different brain layers, for example a ‘lizard brain’ underlying basic physiological functions, is not borne out by evolutionary or physiological evidence. For a start, mammals and reptiles split early in evolutionary terms. Whilst it is true that more primitive functions in our brains evolved earlier in the course of life on Earth, this view of three separate brain systems driving our basic instincts, emotions and logic respectively does not stack up.”Lisa Feldman Barrett, professor of psychology at Northeastern University is another contemporary voice actively debunking the lizard brain myth. In her view, rather than operating as a battleground between ancient instinct, raw emotion and sophisticated logic, the brain is a dynamic, integrated system, whose aim is to keep us alive by predicting and budgeting our energy requirements.Neuroanatomically and behaviourally, if not yet in the popular consciousness, the idea that we all have a lizard brain has been thoroughly discredited. Yet despite the mounting evidence, and the success of more recent frameworks, the triune brain endures. Shockingly, it is still being widely taught in introductory psychology textbooks (as one journal article mischievously titled “Your Brain Is Not an Onion With a Tiny Reptile Inside” showed). The study also highlighted some of the pitfalls of allowing the hypothesis to go unchallenged, which include giving students a false sense of how evolution unfolds, and promoting the idea that human beings have a monopoly on “rational” actions such as deferring gratification – sacrificing a short-term reward for a longer-term gain.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIs culture alive?Read moreSo, what is it about MacLean’s model that we just can’t seem to let go of? Well, as we’ve seen, people really do seem to love threes. But perhaps there’s more to it than that. The triune brain tells us an ego-stroking story about our place in the world: that we really are the pinnacle of evolution, standing apart from other species. It reaffirms heady ideas about our sovereignty over nature, and tells a reassuring story about our logical, orderly, almost computational abilities. We are storytelling creatures, of course, but this is a story that needs updating – to one about how much in common we have with other animals, and how simplistic assumptions about the way our minds work are almost never true.Dr Hannah Critchlow is a neuroscientist and author ofThe 21st Century Brain(Torva).Further readingSeven Deadly Sinsby Guy Leschziner (William Collins,£20)How Emotions are Madeby Lisa Feldman Barrett (Pan, £12.99)Our Brains, Our Selvesby Masud Husain (Canongate, £20)Explore more on these topicsNeuroscienceThe big ideaPsychologyEvolutionBiologyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Readers reply: Is it possible that 3 is the most common number in UK street addresses? | Life and style | The Guardian
description: The long-running series in which readers answer other readers’ questions on various subjects considers a numerological conundrum
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The long-running series in which readers answer other readers’ questions on various subjects considers a numerological conundrum
Content: The magic number.Photograph: papparaffie/Getty Images/iStockphotoView image in fullscreenThe magic number.Photograph: papparaffie/Getty Images/iStockphotoNotes and queriesLife and styleReaders reply: Is it possible that 3 is the most common number in UK street addresses?The long-running series in which readers answer other readers’ questions on various subjects considers a numerological conundrumThis week’s question:Why are national anthems almost always orchestral?Sun 4 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 09.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleItried recently to buy sticky vinyl numbers for a new wheelie bin. At two stores, I could find every number from 0 to 9 except the number 3, which I wanted. Is it possible that 3 could be more common in UK street addresses than other numbers?John Gorrill at No 31, OxfordSend new questions tonq@theguardian.com.Readers replyHaving pondered this situation overnight, my unverified reasoning is that it is influenced solely by the prevalence of short roads and streets in most of the UK. The number 1 is going to figure highly in roads with fewer than 20 houses (a total of 13). The number 2, similarly (an unlucky 13), with roads of fewer than 30 houses. Numbers 3 to 9 obviously feature less in this scenario. I suspect the lack of 3s and above becomes more apparent as the average number of houses per street or road rises. If we had long streets like the US, with house numbers frequently in the thousands, the demand for certain numbers would even itself out.FrankieandDexyI live at No 33 and I have seven bins. Sorry.lexicon_mistressThe question isn’t whether 3 is the most popular number, but whether DIY stores have underestimated how popular 3 is compared with 1 and 2. Like other posters here, they may have considered only main door numbers, ignoring flats or divided houses. In my experience, houses divided into two append a letter (eg 65b), but any more than that use a slash then a second digit (eg 65/3), but rarely higher than 3. Some flats – common in Scotland – use a floor number and a digit or letter modifier (eg 3F2 or 3FC), but as most tenements have fewer than four floors, they rarely require digits higher than 3, even if there are 9 or more flats.The upshot is that while 1 and 2 will be overwhelmingly popular, 3 may be a lot more popular than you might initially expect – closer to the popularity of 1 and 2 than to 4 to 9. But if purveyors of door furniture assumed the opposite, their stock will be constantly short of 3s.HaveYouFedTheFishMaybe you share a house with some others and they all decided, without your knowledge, to pop out and sort it out?parasamgateI appreciate that two might seem like a lot of stores, because of the toll it’s taken on your day, but if I were your PhD supervisor I’d ask for some more data.klingerdingerBenford’s law is the empirical observation that the distribution of leading digits in many large datasets is heavily weighted towards the smaller digits: 1 – 30.1%, 2 – 17.5%, 3 – 12.5%, and so on, up to 9 – 4.6%. It applies to human-generated data (eg finance, vote counts, addresses, areas of geographical divisions) as well as many datasets in nature (populations, gene expression). It has been used for detecting fraud in finance and vote-counting. While this does not answer the question directly, it strongly suggests that it is unlikely that 3 is the most common digit.seameadowBenford’s law concerns how leading digits are distributed in datasets and says 1 occurs in around 30% of labels. It shouldn’t strictly apply to house numbering, because streets are generally short and there aren’t usually enough houses to get to numbers that start with 9. However, in practice, the pattern does approximate to house numbering. This isn’t too hard to demonstrate from address files, or from examining some long streets, for example, Duke Street and Gallowgate (Glasgow) and King Street (Aberdeen).Tangentially, when the kids were young, we did some crafting together to make the new house more homely. There’s a homemade sign on the wall saying WELCOME, except the hobby shop had no more Ls, so we bought a J and turned it around. Guests don’t spot the difference, but to this day I still read it as WEJCOME when I walk past.DorkaliciousYou wouldn’t expect a set of numbers to follow Benford’s law if they were allocated sequentially – as house numbers are. You generally also need a set of numbers which span several orders of magnitude. So, in the UK, at least, the prevalence of short(ish) streets also works against Benford’s law.mutieMaybe the company selling the number stickers badly misjudged the demand for number 3s? Perhaps they stocked heaps and heaps of 1s and 2s, thinking they’re common like commenters do here, and failed to turn out enough 3s to keep up with demand?Randomusername222A sample of a single column of a random page of an Edinburgh telephone directory from a few years ago – 128 addresses containing 236 digits – gives the following:0 – 8%1 – 21%2 – 17%3 – 12%4 – 9%5 – 8%6 – 8%7 – 9%8 – 5%9 – 3%There are several obvious problems with such a calculation. For example, a tenement will probably have an entry for each flat, so the number on the front door will be counted multiple times.ebcdicI was born in No 13, but my superstitious parents refused to acknowledge it (the number, not my birth) and only ever referred to the house by the name they gave it.WormloverMore likely that it’s a fluke. Someone at number 33 bought four of them and now they are sold out. It’s such a low sample size that random noise in the data is larger than any actual effect of sales.NyuszNo1Ordnance Survey provides a few free samples of address data. These cover Inverness, Newport and Exeter. After a bit of spreadsheet work, I find that a total of 218,126 digits appear in street addresses in these locations. These are split as follows:0 – 6%1 – 22%2 – 15%3 – 12%4 – 10%5 – 8%6 – 8%7 – 7%8 – 6%9 – 6%If Exeter, Inverness and Newport are representative, then 3 is not the most common number in UK street addresses.FGBootisDe La Soul, it turns out, were correct: 3 is the magic number. Seems like it does a disappearing act.catchytitledThe average number of houses in a street in the UK is 30, therefore the most common numbers are 1 and 2, equally. Obviously, if the predominant new builds were high-rise flats, this might change but, as far as I am aware, they are not.slojdareNo. If you look at the numbers 1 to 40, the digits 1, 2 and 3 all occur 14 times. I assume that you’d get the same result with the digits 1 to 9 if you went up to 99. Beyond that, 1 is obviously most common between 100 and 199, 2 between 200 and 299, and 3 between 300 and 399. I suspect, though, that 1, 2 and 3 would be equally common between 1 and 399, and that 1 to 9 would be equally common in an infinite road*. 0 wouldn’t be, because addresses are not numbered by mathematicians, so there is no number 0 and we don’t use leading zeros.mutie*The proof has been left as an exercise for the reader.If the road were infinitely long, all the digits including 0 would be used infinity times, so equally common. There’d be no stock of any sticky numbers left anywhere.Randomusername222This can be explicitly checked if you get the official UPRN data for all house and maisonette data (usually used in GIS software), assuming you discount flats that have communal bin rooms. Some houses have one digit and others can go up to four digits, I guess, and some can have letters, for example 9999A or 9999B. So, really, the frequency of number requests per house in an area can be calculated. As 13 is often omitted, the probability of 1 and 3 being requested will be fractionally lower. The lack of availability mentioned is probably due to bad supply and demand management in the store, or poor replenishment of shelves.James Martin, via emailJust buy three sticky vinyl letter Is and dress up in a toga every time you take the bin out.EddieChorepostSurely simpler and cheaper to buy an 8 and use a pair of scissors?WormloverOr two 1s and assume the postie understands you’ve switched to using binary for house numbers.DorkaliciousExplore more on these topicsLife and styleNotes and queriesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Incinerated novels and destroyed warehouses: Russia’s war on Ukrainian books | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: A Ukrainian publishing boom sparked by the 2022 invasion is now under threat from the force and frequency of Russian attacks
Author: Charlotte Higgins
Headline: A Ukrainian publishing boom sparked by the 2022 invasion is now under threat from the force and frequency of Russian attacks
Content: Viktor Kruglov, the co-founder and chief executive of the publisher Ranok, at inspects his burnt-out warehouse.Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The GuardianView image in fullscreenViktor Kruglov, the co-founder and chief executive of the publisher Ranok, at inspects his burnt-out warehouse.Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The GuardianThe Sunday readUkraineIncinerated novels and destroyed warehouses: Russia’s war on Ukrainian booksA Ukrainian publishing boom sparked by the 2022 invasion is now under threat from the force and frequency of Russian attacksCharlotte Higginsin Kharkiv, Kremenchuk, Kyiv and Lviv. Photographs byJulia KochetovaSun 4 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 03.31 EDTShareOn a Saturday morning in August, Viktor Kruglov, the co-founder and chief executive of the publisher Ranok, was at his headquarters in Kharkiv – the eastern Ukrainian city that, along with Kyiv, is the centre of the country’s publishing and printing industry. Built 15 years ago on the site of a former bread factory, the footprint of the premises is about 10,000 sq metres (107,640ft). Books were stacked 12 metres high on rank after rank of shelves.Kruglov, along with five senior colleagues, were on the warehouse floor to discuss the approaching school year. The warehouse was holding 628,000 new schoolbooks. “It was the high season of distribution,” he said, “so we were checking all our processes: how to do it more successfully, how to do it in time.”View image in fullscreenEight million books were destroyed in the drone strike and subsequent fire at Ranok’s warehouse in Kharkiv.The meeting was scheduled for 11am. But a couple of moments after it began, there came “the sound of an explosion, and almost simultaneously I saw a huge fire”, said Kruglov. The impact was about 30 metres from where the staff were gathered, and, as colleagues set about trying to put out the flames, “there came a second strike and I understood that there could be a third, and a fourth, so we started to evacuate”.The munitions used in the attack were jet-powered Shaheds, a recent and insidious escalation of Russian drone technology, faster and harder to intercept than their predecessors. These are the weapons that have been lately terrorising Kyiv during daylight hours, ploughing into the National Academy of Sciences and a working medical clinic in the past week.“Fifty people were on shift that day,” said Kruglov of the warehouse strike, “and I don’t know how to explain how nobody was injured.”The combination of an explosion, jet fuel and a warehouse full of paper was catastrophic. None of the books could be salvaged and 8m were destroyed. It took firefighters a week to bring the flames under control.View image in fullscreenThe burnt remains of sheet music at Ranok’s warehouse, which was destroyed in an attack using jet-powered Shaheds.Several weeks on, smoke still rose from parts of the warehouse. The roof seemed on the verge of collapse, metal beams listing alarmingly, twisted out of shape by the heat.Shafts of sunlight slanted through the damaged roof, illuminating the catastrophe. The smell was terrible, clinging to clothes and hair. As far as the eye could see, the wreckage of books lay in mounds.In some places, engulfed by the firefighters’ water, they had dissolved into a thick, stinking, mud-like slurry. In others, they were charred at the edges but recognisable as what they once were: children’s picturebooks illustrated with animals and flowers, geography textbooks, young-adult fiction. Others were nothing but swollen millefeuilles of blackened pages that flaked away to the touch.View image in fullscreenChildren’s picturebooks illustrated with animals and flowers were among the books destroyed or damaged.A couple of editorial staff, visiting the wreckage for the first time since the attack, looked shaken as they recognised fragments of books they had written or edited. “When you see what was produced with your brain, with your hands, with your imagination, spoiled by Russia, it’s an awful feeling,” said Kruglov, a trim, bald, blue-eyed man in his early 60s.Those 8m books represented more than 85% of Ranok’s total stock, he said. In the main branch of Ranok’s own Knyholand bookstore in Kyiv, the display still looked cheerful and dense in late September – but, predicted Kruglov, there will be shortages this autumn when the books instore run low and there is nothing to replace them.In total, this summer, 13m Ukrainian books have been destroyed by Russian missiles or drones – a third, estimates the government, of all books printed inUkrainethis year.Books, literature, culture and language are not peripheral to Russia’s war on Ukraine – they are bound up in it. The full-scale invasion in February 2022 was prompted, at least in part, by Vladimir Putin’s conviction that Ukraine and Russia have no true separate cultural identity.Kruglov said he was sure his warehouse full of Ukrainian-language, Ukraine-produced books had been deliberately targeted. “It is nowhere near any military facilities and everyone knows it is a book warehouse,” he said.Bohdana Laiuk, a Ukrainian deputy minister for culture, who works on literature and publishing, takes a slightly different view: the recent attacks on books should not be seen in isolation, but as part of the invaders’ recent campaign of attacking warehouses, depots and fulfilment centres of any kind. “They cannot occupy Kyiv,” she said. “So they target warehouses around Kyiv to take the possibility of everyday life from us – and books are part of everyday life.”View image in fullscreenThe books destroyed in the Kharkiv attack represented 85% of Ranok’s total stock, according to the CEO of the publisher.But books are also part of language, and language is part of identity and, often, nationhood. Books are, said Laiuk, certainly considered important by the Russians invaders. “When the Russians occupy, the first thing they do – and we know this from the areas that were occupied and then liberated in 2022 in the Kherson and Kharkiv regions – is to go to the libraries, take the Ukrainian language books out, and destroy them,” she said.Until 2022, about 70% of the Ukrainian book market was Russian-language titles – most imported from Russia, some published in Ukraine.The dominance of Russian publishing had a long history. Its seeds lay in 19th-century decrees under the tsars against publishing in Ukrainian and continued through the Soviets’ promotion of Russian as the language of aspiration, education and culture. Ukrainian writers were purged and Ukrainian literature left in the shadows, shut out from a canon that lionised the Russian novel.After Ukraine’s independence in 1991, the idea of a commercially successful Ukrainian-language novel that tackled modern social issues was so unthinkable that publishers initially suggested to Oksana Zabuzhko that her 1996 novel Fieldwork in Ukrainian Sex be published in Russian translation. She insisted it was published in the language it was written. It became a bestseller, paving the road for waves of contemporary Ukrainian literature.View image in fullscreenBohdana Laiuk: ‘When the Russians occupy, the first thing they do … is to go to the libraries, take the Ukrainian language books and destroy them.’Laiuk characterised the dominance of Russian book imports as a kind of colonialism. “It should be compared to how Russians invested in Ukrainian media outlets, Ukrainian TV channels, Ukrainian newspapers and magazines.” It was a conscious policy, she argued. “This is how Russians think: when they arrive on tanks, everything will be ready for them because they already have this information space.”But in 2022, Ukrainian booksellers abruptly stopped selling Russian imports, in line with the rupture of all commercial ties between the countries. At the same time, swathes of the Ukrainian population switched their day-to-day language from Russian to Ukrainian.They switched reading matter, too, and Ukraine’s publishers fed the appetite with new editions of classic Ukrainian literature from the 1920s, poetry, translations, and new Ukrainian writing. The country’s publishers may publish Russian-language books, as long as at least half their titles are in Ukrainian; in practice the social barriers to doing so, at the moment, would be prohibitive. (Death and the Penguin author Andrey Kurkov, for example, writes his novels in Russian, but they are published only in Ukrainian translation; he writes nonfiction and children’s books in Ukrainian.)“People began to understand that the Russians came here to kill people simply because they were Ukrainian,” Laiuktold me in 2023. “So people are asking: what does it actually mean to be Ukrainian? Literary culture gives us the place to understand who we are.”View image in fullscreenOleksiy Erinchak opened the first of his chain of Ukrainian-only bookstores, Sens, in 2021.Oleksiy Erinchak opened the first of his chain of Ukrainian-only bookstores, Sens, in 2021. In 2024, while the city was under fire, he opened a second, in a huge building on Khreshchatyk, Kyiv’s grandest boulevard, to which he has recently added a third floor, with an expansive events space. He has another branch in the western city of Ivano-Frankivsk and he has just opened a fourth, in a former cinema in Lviv.“When you go to a bookstore like Sens,” said Laiuk, “you feel that you have dignity. You have the right to buy a new book and to choose which one you like. And when you have drones above your head, it gives so much space, inner space in your heart and soul, and in your mind.”The rapid expansion of Sens is a symptom of something unlikely: a Ukrainian publishing boom amid a full-scale invasion of the country. And now, that boom is threatened by the force and frequency of Russian attacks.Kateryna and Artem Sova started their imprint in 2023, in the thick of the new Ukrainian publishing boom. By then Artem had been in the army for nearly a year and Kateryna was several months pregnant, living in her hometown of Kremenchuk, on the River Dnipro in central Ukraine. It was their dream: they had both worked in bookstores and at arts festivals for years. Part of the point for Artem was to keep some chink of his old self alive. “I realised,” he said, speaking in Zaporizhzhia during a break from his military duties, “that I was detached from everything I love.”View image in fullscreenKateryna Sova said she and her husband, Artem, called their publishing house Krapky (Ellipsis) as they wanted reading their books ‘to be an ongoing conversation’.They began withLonely City, a nonfiction work about art and the experience of urban isolation, by the British author Olivia Laing. They had loved it since they read it a decade ago, and were bemused it was not already translated. They wrote to Laing’s agent asking whether they could acquire the rights.“We tried to explain why this book is important for Ukrainians now, and to me personally,” Artem said, recalling. “This experience of being lonely is kind of universal, but it has been multiplied because a lot of people went into the army, and there are so many displaced people in Ukraine: separated couples, destroyed lives.”Laing, to their surprise, agreed: only then did they actually go through the legal process of setting up the company. They called it Krapky – Ukrainian for “ellipsis”, the three dots being their favourite punctuation mark, signifying, said Kateryna, as she sipped coffee in an independent bookshop in Kremenchuk, that they wanted reading their books “to be an ongoing conversation. Something that doesn’t stop when you close the book.” Their aim was for every book they published to be expertly translated and wonderfully illustrated.View image in fullscreenPart of the reason Artem Sova co-founded Krapky was to keep some chink of his old self alive while doing his military service.In 2025, they finally went to Kyiv Book Arsenal – the great annual gathering for publishers, writers and readers in the capital – with a beautifully designed edition of Lonely City. By this year’s Book Arsenal they had several titles already out, and translations of Laing’s To the River and Karen Blixen’s classic, Out of Africa, in the pipeline. In preparation were also works by Flannery O’Connor, among others. “We wanted to get to a position where we were publishing eight to 10 titles a year,” said Kateryna.Recently, they had signed a contract withNova Poshta, the Ukrainian postal service, to handle fulfilment – so that Kateryna was not sending out the books herself to customers and bookstores. She was driving her sister to university on the morning of 28 August when Artem rang. The warehouse where their books were held, on the periphery of Kyiv, had been attacked. Kateryna had to pull off the road in her distress. At the Lviv BookForum, a fortnight later, their stand was empty but for a QR code so visitors could preorder their forthcoming titles. They had nothing physical to sell. All of their books had been destroyed.Ranok is now rushing to reprint textbooks and bestsellers, hoping to get precious teaching materials into schools – and plug the shortfall in cashflow with sales of popular titles. Vivat, a large Kharkiv-based publisher, which lost 16m Ukrainian hryvnia (about £270,000) worth of books in a hit on one of its warehouses this summer, is doing the same. “We’ll definitely continue publishing Ukrainian authors, and the schedule for 2027 is already finalised,” said Vivat’s spokesperson, Kateryna Ilchuk, between events at Lviv BookForum. “But probably yes, it will mean going with more mainstream titles.”View image in fullscreenKateryna Sova shows the very last books that were left for sale after Russian attacks.Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The GuardianSmall literary publishers such as Krapky are the most vulnerable in the current crisis. Another small independent press, Who is That?, recently announced apausein its operations until the end of the war, after the destruction of all of their stock this summer in two separate airstrikes.For debut authors, or writers of less commercial or more experimental titles, this is a bleak moment. Even before the summer drone hits, there had been delays in some books’ publication owing to attacks on printing infrastructure. Ksenia Shpak’s debut young-adult novel – an urban fantasy about a girl internally displaced from eastern Ukraine to the Carpathian mountains – was originally due out in February 2025. It was finally published, by the imprint Zhorzh, in November.But half the print run was in the Ranok warehouse in Kharkiv when it was attacked. “I must say that it’s sad because it was my first published book,” said Shpak, “and now my publisher will focus on their bestsellers, and only after that if they get enough money will they reprint my book.” She mentioned other factors that had lately cooled the Ukrainian publishing boom: a levelling out of demand; the rise in the cost of living. “It feels like there is a snowballing of bad things for our publishing industry,” Shpak added.View image in fullscreenFor publishers such as Ivan Malkovych, the task now is to adapt: spread stocks of book in smaller warehouses across the country, at the expense of super-fast delivery times.“It’s shaky,” said veteran poetry editor, poet and children’s publisher Ivan Malkovych. His premises – in central Kyiv, shared with a male-voice choir, the sound of whose rehearsal wafted through the editorial offices as he spoke – presented an absolute contrast to the desolation of the Ranok warehouse. In one room, a wall of shelves displayed ranks of exquisitely illustrated children’s titles, and handsome volumes of poetry. He began his company amid the economic chaos of the early 1990s, starting with a Ukrainian alphabet book, printed on board a supplier let him have on the vague promise he’d pay for it in six months (the book was a success, and he did). The alphabet began, “A is for Angel”, and the angel has been the publishing house’s good luck charm ever since.‘We just have to adapt’: Kyiv residents prepare for a hard winter aheadRead moreMalkovych has published many children’s books, but none in such quantity as Harry Potter. His editions hit the shelves faster, and were better translated, than the Russian versions (“We Ukrainianised a lot of children that way,” he said.) He lost 40,000 books in the same Nova Poshta warehouse attack that destroyed Krapky’s stock – about $500,000 (£377,800) of losses. “We were always proud of our delivery service – you could order a book at 4am and it would arrive by midday. Now we face big delays,” he said. He was particularly worried about the next Harry Potter release, on 6 October. There had been a lot of pre-orders and he wanted delivery to be synchronised with the rest of the world, despite the full-scale invasion.For publishers like Malkovych – whose staff have elected not to leave Kyiv, despite the oncoming winter and the new Russian jet-powered drones – the task now is to adapt: they will now spread stocks of book in smaller warehouses across the country, at the expense of super-fast delivery times. There is hope for Krapky too: Nova Poshta may reimburse it for some of their lost stock; there has been an outflowing of support from readers who havepreordered forthcoming titles; and it has received a grant from an NGO towards reprinting costs.View image in fullscreenViktor Kruglov remains optimistic after the attack on the warehouse in Kharkiv: ‘I think that we will rebuild everything. And I even know how to do it better.’When Laiuk visitsFrankfurt book fairthis October, she will be promoting a ministry of culture and Kyiv School of Economicsfundraiserfor small Ukrainian publishers like Krapky. But she will also urge global publishers to translate Ukrainian titles. “It’s important to see that the industry is suffering and to see the devastating pictures of burned books. But that is not the whole story. The whole story is that Ukrainian literature is rich and diverse as never before. The best way is to see that is to translate, and to bring new voices to the discourse in your country.”As for Kruglov, despite the devastating loss of 8m books, he was, somehow, optimistic. Surveying the absolute ruin of his Kharkiv premises, he said, “I think that we will rebuild everything. And I even know how to do it better.”

title: ‘You have 10 minutes to decide’: answering the life-changing call to become a kinship carer | Carers | The Guardian
description: Those who have stepped in to keep young family members from going into care in England and Wales say the decision has brought them joy and hardship
Author: Patrick Butler
Headline: Those who have stepped in to keep young family members from going into care in England and Wales say the decision has brought them joy and hardship
Content: From top: kinship carers Clive, Leasa and Alan with Savannah, Luke and EllaComposite: GuardianView image in fullscreenFrom top: kinship carers Clive, Leasa and Alan with Savannah, Luke and EllaComposite: GuardianCarers‘You have 10 minutes to decide’: answering the life-changing call to become a kinship carerThose who have stepped in to keep young family members from going into care in England and Wales say the decision has brought them joy and hardshipPatrick ButlerSocial policy editorSun 4 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 14.09 EDTShareClive vividly remembers the day when, without warning or time to work out what he was really letting himself in for, he became a kinship carer.“The social worker left, the door closed and Savannah was lying there in a carry cot, wrapped up in a pink blanket. She looked so calm and so comfy, absolutely oblivious about what’s just happened.“There was this eerie silence in the house. It was just me and her and a little suitcase with some belongings in it. I burst into tears. I’m a teacher, but training as a teacher does not prepare you for looking after a baby.“I didn’t know how to change a baby’s nappy, I didn’t have a push chair, I didn’t have a cot, I didn’t know where she was going to sleep. I didn’t have anything.”A few hours earlier, Clive, a primary school headteacher, had taken a call at work from children’s services. He assumed it would be about one of his pupils, but it was about his six-week-old niece. Would he, as a family member, take her into temporary care?View image in fullscreenSavannah and Clive. ‘I said yes – and deal with the consequences later.’Photograph: Saskia Albers/Portray Your Story“So I, quite blase, said: ‘Yeah, no problem at all. I’ll need to put a few things in place, so just give me a couple of days.’ They were like: ‘No, she needs to come to you today. We need to drop her off at four o’clock.’“I was kind of like: ‘Well, what happens if I don’t say yes today?’ They said they’d have to come up with ‘other options’. So I started to panic: what if she goes into foster care or for adoption? So I said yes – and deal with the consequences later.”“I went home and just sat there waiting. It was a bit bizarre because I don’t think I’ve ever been home at 3.30pm on a school day before. And then social care came, dropped her off. And that was that.“I’d only ever invested in my career. I was career-driven all the time. And then a baby was sprung on me that I’d never planned for.”Clive, then 32, would now admit he was naive about the consequences of the decision that changed his life. Nine years on, with the “temporary” stay having become permanent, “Uncle Clive” is Savannah’s legal guardian, though she is in regular contact with her birth parents. He adores her, and theirs is a heartwarming kinship success story. She still has the pink blanket. But the path, he admits, while joyful and fulfilling, has not always been smooth.View image in fullscreenClive is now Savannah’s legal guardian, and they have lived together for nine years.Photograph: Saskia Albers/Portray Your Story“I would do it all again. It’s the best thing that could have happened for my niece. But at times it’s been quite isolating and exhausting.”More than 141,000 children inEnglandand Wales are like Savannah, being raised by kinship carers. These are normally relatives, like Clive, or family friends who step in to prevent children whose parents can no longer look after them from entering the care system.Despite the dependence of children’s services on kinship care – twice as many children enter kinship arrangements as are fostered – it remains startlingly informal, with few of the practical, legal and financial supports that accompany fostering or adoption. Often it can seem kinship care isinvisible to policymakers.Clive’s experience – being given just hours to make a momentous decision about whether to take over care of a loved one – is far from unusual. A new survey by the care charityKinshipfound that four in 10 carers were given less than an hour to make a decision. A further fifth had less than 24 hours.Alan and Julie, both 65, were given 10 minutes to decide whether they would care for their severely disabled grandchild Ella, who was then 10 months old. They had just got back home to Leeds after a holiday when they got the call from social services.View image in fullscreenElla, nine, has lived with her grandparents Alan and Julie since she was 10 months old.Photograph: Saskia Albers/Portray Your Story“They said: ‘This place closes in 10 minutes. We need to know if you are prepared to take the child on, or they will go into local authority care and you will probably never see them again,’” Alan recalls. “Of course, it was a no-brainer. We said we’d take her on straight away, as we would any of our grandchildren.”Having made that snap decision, almost all kinship carers report that it changes their lives profoundly. The ramifications are broad and not always immediately appreciated, and official support can be patchy or nonexistent. Overnight, there is an extra person in the home to feed and clothe, who may have suffered trauma and have special needs. There is often an unexpectedstrain on finances, carer health and wider family relationships.Many kinship carers give up work, often at the request of social services. Clive was terrified he would have to abandon his career. He worried he wouldn’t be able to pay the mortgage if that happened, and if he lost the house, Savannah would be taken into foster care.He was lucky: his school was incredibly supportive and allowed him to work flexibly – he recalls bottle-feeding Savannah while delivering a staff training session. He also has a strong network of friends and family. But he knows from support groups organised by Kinship that other carers are not so fortunate.Leasa, 56, and Oly, 57, from west London, say that having made the snap decision to care for their nephews, Jake and Luke, they had to fight for support they expected would be automatic. With their own son at home, there were suddenly five people crammed into their tiny two-bed flat, but the council didn’t seem interested.View image in fullscreenLeasa, Oly, Luke and Jake. ‘My mum thought I was crazy,’ says Leasa.Photograph: Saskia Albers/Portray Your StoryOly recalls he had once enquired about becoming a foster carer, but was told he stood no chance because his home was not big enough. That didn’t seem to matter when it came to kinship care. When he asked his housing association landlord about moving to a bigger flat, just before his nephews arrived, there was little sympathy. “I was told: ‘Why are you making your house overcrowded?’”Leasa and Oly are still in the flat, and for the past five years, they have slept on a sofa bed in the lounge. The room is crammed with storage boxes, and is also where the couple’s nephews do their homework. The arrangement works partly because Oly works night shifts and Leasa, who is a nanny, works during the day.“Some of our friends sat us down and said: ‘What are you doing? Where will you find the money to look after these kids?’ My mum thought I was crazy,” says Leasa. “What people with the power to do something need to understand is that kinship care really does upend your life, physically and emotionally.”Looking back, Oly says they were naive. Eventually, with the help of a lawyer, they got a bigger financial allowance. They don’t regret becoming kinship carers for a minute, but the nagging feeling remains that social services exploited their goodwill.“I feel a bit blindsided by the council,” says Oly. “Sometimes, I think: why didn’t you tell us (about the support available). It didn’t have to be like this, right?”View image in fullscreenOly and Leasa making up the sofa bed they have slept on for the past five years.Photograph: Saskia Albers/Portray Your StoryClive says: “Kinship carers are like the shadow of the care system. We are not well recognised, not well understood or appreciated, and the system almost takes advantage of that. That’s what it feels like.”The chief executive of Kinship, Lucy Peake, says kinship carers save £4.3bn a year that the state would otherwise spend on children’s homes and foster care.“Relatives often say they are told that if they don’t step in, children will go into care,” Peake says. “They step up to do the right thing for children. Kinship carers regularly tell us they felt under pressure to make a decision without enough time, information or clarity about the support available to them.“It’s time their extraordinary contribution to children and our society is recognised,” she adds.Earlier this year, the government launcheda three-year pilot schemein seven local authorities giving kinship carers a financial allowance in line with foster carers for the first time. Foster carers currently receivebetween £170 and £299 a week, depending on where they live and the age of the child. The children’s minister, Josh MacAlister, said the pilot recognised “the vital role [kinship carers] play ensuring families can stay together”.View image in fullscreenAlan, Julie and Ella. ‘She has a way of showing us things,’ says Alan.Photograph: Saskia Albers/Portray Your StoryKinship welcomes the scheme, but points out it covers just 5,000 children. “Unlike foster carers who receive months of preparation and ongoing support, kinship carers have no notice and get little support, forcing many to lose jobs, pensions, savings and even their own retirement to keep a child they love out of the care system,” says Peake.Research shows kinship care is not only cheaper than residential or foster care, but more likely to lead to better outcomes for the child while helping them retain a strong sense of family and identity. Yet the latest Kinship survey found many carers were struggling financially, falling into debt and relying on food banks.For all the stress, many enthuse about the joy kinship caring has brought. Alan talks about lying on the floor next to Ella, watching her smile as he sings Beatles songs to her. She is non-verbal and is only just learning to walk aged nine, but “she has a way of showing us things”, Alan says proudly.Clive says he is often asked at conferences to name his greatest achievement. Once he would have said turning a school around or becoming a headteacher at 28. Now, he says, “keeping my niece in the family means more than any of those accolades”.For Oly, “the best thing is when I look at the boys and they are laughing from the heart. They didn’t do that when they first came. They were in shock. So when I see that laughter, and feel those hugs … yeah, that fills my heart.”

title: Egyptian journalist faces terrorism charges after entire newsroom detained | Egypt | The Guardian
description: Calls for release of six Matsadaash staff after one is charged, while whereabouts of other five remain unknown
Author: William Christou
Headline: Calls for release of six Matsadaash staff after one is charged, while whereabouts of other five remain unknown
Content: Clockwise from top left: Mohamed Ashraf, Omar Helal, Islam Barakat, Mohamed Adel, Mohamed Mahmoud and Abdallah Qadri.Photograph: Matsadaash/APView image in fullscreenClockwise from top left: Mohamed Ashraf, Omar Helal, Islam Barakat, Mohamed Adel, Mohamed Mahmoud and Abdallah Qadri.Photograph: Matsadaash/APEgyptEgyptian journalist faces terrorism charges after entire newsroom detainedCalls for release of six Matsadaash staff after one is charged, while whereabouts of other five remain unknownWilliam Christouin JerusalemSun 4 Oct 2026 11.16 EDTFirst published on Sun 4 Oct 2026 11.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn Egyptian journalist has been charged with joining a terrorist group, days after an entire newsroom was detained in what rights groups have said is a crackdown on press freedoms.Last week, authorities arrested six journalists from the independent fact-checking and investigative platform Matsadaash – literally meaning “don’t believe” – accusing them in a statement of being unlicensed and publishing false news on behalf of the outlawedMuslim Brotherhood.The outlet’s six journalists, Abdallah Qadri, Mohamed Ashraf, Mohamed Adel, Islam Barakat, Mohamed Mahmoud and Omar Helal, were arrested by security forces over the course of two days.On Sunday, Egyptian authorities charged Ashraf with joining a terrorist group and spreading false news, according to a statement by the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights, a NGO. The charges came after an interrogation that lasted from 10pm to 8am and focused exclusively on material published by Matsadaash, the rights group said.Ashraf was to be held for 15 days, pending investigation, while the whereabouts of the other five journalists were still unknown.View image in fullscreenEgyptian authorities have charged the journalist Mohamed Ashraf with joining a terrorist group and spreading fake news.Photograph: Matsadaash/APAbdelrahman Mansour, the co-founder of the platform, denied having any association with the Muslim Brotherhood, a transnational movement that was designated a terrorist organisation by Egypt in 2013 after the former president Mohamed Morsi, a senior Brotherhood figure, was ousted in a coup. Mansour called the arrests “one of the gravest attacks on journalism in Egypt’s modern history”.“My colleagues were doing what journalists should do: asking difficult questions, uncovering facts, and reporting on issues that affect people’s lives.
