They deserve recognition for their work. Instead, their homes were raided, and all six were taken away,” he said. “The government must answer this question: why have you arrested six journalists? What have they done beyond doing their jobs?”The Guardian contacted the Egyptian State Information Service for a comment but did not receive a reply by the time of publishing.Dozens of journalists staged a sit-in outside the Egyptian Journalists Syndicate (EJS) in Cairo on Saturday, demanding the release of the Matsadaash staff. Members said they would keep the sit-in open ended until the journalists were released, and the EJS said it would convene an emergency meeting on Monday.The EJS had filed a request with the ministry of interior and public prosecutor for the release of the journalists, as well as for information on their whereabouts.More than 80 rights groups, including Human Rights Watch and the Committee to Protect Journalists, condemned the arrests as a violation of freedoms, and demanded the immediate release of the Matsadaash staff.The arrests came little over a week after the US government waived its human rights conditions on $320m (£242m) in military aid to Egypt, citing Cairo’s “helpful role” to US national security after the US-Iran war.The US gives about $1.3bn in aid to Egypt annually, but a portion is contingent upon the Egyptian government meeting certain human rights and democracy-related requirements. The US has withheld portions of aid several times since the 2013 coup owing to Egypt’s poor human rights record, but has largely kept funds flowing.This year, Washington waived the human rights requirement in total, as doing so was “essential for the US-Egypt relationship and US national security priorities”, according to a state department memo revealed by Reuters.While saying that he was unsure whether the arrests were linked to the recent waiver, Mansour said: “The use of the national security waiver on human rights conditions by the US by many years, a willingness by other states to look the other way on Egypt’s human rights record … certainly enables violations like this to occur more easily.”Cairo has for years faced criticism for its human rights abuses, with the rights monitor Freedom House saying Egyptian security forces “engage in human rights abuses and extrajudicial killing with impunity”.Since the Egyptian president Abdel Fatah al-Sisi took power in the coup that ousted Morsi, civil liberties have been curbed and domestic political opposition has been violently crushed.Egypt ranks 169th out of 180 countries on the Reporters Without BordersPress freedomindex. Freedom of the press is tightly restricted in the country and independent platforms such as Matsadaash are rare. About 26 journalists are held in Egyptian prisons, according to the EJS.Explore more on these topicsEgyptPress freedomMuslim BrotherhoodMiddle East and north AfricaAfricaNewspapersNewspapers & magazinesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Would slashing migration tank the economy or reset Australia’s living standards? Canada may offer clues | Australian immigration and asylum | The Guardian
description: Annual population growth for the North American nation has slowed to just 0.5% – and the economy is ‘adjusting’
Author: Patrick Commins
Headline: Annual population growth for the North American nation has slowed to just 0.5% – and the economy is ‘adjusting’
Content: Canada has not targeted a specific net overseas migration level. Instead, it has adopted policies to reduce the number of temporary migrants as a share of population.Photograph: Canadian Press/Rex/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenCanada has not targeted a specific net overseas migration level. Instead, it has adopted policies to reduce the number of temporary migrants as a share of population.Photograph: Canadian Press/Rex/ShutterstockAustralian immigration and asylumAnalysisWould slashing migration tank the economy or reset Australia’s living standards? Canada may offer cluesPatrick ComminsAnnual population growth for the North American nation has slowed to just 0.5% – and the economy is ‘adjusting’Get ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastSun 4 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 16.31 EDTShareWould slashing net overseas migration “trash the economy” or deliver the necessary population “reset” to restore Australia’s stagnant living standards?Labor and an ascendantOne Nationhave presented starkly different visions of what a migration program in the national interest looks like.Pauline Hanson, the populist party’s leader, last monthannounced a planto cut the number of temporary migrants in Australia by more than 750,000 over three years by targeting international students and family members of skilled migrants.One Nation’s immigration policy deserves serious discussion – but not for the reason you might think | Alan GamlenRead moreTo achieve that reduction, net overseas migration (Nom) would need to turn negative for three years, the party says, before an ongoing cap of 130,000.That compares withLabor’s longer-term Nom target of 225,000, and to the last official estimate of 292,000 in the year to March.Tony Burke, the home affairs minister,said One Nation’s plan, if enacted, would “trash Australian services andtrash the Australian economy”.Hanson disagrees, and is quick to blame Australia’s high population growth over the past few years for the economy’s woes.In a social media post, she said “vested interest [sic] are warning Australia could face a technical recession if migration is cut”.“Australians have been in a per-capita recession for years. Their lives have been getting worse because of migration.Canadahas shown living standards improve when migration is cut.”Graph showing Australia’s stagnant living standards, with GDP per person in 2026 where it was three years agoFor those looking for international comparisons, Canada has long been a type of sister country to Australia – similar size, similar culture, similar economy.And the North American nation is in the midst of a dramatic migration adjustment that has flattened population growth.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailUnlike Hanson, Canada’s policymakershave not targeted a specific net overseas migration level. Instead, they have rolled out a suite of policies to reduce the number of temporary migrants as a share of population from a peak of 7.6% in 2024, to 5%.Canada is about halfway to this goal. The government has done this by reducing temporary arrivals, particularly international students, making it harder to extend stays and giving some temporary migrants permanency.Graph showing a dramatic reduction in Canada’s annual net international migrationAnnual population growth has slowed from 3.1% in early 2024 to just 0.5% now.So how well has Canada’s economy coped? And what does their experience tell us about how Australia should respond to growing calls for a more hardline approach to migration?‘Canada’s economy is not broken. It is adjusting’In May, the CD Howe Institute, a leading Canadian thinktank, issued a report on the country’s economy in a “lower immigration era”.The title was “resetting expectations”.Modelling by the report’s authors, Don Drummond and Parisa Mahboubi, estimated that employment in Canada could fall this year and the next.Real GDP growth in 2026 may be no more than 0.5%, they forecast, and “little more” than 1% on average in the long term.Falling employment would normally be cause for alarm, but Drummond and Mahboubi say this is actually “what a normally operating labour market delivers, given the demographic shifts underway”.“These are not signs of a struggling economy,” they said.“Canada’s economy is not broken. It is adjusting. Understanding that adjustment is a precondition for sound policy in the years ahead.”View image in fullscreenThe Canadian economy has been ‘relatively resilient’, experts say. Pictured: Vancouver.Photograph: Charles Mistral/AlamyNathan Janzen, the assistant chief economist at the Royal Bank of Canada, agrees with this assessment.“What the population shifts have done has changed how we need to interpret economic data.”The university sector has been hit particularly hard by the tighter migration rules. The government also provided exceptions to migrants working in areas of particular labour shortages, such as agriculture and the care economy.But overall, Janzen says, “the Canadian economy has been relatively resilient”.“If our population estimate numbers are right, we could have negative employment growth and still have falling unemployment. And the per capita economy looks like it’s getting better.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionCanada’s recession and ‘cyclical factors’ at playBut economists warn against assuming Canada’s experience would be replicated here.Jonathan Kearns, the chief economist at Challenger, says the first point to make is that Canada’s post-pandemic surge was far larger than Australia’s.“While people here get excited about our post-Covid immigration, it was nothing compared to theirs,” Kearns says.Even now, Canada’s population still sits 5% above where it would have been expected to be based on pre-Covid trends.In comparison, Australia’s population is tracking just 0.2% above its pre-pandemic trend line.“So the decline [in Canada’s population growth] has to be taken in context of the massive run-up,” Kearns says.Graph showing total population versus pre-pandemic trend for Canada and AustraliaCanada also began its migration crackdown at a time of high unemployment in the wake of an aggressive series of interest rate hikes by the Bank of Canada.In contrast, were Australia to crack down hard on migrants, it would do so with a tight labour market where unemployment sits at 4.6% and at a time of widespread labour shortages.Luci Ellis, Westpac’s chief economist, says: “I don’t think you can just point to Canada and say, ‘Look, they did OK.’”Ellis says there are cyclical factors at play that help explain Canada’s apparent economic resilience to its migration crackdown.“It’s also because they are recovering from a recession,” she says.The challenge of ageing populationsWhile Canada’s economy has, so far, coped with the country’s stricter migration policies, there is little appetite for them to be a permanent feature in a nation that remains open to immigration.Canada, like Australia, is ageing. That means a shrinking share of taxpaying workers to fund the cost of providing pensions, aged care and health services to older Canadians.Think Australia would be better off with less migration? The numbers tell a different storyRead moreThe CD Howe Institute analysis shows that if the current era of low population growth became a permanent one, then Canada’s economy would be about 11.5% smaller by 2060, compared with official government projections.“The implications for fiscal sustainability are significant,” the authors said. “This gap translates into structurally weaker revenues and higher debt ratios.”Janzen says that, without immigration, “labour shortages are going to be a structural feature of the economy”.“The view is that this will be a temporary adjustment, before we return to something more like historical rates of immigration.”And while Australia may not want to exactly replicate our North American peer’s dramatic migration reset, there remain legitimate questions around how we can better manage a temporary migration program that has ballooned over recent years.Ellis believes Australian employers have become too reliant on overseas labour, from chefs to workers in rural areas, and that this has come at the expense of training and hiring locals, even if it means paying higher wages.“By choosing higher population growth with a high temporary component, we have made it easy for employers to look offshore any time they need to find someone for a job. There are definitely industries that have grown to be reliant on that,” she says.“That degrades your ability and willingness to train your local workforce.”Patrick Commins is Guardian Australia’s economics editorExplore more on these topicsAustralian immigration and asylumAustralian economyAustralian politicsLabor partyOne NationMigrationCanadaanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Polls close in first round of Brazil’s high-stakes presidential election | Brazil | The Guardian
description: Leftwing incumbent Lula trying to fight off close rival Flávio Bolsonaro, far-right son of jailed ex-president
Author: Tiago Rogero
Headline: Leftwing incumbent Lula trying to fight off close rival Flávio Bolsonaro, far-right son of jailed ex-president
Content: Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (left) is seeking a fourth term, with the far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro standing in his way.Composite: Isabella Finholdt/NurPhoto/Shutterstock, Douglas Shineidr/GettyView image in fullscreenLuiz Inácio Lula da Silva (left) is seeking a fourth term, with the far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro standing in his way.Composite: Isabella Finholdt/NurPhoto/Shutterstock, Douglas Shineidr/GettyBrazilPolls close in first round of Brazil’s high-stakes presidential electionLeftwing incumbent Lula trying to fight off close rival Flávio Bolsonaro, far-right son of jailed ex-presidentTiago Rogeroin Rio de JaneiroSun 4 Oct 2026 09.52 EDTFirst published on Sun 4 Oct 2026 04.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe polls have closed in the first round of Brazil’s highly polarised and high-stakes presidential election that could change not only the direction of Latin America’s largest country but that of the entire region.The election pits the leftwing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, who is seeking a fourth non-consecutive term, against the far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro, an ally of Donald Trump and the son of the former president Jair Bolsonaro, who is serving a 27-year sentencefor attempting a coupafter his failed 2022 re-election attempt.Late on Sunday Bolsonaro was leading Lula in partial results. With results in from almost 65% of the country, Bolsonaro had 49.8% to Lula’s 42.25%, while several other candidates stood in the single digits.Lula and Bolsonaro have alternated as frontrunners in the final stretch, making the outcome unpredictable. In recent days both have focused on persuading undecided voters in hopes of reaching 50% plus one vote; if neither does, there will be a runoff on 25 October.Brazil is one of the few Latin American countries that still has a leftwing government after a wave of rightwing and far-right electoral victories across the region andthe US takeover of Venezuelaafter the capture of Nicolás Maduro.The 80-year-old Lula has positioned himself as one of the last regional leaders still willing to say no to Trump, and has recently accused the US president oftrying to interferein Brazil’s election inBolsonaro’s favour.View image in fullscreenLula embraces a child as he leaves a polling station in São Bernardo do Campo after casting his vote on Sunday.Photograph: Alexandre Meneghini/ReutersLike his father, who was Brazil’s president during Trump’s first term, Flávio Bolsonaro, 45,frequently praisesthe US president and has pledged to join the US-led anti-drug-cartel coalition that haskilled dozens of people in airstrikesand carried out military operations across the region.Voting on Sunday morning in São Bernardo do Campo, the industrial city where hispolitical career begannearly half a century ago, Lula said: “People will have to choose between strengthening democracy and barbarism.” The incumbent played down polls released on Saturday that showed the race was wide open – they suggested either candidate could finish ahead and force a runoff, or even win outright on Sunday. “The poll that matters will be carried out today,” he said.View image in fullscreenFlávio Bolsonaro with his wife, Fernanda, after voting in Rio de Janeiro.Photograph: Silvia Izquierdo/APFlávio Bolsonaro, who voted in Rio de Janeiro’s north zone, urged supporters of other rightwing candidates to switch to him in a “protest vote”. “Our internal polls show people who would have voted for other candidates, who are also against Lula, already voting for Flávio Bolsonaro … I hope it’s enough to give us victory in the first round,” he said.Claudinei Ferreira Viana, 45, a workshop manager in Pinhais in Paraná state, is one of the senator’s supporters. “My first choice would be Jair Bolsonaro but, since he isunder house arrestand there is no other rightwing candidate strong enough to take on the current president, I’m going with Flávio,” he said.3:43How Trump is meddling in Brazil’s election – explainerAt the beginning of the year,polls suggestedBolsonaro voters would have preferred a ticket led by the São Paulo governor, Tarcísio de Freitas, or the former first lady Michelle Bolsonaro. But the former president chose his eldest son.The campaign was also marked by a scandal in which the senator wascaught on tapeasking a banker accused of corruption for $26.8m (£20m) to fund afilm about his father, as well as speculation that Bolsonaromight stripthe country’s widely cherished patron saint of her status, but he has nevertheless remained highly competitive.View image in fullscreenFlávio Bolsonaro during an open-top campaign parade through the Campo Grande district of Rio de Janeiro on Saturday.Photograph: Bruna Prado/APFor many analysts, that reflects a combination of a straightforward transfer of his father’s voter base – Jair Bolsonaro lost to Lula by less than two percentage points in 2022 – and an anti-Lula vote, with the president still facing highrejection ratesdespitestrong social and economic indicators.The incumbent’s campaign has also been hit by corruption allegations – still under investigation – involving his son and a former aide, as well as ascandal involving supreme court justices, which, despite having no connection to Lula, is seen as fuelling an “anti-system” vote and by extension an anti-incumbent one.View image in fullscreenLula parading through São Paulo on Saturday.Photograph: Sebastião Moreira/EPABrazilians will also elect 27 state governors, members of state legislatures, all 513 federal congress members and 54 of the country’s 81 senators in Sunday’s vote.AMC, 40, who asked to be identified only by her initials because she fears reprisals from the local conservative government where she works in the interior of Amazonas state, will vote for Lula on Sunday “because of the many programmes he created to support the most vulnerable groups”.“Jair Bolsonaro weakened protections for Indigenous peoples, and everything Lula has done over the past four years to strengthen those protections andprotect the Amazonwould beseriously threatenedif his son came to power,” she said.Explore more on these topicsBrazilLuiz Inácio Lula da SilvaJair BolsonaroAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: US Coast Guard finds debris of missing air ambulance off coast of Massachusetts | Massachusetts | The Guardian
description: The plane was undertaking a medical evacuation from Bermuda with six people onboard when it lost contact
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The plane was undertaking a medical evacuation from Bermuda with six people onboard when it lost contact
Content: A US Coast Guard ship patrols off the California coast in 2024.Photograph: APView image in fullscreenA US Coast Guard ship patrols off the California coast in 2024.Photograph: APMassachusettsUS Coast Guard finds debris of missing air ambulance off coast of MassachusettsThe plane was undertaking a medical evacuation from Bermuda with six people onboard when it lost contactKeely Aouga and agenciesSat 3 Oct 2026 23.38 EDTFirst published on Sat 3 Oct 2026 13.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe US Coast Guard said late on Saturday it had found debris from a medical transport aircraft off the shore of ⁠Massachusetts’s Nantucket Island and ⁠was searching for ​the six people who were onboard.The jet lost contact with the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) during a flight fromBermudato Boston on Saturday morning. In a statement to the Guardian, an FAA spokesperson said that the agency issued a search-and-rescue alert notice for a Gulfstream G-100 at about 1.20am local time Saturday.The Canadian-registered air ambulance jet had four crew members and two passengers onboard when it departed Bermuda’s LF Wade international airport overnight for the flight to Massachusetts, according to a statement from the Bermuda airport’s operator, Skyport, obtained by theAssociated Press.Four Canadians ​were on the plane, the Canadian minister ‌of transport Steven MacKinnon posted, adding: “We are closely monitoring the situation and are working with the relevant authorities ‌as search and rescue efforts continue.”The other two passengers were Bermudian nationals, the coast guard said. Searches would continue throughout the night near Nantucket, an island community south of mainland Massachusetts.The Bermuda government was in contact ​with US authorities ​and the families of the passengers, the Bermuda premier, David Burt, posted.The aircraft, registered to Latitude Air Ambulance, departed Bermuda at 12.41am on Saturday according to data from flight-tracking website ‌FlightAware. The plane was flying at 24,000ft (7,300 metres) for much of the journey before descending 13,000ft in about two minutes shortly ​before flight controllers lost contact, data showed.TV stationBoston25 posted an audio clip from Boston Logan international airport in which an air traffic controller can be heard asking the Gulfstream pilot: “You said you’re coming in blind? Is that what you said?”The controller ⁠then asked whether the plane was declaring an emergency. No response was ​heard.Latitude is based in ​Ontario, Canada, and provides medical evacuation ​services.NBC Newsreportedthat the plane was carrying out a medical evacuation in Bermuda, citing a statement from Clarence Togeretz, the director of flight operations at Latitude.“We always get rather concerned when our crew doesn’t report to us in a timely manner,” he told NBC News. “But I will say that again, optimistically and positively, that doesn’t mean that the worst has happened.”NBC also reported that the Massachusetts port authority, which operates Boston Logan international airport, said the aircraft did not arrive as scheduled. A port authority spokesperson said: “Our thoughts are with those on board and their loved ones as the search continues.”The FAA is coordinating with the Rescue Coordination Center and the US Coast Guard to locate the aircraft.Explore more on these topicsMassachusettsBermudaBostonPlane crashesAir transportAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: US marine arrested in Japan on suspicion of killing woman, police say | US military | The Guardian
description: Suspect allegedly killed woman at hotel in Okinawa as prime minister calls crime ‘exceptionally brutal and vicious’
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Suspect allegedly killed woman at hotel in Okinawa as prime minister calls crime ‘exceptionally brutal and vicious’
Content: US MV-22 Osprey aircraft parked at Marine Corps air station Futenma, Okinawa, Japan, on 18 February 2025.Photograph: Hiro Komae/APView image in fullscreenUS MV-22 Osprey aircraft parked at Marine Corps air station Futenma, Okinawa, Japan, on 18 February 2025.Photograph: Hiro Komae/APUS militaryUS marine arrested in Japan on suspicion of killing woman, police saySuspect allegedly killed woman at hotel in Okinawa as prime minister calls crime ‘exceptionally brutal and vicious’Agence France-Presse and Guardian staffSun 4 Oct 2026 09.46 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 18.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA US marine stationed onJapan’s southern island of Okinawa is accused of murdering a Japanese woman and has been arrested on suspicion of murder, police said on Sunday.The suspect allegedly “killed [a] 39-year-old woman at a hotel in Naha and stole her wallet” as well as her backpack, local police told news media outlets.Citing police, NBC Newsreportedthat the suspect charged in the case was identified as Lance Cpl Devin Jacob Ballard, 20. Anna Yagi was identified as the victim.Ballard denied the allegations, police said, according to NBC.Crimes including rape, assault, hit-and-run and drunk driving by US personnel have long sparked protests on Okinawa. The island bears a disproportionate burden of hosting about 70% ofUS militaryfacilities in Japan.US ambassador George Glasspostedon social media that he had spoken with Japan’s foreign ministry and Okinawa’s governor, offering “sincere condolences to the victim’s family” and pledging cooperation into the investigation of her death.The Japanese prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, saidJapanhad lodged a protest with US authorities and called the crime “exceptionally brutal and vicious”.The government has urged the US “to provide maximum cooperation with the investigation, enforce stricter discipline amongUS militarypersonnel, and take thorough measures to prevent the recurrence of similar crimes”, Takaichi said.Public broadcaster NHK and other Japanese media outlets, citing investigation sources, reported that CCTV footage from near the scene showed a foreign man entering a room with a woman and later leaving with her belongings.Police then found a 20-year-old man who matched the description of the suspect seen in the footage and asked him to accompany them voluntarily to a local police station, where he was arrested, NHK reported.“We have lost a family member and are deeply saddened,” Yagi’s brother said through local police, according to the Asahi Shimbun daily newspaper. “My parents, in particular, are utterly devastated at the loss of their daughter.”The US has about 54,000 military personnel stationed in Japan, mostly on Okinawa.Crimes committed by US personnel in Japan have been a thorn in relations between the close security allies.“Incidents and accidents involving US military personnel cause great anxiety among the local community and must not be allowed to happen,” Japan’s defense minister Shinjiro Koizumi said.In June 2025, a Japanese courtsentencedUS marine Jamel Clayton – then 22 – to seven years in prison after being convicted of choking and sexually assaulting a woman in her 20s.Earlier, in 2017, former US marine and civilian military base worker Kenneth Shinzato was sentenced to life in prison for the rape and murder of a local woman in Okinawa.The same year, US forces in Japan banned all personnel from consuming alcohol after an intoxicated American marine crashed his vehicle into a mini-truck, killing its 61-year-old local driver.According to the Yomiuri Shimbun newspaper, about 6,000 US military personnel have been arrested since Okinawa was returned to Japan from the US in 1972 after the second world war.The number of arrests in a year hit 80 in 2024, the highest in 20 years.Explore more on these topicsUS militaryJapanUS crimeAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: UK car industry faces ‘difficult trade-off’ between Chinese and EU markets | Automotive industry | The Guardian
description: Britain under pressure to put tariffs on cheap Chinese vehicle imports ahead of protectionist trade measures
Author: Alex Daniel
Headline: Britain under pressure to put tariffs on cheap Chinese vehicle imports ahead of protectionist trade measures
Content: Chinese EVs wait to be shipped for export at Yantai Port in Yantai City, Shandong Province, China.Photograph: Costfoto/NurPhoto/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenChinese EVs wait to be shipped for export at Yantai Port in Yantai City, Shandong Province, China.Photograph: Costfoto/NurPhoto/ShutterstockAutomotive industryUK car industry faces ‘difficult trade-off’ between Chinese and EU marketsBritain under pressure to put tariffs on cheap Chinese vehicle imports ahead of protectionist trade measuresAlex DanielSun 4 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 14.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBritain’s car industry is grappling with a “difficult trade-off” between China andEurope, as manufacturers struggle to balance the benefits of both markets ahead of looming trade measures that could restrict UK exports to the EU.The UK is an outlier in choosing not to put import taxes on Chinese vehicles, even as the US hasshut them out almost entirely, and the EU imposesduties of up to 45%.EU officials reportedly warned Andy Burnham last month that the UK must put tariffs on cheap Chinese vehicles otherwise Brussels would impose protectionist“made in Europe” barrierson British exports to the bloc, hitting British carmakers in their largest market.Ministers have so far resisted such calls, with Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary, arguing any levies would “probably be reciprocated” – costing UK manufacturers sales inChina.Tariffs would also raise prices for British drivers, who haveflocked to cheaper Chinese models, and could deter brands such as Chery, which isin talks to build cars at Nissan’s Sunderland plant, from investing further in the UK.“There is a difficult trade-off,” said Emily Sawicz, of the consultancy RSM UK, adding that the UK “cannot afford to drift between the two indefinitely”. Chinese investment could be a “lifeline” for carmakers, while access to Europe would also be “crucial” for smaller manufacturers.“Being excluded risks UK suppliers becoming increasingly shut out of those European opportunities,” she added. “Manufacturers need clarity on which direction the government intends to take so they can make long-term investment decisions.”Ian Plummer, commercial director at Autotrader, said competition from Chinese brands had made cars more affordable and “is encouraging more people to go and buy a new car”.Brands such as BYD, Omoda and Jaecoo more than tripled their share of the UK new car market in the first eight months of 2026, reaching 12% of sales, according to industry figures.Figures released on Friday showed that British new car ⁠registrations rose 12% in the year to September, the best month for annual growth since 2017. The preliminary data from the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders (SMMT) showed the boom was powered by a demand for electric vehicles and Chinese brands, with the Jaecoo 7 and BYD’s ​Sealion ‌7 among the top sellers.The trade body said on Wednesday that the European Commission’s made in Europe rules, which restrict subsidies, tax breaks and public procurement contracts to vehicles built within the EU, pose an existential threat to British car production. The EU accounted for 58% of UK car exports in the first half of the year, compared with about 4% for China.Mike Hawes, the SMMT’s chief executive, said: “The UK and EU automotive industries are deeply integrated, so effectively excluding British-produced vehicles from their largest market would assure mutual damage.”.Massimiliano Messina, Nissan’s chair in Europe, said last month: “Europe cannot have a Trojan horse where the Chinese are going to flood the market through the UK.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionVictor Zhang, the deputy UK chief of Chery, which owns the Jaecoo and Omoda brands, rejected that claim, saying: “Most of what we sell are super-hybrids, not the cars that those tariffs are about, and the cars we sell here stay here.”He added: “Tariffs can come and go, but we won’t change our ongoing investment in the UK.”Brussels raised its own tariffs on Chinese EVs in 2024, triggering a decline in what was then an accelerating sales trajectory. It is now facing calls for fresh barriers to be imposed on importing hybrid electric vehicles, potentially quotas or price floors.Imports of plug-in and battery hybrid carsrocketed after the EU tariffs were imposedon EVs, underlining China’s ability to pivot its export efforts when hit by trade barriers.Others in the industry believe tariffs could help protect the UK’s manufacturers, whose market share in Britain continues to be eroded Chinese firms.Tim Tozer, a former chair of Vauxhall, said that tariffs were “vital” to stop Britain’s car sector “atrophying”. He said: “We are at last knockings now, trying to save the industry.”He added that Reynolds was “whistling in the wind” with hopes of continuing to export to China en masse, arguing the market had become “fiercely nationalistic,” with buyers increasingly loyal to domestic brands “because they’re bloody good”.Explore more on these topicsAutomotive industryEuropean UnionChinaTrade policyManufacturing sectorAsia PacificEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: No bail for P-plater over Newcastle crash that left five-year-old in induced coma and injured nine other NRL fans | Newcastle and the Hunter | The Guardian
description: Indika Bambrick Samarasinghe, 18, appears in court on dangerous driving offences after car struck Knights supporters lining streets to farewell their team
Author: Andrew Messenger
Headline: Indika Bambrick Samarasinghe, 18, appears in court on dangerous driving offences after car struck Knights supporters lining streets to farewell their team
Content: Ten people were left injured after a car allegedly driven by 18-year-old P-plater Indika Bambrick Samarasinghe careered into the crowd near a major roundabout near Newcastle on Saturday morning.Photograph: Supplied By ABC News/PR IMAGEView image in fullscreenTen people were left injured after a car allegedly driven by 18-year-old P-plater Indika Bambrick Samarasinghe careered into the crowd near a major roundabout near Newcastle on Saturday morning.Photograph: Supplied By ABC News/PR IMAGENewcastle and the HunterNo bail for P-plater over Newcastle crash that left five-year-old in induced coma and injured nine other NRL fansIndika Bambrick Samarasinghe, 18, appears in court on dangerous driving offences after car struck Knights supporters lining streets to farewell their teamGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastAustralian Associated Press andAndrew MessengerSun 4 Oct 2026 15.56 EDTFirst published on Sat 3 Oct 2026 23.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA driver whose car careered into a crowd ofNewcastle Knightssupporters – leaving children as young as five injured – will be kept in custody as the community rallies to support those hospitalised after the crash.Ten people were left injured after a car allegedly driven by 18-year-old P-plater Indika Bambrick Samarasinghe careered into the crowd near a major roundabout on Saturday morning.Six people remain at the John Hunter hospital with injuries caused by the collision, according to the Hunter New England Local Health District chief executive, Tracey McCosker. As of 4pm Sunday, five people were in a stable condition.A five-year-old girl who had been placed into an induced coma with critical injuries, although her condition has stabilised.Five-year-old girl in a coma and P-plater charged after car hits crowd of NRL fans in NewcastleRead moreSamarasinghe was taken to hospital for mandatory testing and subsequently charged with nine offences, including dangerous driving occasioning grievous bodily harm, negligent driving and causing bodily harm by misconduct.He did not make any application for release during a brief court appearance on Sunday, and he was formally refused bail. The judge also endorsed a warrant for a health assessment.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailThe bail court was told the most serious offence of dangerous driving occasioning grievous bodily harm carried a maximum jail term of seven years.He will next appear at the Newcastle local court on 15 October.Chris Clancy was among those injured in the crash, after joining thousands of Newcastle Knights fans to lined the streets to farewell their team as the players travelled to Sydney for the grand final.“We’re there at the roundabout having fun – cars going past, beeping their horns, people waving,” Clancy said.“The next thing, this car stops [at] the roundabout and then he just floored it on the wet ground, lost it.“It happened in seconds, but when you stand there, seeing the car coming at you, I honestly thought I was going to die. It just felt like slow motion.”Clancy suffered small fractures in his ribs and spine, a broken collarbone, and small fractures in his foot.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionInvestigators did not believe the incident was deliberate but declined to comment on reports the vehicle was being driven erratically before the crash.Multiple fundraisers have been established for the victims of the incident, including one for the five-year-old girl and another for Wallsend grandfather Dave Martin.Martin was injured after being struck by the car while trying to protect his two young granddaughters, sustaining multiple fractures in both legs and undergoing a lengthy surgery.He was known in Wallsend for his love of the Knights, often decorating his barber shop on Nelson Street with team paraphernalia.The Knights’ chief executive, Peter Parr, expressed deep concern for those affected by the crash.“Newcastle is a strong community,” he said.“We have seen that strength throughout this week, and today we need to draw on it again with compassion, care and support for those who need it most.”Explore more on these topicsNewcastle and the HunterNew South WalesNewcastle KnightsNRLnewsShareReuse this content

title: Australia and Turkey criticised for hosting UN climate conference while embracing coal | Cop31 | The Guardian
description: Global campaign group 350.org urges Cop31 hosts to announce a coal phase-out date and national roadmaps to get off fossil fuels
Author: Adam Morton
Headline: Global campaign group 350.org urges Cop31 hosts to announce a coal phase-out date and national roadmaps to get off fossil fuels
Content: The Cop31 UN climate change summit is being held in the Turkish city of Antalya next month. Both Turkey and Australia will host the fortnight-long talks.Photograph: Goksel Yapar/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Cop31 UN climate change summit is being held in the Turkish city of Antalya next month. Both Turkey and Australia will host the fortnight-long talks.Photograph: Goksel Yapar/AFP/Getty ImagesCop31Australia and Turkey criticised for hosting UN climate conference while embracing coalGlobal campaign group 350.org urges Cop31 hosts to announce a coal phase-out date and national roadmaps to get off fossil fuelsSign up for climate and environment editor Adam Morton’s free Clear Air newsletter hereAdam Mortonin Nadi, FijiSun 4 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 16.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe hosts of the next major United Nations climate conference,Turkeyand Australia, are facing criticism for being partners in a coal supply chain while remaining near silent on the need for a global deal to rapidly get off fossil fuels.With theCop31summit in the Turkish Mediterranean city of Antalya just a month away, the two countries running the fortnight-long talks have been accused by activists of a “vacuum of action” on plans for a transition away from coal, gas and oil – a key goal of many nations at the talks.Preparations for Cop31 will kick up a gear this week with a small group of national leaders, including the Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese, expected to join representatives of more than 50 countries for a preparatory meeting in Fiji and Tuvalu.Australia’s big polluters rely on carbon offsets for climate credibility. But the system looks like a house of cards | Adam MortonRead morePre-summit meetings are typically bureaucratic gatherings, but expectations for his year’s event were elevated after Australia – which has the new role of “president of negotiations” at Cop31 – pushed to hold it in the Pacific, and invited leaders to attend, arguing it would highlight the plight of low-lying island nations.Few leaders from outside the region accepted.The Fijian government named five expected attenders – from Thailand, Antigua and Barbuda, Cape Verde, the Maldives and Timor-Leste – but some have since cancelled. They include the Thai prime minister, Anutin Charnvirakul, asBangkok suffered severe flooding.Sign up to get climate and environment editor Adam Morton’s Clear Air column as a free newsletterThe meeting is being held just days after a New South Wales regulatorapproved the largest coalmine expansionin the Australian state’s history. Joint owners Yancoal and Glencore estimate the 19-year life extension for the Hunter Valley Operations thermal coalmine could lead to 809m tonnes of heat-trapping carbon dioxide emissions if it wins federal approval.A report, by campaign group350.org, cited UN Comtrade data suggesting the supply of coking and thermal coal from Australia to Turkey had been responsible for more than 75m tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions since the signing of the landmark Paris climate agreement in 2015. It said the countries were now expanding their trade in liquified natural gas (LNG).The organisation said this had continued while the Cop31 presidents largely ignored fossil fuels – the primary cause of the climate crisis – in public comments before the summit. Three letters to countries setting out the mission and expectations for the summit, twofrom the Turkish governmentand onejoint letter with the Australians, did not mention fossil fuels. Albanese also did not mention fossil fuels ina keynote speech at Climate Weekin New York two weeks ago.Andreas Sieber, 350.org’s head of political strategy, said the hosts should be following the previous host, Brazil, in working on a roadmap to accelerate a transition away from dirty fuels. He said both countries should announce coal phase-out dates as a first step.“Amidstthe biggest energy crisis in history, it is extraordinary that the Cop31 presidency continues to ignore the central issue of fossil fuels,” Sieber said. “Rather than leading the transition away, both countries are still expanding fossil fuels at extreme rates.”Australia hasaccelerated its clean energy expansionat home, but remains one of the world’s biggest exporters of coal and LNG, with shipments this yearexpected to be worth more than A$140bn. The350.orgreport said Turkey was Europe’s biggest coal-power generator and it had signalled it could expand its coal and gas power capacity by about 30% by 2035.Australian climate change minister, Chris Bowen, has argued at previous summits that the world needs to move away from dirty fuels, including declaring at the Cop28 conference in Dubai that“the age of fossil fuels will end”. He told the Guardian on Sunday that Australia was a fossil fuel-exporting country, but acting on climate change was in its national, economic and strategic interest.He said Treasury analysis had found Australia could have an impact on global emissions by becoming a renewable energy exporter. “Our trading partners are pursuing their own energy transitions. We want to help them do that, so we remain a reliable trading nation,” Bowen said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When he publishesSign up toClear Air AustraliaAdam Morton brings you incisive analysis about the politics and impact of the climate crisisEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTurkey and Australia are sharing hosting duties at Cop31 in a unique agreement struck after a protracted standoff. Turkey has ultimate responsibility, including running a massive green trade fair, but Bowen has been appointed “president of negotiations” for the formal talks between nearly 200 nations.What is El Niño, what causes it and can we reduce the risks?Read moreThe Cop30 summit in Brazil last yearavoided collapse, but could manage only a voluntary agreement to begin discussions on a roadmap to phase out fossil fuels after oil-producing countries opposed stronger wording.Frustration over the impasse prompted 57 national governments to holda separate conference on how to transition away from fossil fuelsin Colombia in April. Turkey and Australia were represented at the Colombia meeting by senior officials.Vanuatu’s climate change minister, Ralph Regenvanu, said it would be “deeply disappointing” for Pacific countries if Australia extended the life of a major coalmine as it led the Cop31 negotiations. “This decision sends the wrong signal at a critical time,” he said,Bill Hare, the chief executive of the Climate Analytics, a science and policy institute, said it would be “interesting to see” if Turkey and Australia could set aside their “addiction to fossil fuels”. He said the Australia Labor government had approved 37 fossil fuel developments for export since its election in 2022, while Turkey under president Recep Tayyip Erdoğan seemed “fixated on prioritising digging up and burning coal … and establishing itself as a regional fossil gas hub”.Cop31 will be held amid rising concern about the impact of what has been described as a“super El Niño” weather pattern, and after the UN Environment Programme warned the worldwould breach the 1.5C global heating goalincluded in the Paris agreement.The UN agency warned every fraction of a degree of temperature rise would intensify destructive extreme weather, glacier melt, ecosystem loss, and island and coastal city submersion, and called for immediate and sustained cuts in emissions.Explore more on these topicsCop31CoalFossil fuelsTurkeyClimate crisisEnergy (Australia news)Energy (Environment)newsShareReuse this content

title: Bosnian Serb nationalist Dodik declares party victory in Bosnia election | Bosnia and Herzegovina | The Guardian
description: Staunchly pro-Russia politician has dominated campaign and inflamed divisions despite not appearing on ballot
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Staunchly pro-Russia politician has dominated campaign and inflamed divisions despite not appearing on ballot
Content: Formerly the president of the country’s Serb-majority entity of Republika Srpska, Dodik has been banned from holding public office.Photograph: Marko Đurica/ReutersView image in fullscreenFormerly the president of the country’s Serb-majority entity of Republika Srpska, Dodik has been banned from holding public office.Photograph: Marko Đurica/ReutersBosnia and HerzegovinaBosnian Serb nationalist Dodik declares party victory in Bosnia electionStaunchly pro-Russia politician has dominated campaign and inflamed divisions despite not appearing on ballotAssociated PressSun 4 Oct 2026 16.42 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 16.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBosnian Serb nationalist politician Milorad Dodik has declared victory for his party in an election in Bosnia shaped by economic pressures, the prospect of the Balkan nation joining the European Union and ethnic tensions that have divided the country since its brutal 1992-95 war.Dodik is a staunchly pro-Russia politician who, despite not appearing on the ballot, has dominated the campaign and inflamed divisions with separatist rhetoric that has sparked fears of renewed instability in Bosnia.Formerly the president of the country’s Serb-majority entity of Republika Srpska, Dodik was banned from holding public office after being convicted last year of defying decisions by the international envoy overseeing the 1995 peace agreement that ended the war.With nearly 90% of votes counted, Dodik’s ally Željka Cvijanovićof the rightwing Alliance of Independent Social Democrats had more than 55% of the votes to take one of the three seats in the country’s tripartite presidency, leading her nearest opponent by about 30 percentage points.Speaking at a news conference late on Sunday, Dodik said his nationalist party would also hold a “vast majority” in Republika Srpska’s assembly, and credited US president Donald Trump’s “magnificent victory” in 2024 and Russian president Vladimir Putin’s support for the election win.“No one should ask us to change our politics,” Dodik said. “We will not give up, but continue for our people … I cannot believe that we smashed it like this.”About 3.4 million voters were eligible to choose the three members of the country’s multi-ethnic presidency, lawmakers for the national parliament and heads of institutions for the country’s two entities: the Muslim-majority Federation ofBosnia and Herzegovinaand Republika Srpska, which is dominated by ethnic Serbs.With more than 94% of votes counted on Sunday, Darijana Filipović of the nationalist Croatian Democratic Union of Bosnia and Herzegovina held a commanding lead for the Croat seat on the presidency, while the incumbent Bosniak member of the presidency, Denis Bećirović of the Social Democratic party, led his nearest opponent, Bakir Izetbegović, by fewer than three percentage points.Can anything politicians say at Sunday’s election stop young people from leaving Bosnia?Read moreBoth Filipović and Bećirović declared victory in their races late on Sunday before all votes were counted.Bosnia’s central election commission said that 1,432,269 votes were cast in total, a turnout of 42% that was down by about 8% from Bosnia’s last election in 2022.Bosnia has a complex web of governing institutions that were created by a US-brokered peace agreement in 1995 in an effort to manage the ethnic divisions between Muslim Bosniaks, Orthodox Serbs and Catholic Croats that gave rise to the war.Yet Dodik has consistently tested those limits, openly defying Bosnia’s national government in the capital Sarajevo and making moves for Republika Srpska to separate from the country.At his party’s final election rally on Friday night in Banja Luka, Republika Srpska’s administrative capital, Dodik told supporters that Bosnia “is dead”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“It is an impossible country. It doesn’t make any sense,” Dodik said at the rally, which was also attended by Russian ambassador Igor Khalabukov.Such political and ethnic divisions – in which the country’s Bosniaks, Serbs and Croats largely vote along ethnic lines – have blocked Bosnia’s progress toward joining the EU despite the bloc’s efforts to encourage the country’s divided leaders to work together for reform.Dragan Bursać, an analyst, said that despite Dodik not appearing on the ballot for the first time in nearly 30 years, he “is still in command. He is everywhere.”“It is obvious that these measures to ban him from political life are not working, and he is using them,” Bursać said.One of the poorest countries in Europe, Bosnia is still struggling to recover decades on from the war, which started in 1992 after the country declared independence from the Serb-led former Yugoslavia and ethnic Serbs took up arms to carve out their own state and join Serbia. The conflict killed more than 100,000 people and displaced millions.Bosnia’s wartime wounds were recently revived by a public homage in Serbia and among Bosnian Serbs to the wartime army commander Ratko Mladić, who died in late August while serving a life sentence for genocide and other war crimes.Explore more on these topicsBosnia and HerzegovinaEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Russia strikes Kyiv bridge as German chancellor visits Ukraine in show of support | Kyiv | The Guardian
description: Attack shortly after Friedrich Merz arrived on unannounced visit intended to underline Germany’s backing
Author: Pjotr Sauer
Headline: Attack shortly after Friedrich Merz arrived on unannounced visit intended to underline Germany’s backing
Content: Soldiers inspect the damage from a Russian drone strike on the Northern Bridge in Kyiv.Photograph: Mykola Tymchenko/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSoldiers inspect the damage from a Russian drone strike on the Northern Bridge in Kyiv.Photograph: Mykola Tymchenko/AFP/Getty ImagesKyivRussia strikes Kyiv bridge as German chancellor visits Ukraine in show of supportAttack shortly after Friedrich Merz arrived on unannounced visit intended to underline Germany’s backingPjotr Sauerin KyivSun 4 Oct 2026 12.12 EDTFirst published on Sun 4 Oct 2026 07.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRussia has struck another major bridge in Kyiv as the German chancellor,Friedrich Merz, arrived in the capital in a show of support for Ukraine.A Russian drone hit Kyiv’s key Northern Bridge over the Dnipro River, marking the fourth consecutive day thatRussiahas targeted bridges used by tens of thousands of residents commuting between the city’s two banks. Video footage showed cars driving across the bridge as the drone plunged into the roadway and exploded in a burst of fire. Two people were injured in the strike, said Kyiv’s mayor, Vitali Klitschko.The attack came shortly after Merz arrived in the city on an unannounced visit intended to underline Germany’s backing of Ukraine, as the country enters one of the most precarious periods since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022.Germany has become Ukraine’s biggest provider of military aid since Merz entered office in May 2025, surpassing the US as American support has declined.Russian drone strikes North Bridge in Kyiv, UkraineKyiv has comeunder near-constant attackfrom Russia’s new jet-powered drones in recent weeks, as an intensifying strike campaign increasingly disrupts everyday life in the capital and threatens to leave the city without power this winter.On his visit, Merz announced that Germany would fund the joint production of drones designed to intercept Russia’s jet-powered drones, adding that “significant technical breakthroughs” in recent weeks were speeding up production.“This will quickly and tangibly strengthen Ukraine’s air defence,” he said. “And this strengthening is urgently needed.”The German leader got a taste of the new reality of daily life in the Ukrainian capital. Air-raid sirens sounded repeatedly during his visit, including as Volodymyr Zelenskyy showed him the badly damaged National Academy of Sciences building, wherea Russian drone strike killed two people last week.The Ukrainian president told Merz that people inKyivwere suffering “terrible nights and days” from the relentless attacks, and called Ukraine’s Russian adversaries “absolute barbarians”.“We can see the entire pointlessness of this war at this place,” said Merz, adding as he arrived that Ukraine “needs all our support in the coming weeks”. “If Russia is not stopped, its war machine will sooner or later turn against us,” he said.View image in fullscreenVolodymyr Zelenskyy (left) and Friedrich Merz in Kyiv on Sunday.Photograph: dts News Agency Germany Bundesregierung/Tobias Koch/ShutterstockRussia had already damaged Kyiv’s Northern Bridge and repeatedly struck its Southern Bridge. Although the crossings remain standing, repeated attacks and the threat of further strikes have prompted the city’s authorities to restrict or suspend traffic on five of the city’s six road bridges over the Dnipro, causing temporary closures and large traffic jams.If Moscow succeeds in seriously damaging Kyiv’s bridges, it could create a logistical nightmare for the city of 3 million people, whose crossings over the Dnipro were last destroyed on a large scale as Nazi German forces retreated in 1943. More than a third of residents live on the left bank while much of the city’s employment and infrastructure is concentrated on the right.View image in fullscreenA Russian jet-powered drone strikes a bridge in Kyiv on 2 October.Photograph: Valentyn Ogirenko/ReutersThe attacks form part of a broader Russian campaign against civilian and industrial infrastructure inside Ukraine. In recent weeks, strikes have hit logistics hubs, railway lines, datacentres, medical storage facilities and steel plants, alongside a sustained assault on the country’s energy system that is expected to intensify over the winter.“He [Putin] is counting on constant escalation. He wants this very much,” Zelenskyy said at a press conference alongside Merz. “This is an answer to everyone – to those who believe that all you have to do is simply ask Putin and he will end the war for real. It won’t happen, simply.”Russia’s foreign ministry on Saturday warned foreign nationals and diplomatic staff against remaining in or travelling to Ukraine. “Responsibility for any possible adverse consequences lies entirely with those who choose to disregard this warning,” the ministry said.mapA number of foreign ambassadors, including Germany’s, responded on social media that they intended to remain in Kyiv.“The EU delegation is staying,” the European Union ambassador, Katarína Mathernová, wrote on X on Sunday. “Threatening us will not stop Europe’s support for Ukraine. It only reminds us why that support matters.”In Moscow, some pro-war commenters noted with glee that the Russian strikes had continued despite Merz’s arrival. “Russia used to pause strikes on Kyiv during visits by European politicians. Not any more,” wrote Sergei Markov, a prominent pro-war commentator.The trip is Merz’s second to Ukraine since becoming chancellor. He has been among Kyiv’s most outspoken supporters in Europe and a leading voice warning about Russia’s hybrid campaign against other nations.Incinerated novels and destroyed warehouses: Russia’s war on Ukrainian booksRead moreLast month, Germany formally accused Moscowof being behind a suspected plot targeting Leipzig/Halle airport, a key logistics hub for western military aid to Ukraine. But Merz is also facinggrowing discontentat home over his support for Ukraine, as his approval ratings fall.Germany’s far left and far right are sceptical of support for Ukraine and want Berlin to scale back aid. The pressure has intensified as the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD)has made big electoral gains.Alice Weidel, the AfD’s co-leader, wrote in a social media post: “Merz is travelling to Ukraine on Germany’s national holiday and promising further billions in German taxpayer money that is missing from the pension and health insurance funds, while Germany is mired in its worst energy crisis.”Explore more on these topicsKyivUkraineRussiaGermanyFriedrich MerzEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: More than 400 schools in France to be closed on Monday as more protests planned | France | The Guardian
description: Education minister says 24 schools have been burnt or ransacked and 78 staff members injured since student unrest began last month
Author: Rory Carroll
Headline: Education minister says 24 schools have been burnt or ransacked and 78 staff members injured since student unrest began last month
Content: High-school students protesting in France.Photograph: Nacho Doce/ReutersView image in fullscreenHigh-school students protesting in France.Photograph: Nacho Doce/ReutersFranceMore than 400 schools in France to be closed on Monday as more protests plannedEducation minister says 24 schools have been burnt or ransacked and 78 staff members injured since student unrest began last monthEurope live – latest updatesRory CarrollSun 4 Oct 2026 11.08 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 15.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMore than 400 schools inFrancewill be closed or partly closed on Monday as authorities brace for another week of student protests.Lessons will be totally or partly suspended in 400 to 500 schools because security conditions “have not been fulfilled”, the education minister, Édouard Geffray, said on Sunday.The minister said 24 schools had been burnt or ransacked and 78 education staff members injured. The number of school closures on Monday would be comparable to Friday’s but the government envisaged a “partial, progressive return to lessons”, said Geffray.Thousands of teenagers staged widespread demonstrations anderected barricades last weekto protest against what they said was underfunding and neglect of the education system.View image in fullscreenStudents block the entrance to Ampere high school in Lyon.Photograph: Konrad K/Sipa/ShutterstockClashes with riot police left hundreds of people injured, led to more than 5,000 arrests, mostly of minors, and jolted President Emmanuel Macron’s centrist administration.There was a lull at the weekend, but protest organisers called for renewed demonstrations on Tuesday because the government had failed to produce “concrete measures”.Authorities say political agitators have infiltrated the protest, which started at a Paris school on 17 September and spread across the capital and the rest of France.“There are activists – particularly from the far left – who have infiltrated the high school student movement, hijacked it from the students themselves, and engaged in extreme violence,” said Geffray. “Clearly, this poses a risk to both our staff and our students.”The injured education staff members were deliberately targeted, “something we have never seen before”, said Geffray.The protestscaught the government by surpriseand confronted Macron with his worst crisis in months. Images of burning barricades and police using teargas, batons and other methods to disperse protests have dominated TV news.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenSecurity forces are stationed at Place de la Nation in Paris on Friday during the student protests.Photograph: Giulia Morici/NurPhoto/ShutterstockStudent grievances include overcrowded classes of up to 40 children in crumbling buildings, poor teacher pay, staff absences and an unequal system in which social background determined success. Other factors are an opaque and difficult online system for university applications as well as the sweltering temperatures in classrooms duringheatwaves.Protesters have accused the state of disengaging from secondary education and cited difficult conditions such as leaks, cockroaches, collapsed ceilings and decayed buildings. Others have complained about excessively long school days and a lack of teaching staff.The government said the grievances were legitimate but condemned what it called “urban violence”. On Sunday, police detained a 16-year-old in relation to an assault of a teacher in La Ciotat, a town on the southern coast between Marseille and Toulon. The teacher, 59, was doused with gasoline and struck during a protest on Friday.The government is also under pressure from trade unions that called a day ofstrikes last weekto compel the new prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, to rethink budget cuts and consider a form of wealth tax on the super-rich. The CGT trade union exhorted workers to sustain the pressure with demonstrations this week.Explore more on these topicsFranceProtestEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: French education minister says up to 500 schools could remain closed on Monday after student protests – as it happened | Europe | The Guardian
description: At least 5,000 people, mainly teenagers, have been arrested while dozens of people, including students and teachers, have been injured
Author: Frances Mao
Headline: At least 5,000 people, mainly teenagers, have been arrested while dozens of people, including students and teachers, have been injured
Content: 08.06 EDTFrance to keep up to 500 schools closed on MondayThe education minister says 400- 500 high schools will remain partially or fully shut following a week where riot police clashed with high school students as protests on classroom conditions have spread nationwide.Lessons will be “totally or partly suspended” given the unrest, says Education Minister Edouard Geffray.He said 24 schools had been “burned or ransacked” since the start of the movement.At least 5,000 people, mainly teenagers, have been arrested while dozens of people, including students and teachers, have been injured. Unions are calling on teachers to strike.Protesting students carry out blockading action near place de la Nation, in Paris, on 2 October 2026.Photograph: Thomas Samson/AFP/Getty ImagesThe protests began last week in the Paris region, with students staging sit-ins over conditions like overcrowding in classrooms, teacher shortages and dilapidated buildings.The rallies in some cases have become more violent with protesters wearing masks and setting off fires in the street and vidoes showing police officers using batons on students.More protests had been scheduled for Tuesday this week, prompting law enforcement this weekend to say the situation had grown “out of control”.Paris police chief Patrice Faure told students to abandon their school blockades to return to peaceful forms of protest and suggested to parents there was influence from “professional rioters”.Read more on the protestshere:Fires, fury and hundreds of arrests as France gripped by student protestsRead moreShareUpdated at08.14 EDT

title: Jacob Rees-Mogg accuses Tucker Carlson of ‘verging on defending Hitler’ | Tucker Carlson | The Guardian
description: Former Tory minister defends UK decision to enter war in podcast with US rightwinger and Putin sympathiser
Author: Rowena Mason
Headline: Former Tory minister defends UK decision to enter war in podcast with US rightwinger and Putin sympathiser
Content: Carlson repeatedly suggested to Rees-Mogg that the west was to blame for inviting Russian aggression and said of the prospect Britain could have lost to Hitler: ‘Who cares?’Composite: Chip Somodevilla, Leon Neal/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenCarlson repeatedly suggested to Rees-Mogg that the west was to blame for inviting Russian aggression and said of the prospect Britain could have lost to Hitler: ‘Who cares?’Composite: Chip Somodevilla, Leon Neal/Getty ImagesTucker CarlsonJacob Rees-Mogg accuses Tucker Carlson of ‘verging on defending Hitler’Former Tory minister defends UK decision to enter war in podcast with US rightwinger and Putin sympathiserRowena MasonWhitehall editorSun 4 Oct 2026 06.53 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 15.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe former Tory ministerJacob Rees-Mogghas found himself defending Britain’s decision to fight against Adolf Hitler after inviting the US rightwinger and Vladimir Putin sympathiser Tucker Carlson into his home for an interview.During the encounter, Carlson repeatedly suggested the west was to blame for inviting aggression fromRussiaand said of the prospect that Britain could have lost to Hitler: “Who cares?”Rees-Mogg, who lost his parliamentary seat in 2024, appears to have agreed to host Carlson’s podcast show after carving out a post-politics career as a commentator.Carlson set up the show after leaving Fox News and losing faith with Donald Trump, largely citing the US president’s willingness to get involved in foreign wars. Carlson has interviewed Putin and taken a sympathetic position towards Russia overUkraine.In the lengthy debate on foreign policy and global tensions, the US commentator repeatedly goaded Rees-Mogg over the smallness of the UK armed forces and suggested Russia was more powerful.Rees-Mogg explained that the UK economy was bigger and made the case that Britain and western allies had to support Ukraine and deter Russian aggression.Carlson went on to question why Britain bothered entering the second world war and claimed Germany had a legitimate claim over parts of Poland.Rees-Mogg said: “Otherwise we’d be speaking German.”Carlson replied: “Who cares? There are a lot of people in Britain who can’t speak English. So it would be nice to have at least a European language spoken in your country.”During the interview, Rees-Mogg said he was very surprised that Carlson was “verging on defending Hitler”, adding: “I think this is not really what you want to be doing.”Carlson replied: “Yeah, I guess I’m just a secret Nazi. I’m actually not a secret Nazi … and hardly a public Nazi.”Rees-Mogg responded that he was reassured, before saying that “Germany would have invaded us” if the UK had not gone to war.The interview has raised eyebrows in the US as well as Britain, with the Republican Mike Huckabee, the US ambassador to Israel, posting on X: “When it seemed impossible for Toxic Tucker to descend deeper into the sewer here he goes opining that UK should have let Nazis take over. Forget that Hitler murdered 11 million people? I thought Tucker was against killing? He needs help. Serious help.”Explore more on these topicsTucker CarlsonJacob Rees-MoggAdolf HitlerSecond world warVladimir PutinRussiaUkrainenewsShareReuse this content

title: As it happened: Israel condemns Green party passing ‘Zionism is racism’ as a ‘stain on history of UK’ | Politics | The Guardian
description: Party formally adopts policy which equates Zionism with racism, a move has alarmed some Jewish members
Author: Andrew Sparrow
Headline: Party formally adopts policy which equates Zionism with racism, a move has alarmed some Jewish members
Content: 10.35 EDTIsraeli foreign ministry condemns Green party vote as 'stain on history of UK'TheIsraeli foreign ministryhas issued a statement condemning the Green party in the light of today’s vote, Tom Scotson from the Sunreports.In the statement, the foreign ministry said:double quotation markThe shocking resolution adopted today legitimises armed struggle, calls for a Palestinian state “from the river to the sea” - meaning the destruction of the State of Israel - and labels as “racist” the aspiration of the Jewish people for self-determination.This goes far beyond the boundaries of legitimate political debate. As long as this resolution remains in place, it will stand as a stain on the history of the United Kingdom.Share

title: Children’s books with Black main characters down 8% in a year, study shows | Children and teenagers | The Guardian
description: Only 150 of 2,189 titles published in UK for young children last year focused on minority ethnic, disabled or neurodivergent characters
Author: Emma Loffhagen
Headline: Only 150 of 2,189 titles published in UK for young children last year focused on minority ethnic, disabled or neurodivergent characters
Content: Just 47 of the 2,189 books published for under-10s in 2025 featured a Black main character,Photograph: MBI/AlamyView image in fullscreenJust 47 of the 2,189 books published for under-10s in 2025 featured a Black main character,Photograph: MBI/AlamyChildren and teenagersChildren’s books with Black main characters down 8% in a year, study showsOnly 150 of 2,189 titles published in UK for young children last year focused on minority ethnic, disabled or neurodivergent charactersEmma LoffhagenSun 4 Oct 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 19.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe number of children’s books featuring Black main characters fell by almost 8% last year, according to research into diversity in UK publishing.Just 47 – or 2.1% – of the 2,189 books published for under-10s in 2025 featured a Black main character, a 7.8% fall from the previous year, according to Inclusive Books for Children. Black children make up about 8.5% of that age bracket in England and Wales.Representation of south Asian main characters fell by 14.3 percentage points to 1.4%, despite children of south Asian heritage making up about 12.4% of the population of under-10s. Just three books featured main characters of Middle Eastern and North African (MENA) heritage, down 50% from the previous year. This represented 0.1% of surveyed books, compared with the group’s 2.2% share of the population.The research by the literacy charity found that only 150 books – 6.9% of those surveyed – featured main characters from minority ethnic, disabled or neurodivergent backgrounds. Of these, 37.3% were written or illustrated by creators who did not share the background of their characters.View image in fullscreenThe author Sheena Patel says children need books ‘that reflect both the lives they live and the ones they don’t’.Photograph: Antonio Olmos/The ObserverThe author Sheena Patel said: “At an age when children are figuring out the world around them and where they fit in, it’s vital they have access to funny, inspiring, adventurous books that reflect both the lives they live and the ones they don’t. We must do better.”The report surveyed baby and toddler books, picture books and fiction for children aged up to nine. It found that representation of disabled characters in picture books fell sharply: the number with disabled main characters dropped by 60% in 2025, to just two titles. Neither was by a disabled creator.The survey also highlighted what it described as a lack of “incidental representation”: stories in which a main character’s identity does not explicitly drive the plot of the story.Dr Stella Louis, an early years consultant, trainer and author, pointed to this “continued reliance” on books where identity itself was the story. “Why can’t a child simply be south Asian, disabled, neurodivergent or bilingual and also be the hero of an ordinary story about friendship, adventure, loss or joy?” she said.The report found that all three books published in 2025 with MENA main characters were refugee narratives. The study authors said children of MENA heritage needed stories covering a broader range of themes and experiences.“As an Arab author, it is painful to see the number of children’s fiction books representing our region decline from six to only three in 2025,” said Nadine Kaadan. She said the fact that all three books published were focused on refugee experiences risked reinforcing a “single story” about the region, defining it through “war and displacement rather than our rich cultures and heritage”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThere were some signs of progress. Neurodivergent representation increased in picture books, from three titles in 2024 to 13 last year. In the baby and toddler category, the number of books with marginalised main characters rose by 29.4%.Jack Hope, a children’s book consultant, said: “When children’s enjoyment of reading is at a significant low, it’s more important than ever that the stories children encounter reflect their lives, identities, experiences and emotions.“These figures need to be more than mere statistics and a call to action for continued change and improvements.”Explore more on these topicsChildren and teenagersPublishingRaceBlack British culturenewsShareReuse this content

title: Money stolen by scammers hijacking UK social media accounts rises 400% | Scams | The Guardian
description: Many cases involve criminals using other people’s identities to sell fake event tickets to friends and family
Author: Rupert Jones
Headline: Many cases involve criminals using other people’s identities to sell fake event tickets to friends and family
Content: The total reported amount stolen via email and social media account hacking reached £6.3m in the 2025-26 financial year, compared with £1.2m in 2024-25Photograph: Tim Goode/PAView image in fullscreenThe total reported amount stolen via email and social media account hacking reached £6.3m in the 2025-26 financial year, compared with £1.2m in 2024-25Photograph: Tim Goode/PAScamsMoney stolen by scammers hijacking UK social media accounts rises 400%Many cases involve criminals using other people’s identities to sell fake event tickets to friends and familyRupert JonesSun 4 Oct 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe total amount stolen by criminals who hack into people’s emails and social media accounts and then pretend to be them has risen by more than 400% in a year, official UK data shows.In many cases, the scammers are hijacking people’s accounts in order to use their identity to sell fake event tickets – such as to sold-out gigs – to unsuspecting friends and family.The total reported amount stolen via email and social media account hacking reached £6.3m in the 2025-26 financial year, compared with £1.2m in 2024-25, according to the Report Fraud service run by the City of London police, which holds national responsibility for economic crime.However, the true total may be much higher as many scam victims do not report the crime, often because they feel embarrassed, and sometimes because the individual amount of money involved was relatively small.The Guardianpreviously featured the caseof a music fan whose Instagram account was targeted by hackers, who used her identity to advertise tickets to an Oasis gig and stole £1,400 from her friends. She said the hackers impersonated her so well that her friends and family genuinely thought they were speaking to her.Others have been scammed by fraudulent WhatsApp and text messages in which a criminal pretends to be their child or a relative who is in an emergency situation and urgently needs cash. This has been dubbedthe “Hi mum” scam.Data from Santander has shown that among customers of the bank, fraudsters pretending to be someone’s son were the most successful at extracting cash, followed by daughters.Ch Supt Amanda Wolf, head of Report Fraud operations, said: “For most people, being hacked isn’t just a cyber issue – it’s personal. It can leave victims locked out of important accounts, worried about what information has been accessed, and concerned that criminals may use their identity to target others.”She added that what starts with one compromised account “can quickly impact family, friends and colleagues as fraudsters exploit trusted relationships to commit further fraud”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionReport Fraud is launching an awareness campaign urging the public to protect their online accounts from hackers by switching to passkeys where they are available. A passkeyuses an individual’s device and biometricsto authenticate them and cannot be hacked like a password.Explore more on these topicsScamsSocial mediaHackingConsumer affairsCrimenewsShareReuse this content

title: Strikes by North Sea oil workers could ‘severely disrupt’ UK fuel supplies | Oil | The Guardian
description: Union says staff left with no choice but industrial action after breakdown in pay talks with Texas oil firm Apache
Author: Kalyeena Makortoff
Headline: Union says staff left with no choice but industrial action after breakdown in pay talks with Texas oil firm Apache
Content: The Forties Bravo oil platform in the North Sea.Photograph: Allan Coutts/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe Forties Bravo oil platform in the North Sea.Photograph: Allan Coutts/AlamyOilStrikes by North Sea oil workers could ‘severely disrupt’ UK fuel suppliesUnion says staff left with no choice but industrial action after breakdown in pay talks with Texas oil firm ApacheKalyeena MakortoffSun 4 Oct 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA looming strike by oil workers in the North Sea could “severely disrupt” UK fuel supplies, theUniteunion has said, adding that staff were left with no choice after a breakdown in pay talks with the Texas oil company Apache.The union said Apache workers had “emphatically” backed strike action after being given what it said was an
