unacceptable pay offer that amounted to a real-terms pay cut for many employees, at a time when the company was “raking in eye-watering profits”.Unite said the operator had also set deadlines for reaching an agreement over back pay and indicated payments could be withheld, “leaving workers potentially thousands of pounds out of pocket”.Apache said it had “engaged constructively throughout the pay discussions” and added that it had offered a 4% pay increase for staff, “whose earnings already place them among the highest earners in the UK and whose offshore rota averages 153 working days a year”.Strike action could begin later this month, according to the union, and could involve more than 160 Apache offshore workers, including electrical experts, production technicians and radio operators.Any action would affect the Forties and Beryl oilfields, and could lead to one of the critical North Sea platforms, known as Charlie, “being brought to a standstill”, Unite said.That could ultimately result in the entire Forties pipeline system in the North Sea – which is said to handle almost a third of the UK’s oil and gas – “going down”, the union said, adding that the disruption could also ripple out and affect other large North Sea operators.Unite blamed the potential disruption on Apache’s failure to reach a pay deal, saying the company’s behaviour could have “far-reaching consequences for workers, operators and consumers”.Consumers have already beengrappling with rising fuel and gas pricesbecause of the US-Israel war on Iran, which has been disrupting supplies of crude and refined oil products from the Gulf.On Friday, British motorists were dealt a fresh blow when it emerged that the average price of diesel hadclimbed to a record £2 a litre.At the same time it was announced that leaders of G7 nations wouldrelease up to 100m barrelsof their emergency diesel and crude oil stockpiles after Donald Trump threatened to cut off supplies of US diesel.Commenting on the potential strike action, the Unite general secretary, Sharon Graham, said: “We will not tolerate unacceptable pay offers.”Stevie Davies, a Unite industrial officer, said any disruption to Apache’s platforms “would have a direct hit on the Forties pipeline and potentially severely affect the UK’s fuel supplies”.The Texas-based APA Corporation, which is the parent company behind Apache North Sea Production, reported $1.4bn (£1.1bn) in after-tax profits and $9.2bn in revenues for last year.“We believe our final offer to the union is fair and recognises the contribution of our offshore workforce, alongside the wider benefits in our total rewards package,” Apache said. “The proposed pay increase is also in line with that awarded to our non-unionised employees earlier this year.”Apache also said it had contingency plans in place, and that it did not expect any strike action to affect other producers and their ability to operate through the Forties pipeline system. The plans included keeping “experienced personnel” on key sites, and it said any reduction in pipeline pressure as a result of industrial action would be similar to what occurred during routine maintenance outages.“As a responsible operator, we are planning to maintain safe operations throughout any industrial action,” Apache added.Planned strikes by Neo Next offshore workers, organised by Unite,were called off this summerafter they secured a deal that the union said lifted the pay package by more than £4,000. The deal was reached days before workers were due to start a series of strikes from 22 July.Ineos, which operates the Forties pipeline system, was contacted for comment.Explore more on these topicsOilOil and gas companiesEnergy industryCommoditiesIndustrial actionTrade unionsUnitenewsShareReuse this content

title: US bombers pulled from RAF Fairford base after suspected terror plot | US military | The Guardian
description: Aircraft leave Gloucestershire base to return to US following arrest of dual British-Iranian national in central London
Author: Dan Sabbagh
Headline: Aircraft leave Gloucestershire base to return to US following arrest of dual British-Iranian national in central London
Content: A US Air Force Rockwell B-1 Lancer bomber seen at RAF Fairford on 29 September.Photograph: Ben Birchall/PAView image in fullscreenA US Air Force Rockwell B-1 Lancer bomber seen at RAF Fairford on 29 September.Photograph: Ben Birchall/PAUS militaryUS bombers pulled from RAF Fairford base after suspected terror plotAircraft leave Gloucestershire base to return to US following arrest of dual British-Iranian national in central LondonDan Sabbagh,Marina Dunbar,Charlie MoloneySun 4 Oct 2026 17.25 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe US Air Force has pulled its bombers from RAF Fairford following an investigation into an alleged planned terror attack at the base.The bombers were redeployed back to their home bases in the US, according to a Pentagon official who was not authorised to discuss sensitive military movements and spoke on Sunday on condition of anonymity.A Pentagon spokesperson said: “While ⁠operational security precluded us from confirming the movement of our ​assets and forces in ‌real time, we can acknowledge ‌now that all US bombers that were deployed to ‌RAF Fairford have redeployed to their home stations in the United States.”At least 10 B-1 bombers of 12 flew out of Fairford on Sunday, including some that arrived on rotation less than a week ago, underlining the haste of the departure and the apparent significance given by the US to the threat.There was no immediate comment from the UK Ministry of Defence, though the rapid pace of the withdrawal will heighten concerns in the area around the RAF base in Gloucestershire.According to reporting by US media, the withdrawal appears to be in response to fresh or renewed security concerns about safety on the base.A report in the New York Times said: “American officials on Sunday declined to specify the nature of the new information that prompted the rapid withdrawal of the Air Force bombers, some of which had just arrived in the past week as part of a normal rotation of forces.“One US official said the new information was part of the same threat warnings that surfaced three weeks ago, but specific details and a sense of urgency spiked in the past 24 hours, alarming commanders.”A dual British-Iranian national was arrested in central London last week on suspicion of plotting a terror attack, following a security incident at RAF Fairford in late September. In total, six people have been taken into custody and then released on bail during the investigation.Suspect in RAF Fairford case called police to report incidentRead moreBritish authorities have linked the incident to Tehran. Iran has denied involvement.RAF Fairford, located 100 miles (160km) west of London, has been used by American bombers during decades of conflicts in the Middle East.Its use in recent months came after then prime minister Keir Starmer granted Washington permission to use British bases for “defensive” strikes against Tehran.TheUS militarystill maintains a sizeable presence in the Middle East. On Thursday, a US official said the recently deployed USS Theodore Roosevelt aircraft carrier as well as the USS Makin Island amphibious readiness group – a group of ships that together carry more than 7,000 sailors and 2,000 Marines – were heading for the region. The official said the move could result in three carriers being in the region as early as the end of October.Explore more on these topicsUS militaryMilitaryRoyal Air ForcenewsShareReuse this content

title: White House defends new press aide who posed with rifle in ‘Fuck Joe Biden’ shirt | Trump administration | The Guardian
description: Beni Rae Harmony, 24, has been ‘a trusted voice for the MAGA movement as a White House correspondent’, White House says
Author: Robert Mackey
Headline: Beni Rae Harmony, 24, has been ‘a trusted voice for the MAGA movement as a White House correspondent’, White House says
Content: Donald Trump takes questions from members of the media, including Beni Rae Harmony, on Air Force One after a two-day visit to Ireland, on 13 September.Photograph: Kylie Cooper/ReutersView image in fullscreenDonald Trump takes questions from members of the media, including Beni Rae Harmony, on Air Force One after a two-day visit to Ireland, on 13 September.Photograph: Kylie Cooper/ReutersTrump administrationWhite House defends new press aide who posed with rifle in ‘Fuck Joe Biden’ shirtBeni Rae Harmony, 24, has been ‘a trusted voice for the MAGA movement as a White House correspondent’, White House saysRobert MackeySun 4 Oct 2026 19.38 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 19.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe White House has defended a newly hired press aide who posed for a holiday photograph in 2021wearing a “Fuck Joe Biden” T-shirtand holding a rifle.Beni Rae Harmony, the new assistant White House press secretary,revealedon Friday that she was going to work for Donald Trump just days after covering him as a correspondent for Real America’s Voice, a partisan rightwing outletoriginally createdas a video podcast platform for the president’s former adviser Steve Bannon.According toa LinkedIn profile, Harmony, 24, previously worked asa producerfor the far-right Turning Point USA host Jack Posobiec – and as a press aide “focusing on crisis management” for two far-right Republicans: congressman Paul Gosar of Arizona and former congressman Matt Gaetz of Florida.In 2021, whenGosar was censuredby the US House for posting an animated video that depicted him killing Democratic congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and attacking Joe Biden, Harmony recordedan outraged defense of her bossfor his YouTube channel.The photograph of Harmony and an older man posing with rifles in matching anti-Biden shirts, in front of Christmas decorations, was reportedly posted on Instagram in November 2021 by a far-right Republican House candidate, Jarome Bell, who mounted a failed campaign for Congress in 2022.A screenshot of that post,published by the Daily Mirror, shows that it included the caption: “My campaign Public Affairs Director @beniraeharmony is a beast. This is how we roll.”Harmony appeared to verify the authenticity of the photograph in December 2021, when it wasshared on social mediaby an anti-Maga outlet, PatriotTakes, which alsoidentified heras an aide to Gosar.The next day, Harmonyrepliedto the PatriotTakes post of the image with another image of herself, wearing the same shirt in the same location and grinning into the camera. When another social media user posted a sarcastic question about the relationship between the older man and the young woman seen in the image, asking: “Daughter or date?”,Harmony repliedwith a one-word answer: “Uncle.”Biden at the time was serving his lone term in the Oval Office, and Trump supporters chanting “Fuck Joe Biden” at a Nascar race that autumn inspireda viral memefeaturing a variation of the slogan.Harmony did not reply to requests to comment on the photograph. But the White House press office responded with a statement from a deputy press secretary, Anna Kelly, who praised the new hire for her advocacy of Trump’s Make America Great Again movement, while ostensibly covering the president as a journalist.“Beni Rae Harmony has been a trusted voice for the MAGA movement as a White House correspondent,” Kelly wrote. “She will be an outstanding addition to President Trump’s communications team as an Assistant Press Secretary – we look forward to having her on board!”Harmony joins a White House press office that has taken unprecedented steps to ensure that the president is surrounded at all times by correspondents from partisan outlets who shower him with praise, and limit or deny access to reporters from nonpartisan outlets who challenge him.Trump hastried to ban CNN, Politico and MS Nowfrom the White House entirely, for what he considers overly negative coverage, and his aides now select which outlets are in place to ask him questions, with frequent slots reserved for correspondents who openly support him.Harmony became the White House correspondent for Real America’s Voice after her predecessor, Brian Glenn, fell out of favor with Trump when his partner, Marjorie Taylor Greene, broke with the president and accused him of betraying the Maga movement.Glenn had previously worked hard to advance Trump’s political agenda when invited by the president to ask questions. In 2025, for instance, Glennpointedly askedUkraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, why he refused to wear a suit in the Oval Office, a question that inflamed an already volatile encounter.Duringa press availability on Air Force Onelast month, Trump approached reporters with a sheaf of papers in his left hand. Harmony asked Trumpa series of friendly questionsthat seemed designed to help him score political points. AsTMZ reportedon Friday,Associated Press photographstaken during that exchange showed that Harmony’s name was at the top of the first page in the president’s hand, suggesting that he might have been holding her résumé as he took her questions.Harmony achieved a measure of celebrity in the rightwing media in 2025, when she left her job as an on-air host at a local TV station in Springfield, Illinois, after deliveringan on-air tributeto the late Charlie Kirk, describing him as her first boss and mentor.The station’s news directordeniedthat Harmony had been suspended over the tribute, as she claimed, and clarified that she had never been a member of its news team, and instead hosted a program run by the channel’s sales department that featured clients who paid to be interviewed on television.Explore more on these topicsTrump administrationUS politicsUS press and publishingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump names intelligence chief Jay Clayton as new White House AI czar | Trump administration | The Guardian
description: Clayton had said AI was a ‘gamechanger’ but also posed ‘a threat’ during his confirmation hearing
Author: Ariana Baio
Headline: Clayton had said AI was a ‘gamechanger’ but also posed ‘a threat’ during his confirmation hearing
Content: Donald Trump with Jay Clayton, the director of national intelligence, in Washington DC on 29 September.Photograph: Alex Brandon/APView image in fullscreenDonald Trump with Jay Clayton, the director of national intelligence, in Washington DC on 29 September.Photograph: Alex Brandon/APTrump administrationTrump names intelligence chief Jay Clayton as new White House AI czarClayton had said AI was a ‘gamechanger’ but also posed ‘a threat’ during his confirmation hearingAriana BaioSun 4 Oct 2026 13.45 EDTFirst published on Sun 4 Oct 2026 09.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trump on Sunday namedJay Clayton, the director of national intelligence, to also serve as the new White House AI czar.Clayton,who leads the US’s 18 intelligence agencies, previously served as the top federal prosecutor in Manhattan and led the Securities and Exchange Commission during Trump’s first term.During hisSenate confirmation hearing, Clayton said AI was a “gamechanger” but it also posed “a threat”.“When something’s both an opportunity and a threat, you better get your arms around it,” Clayton told lawmakers when asked about AI.CBS News was the firstto report that Clayton would be appointed White House AI czar.In a social media post on Sunday, Trump announced that Clayton would lead what the US president called “the Super Intelligence Force (SIF)”.Trump’s post also said the SIF would “coordinate the federal government’s engagement with consumers, public interest groups, religious organizations, critical infrastructure providers, and super intelligence companies”.Among those reacting on Sunday to Trump’s invoking the term “super intelligence” was SpaceX chiefElon Musk. Musk said on his social media platform X that SI was “better” than AI – and that he wasrenaminghis aerospace company’s AI unit from SpaceXAI to SpaceXSI.Senator Mark Warner, a Virginia Democrat who is vice-chair of the Senate select committee on intelligence, cautiously welcomed the appointment of Clayton, while noting that “the administration hasresistedmeaningful safeguards without offering a serious alternative for addressing the national security risks posed by increasingly powerful AI systems”.“I look forward to working with Director Clayton on ensuring the United States stays ahead of China and other adversaries, strengthening the security and resilience of our most advanced AI systems, and establishing rigorous testing and safeguards so that increasingly powerful systems remain secure, reliable, and under human control,” Warner added.In September, Trumpannouncedhe wascreating an “AI Force”and a czar to oversee the technology’s growth and monitor for “bad” development. The announcement came aftertech industry leaders warned that AI was developing too rapidlyto control and that it could harm humans.The president has largely brushed asideconcerns about AI developmentand the construction of datacenters, which power the technology.Trump has insisted continued development is paramount to defeating China in the global AI race.But to address concerns, the president created an advisory committee in addition to the czar – whom he previously promised would be led by a “high IQ” individual. Trump also recently met with AI industry leaders to discuss concerns.On Tuesday,Trump and six executives signed an AI accordat the White House, promising to create internal and external monitors to ensure the technology is used as intended and any safety issues are addressed.Trump had initially created the AI and cryptocurrency czar position when he returned to the White House in January 2025.David Sacks, the venture capitalist and tech businessman, served as the administration’s AI and cryptocurrency czar until March 2026, when he reached his employment limit under his designation as a “special government employee”.Sacks still co-chairs the President’s Council of Advisors on Science and Technology.Trump previously floated Clayton’s name as a potential AI czar, tellingAxiosin September that Clayton was “a good man” and the prospect of appointing him was “a good idea”.Explore more on these topicsTrump administrationAI (artificial intelligence)Donald TrumpUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: After a deadly paper mill explosion, a community in Washington state looks to a key House race | Washington state | The Guardian
description: In a district shaken by the deaths of 11 workers, Democrat Marie Gluesenkamp Perez faces a stiff challenge to keep her seat
Author: Lok Darjee
Headline: In a district shaken by the deaths of 11 workers, Democrat Marie Gluesenkamp Perez faces a stiff challenge to keep her seat
Content: Community members hold photographs of loved ones during a vigil following the fatal chemical storage tank failure in Longview, Washington, on 26 May.Photograph: Mathieu Lewis-Rolland/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenCommunity members hold photographs of loved ones during a vigil following the fatal chemical storage tank failure in Longview, Washington, on 26 May.Photograph: Mathieu Lewis-Rolland/Getty ImagesAmerican crossroadsWashington stateAfter a deadly paper mill explosion, a community in Washington state looks to a key House raceIn a district shaken by deaths of 11 workers, Democrat Marie Gluesenkamp Perez faces a stiff challenge to keep her seatLok DarjeeSun 4 Oct 2026 13.27 EDTFirst published on Sun 4 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn a misty morning in May in south-westWashington state, Laura Oltmann, a 41-year-old dietitian, had barely clocked in when an unfamiliar overhead announcement echoed through the hospital.“We get overhead pages for different types of emergencies. But this one, we don’t get very often,” recalled Oltmann.Doctors, nurses and staff began guessing what could have happened. Perhaps it was a train derailment. Maybe a major highway crash. As the speculation grew, so did the uncertainty. Staff started calling one another. The answer shook them all. “Someone mentioned there had been an explosion at this plant, and that we were probably going to be getting some patients from there,” Oltmann said.Forty miles south, in the port city of Longview, residents had awakened to a thunderous boom. At approximately 7.18am, as workers changed shifts at a paper mill company,Nippon Dynawave Packaging, a tank of white liquor, acaustic chemical usedin the paper-making process, imploded. Hours passed with no explanation of what had caused it or how it could have happened at all, and suspicion began to brew.With roughly a thousand people working at the mill, thousands more were waiting for a phone call. Parents called children. Wives called husbands. Grandparents called grandchildren.View image in fullscreenDamage at the Nippon Dynawave Packaging mill in Longview, Washington, after an implosion on 26 May.Photograph: Karen Ducey/The Seattle Times/AP“For those that did not get that response,” saidJeff Wilson, a Republican state senator representing Longview, who also sits as the port commissioner, “all they got was silence.” In the end,11 people were killedin one of Washington state’sdeadliest industrial accidentsin nearly a century.Nowhere was that impact felt more deeply than in Longview itself, a working-class city ofabout 38,000 peoplewhose economy and identity have long been tied to the paper industry, shipping and logging. For generations, families have depended on the mills for their livelihoods. The disaster struck at something the city had long regarded as permanent: the mills where generations had gone to work, and helped many send their children to college or put down a down payment on a home.The implosion rippled through nearly every corner of a community affected by mill closures and economic change. Those concerns will likely have an impact at the ballot box. As summer turned toward fall and the leaves along the Columbia River began to turn yellow, memorial services gave way to campaign rallies. The same communities that had gathered around grieving families were preparing for one of the country’s most closely watched House races in November.Nearly two months after the implosion, on 8 July, Wilson still spoke first about the workers, the funerals he had attended, the families and the co-workers who ran toward danger looking for one another. He recalled brothersTyler and Brad Covington, 27 and 29; he said: “They went to work together. And then they died together.”Before entering politics, Wilson spent more than 23 years cleaning tanks at the Nippon Dynawave mill. In the aftermath of the tragedy, he worked routinely with Democratic congresswomanMarie Gluesenkamp Perez’s office as local, state and federal officials responded to the disaster, his role in Olympia intersecting with hers in Washington.View image in fullscreenMarie Gluesenkamp Perez speaks to reporters outside the Nippon Dynawave on 26 May.Photograph: Mathieu Lewis-Rolland/Getty ImagesThough he declined to endorse her re-election, Wilson credited the Democratic congresswoman with being “present and accountable” and praised her for asking questions rather than “rubber-stamping anything”.For a community divided by many of the same political forces pulling at the rest of the country, the disaster briefly created a sense of togetherness, as the whole community grieved the deaths of many of their neighbor and family members.“Natural disasters will tend to bring people together,” said Mark Alan Smith, a political science professor at the University of Washington who studies American politics and religion. “It’s something people can unify around … across race and class and other divisions.”On 4 August, Gluesenkamp Perez and Republican state senator John Braun advanced from a field of nine to face off for the district’s congressional seat in November. Braun finished first with about39.7% of the votetoGluesenkamp Perez’s 36.4%. Brent Hennrich, the progressive Democratwho arguedthat Gluesenkamp Perez no longer represented many of her party’s voters,took 16.7%.The results exposed the competing pressures facing Gluesenkamp Perez heading into the general election. Braun, who netted a Trump endorsement in April andmillions in pro-Trump money,finished ahead of the incumbent. Meanwhile, Hennrich’s showing demonstrated the size of the progressive bloc she will have to contend with in November. Many of those voters remain angry over parts of her vote on theSafeguard American Voter Eligibility (SAVE) Act(which would require proof of citizenship to vote), ICE funding, and a bill restricting how public schools address gender identity.When asked about those direct criticisms of the congresswoman – whom many on the left feel has drifted from the party – her campaign responded with a written statement to the Guardian that cast her independence as the reason south-west Washington should return her to office. “DC has enough career politicians following national agendas,” said campaign manager Timothy Gowen. “Southwest Washington deserves an independent representative who delivers real results. Marie will always be loyal to her district first.” The statement did not address questions about her voting record or the primary result.View image in fullscreenJohn Braun at the capitol in Olympia last year.Photograph: Lindsey Wasson/APThe race stretches far beyond Longview and the nearby city of Battle Ground. Washington’s third congressional district runs from the Pacific coast through the timber towns of the lower Columbia and inland farm country to Vancouver and the fast-growing suburbs north of Portland. Logging, paper mills, agriculture, shipping and manufacturing still shape daily life across much of it, while its politics pull hard in opposite directions.That geography has forced Gluesenkamp Perez to build an unusual coalition. Her political survival has depended partly on voters who do not ordinarily identify withDemocrats, including moderates and conservatives drawn to her emphasis on the trades, guns and independence from her party. But that same positioning has alienated Democrats who believe she has moved too far from them.“Two years ago, people reported having to hold their nose and vote for her, because she was better than [former opponent and one-time counter-intelligence official] Joe Kent,” said LaDonna Kirkpatrick, chair of the 18th Legislative District Democrats, speaking in a personal capacity. “But now we’re in a situation where I’m hearing from so many people that even if she wins the primary, they will not vote for her. And the frustration is real. I’m feeling that personally.”Thea Zaine, chair of the 20th Legislative District Democrats, speaks for the bloc of progressive Democrats whose discontent showed up in the primary returns. Her organization was the only Democratic party body in the district to endorse Hennrich.“We believe in protecting immigrants. She’s voted to give more money to ICE,” Zaine said. “She voted to give funding to wars in Iran. And she takes money from Aipac, and she’s voted to fund the genocide in Gaza.”Gluesenkamp Perez’s record on Iran, however, is more complicated than Zaine suggested. The Democratic representative voted for war powers resolutions directing the removal of US forces from the unauthorized war with Iran, while also breaking with most Democrats to support thebroader $1.15tnNational Defense Authorization Act.For Zaine, those votes have made the choice straightforward. But not every young, left-leaning voter who shares her frustration has reached the same conclusion.Tanner Manley, 25, an incoming law student who lives near Vancouver and describes himself as left-leaning, shares much of the critique. He plans to vote for Gluesenkamp Perez anyway.View image in fullscreenProtesters gather in front of the Henry M Jackson federal building in Seattle, on 11 June 2025.Photograph: Rio Giancarlo/Getty Images“Of course, I wish more progressive candidates were viable here, and that Marie would take a clear moral stand on Israel and reject Aipac funding the way she refuses corporate Pac money,” he said. “In another race with different options, I’d likely support a different candidate.”What keeps Manley with her is closer to home. After the Longview disaster, the US Chemical Safety and Hazard Investigation Board, the independent federal agency investigating the tank failure at the Longview paper plant, faced elimination under the administration’s proposed budget. In June, Gluesenkamp Perez backed an amendment restoring$14m for the agency, which passed the House appropriations committee with Republican support.“That might not satisfy progressives watching from the other side of the country,” Manley said, “but try telling people in this district that that kind of fight in Congress doesn’t matter.”Neither candidate’s campaign has made the Longview tragedy a centerpiece of the race. A recent poll underscores how little room both candidates have: the survey, conducted byDHM Research for Oregon Public Broadcasting, foundBraun at 48%andGluesenkamp Perez at 47%after undecided voters were asked which candidate they leaned toward, with 5% still undecided.Smith, of the University of Washington, said events that bring communities together can be difficult to translate into partisan advantage.“In order for something like that to affect how people vote, somebody has to channel it,” Smith said. “It’s hard to channel anything where everybody agrees.”That could change, he said, “if you can somehow link your opponent to some negative aspect” of the event. So far, neither campaign has done so. And Wilson praised Gluesenkamp Perez’s handling of the disaster.“She’s been representing, you know, from the federal angle, well on this,” he said.The response also fit the political identity Gluesenkamp Perez has cultivated in south-west Washington, where she has emphasized the trades and the economic pressures facing rural and working-class communities. In aninterview with OPB, she described watching the decline of industries that have long sustained towns across the region.“Mill after mill close in our region,” she said. “It’s just got people really at high anxiety levels.”A recent poll underscores how little room both House candidates have. The survey, conducted byDHM Research for Oregon Public Broadcasting, foundBraun at 48%andGluesenkamp Perez at 47%after undecided voters were asked which candidate they leaned toward, with 5% still undecided.About three miles north of Nippon Dynawave, at the Pentecostal church where Ron Peterson is pastor, the disaster remains part of the community’s memory.For Peterson, 38, the tragedy had briefly brought together people who otherwise disagreed about much else. But when I asked him about politics, he drew a distinction.View image in fullscreenA vigil for the victims of the explosion.Photograph: David Ryder/Reuters“We don’t win politically,” he said. “We win spiritually.”A few miles south, and across a district where the divisions are not only political, Chydell Armijo, 35, mother of two, was thinking about something more immediate. She had little enthusiasm for either political party. What worried her was whether people like her could still build a stable life: whether a small business could survive, whether her children could find opportunity and whether working people could still move up.“I honestly feel like everybody is struggling,” Armijo said. “There is no such thing as middle class any more.”For all the attention on which party will control this congressional seat after November, Armijo saw a divide that would remain regardless of who won.“Our economic system has become difficult, in many ways, for us to climb,” she said.Explore more on these topicsWashington stateAmerican crossroadsHouse of RepresentativesUS politicsWest CoastDemocratsRepublicansnewsShareReuse this content

title: Mass shootings leave two people dead in Georgia and 12-year-old girl dead in Baltimore | US crime | The Guardian
description: At least 25 injured at block party shooting in Georgia and three wounded in Baltimore park shooting, officials say
Author: Michael Sainato
Headline: At least 25 injured at block party shooting in Georgia and three wounded in Baltimore park shooting, officials say
Content: There had been at least 355 mass shootings reported in the US so far for the year as of Sunday.Photograph: José Luis Magaña/APView image in fullscreenThere had been at least 355 mass shootings reported in the US so far for the year as of Sunday.Photograph: José Luis Magaña/APUS crimeMass shootings leave two people dead in Georgia and 12-year-old girl dead in BaltimoreAt least 25 injured at block party shooting in Georgia and three wounded in Baltimore park shooting, officials sayMichael SainatoSun 4 Oct 2026 11.23 EDTFirst published on Sun 4 Oct 2026 11.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTwo people were killed and at least 25 others injured when ashootingerupted at a homecoming block party in Vienna, Georgia, early on Sunday, according to authorities.In another high-profile mass shooting in the US over the weekend, a 12-year-old girl was shot and killed and three other people were wounded after gunfire evidently broke out over a parking spot in aBaltimorepark on Saturday, officials said.The violence in Georgia occurred at a gathering of more than 1,000 people, local sheriff Craig Peavy told area news outletWMAZ. Shots were fired at about 50 people in two locations about a block apart just after 1am on Sunday, Peavy told WMAZ.The pair killed at the scene were not immediately identified. The identity of the suspects, or a possible motive for the gunfire, also were not immediately identified.Peavy added that about 25 people were taken to the hospital, as many as 35 people may have been wounded, and deputies were monitoring the crowd at the time of the shooting.Meanwhile, with respect to the shooting in Baltimore, police commissioner Richard Worley said two suspects were being sought after two different types of gun cartridges were found at the scene of the violence near a youth football event at Leon Day Park.“What we know is that there was some type of argument between two cowards, and of course they both opened fire on each other,” Worley said at a Saturday nightnews conference. “The dispute most likely occurred from a stupid parking spot, and they get into a fight, and the two cowards pull guns on each other.”Worley said the 12-year-old girl who was killed in that case was a bystander at a nearby field, who was hit when one of the shooters “fired multiple rounds down range”.A 25-year-old woman with the girl was shot, too. So were two men, aged 23 and 28, according to police. None of the three wounded victims were believed to have life-threatening injuries, police said.The 12-year-old girl waspronounceddead at the scene, and paramedics took the woman to the hospital. The two other victims walked into a nearby hospital with injuries.“Two grown men got into an argument, and now a 12-year-old is gone,” the Baltimore mayor, Brandon Scott,saidto reporters. “What happened out here today, is one of the most disgusting things I’ve ever seen in my life because that baby was just out here, at homecoming for this youth football league is out here every single day, trying to keep young people safe, trying to keep young men and young women on the right path.”There had been at least 355 mass shootings reported in the US so far for the year as of Sunday, which was the 277th day of 2026, according to theGun Violence Archive. The archive, a nonpartisan reference resource, defines mass shootings as cases in which at least four victims are killed or wounded.The US perennially has high rates of such shootings, fueling calls from some quarters for more substantial federal gun control. But Congress has not passed such measures over the years.Explore more on these topicsUS crimeGeorgiaBaltimorenewsShareReuse this content

title: JD Vance flexing Maha connections as he eyes 2028 election | JD Vance | The Guardian
description: Considered Republican frontrunner for presidential election, Vance is cozying up to the movement – as it splits
Author: Melody Schreiber
Headline: Considered Republican frontrunner for presidential election, Vance is cozying up to the movement – as it splits
Content: JD Vance (left) and Robert F Kennedy Jr at the Make America Healthy Again summit in Washington DC on 29 September.Photograph: Nathan Howard/ReutersView image in fullscreenJD Vance (left) and Robert F Kennedy Jr at the Make America Healthy Again summit in Washington DC on 29 September.Photograph: Nathan Howard/ReutersJD VanceJD Vance flexing Maha connections as he eyes 2028 electionConsidered Republican frontrunner for presidential election, Vance is cozying up to the movement – as it splitsMelody SchreiberSun 4 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 10.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJD Vance, widely considered to be the Republican frontrunner for the presidential election in 2028, is aligning himself with the Make America Healthy Again (Maha) movement as some say it is shedding its grassroots supporters in favor of political and corporate interests.The US vice-president has positioned himself as the inheritor of Make America Great Again (Maga), and attaching himself to Maha, which many in the Trump administration believe helped to win the 2024 election, signals a greater overlap between the two movements as the administration’s popularity plummets amid the war in Iran and rising prices.More than two-thirds (68%) of rural Maha supporters said that Trump’s health policies have “had a negative effect or no impact on the health of people where they live”, according in a new AP-KFFsurveythat highlights the disconnect between the sprawling political project and its grassroots support, especially in rural areas that overwhelmingly supported Trump in the 2024 election. More Americans view the president and vice-president unfavorably than favorably, according to a Januarysurveyby Pew Research.At the Maha summit in Washington DC on Tuesday, Vance traded jokes about memes and the “carnivore” diet of meat and fermented foods withRobert F Kennedy Jr, the secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and the leader of Maha.But Vance also highlighted his role in identifying what he says is fraud in Medicaid, Medicare and the Affordable Care Act marketplace – blaming it on immigrants, especially undocumented immigrants.“We’ve found close to $250bn in fraud just since I’ve been leading the anti-fraud task force,” Vance claimed, though the administration has releasedscant detailson who has been unenrolled from these programs and why the activity was considered fraudulent.Vance said that “the states that administer the programs don’t enforce them at all”, claiming that undocumented people were receiving Medicare benefits, though there is no documentation that this is occurring. “Cut that shit out and be honest about your intentions. It’s about giving benefits to illegal aliens,” Vance said to applause.Kennedy alluded to the more cost-efficient health systems of Europe, which have universal healthcare, to speak about the inefficiencies of the health system in the US, where costs have been “allowed to get out of control”. Vance seemed to point to the need for stronger regulation of the health system, saying that programs like Medicaid and Medicare are stronger when fraud can be detected – though the Trump administration has largely focused on deregulation.Speaking at the event, Vance underlined “the politics that Maha is stirring up”, said Art Caplan, professor emeritus at the NYU Grossman School of Medicine. “I think Vance was there making a calculation. He wants to replicate what Trump did, get the Maha devotees on his side, not Rubio’s.”Vance poked fun at secretary of state Marco Rubio, his closest political rival, saying Rubio “doesn’t have a great poker face”, which makes for “absolutely incredible” meme material. “Bobby and I are on a text chain with a bunch of the cabinet secretaries, where we’re basically beating social media to the memes,” Vance said, describing one image of Marco in a blonde wig after Dolly Parton died.The second annual summit showcased the fracturing of the Maha movement, which has often been an uneasy alliance among environmental, nutrition and anti-vaccine activists, and political and corporate actors. The event appeared to eschew the former and prioritize the latter, featuring companies like UnitedHealth, Walmart and Anthropic, including companies with active business before the US government. Grail, an experimental cancer-treatment company whose approval is currently before the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA), was a top sponsor.Companies that paid $300,000 were given the option of speaker slots, as well as a private dinner with Kennedy and Mehmet Oz, the administrator for the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS), according toreportingby Bloomberg.The Maha Center, which organized the event, is one of many Maha-affiliated endeavors headed by Tony Lyons, a longtime vaccine critic, who has paid Kennedy$4min the past year. Tickets were available for “Maha members” who pay $6,000 a year to Maha Holdings, whosesole board memberis Finn Kennedy, Kennedy’s 29-year-old son.“The Maha summit, I thought, was a giant conflict of interest,” said Caplan, adding that the “ethically disturbing” event appeared to be “pay to play” to access high-ranking officials in the Trump administration. Speakers included Oz; Brooke Rollins, secretary of the US Department of Agriculture; and Stefanie Spear, a top Kennedy aide. “Normally, you don’t get a chance to cozy up to FDA officials. That’s troubling,” Caplan added.While Maha appears to be fracturing in favor of corporations, it could still prove a powerful movement for Vance, Caplan said: “If he can get half of what Trump got, even if there’s a split, he’s doing well.”The strong focus on corporations was not lost on Maha activists. “Why are they excluding our voices?” Mary Talley Bowden, a doctor who opposes Covid vaccines and wasreprimandedfor stealthily providing unproven Covid treatments,saidon X.The lineup did not “reflect the issues that birthed the original Maha movement and drove voters, especially women, to show up and vote for this coalition”,saidKelly Ryerson, also known as the Glyphosate Girl. Some of the speakers “could not be less Maha”, she added.Maha has been “captured” by the very corporate interests it sought to fight, Robert Malone, a conspiracy theorist who voted to restrict vaccines while he was a member of the now-halted vaccines advisory committee,wroteon his Substack – decrying the “incestuous nature” of Maha, where “conflicts of interest seem to multiply by the day”.Kennedy, who has long railed against corporate influences affecting Americans’ health and wellbeing, was notably quiet about corporate power at the event. Instead, he praised companies like OpenAI, which has millions of dollars in US government contracts.“Today, it would be malpractice for a doctor to make a diagnosis or to make a prescription without at least checking AI,” he said, attributing the quote to OpenAI’s Sam Altman. Kennedy added that large language models “can give you a second opinion that is much better informed than any doctor in the country”. About a third (32%) of Americans consult AI for medical information and advice, though AI chatbots are inaccurate about25%of the time.“We’re never, ever again going to be able to be dominated by public officials who tell us ‘trust the experts’,” Kennedy said.“If somebody tells you ‘masks work, trust the experts’, AI may tell you otherwise. If somebody tells you ‘social distancing works, trust the experts’, AI may correct that. And if somebody tells you that ‘a vaccine will prevent transmission and infection, so you need to take it to protect your grandmother’, AI may say ‘it actually doesn’t do that’, So it really has the capacity to dominate us and free us from medical tyranny,” Kennedy said.His “fringy science agenda was on full display”, Caplan said. If Kennedy aligns himself with Vance and Vance wins the election, “it gives him power to pursue some things that he cares about”.Vance has longseenKennedy’s faction as essential for Trump’s success, and he also spoke at the Maha summit in 2025. But fewer than one in four Americans (23%) view Kennedy favorably, according to a newsurveyfrom the Annenberg Public Policy Center.Explore more on these topicsJD VanceRobert F Kennedy JrUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: MS Now connects ‘blue dots’ at Texas fan event: ‘I always feel hope when I watch them’ | Media | The Guardian
description: Network at receiving end of White House press ban recently chose red state to host fan event as part of broader outreach
Author: Jeremy Barr
Headline: Network at receiving end of White House press ban recently chose red state to host fan event as part of broader outreach
Content: Jacob Soboroff takes a question from the audience at MS Now’s live fan event in Texas on 26 September 2026.Photograph: Amy Mikler Kenyon/Amy Mikler Kenon/MS NOW © Versant Media.View image in fullscreenJacob Soboroff takes a question from the audience at MS Now’s live fan event in Texas on 26 September 2026.Photograph: Amy Mikler Kenyon/Amy Mikler Kenon/MS NOW © Versant Media.MediaMS Now connects ‘blue dots’ at Texas fan event: ‘I always feel hope when I watch them’Network at receiving end of White House press ban recently chose red state to host fan event as part of broader outreachJeremy Barrin Arlington, TexasSun 4 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 08.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn 2024, Donald Trump and JD Vance carried Tarrant county,Texas, by 42,125 votes. So why, on the afternoon of 26 September, was the arena at the University of Texas-Arlington filled with nearly 5,000 super fans cheering for liberal media darlings Rachel Maddow and Lawrence O’Donnell like they were rock stars?After two years of hosting the network’s annual fan event in dark blue New York City,MS Now(formerly MSNBC) got wind that something was happening in Texas. The state, which hasn’t elected a Democrat to the US Senate in 37 years, might do so next month, when 37-year-old James Talarico, Texas state representative, goes up against the Republican nominee, Ken Paxton, a well-known but controversial figure who ousted incumbent John Cornyn in the party’s primary with Donald Trump’s backing.“We wanted to be bigger and bolder. We wanted to go to a story that really matters (and this is one of the most important stories of the season), and we wanted to keep growing our live events business,” Marcus Mabry, senior vice-president of content strategy for MS Now, said in an interview. And, he noted, “everything is bigger in Texas”.While MS Now has a relative monopoly on older liberal Americans who still watch linear television, the network sees potential outside of its traditional coastal strongholds – much like the national Democratic party. Several MS Now hosts hinted at that growth opportunity in their on-stage remarks throughout the day’s programming.View image in fullscreenRachel Maddow hosts a discussion at MS Now’s annual live fan in Texas on 26 September 2026.Photograph: Amy Mikler Kenyon/Amy Mikler Kenon/MS NOW © Versant Media.“I will say, in the state of Texas, you might have a lot of neighbors that don’t vote like you, but it doesn’t mean they can’t tomorrow,” Stephanie Ruhle, an MS Now host, told the crowd. “I met so many people today whose eyes were filled with tears, and they said: ‘I’m the sole blue dot in Texas.’ How great that you are outstanding. How great that you are a special voice.”Or, as Mabry put it: “I think right now the opportunity for any journalism in the country is to stop speaking red and blue, and to start speaking to people as individuals.”In a holding room before his on-stage interview with Stacey Abrams, a former Georgia state representative, Chris Hayes, an MS Now host, said viewers seem to be more “locked into the news” lately after a period of post-election malaise (and softer television ratings) in late 2024 and early 2025, particularly now that Democrats face good odds in next month’s midterm elections. “There are thousands and thousands of people here – in the middle of Texas,” he said of the event.Comparing the vibes with the months after Trump took office, “it feels like another world. … We’ve had the most intense stress test in the American constitutional republic in my lifetime, and I don’t think anything is determined yet, but it certainly feels better than a year and a half ago.”The network is feeling that surge of interest. So far this year, MS Now’s primetime lineup is averaging 1.3 million viewers, up 11% from 2025. The network has seen an even bigger increase among viewers aged 25 to 54, the demographic most prized by advertisers.View image in fullscreenChris Hayes smiles with fans at MS Now’s live fan event in Texas on 26 September 2026.Photograph: MS NowThe event – Together In Texas: We the People 2026 – also served as something of an in-person illustration of the network’s first major direct-to-consumer offering, a membership plan – for $7.99 per month or $79.99 annually – that gives subscribers access to two daily Q&As with top hosts and reporters, a moderated discussion community for members, exclusive content, a curated daily briefing and even a collection of guided meditations. (Those in the Founders tier of the membership program had access to a special lounge at the event space.)“We’re still telling the audience what they need to know, but we’re also asking them, ‘What do you want to know, and how can we actually have a relationship where we actually are more than just delivering news to you as the voice of god,’ which fewer and fewer audience actually wants,” Mabry said. “I hope our business is learning that, because that’s the only way we survive. And we have to survive – it’s important for democracy.”With MS Now leaning into direct-to-customer products, fan service was the name of the game at the event. At one point, Rebecca Kutler, the network president, happily agreed to photograph several attendees who wanted to take photos with Laura Barrón-López, MS Now White House correspondent, after a panel on the network’s expulsion from the building – seemingly without realizing who their amateur photographer was. “I’ll do any job!” Kutler told the Guardian.Ruhle served as the event’s unofficial “cheerleader”, as one attendee said, hyping up the crowd and taking photos with fans.“Those are the people that we work for,” she said in an interview. “When you talk about the media being disconnected from the people, we are no longer – or we shouldn’t be – in the presentation business. No longer should we be sitting in newsrooms deciding here’s what we’re going to make or here’s how it has to look.”View image in fullscreenStephanie Ruhle in the crowd at MS Now Together in Texas.Photograph: Amy Mikler/MS Now“This isn’t a political rally,” Ruhle said of the event. “This is what America is … These people make our shows better. Why wouldn’t you want to be with them?”Ahead of the event, several attendees said it was a no-brainer for MS Now to host the event in Texas – and said they were committed to watching the network as a purveyor of both reliable information and a much-needed sense of optimism.Ronnie Thomas, a 47-year-old Dallas resident who works in automotive sales, said he was “very happy” to be able to see Maddow and his other favorite hosts with only a short drive.“I like getting more of the truth,” his wife Rachael, also 47, said. “And it feels like they are closer to what the true state of things are compared to some of the things we see on other stations.”Former Republican Leslie Lesher, 73, and her spouse Joni Dennis, 68, said they watch MS Now “almost all day” every day.“These are our favorite people,” Lesher said. “I know they have knowledge that we don’t have. I always feel hope when I watch them.”Ruhle shared her sentiments. “A lot of people are scared about the state of the world,” she said. “They’re scared of the state of democracy. And I just think we’re all in this together.”Explore more on these topicsMediaMS NowTexasUS politicsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Republicans say they hate communists. So why do they like Donald Trump? | US economy | The Guardian
description: Trump supporters may be surprised to learn the state takeover of means of production is not driven by the left
Author: Eduardo Porter
Headline: Trump supporters may be surprised to learn the state takeover of means of production is not driven by the left
Content: ‘The president’s statist leanings mark a dramatic break with the market-focused presidencies of his recent predecessors, Democrat and Republican.’Photograph: Mark Makela/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘The president’s statist leanings mark a dramatic break with the market-focused presidencies of his recent predecessors, Democrat and Republican.’Photograph: Mark Makela/Getty ImagesUS economyAnalysisRepublicans say they hate communists. So why do they like Donald Trump?Eduardo PorterTrump supporters may be surprised to learn the state takeover of means of production is not driven by the leftSun 4 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 07.02 EDTShareAmericans will never accept the Democratic party’s slide to the left, or so desperateRepublicansare hoping.With the midterm elections fast upon us, Zohran Mamdani’s promise of a few city-run bodegas in New York City will scare the bejeezus out of middle America. Disgust over the democratic socialists’ unicorn-and-puppy promises of aworld without capitalismwill keep the Republicans in power.Leading the charge against the new reds-under-the-bed is Donald Trump. “Together, we will defeat communism,” Trump promised in hisrecent TV ads.Trump’s supporters might be surprised to discover that the United States is, indeed, sliding in the direction of a command and control economy. But the state takeover of the means of production is not being driven by the left. The grab for the US’s productive resources is the project of none other than Trump – who, it’s a fair guess, has never read Lenin.The latest evidence comes in data crunched bythe V-Dem projectin Sweden, which measures the erosion of democracy around the world. It built a scale to gauge “state ownership of the economy”. Asnoted by Cullen Hendrixfrom the Peterson Institute for International Economics, from 2002 to 2024, the US ranked among the four countries with the least state control. In 2025, the first year of Trump’s second term, it dropped from second place to 16th.By November of last year, the Trump administration had spent more than $10bntaking stakesin companies he deemed essential for national security, from Intel to a range of ventures mining for critical minerals. It also acquired an option to take a stake in Westinghouse, which makes nuclear reactors. And it blackmailed Nippon Steel into granting Trump’s Washington a “golden share” in exchange for the go-ahead to purchase US Steel.To be fair, Trump’s acquisitiveness notwithstanding, the US is not even close to flirting with the flavor of socialism favored by the Soviet Union and its satellites in the second half of the 20th century. By the V-Dem accounting, Washington’s stake in the economy is still smaller than in 163 countries.Government-run companies are a standard feature in many market economies. The Norwegian government has a majority stake in its massive oil company, which puts the country in 18th place. Even “communist” countries are pretty capitalist: private companies contribute60% of China’s GDP.And in a geopolitical landscape shaped by competition with China, there isa reasonable caseto be made for Washington to take equity stakes in industries that are critical for American leadership and security, and which might not develop autonomously in competition with rivals heavily subsidized by Beijing.Yet Trump’s wanton lunge for private assets lacks the discipline required for this kind of strategic positioning.The president’s statist leanings mark a dramatic break with the market-focused presidencies of his recent predecessors, Democrat and Republican. The question is, what motivates him? His appetites are embedded in a body of thought that is skeptical, if not outright hostile, towards essential building blocks of the global market economy. He has pushed backagainst globalizationsince his first term in office, seemingly drawn to the Marxist-inspireddependency theory, which washed across Latin America in the 1960s and 1970s proposing protectionism and state industrial policy as a path to economic development.His lust to control the economy is there for all to see. Though the supreme court alreadyslapped downhis attempt to take over trade policy from Congress, he is still threatening to “STOP TRADING WITH COUNTRIES WITH WHICH WE HAVE A DEFICIT”. His promise to give $5,000 to every American if Republicans maintain control of Congress in November’s elections underscores how he views the state’s coffers as his private piggy bank. Even his commie-bashing ads were paid for by taxpayer dollars.Still, he clearly has no interest in the dictatorship of the proletariat, caring little if at all for the fate of the downtrodden. Hispreferred flavor of redistributiontakes from those on the bottom to give to those on the top.If anything, Trump reminds us that socialism is not the only ideological justification for state projects to take control over resources and wealth.Watching the US presidentbow to Xi Jinpinglast week, it’s tempting to think that Trump wants to emulate China’s leader. Xi gets to rule unimpeded over more than one billion Chinese. He gets to shape China’s society and economy at will – purging this rival, raising that sycophant to power.But Xi’sChinais too disciplined for Trump. The Chinese leader still relies on hordes of technocrats to execute a coherent strategy aimed to achieve technological superiority. The US president doesn’t have the attention span for this kind of thing.Rather, Trump’s model might be Vladimir Putin, who rules Russia like a fiefdom. Or maybe one of those dictators the US used to support in Latin America during the cold war: Haiti’s Papa Doc Duvalier or Anastasio Somoza in Nicaragua, who saw government as a tool to enrich their families and cement dynasties in power. If nothing else, Trump’s dealings with crypto suggest he views his administration as a road to family riches.Karl Marx may not be Trump’s guiding light. But his writings can help understand Trump’s place in history.Marx proposesthat his tome The 18th Brumaire of Louis Bonaparte, about the 1851 coup that brought Louis-Napoléon Bonaparte to power in France, was meant to “demonstrate how the class struggle in France created circumstances and relationships that made it possible for a grotesque mediocrity to play a hero’s part”.Americans may be grateful that their most recent class struggles didn’t produce a homegrown Lenin. But they did deliverDonald Trump.Perhaps this does not condemn the US to an autocratic future. Hendrix points out that while Trump “clearly wants to be king”, the US’s political economy may not let him. Putin managed to establish autocratic rule over a fairly primitive, oil-based economy. This kind of control “is much harder to achieve in a modern complex economy” such as that of the United States, Hendrix noted. You can’t simply seize the oil to run the place.Though Trump may fail, Americans’ acquiescence as he grabs for power raises a question for those who freak out over Mamdani’s city-run bodegas: why is Trump’s lurch to take over the American economy any better than what they hear from the Democratic Socialists of America?Eduardo Porter is a journalist focused on economics and politics. He writes the newsletterBeing Thereon SubstackExplore more on these topicsUS economyDonald TrumpCommunismRepublicansChinaUS politicsanalysisShareReuse this content

title: ‘The violence is off the scale’: staff and passengers at risk as assaults on trains in Great Britain soar to record high | Public transport | The Guardian
description: Cases of abuse, spitting, head-butting and sexual harassment, have spiked as transport police numbers have dwindled
Author: Gwyn Topham
Headline: Cases of abuse, spitting, head-butting and sexual harassment, have spiked as transport police numbers have dwindled
Content: Rail staff feel increasingly under threat, with many wearing bodycams to log violence.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenRail staff feel increasingly under threat, with many wearing bodycams to log violence.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianPublic transport‘The violence is off the scale’: staff and passengers at risk as assaults on trains in Great Britain soar to record highCases of abuse, spitting, head-butting and sexual harassment, have spiked as transport police numbers have dwindledGwyn Topham,Stephen Morris,Nicola Slawson,Hannah Al-OthmanandEve LivingstonSun 4 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 12.49 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen a train was halted outside Exeter St Davids station on Monday, rail staff leapt to one conclusion: there had been a violent incident on board.“Someone will have kicked off,” one staff member said. “It happens all the time. My boss got head-butted recently.”On this occasion, they were wrong – but their assumption told a tale. Figures released late last month showed the number of reported assaults on Great Britain’s railways had risen by a fifth, to a record high of almost 25,000 incidents in a year.Staff in particular have felt increasingly under threat. While the total numbers reported by the Office of Rail and Road in 2025-26 covered threats, verbal abuse, and contact that might not have resulted in any injury, they included nearly 2,500 physical assaults on workers – an average of about seven every day.Reported assaults on Great Britain’s railways rise by fifth in a yearRead moreTheir unions said the numbers were horrendous, but unsurprising: the RMT and TSSA unions have campaigned for more staffed stations and policing, after the number of BritishTransportPolice (BTP) officers fell by more than 10% between 2024 and 2026.Many rail staff wear body cams to record and log incidents of violence. “I think it’s so sad that we have those,” said Dave*, a rail worker in south-westEngland. However, after 20 years in the job, he said: “The threats, the abuse, the violence we see is off the scale.”Drink and drugs play a part, he added. “We’re also seeing a lot more people with mental health issues. If you’re out on the street you can steer clear, but if you’re on a train or a platform you can’t. Our workplaces are becoming more and more dangerous.”‘Now it’s mostly bad days’Steve, a guard based in the north of England, was punched in the head by a passenger: “It was my last train of the night. I’ve had to look away to see the door controls and the next thing I know, I’m waking up on the platform.”Every guard gets verbally abused on a daily basis, he said, with behaviour worsening since the pandemic: “Now it’s mostly bad days, and you’re searching for good days, where nothing’s said, or nothing happens. The amount of times we’re getting threatened now with physical attacks, even when you walk through the train and say, ‘Tickets, please.’”View image in fullscreenEven a simple request for tickets can trigger abuse.Photograph: UK Stock Images Ltd/AlamyEven those working on the infrastructure can be on the receiving end. One rail contractor, Liam, based in Somerset, said: “We’re there working on the tracks and we sometimes get sworn at and even spat at. It’s just a minority, but somehow they think we’re responsible for slow journey times, cancelled trains. We’re in bright orange so we’re easy targets.”The railway is by no means unique: bus drivers have faced repeated abuse and threats, as the Unite union has highlighted. Transport for London staff working on roads are issued with “spit kits”, or forensic saliva collection tubes, so common is that form of assault.Violence against women and girls is of particular concern; at the Labour conference this week, the minister for buses and local transport, Simon Lightwood, described it as a “national emergency”.View image in fullscreenKim McGuinness said women need to know ‘that if you raise an alarm something is going to be done’.Photograph: DEW/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.Speaking alongside him, the mayor for the north-east, Kim McGuinness, said that as well as measures such as more staffing, lighting and CCTV, a crucial point for women was “knowing that if you raise an alarm something is going to be done. It’s a choice to use public transport or not … if you’re accepting 50% of the population don’t feel safe, that’s not good.”The rail industry and police say some of the sharp rise in recorded assaults on passengers – up 36% last year – is due to greater reporting, including using discreet text messaging to the BTP.But while many more incidents are now reported, plenty are not.‘Tearful, angry and scared’Emily, 24, was travelling home on a late-night train between Glasgow and Edinburgh last year when a stranger made a beeline for her. “He immediately tried to start a conversation and wouldn’t give up even when I showed no interest. He was asking what I’d been up to, whether I had a boyfriend, complimenting my outfit, and then it escalated really quickly.”The man began rubbing Emily’s upper thigh and asking her intrusive questions about her sex life. “I froze and didn’t know what to do. I looked around but everyone else was oblivious. I tried to move but I was on the inside seat and he just grabbed my leg harder and leaned in towards me,” she said.She managed to manoeuvre out of the seat and away from the man, who “shouted aggressively and called [her] a bitch”. Other passengers looked round but did not intervene. She moved to another carriage and arrived home shaken but decided not to report the incident.“I wanted to just move on,” Emily said. “But I never used to think twice about getting on a train by myself at night and now I’m much more nervous.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenPassengers are becoming more nervous about taking public transport.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianEdward, a trans man, was travelling home to Staffordshire with his partner, a trans woman, after a weekend inWales. On a packed train from Aberystwyth, a man began loudly making homophobic comments and became confrontational.“Normally in that situation I just walk on, but I physically couldn’t, we were so crammed,” Edward said. He finally yelled back, repeating: “You’re shouting homophobic abuse in front of your children.”A railway worker eventually intervened and told the assailant and his family to move to another carriage. Edward chose not to report the incident to police, dissatisfied with the response to previous incidents. He now tries to avoid public transport: “I felt tearful, angry and scared afterwards.”Tell us: have you recently been assaulted on Great Britain’s railways?Read more‘It’s put me off trains’A fraction of passenger reports end up with arrest or prosecution. Last year, Sam was travelling north from London on a train packed with football supporters. As she tried to reach her reserved seat, a drunken man confronted her and pushed her backward.She instinctively pushed him back. “Then I thought, what have you done?” she said. Other men began throwing beer cans while one held her by her rucksack. “I was being pushed and shoved … they were throwing punches as well.”Amid the assault, one man deliberately grabbed her breasts. “I realised: ‘Oh no, I’m trapped on here with them for the next two hours’,” she said. “There’s nowhere to go. There’s nowhere to get off.”Two BTP officers on the train got through to take a statement from Sam. The investigation was later dropped after police were unable to identify her assailant.The experience had a big impact, leaving her “not doing a lot of things I used to do. It’s put me off trains massively. I think if faced with a train like that, I would just not board it.”View image in fullscreenTransport police say offenders can expect a ‘robust response’.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianThe BTP assistant chief constable Ian Drummond-Smith said: “We will never tolerate violence or abuse directed at passengers or staff on the railway, and anyone committing these crimes can expect a robust response from us.”He noted that when staff had body-worn recording, police brought offenders to justice in about 85% of incidents. “Anyone who witnesses violence or abuse on the railway should report it to us by texting 61016, or call 999 in an emergency,” he said.The Department for Transport said the rise in assaults was “deeply concerning and unacceptable”. It has awarded a £63m increase in BTP funding by 2028-29, allowing more than 200 additional officers to be recruited, and investments in better CCTV and body-worn video. Dozens of new BTP officers will be specialised in tackling violence and intimidation against women and girls.* Names have been changedThe headline of this article was amended on 4 October 2026 to correctly refer to Great Britain rather than the UK.Explore more on these topicsPublic transportRail industryTransportRail transportPoliceCrimeEnglandfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: NFL roundup: Rams escape against Eagles, Chiefs win thriller but Thornton suffers gruesome injury | NFL | The Guardian
description: Kyren Williams ran for two touchdowns in the final four minutes as Matthew Stafford and the Los Angeles Rams rallied from a 10-point deficit
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Kyren Williams ran for two touchdowns in the final four minutes as Matthew Stafford and the Los Angeles Rams rallied from a 10-point deficit
Content: The Rams celebrate their late win over the Eagles.Photograph: Chris Szagola/APView image in fullscreenThe Rams celebrate their late win over the Eagles.Photograph: Chris Szagola/APNFLNFL roundup: Rams escape against Eagles, Chiefs win thriller but Thornton suffers gruesome injuryRams score two touchdowns in final four minutesKansas City Chiefs edge Las Vegas to stay unbeatenLamar Jackson leaves stadium in protective bootDrake Maye finds form in Pats win over BillsAgenciesSun 4 Oct 2026 17.02 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 20.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLos Angeles Rams 24–20 Philadelphia EaglesKyren Williams ran for two touchdowns in the final four minutes as Matthew Stafford and the Los Angeles Rams rallied from a 10-point deficit to beat the Philadelphia Eagles. The Rams had struggled offensively all afternoon and a win seemed out of reach until late in the fourth quarter, when Eagles coach Nick Sirianni decided against kicking a chip-shot field goal that would have made it a three-score game and instead went for it on fourth down. The Eagles failed to convert, giving the Rams new life. Stafford led touchdown drives of 98 and 79 yards, with Williams scoring the go-ahead touchdown from seven yards out. Both teams are 2-2 on the season.Kansas City Chiefs 30–27 Las Vegas RaidersPatrick Mahomes remained undefeated at Allegiant Stadium, passing for 225 yards and two touchdowns, and Kenneth Walker III rushed for 177 yards and two TDs to lead the Chiefs to a tight victory over the Las Vegas Raiders. Walker’s two-yard touchdown run with 3:21 left put the Chiefs ahead for good at 23-19. It was set up by Tyquan Thornton’s 55-yard reception on the previous play. Thornton suffered a serious injury on the catch and was carted off the field. Kirk Cousins passed for 365 yards and two touchdowns for the Raiders, who fell to 3-1 and had a chance to win before Cousins was intercepted in the final minute. The Chiefs are 4-0.New England Patriots 29–26 Buffalo BillsDrake Maye completed 22 of 37 passes for 269 yards and three touchdowns, including a late, go-ahead TD pass ⁠to Efton Chism III, to lead the New England Patriots to victory. Chism’s leaping, one-handed ⁠23-yard TD ​catch plus Maye’s pass to Rhamondre Stevenson for the two-point conversion gave the Patriots a 29-26 lead with 1:50 to play. Craig ⁠Woodson intercepted a Josh Allen pass at the New England 19-yard line on the ensuing possession, and the Patriots (2-2) were able to run ⁠out the clock and hand Buffalo (3-1) their first loss in their new stadium.Denver Broncos 14–24 San Francisco 49ersBrock Purdy threw two touchdown passes and Christian McCaffrey ran for a score to lead the undefeated San Francisco 49ers to victory over the Denver Broncos (2-2). Both offenses struggled to generate offense on a hot day in the Bay Area but the 49ers took advantage of a fumbled punt return by Marvin Mims Jr to set up a short touchdown drive in the third quarter that gave them the lead for good.Dallas Cowboys 34–30 Houston TexansCeeDee Lamb had a career-high 17 catches for 189 yards and his 12-yard TD reception with 40 seconds left lifted the Dallas Cowboys to a win over Houston to keep the Texans winless. Javonte Williams ran for a career-high three touchdowns – all in the second half – to help the Cowboys to the victory. Dallas trailed by four points after a six-yard touchdown run by Woody Marks with less than three minutes to play. Dak Prescott then orchestrated an 11-play, 74-yard drive that included a fourth-down conversion and capped it with the throw to Lamb to give the Cowboys (2-2) the victory.Tennessee Titans 18–24 Baltimore RavensLamar Jackson threw for 222 yards and two touchdowns on 15-of-20 passes but exited early in the Ravens’ 24-18 victory over ⁠the Tennessee Titans. The Ravens (3-1) snapped a four-game losing streak in their home stadium but needed their defense to hang ⁠on after the Titans (0-4) ⁠held them ​scoreless in the second half without Jackson, who did not play in the second half. Jackson was sacked on Baltimore’s final play of ⁠the second quarter by Jermaine Johnson II, who landed on Jackson’s left ankle. Jackson left the stadium in a protective boot after the game. “He was just dealing with a little bit of an ankle,” the Ravens head coach, Jesse Minter, said. “I don’t know enough about it right now, but we’ll have to see where that’s at.”Los Angeles Chargers 23–30 Seattle SeahawksEmanuel Wilson caught a touchdown pass and ran for another score and the Seattle Seahawks handed the Los Angeles Chargers a fourth straight loss to start the season. Sam Darnold threw for 168 yards and two touchdowns for the defending Super Bowl champions who are now 3-1 after rebounding from last week’s 33-31 loss to the Washington Commanders. Justin Herbert threw for 189 yards a touchdown and two interceptions for the 0-4 Chargers.Arizona Cardinals 24–36 New York GiantsJameis Winston threw three touchdowns passes to offset a pair of interceptions, Deonte Banks had a pick-six in the final seconds and the New York Giants (3-1) won another not-so-pretty game, defeating the Arizona Cardinals. Making his second start in place of injured franchise quarterback Jaxson Dart, Winston again did what he needed to do to engineer a victory with TD passes to Malachi Fields, Malik Nabers and Theo Johnson. The Cardinals (1-3) lost a third consecutive game since opening the season with a win in coach Mike LaFleur’s debut.New York Jets 12–23 Chicago BearsKyle Monangai rushed for 146 yards and two touchdowns and the Chicago Bears (3-1) stuffed the New York Jets for a 23-12 victory. Devin Bush, Austin Booker and Dayo Odeyingbo each had a sack as Chicago limited New York to seven first downs and 157 yards overall. The Bears have allowed a total of 28 points in three games since their wild 59-37 victory at Carolina in their season opener. Tyson Bagent passed for 268 yards for Chicago, and Cairo Santos kicked three field goals. Minkah Fitzpatrick ended New York’s NFL-record interception drought at 20 games, but the Jets (1-3) dropped their third consecutive game.Miami Dolphins 10–15 Minnesota VikingsTJ Hockenson had 13 receptions for 119 yards, and the Minnesota Vikings held on for a close ⁠win over the Miami Dolphins. Kyler Murray completed 27 of 37 passes for 247 ⁠yards for Minnesota, ⁠who are ​4-0 for the 11th time in franchise history. Aaron Jones Sr finished with 128 all-purpose yards (94 rushing, 34 ⁠receiving) and Will Reichard kicked five field goals. Ollie Gordon II had nine carries for 100 yards and a touchdown to lead ⁠Miami (0-4). Malik Willis completed nine of 17 passes for 85 yards and ​lost a fumble.Jacksonville Jaguars 22–17 Cincinnati BengalsTrevor Lawrence passed for 227 yards and a touchdown, Jacksonville’s defense forced two critical turnovers and the Jaguars held off the Cincinnati Bengals. Joe Burrow passed for 428 yards for the Bengals (2-2), who lost All-Pro wide receiver Ja’Marr Chase to a concussion in the second quarter. Tee Higgins had 11 receptions for 151 yards. Burrow, who completed 39 of 54 passes, also had two costly interceptions – one that Jacksonville (3-1) converted into a touchdown and the other when the Bengals were in the red zone. The Bengals had a final chance to rally and drove to the Jaguars 21, but Chase Brown was stopped short on fourth down. Higgins also suffered an adductor injury near the end of the game, and could join Chase on the sidelines.Green Bay Packers 17–14 Tampa Bay BuccaneersJordan Love threw two touchdown passes and the Green Bay Packers’ defense forced a pair of interceptions en route ⁠to victory over the Tampa Bay Buccaneers. Love completed 22 of 30 passes for 197 yards ⁠and Tucker Kraft ⁠had six ​catches for 42 yards and a score for the Packers (2-2), who moved to 2-0 on the road. Rookie quarterback Jalon Daniels, making ⁠his first career start, completed 19 of 27 passes for 148 yards and a touchdown for Tampa Bay (0-4). Daniels also rushed for 55 yards as he played in place of the ​injured Baker Mayfield.Indianapolis Colts 30–13 Washington CommandersJonathan Taylor rushed for two touchdowns and Colts quarterback Daniel Jones ran one in and Indianapolis beat Washington in London after the Commanders lost yet another quarterback to injury. Marcus Mariota, who was starting in place of the injured Jayden Daniels, left the game after Washington’s second drive because of a knee injury. Third-string rookie quarterback Athan Kaliakmanis was called into action. Taylor rushed for 95 yards on 20 carries as the Colts overcame two turnovers from Jones, who completed 19 of 34 passes for 134 yards with an interception and a fumble.Explore more on these topicsNFLUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Unequivocally false’: WNBA players push back on Fever GM’s defense of fans’ behavior | Indiana Fever | The Guardian
description: Indiana Fever players past and present have pushed back on an assertion that the team’s fans are not an issue
Author: Guardian sport
Headline: Indiana Fever players past and present have pushed back on an assertion that the team’s fans are not an issue
