Content: Indiana Fever have attracted plenty of attention due to players like Caitlin Clark and Sophie Cunningham.Photograph: Bobby Goddin/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenIndiana Fever have attracted plenty of attention due to players like Caitlin Clark and Sophie Cunningham.Photograph: Bobby Goddin/Getty ImagesIndiana Fever‘Unequivocally false’: WNBA players push back on Fever GM’s defense of fans’ behaviorIndiana GM said team’s fans were unfairly attackedFormer player Brianna Turner says fans are an issueKelsey Mitchell says some fans do not like herGuardian sportand agenciesSun 4 Oct 2026 17.44 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 17.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIndiana Fever players past and present have pushed back on an assertion that the team’s fans are not an issue.On Saturday the Fever’s general manager, Amber Cox, defended Indiana’s fanbase after a series of criticisms over their conduct this season.“The attacks on our fanbase have no basis in reality, and they need to stop, especially with members of the media,” Cox said. “I’m talking about media who have never been to a game at Gainbridge Fieldhouse. Every organization in the league, every organization throughout professional sports, all the way down to youth rec leagues, have to deal with occasional bad behavior from spectators. And anyone who crosses the line in an arena or online needs to be held accountable. I want to be really clear about that: There is a line, and people need to be held accountable if they cross it.”The eternal whirring of the Caitlin Clark conspiracy machine has shifted into a new gear | Andrew LawrenceRead moreCriticism of Fever fansoccurred againin Game 2 of Indiana’s playoff series with the Las Vegas Aces. Four-time MVP A’ja Wilson confronted a Fever fan after he had shouted and pointed at her. The man was taken to the back of the arena before returning to his seat when it was determined he had not broken the fan code of conduct.“We did not have one fan pointed out by a player who violated theWNBAcode of conduct this season. Not one fan was removed from a game,” Cox said. “Our fans love this team. They’re going to cheer, they’re going to boo and sometimes they might point. It’s a home-court advantage for a reason, and it’s the same for the Pacers. And all of that is within the code of conduct.”However, Fever player Brianna Turner, who now plays for the Aces, disagreed with Cox’s comments.“This is an unequivocally false statement,” Turnerwrote on social media. “Players inside and outside the organization have repeatedly issued complaints with the Fever fanbase. While it’s not all Indy fans, it’s certainly a trend. To say the attacks have ‘no basis in reality’ is disingenuous.”Kelsey Mitchell, who had a career-best season with the Fever, said on Saturday that playing in Indiana can be difficult at times because of interactions with some of the team’s fans. She has spent her entire career with the Fever since she was drafted in 2018.“I don’t think people really understand how much we endure,” said Mitchell, who is a free agent this offseason. “Like, if I showed y’all my DMs about the hate and all of the stuff that comes with being a professional athlete, but specifically being an Indiana Fever basketball player, it’s a lot that goes into that. And those days are hard as hell.”Mitchell is entering free agency and said she would “be selfish where my career is going”, indicating it was tough being Caitlin Clark’s teammate at the Fever.“Playing with [Clark] and having the eyes that she’s got [on her], we get a lot of flak just from being on her team,” Mitchell said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Weekly for the 2026 WNBA seasonSign up toWNBA 30A limited run women’s basketball newsletter dedicated to the league’s historic 30th season.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMitchell has had a superb season, averaging 24.7 points a game, but said it could still be a struggle playing for the team.“Showing up every day to compete for fans that may or may not like you is hard,” Mitchell said Saturday. “… I think this organization is unbelievable, man, but I think that when it comes to, like, really trying to be yourself, it hasn’t always been easy.”Mitchell also paid tribute to the team’s part in her career, adding that “everything I’ve grown to be is [due to] the Fever.”Fever lost their playoff seriesagainst the Aces 2-1.Explore more on these topicsIndiana FeverWNBABasketballUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Insane’: F1 drivers unite over engine regulations after chaotic Bahrain GP | Formula One 2026 | The Guardian
description: Kimi Antonelli and Lewis Hamilton led the criticism for Sunday’s Bahrain GP after the race was delayed for 53 minutes because of software problems in the wet conditions
Author: Giles Richards
Headline: Kimi Antonelli and Lewis Hamilton led the criticism for Sunday’s Bahrain GP after the race was delayed for 53 minutes because of software problems in the wet conditions
Content: Kimi Antonelli joined Lewis Hamilton in criticising the FIA after farcical scenes in Sepang.Photograph: Antoine Lapeyre/Reveries Agency/ABACA/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenKimi Antonelli joined Lewis Hamilton in criticising the FIA after farcical scenes in Sepang.Photograph: Antoine Lapeyre/Reveries Agency/ABACA/ShutterstockFormula One 2026‘Insane’: F1 drivers unite over engine regulations after chaotic Bahrain GPAntonelli and Hamilton led the criticism in SepangRace delayed after software problems in wet conditionsGiles RichardsSun 4 Oct 2026 11.30 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFormula One drivers issued a damning condemnation of the sport’s current engine regulations that caused the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia to open with farcical scenes of cars stopping on track and unable to accelerate because of software problems in the electronics that control the engines.Red Bull’sMax Verstappen won in Sepangbut only after F1 suffered the embarrassment of a host of cars barely able to complete two ­formation laps in the wet as they were making their way to the grid.Max Verstappen wins chaotic F1 Bahrain GP in Malaysia amid farcical scenesRead more“It was insane,” said the championship leader Kimi Antonelli of Mercedes. “At some point we were five-wide in the straight, because we couldn’t understand what was going on.”Lewis Hamilton was one of the field who ground to a halt. “I had to stop on-track, stop the car, the engine, and restart it. I’ve never done that before,” he said, while Verstappen reiterated his previous criticism of the engine regulations. “What can you say? It’s not what you want for the sport. I hope there is a lesson learned,” he said.The issue was caused by software designed to control the engine but which had been insufficiently tested in low-grip, wet conditions which led to what the sport’s governing body the FIA called “an unintended loss of power”.The start had to be aborted and the field returned to the pit lane to have the software updated in a delay that lasted 53 minutes, leading to a ­chorus of disapproval from the drivers who were already dissatisfied with the current engine formula.The defending world champion, Lando Norris, who finished ninth for McLaren and is one of many who have been critical of the engine regulations, described it as “just ­horrible” and noted once more that it demonstrated the sport had taken a wrong turn, adding: “We shouldn’t have any of that stuff, the electronic side.”The formula, an almost 50-50 split between electronic and combustion power, will not be changed this ­season with a minor adjustment next year and more serious change in 2028, but the issue had once more raised the question of how the sport reached this point.View image in fullscreenThe safety car leads Max Verstappen in a wet formation lap.Photograph: Clive Mason/Getty Images“[F1] needs to have a hard look at themselves and see how we ended up in this situation,” said Williams’ Carlos Sainz. “It is clear the regs are extremely complicated for the drivers, for the teams, for the power units, for the manufacturers. It is too complicated. Again, my only question mark is who five years ago decided that this was the direction to go?”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe FIA did act swiftly to ­rectify the problem with the software update but their single-seater director Nikolas Tombazis admitted the regulations and the “software bug” had caught the governing body out.“We didn’t manage to test the software as extensively as we would have liked because there’s been very little wet running this year and there was a bit of a combination of circumstances which caused this bug to kick in,” he said.“Basically, the formation lap, some cars went very slowly, almost came to a standstill. There was a bit of a ­concertina effect between cars, and some cars almost stopped completely. That bug prevented the power to be redeployed and for the cars to start again. I think if we had a bit more testing, we probably would have managed to catch it in time and not to have such a situation.”Explore more on these topicsFormula One 2026Formula OneMotor sportnewsShareReuse this content

title: Jesse Marsch: ‘We Americans have been inundated with propaganda since we were young’ | Canada | The Guardian
description: As he prepares to face his home nation, the Canada manager reflects on his adopted country’s soccer, its prime minister, and its place in the world
Author: Joe Callaghan
Headline: As he prepares to face his home nation, the Canada manager reflects on his adopted country’s soccer, its prime minister, and its place in the world
Content: Jesse Marsch led Canada to a last 16 exit at the World Cup this past summer.Photograph: Chris Young/The Canadian Press/APView image in fullscreenJesse Marsch led Canada to a last 16 exit at the World Cup this past summer.Photograph: Chris Young/The Canadian Press/APCanadaInterviewJesse Marsch: ‘We Americans have been inundated with propaganda since we were young’Joe Callaghanin MontrealAs he prepares to face his home nation, the Canada manager reflects on his adopted country’s soccer, its prime minister, and its place in the worldSun 4 Oct 2026 07.30 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 08.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePeak leaf hasn’t yet arrived in Montreal but the bursts of gold and butterscotch up on the hill that gave this place its name still mushroom out by the hour.Sitting in a glass-panelled hotel mezzanine at the foot of Mount Royal,Canadamen’s coach Jesse Marsch has his mind on another harvest. When this extended autumnal international window ends, he will decamp to Italy, where the olive crops at his Tuscan villa are ready for reaping.Flight paths between Canada and Europe have been busy lately, and figurative transatlantic distances are closing fast. As Canada’s relations with the noisiest neighbour to the south stretch and fray, Canadian prime minister Mark Carney isforging alliances with the EUso close that the bloc is apparently inventing new membership categories.How Promise David emerged from Maltese shadows into the Premier LeagueRead moreAs an American residing in Europe who is also a Canadian leader with robust approval ratings, Marsch is watching. To him, it feels right.“I’ve always thought Canada was a little bit more European than the US anyway. Right?” Marsch tells the Guardian. “But certainly now there’s enough happening politically and economically that you would say, we’re looking much more like that. There’s talk of [Canada becoming an associate EU member]even actually happening. I like that aspect.“There’s a uniqueness to Canada in terms of how truly multiethnic this country has become. You can see that Canada is not just a North American country any more, you know? That bodes well for our sport and for the makeup of our team, the makeup of our fans.”Having led Canada’s men tohistoric highsat this summer’s World Cup, Marsch is feeling his way into his second act in the job. Some of his sideline displays –we’ll get tothatmeme– may have irked outsiders, especially in his homeland, during the tournament. Yet, having extended for four more years, Marsch is someone an overwhelming majority of Canadians are happy to have at the helm. There are more than a few cross-points between Marsch and Carney.“My impression is that first of all, he is a really smart guy, but a really normal guy,” Marsch says of Carney, who attended a number of Canada’s World Cup matches. “Sometimes you meet a US president, and you’re overwhelmed, maybe by their presence, the position itself. I’ve met Clinton, George Bush Sr, Obama, Trump, Biden. Oh, and Carter. Six in person. Carney, compared to all of them, the closest would be Obama. A real air of intelligence, but a real air of being a regular guy. I think that that’s perfect for this country and this moment.“He has shown great support for us. I made a joke with him that ‘I heard you’re an Everton fan?’ and he goes, ‘Yeah’. And I go, ‘I’m sorry about that’. He replies: ‘Why does everybody say that? Everybody has to pick their team and stick by them.’ I said, ‘I appreciate that you don’t switch from Everton to Arsenal or Liverpool, like everybody else’. There’s something so genuine [about] that. Could a president of the US ever be an Everton fan? No chance.”View image in fullscreenCanada prime minister Mark Carney greeted Marsch’s team in the locker room after the team’s win over Qatar at the 2026 World Cup.Photograph: Jared C Tilton/Fifa/Getty ImagesCircumstances, as well as natural impulses, have led Marsch to play statesman during this prolonged cooling of relations between Canada and his home country. He’s been defiant – lashing out at Donald Trump’s “51st state” barbs – then more deft. Sometimes, especially when it comes to the US Soccer Federation he said led him on with a job offer only to renege, he finds it hard to hide his disdain.This window is the start of turning the page to the next phase of his Canada project. He admits, with a chuckle, that the four years stretching ahead feel long but there are imminent goals – a first trophy in 25 years, cracking and consolidating inside the world’s top 24.A win over Chile in Toronto and 2-0 win over Peru here on Saturday afternoon in games billed as The Homecoming made for a solid start. New caps have been handed out. Key players arrived thriving in new surroundings, none more than Jonathan David at Atlético Madrid. Extended injury absences and the awkward non-attendance of captain Alphonso Davies (skipping the window to honeymoon) have been overcome.But Tuesday’s clash with the US in Saint Paul means more American questions are coming. Looking back, the Folarin Balogun affair feels absolutely tailor-made for a Marschian verdict. He, of course, has thoughts.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice weeklySign up toSoccer DeskJonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion‘A surprising success’: US, Mexico and Canada fans on hosting the World CupRead more“Well, this is a deep conversation,” he says, leaning back. “We, as Americans, have been inundated with propaganda since we were young. We’re the No 1 country in the world, we deserve everything, we dominate everything, No 1 in every aspect of life. This is what we’ve been told. So, when things happen and we don’t feel like we’re in control of it … we feel like we deserve to be treated differently because we’re Americans. That is one of the things that infuriates the rest of the world about Americans. And Americans don’t know that if they don’t ever leave the country.“So what I feel when the Balogun ruling happens is that would never happen in any other country in the world, and this is why everyone around the world hates America. That was proven to be so. The US had had a good World Cup, was doing well. All that switched in one moment. But do I think that that’s about corruption and unfairness? The problem is, football is inundated with this kind of stuff.”The memeis another World Cup leftover. “I’ve had all kinds of people ask me what it was, was it a meat slicer?” he says of his sideline gyrations during their match against Qatar. The incident spawned a gif which has been used plenty in the Marsch family WhatsApp since. “I don’t know what I’m doing sometimes. As soon as I’ve done it, I’m like: ‘Why did I do that? I’m such an idiot’.”He doesn’t feel fooled, however, by the sport’s latest, arguably greatest, modern corruption crisis. Defeats to Manchester City in 2022-23 didn’t help the Leeds United side Marsch had managed when they missed safety by five points. That campaign is not one of the “sham” seasons which were part of the damning verdict against City last week. But he’s adamant the unfairness extended to his time in England.“I think Man City should be punished severely. I think they should have to go down, and by the way, everyone knew about it. Everyone knew,” says Marsch, who also pointed to Everton and Nottingham Forest later being deducted points for issues in the same season when Leeds were relegated below both.“That summer [2022], us and Man City were the only teams that said we made money. For us, we did make money, because we sold Raphinha, we sold Kalvin Phillips [to City]. We had a lot left over from what we bought. At the time, we weren’t in a position financially to not save. Our ownership didn’t have deep pockets. Whereas when Man City says this, I was literally like, ‘Are you kidding me? Is this some kind of joke?’“When they said they got Erling Haaland for £52m, it’s like: ‘Yeah, OK, sure!’ So, I knew there were inconsistencies in it, but what can you do? You just put your arms in the air and go, ‘This is football’.”Explore more on these topicsCanadaUSAUS sportsinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Hallgrímsson calls on Uefa to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future after bad-tempered draw | Nations League | The Guardian
description: Troy Parrott’s first-half penalty for Ireland was cancelled out by Israel’s Dor Peretz in a 1-1 draw but tensions spilled over between the sides at various points
Author: Guardian sport
Headline: Troy Parrott’s first-half penalty for Ireland was cancelled out by Israel’s Dor Peretz in a 1-1 draw but tensions spilled over between the sides at various points
Content: Ireland’s Jayson Molumby and Jason Knight argue with Eli Dasa and Oscar Gloukh, of Israel, as tensions spilled over.Photograph: Stephen McCarthy/Sportsfile/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenIreland’s Jayson Molumby and Jason Knight argue with Eli Dasa and Oscar Gloukh, of Israel, as tensions spilled over.Photograph: Stephen McCarthy/Sportsfile/Getty ImagesNations LeagueHallgrímsson calls on Uefa to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future after bad-tempered drawGuardian sportand agenciesSun 4 Oct 2026 17.13 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Republic of Ireland’s manager Heimir Hallgrímsson has called on Uefa to keep his side away from Israel in future draws after a pair of fixtures he admitted “has been tough on us all”. Ireland were pegged back to a draw in another tetchy encounter, this time played without fans at TSC Arena in Backa Topola, Serbia.Hallgrímsson did not want to comment on a half-time confrontation, after which it is understood a member of his backroom staff alleged he was spat at by an Israeli player – something the Icelandic manager said was better left to a disciplinary committee.“We need now some time to reflect and go forward,” he said. “It’s also the best time to find your enemies when you’re lying on the ground and people are kicking you. It’s easy to see who was trying to kick you.”Denmark sink Wales as Rasmus Højlund makes Danny Ward pay for blunderRead moreAsked on RTE whether the two sides should be playing in the future, he said: “No, they shouldn’t. That’s not ours to decide, that’s Uefa. I wouldn’t want or wish any national team to go through what we have gone through these two weeks. Uefa needs to step in and do something.’Troy Parrott’s first-half ­penalty was cancelled out after the break in the Group B3 game. Parrott, who has now scored 10 times in his past seven competitive internationals, fired the Republic in front from the spot in the 39th minute before Dor Peretz drew the sides level two ­minutes after the restart.Ireland players again wore black armbands and bowed their heads ­during the Israeli national anthem before the teams’ secondNations Leaguemeeting on Sunday. The Israeli players also wore black armbands in memory of the people killed in the Hamas-led attacks on Israel on 7 October 2023.Ireland goalkeeper Caoimhín Kelleher stepped in as captain for Dara O’Shea – who was excused to be with his wife for the birth of their child – and he pointedly avoided shaking hands with the Israel captain Peretz, despite completing the usual pre-match formality with the referee and one of his assistants.Kelleher repeated O’Shea’s actions before the first match in Debrecen, Hungary last week, when O’Shea declined to shake the Israel captain Manor Solomon’s hand. Ireland went on towin that game 3-0 through three first-half goals. Solomon was dropped to the bench for Sunday’s match. The Israel forward Sayed Abu Farchi was back in the squad after serving a suspension for getting sent off following his goal celebration during Israel’s 3-1 defeat to Austria last month.Finn Azaz, whose mother has Israeli heritage, was among the Irish substitutes after playing from the start against Austria on Thursday.View image in fullscreenThe Ireland goalkeeper Caoimhín Kelleher avoids shaking hands with the Israel captain Dor Peretz before the game.Photograph: Andrej Čukić/EPAIreland had started to find some fluidity when Dunne won a penalty. The Israel goalkeeper Assaf Tzur scrambled to smother the ball, and Jimmy Dunne was brought down under the challenge, with the spot-kick confirmed after a lengthy VAR check.Peretz levelled the scoring two minutes after the restart. An Oscar Gloukh effort took a favourable deflection off Liam Scales and into the path of the acting captain, who gave ­Kelleher no chance with a low finish.YesterSunday’s game was initially supposed to be played in Dublin, but the Football Association of Ireland moved the game to a neutral venue for “operational reasons” in June following widespread calls for a boycott in protest of Israel’s actions in Gaza. The FAI said the game would be played with no fans present.It followed the FAI’s own motion the previous November calling on Uefa to ban Israel from club and international competitions.The difficult atmosphere between the sides spilled over during a clash as the sides entered the tunnel at half-time. Officials then broke up a second altercation in three minutes of added time, and there were more heated words exchanged after the final whistle.Explore more on these topicsNations LeagueRepublic of IrelandIsraelmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Djokovic rolls back years to beat Zverev as Sabalenka swept out in China Open | Tennis | The Guardian
description: Novak Djokovic ousted Alexander Zverev from the China Open, beating the top seed 4-6, 6-4, 6-4 to set up a semi-final with Daniil Medvedev
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Novak Djokovic ousted Alexander Zverev from the China Open, beating the top seed 4-6, 6-4, 6-4 to set up a semi-final with Daniil Medvedev
Content: Novak Djokovic stretches to reach a backhand in his quarter-final victory over Alexander Zverev.Photograph: Yanshan Zhang/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenNovak Djokovic stretches to reach a backhand in his quarter-final victory over Alexander Zverev.Photograph: Yanshan Zhang/Getty ImagesTennisDjokovic rolls back years to beat Zverev as Sabalenka swept out in China OpenNovak Djokovic into semi-finals after 4-6, 6-4, 6-4 winAryna Sabalenka loses to 34th-ranked BartunkovaAgence France-PresseSun 4 Oct 2026 11.33 EDTFirst published on Sun 4 Oct 2026 05.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNovak Djokovic rolled back the years to oustAlexander Zverevfrom the China Open on Sunday, beating the top seed 4-6, 6-4, 6-4 to set up a semi-final with Daniil Medvedev.Women’s tennis tour announces prize money parity with men in ‘major milestone’Read moreThe 39-year-old electrified a packed crowd in Beijing, where he extended an astonishing winning streak to 32 matches. Djokovic got off to a poor start, double-faulting twice in the first game to help Zverev, a decade his junior, break serve instantly.Boos filled the stadium soon afterwards when the umpire agreed to replay a point Djokovic had won, after Zverev complained about a flicker in the LED panels during play. The German saw out the first set from there, but a valiant Djokovic roared back to seal the second with a cross-court winner to break serve and force a decider.The 24-time grand slam champion faced 19 Zverev aces throughout the match but held steady on his own serve to go 5-4 ahead in the final set. He then broke the world No 2 to take the set and the match, seemingly defying his recent physical difficulties with victory in a gruelling two hours and 34 minutes.Djokovic will face Medvedev in the final four after the former world No 1 dispatched Francisco Cerúndolo 7-6, 6-3.View image in fullscreenAlexander Zverev shows his frustration during his quarter-final defeat by Novak Djokovic.Photograph: Pedro Pardo/AFP/Getty ImagesPoland’s Hubert Hurkacz also advanced to the semi-finals after beating Karen Khachanov, and will play Australia’s Alex de Minaur who survived a gruelling test to beat Andrey Rublev 1-6, 6-2, 6-3.Aryna Sabalenka was swatted aside in straight sets by Nikola Bartunkova in the third round of the China Open on Sunday, leaving the event without its top two seeds.Bartunkova, the world No 34, sent down four aces to beat the former world No 1 6-4, 6-3 in one hour and 35 minutes. “I focused on myself, to be calm,” Bartunkova said. “She’s a legend … so I’m really happy that I won the match.” Bartunkova, 20, next faces Austria’s Sinja Kraus in the round of 16.Second-seeded Sabalenka squandered five chances to break serve in the sixth game of the first set, with Bartunkova strong on defence and firing deep.The 28-year-old from Belarus put on a cap for the eighth game of the first set as the women switched between playing in the shade and the sun, but it did not turn the tide in her favour.View image in fullscreenAryna Sabalenka leaves the court after losing in straight sets to Nikola Bartunkova at the China Open.Photograph: Maxim Shemetov/ReutersA frustrated Sabalenka tossed her racket at a break down in the fourth game of the second set, and lost on the first match point when she returned into the net. Top seed Elena Rybakina – who replaced Sabalenka as world No 1 – was ousted by Alina Charaeva in the second round on Saturday. On Sunday she withdrew from the Wuhan Open with a foot injury she said had hampered her against the world No 118.Explore more on these topicsTennisNovak DjokovicAlexander ZverevAryna SabalenkanewsShareReuse this content

title: Let’s stop doubting Thomas Tuchel: England are impressive and Euro 2028 is the target | England | The Guardian
description: Coming third in the World Cup was really not a disaster, and Saturday’s rout of Croatia and building the team around Jude Bellingham are good signs
Author: Barney Ronay
Headline: Coming third in the World Cup was really not a disaster, and Saturday’s rout of Croatia and building the team around Jude Bellingham are good signs
Content: Thomas Tuchel celebrates after England’s 7-0 Nations League win over Croatia in Rijeka on Saturday.Photograph: Paul Childs/Action Images/ReutersView image in fullscreenThomas Tuchel celebrates after England’s 7-0 Nations League win over Croatia in Rijeka on Saturday.Photograph: Paul Childs/Action Images/ReutersEnglandLet’s stop doubting Thomas Tuchel: England are impressive and Euro 2028 is the targetBarney Ronayin RijekaComing third in the World Cup was really not a disaster, and Saturday’s rout of Croatia and building the team around Jude Bellingham are good signsSun 4 Oct 2026 17.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 21.30 EDTShareMove fast and fix things. It has been a fine week so far forThomas Tuchelas he attempts the cyclical task of soldering together not just an England team, but a way of looking like one, all the while being battered by the to-and-fro conflicting winds of England managerdom.There is nothing new here. This is a job that involves not just picking the right players and making high-stakes calculations over your second-half substitutions, but carrying out these basic duties while wrestling with aggrieved members of the Thuggee cult on a collapsing rope bridge outside the Temple of Doom, and simultaneously having your heart ripped out.No other nation makes quite the same twin-track demands. Manage the games. Yeah, do that obviously. But also tell us who we are and how we should play. This is why the job will always take its pound of mince meat, why these people end up drained and hollowed out, an empty tracksuit resigning in the Wembley toilets, Roy Hodgson in Nice looking like a desiccated vampire, saying “I don’t know why I’m here”.Bellingham stands out for high-grade England but Uefa sends out wrong message on racism | Barney RonayRead moreIt is also why it was heartening in Rijeka to see Tuchel gripped with the familiar energies, still whirling about on the touchline in penitent black shoes and black trousers, looking as ever like a famine-ridden earl out taking the hounds for a walk, while simultaneously cracking the Enigma code in his hunting shed.It feels absurd to say that Tuchel is now safe in the job, if only because the idea he wouldn’t be is so hysterical. Tuchel was never realistically in any trouble. But such is the nature of a role where you’re only ever a few rapid-fire defeats away from the incredible twin feat of a greatest-ever overseas World Cup and a near-instant heaving from the job.We should of course keep a sense of scale over a couple of Nations League wins against underpowered opponents. The7-0 steamrollering of Croatiawas always a strange affair. From the moment the doors opened the whole occasion felt like a youth club association sports day, where everyone gets a medal at the end and the teachers do a disco dance routine.It was an atmosphere that seemed to communicate itself to theCroatiaplayers even as they were warming up in a notably fun and jokey way, cheered by shrill groups of junior ultras, and blasted by the Croatian version of We Didn’t Start the Fire through the ear-shredding speaker system.Croatia played from the first minute like a team recovering from a dose of herbal sleeping tablets. Luka Modric’s every touch was met with the kind of noise more usually associated with an appearance by a Korean boyband at an Apple Store launch event, but one of the great players of the age was simply run over by England’s youthful and hungry midfield.View image in fullscreenJude Bellingham was superb in the win over Croatia, as he was during the World Cup.Photograph: Igor Soban/Pixsell/MB Media/Getty ImagesThese are also the teams you play, however. Croatia were decent enough at the World Cup. Mainly, though this came at an absolutely vital moment in the age of Tuchelism. The next 20 months are basically it, the engine room, the space where Tuchel gets to decide how good his team can be, leading in to a tournament England will never have a better chance of winning.The only questions that really matter right now are: is there vision of a team and a way to play? And do we have forward progress? The answers to both of which are yes.England were good in an interesting way in Croatia. We’re used to England teams that seem powerful but also flawed. In Rijeka they looked likea World Cup semi-finalistthat has used that experience to improve, strong in every area, physically, technically and in its basic balance.At times in the current era England have brought to mind the Gareth Southgate team of 2019 into 2020, when some key new players entered a blooming environment, and suddenly they were blowing away mid-range opponents. The Covid break would complicate that arc. An unprovable counter-factual: nudge those first Southgate Euros forward a year and England might have had themomentum to overpower Italyin the final.There are two aspects to Tuchel’s England this time around. First, the reckoning up with the mistakes of the recent past. Why, oh why didn’t he take Cole Palmer? Well, maybe for the same reason Palmer’s not here now. Well, why of why, then, didn’t he take Phil Foden? This has also answered itself. The same goes for not selecting the back-up striker who is now, it turns out, playing in Saudi Arabia. It is entirely legitimate to still disagree with all these things. But it feels clearer that there was logic and reasoning here.The past can re-litigate itself. The second key element is the sense of progress. This was always likely to be the case. It takes time to get to know your players. Tuchel had never been to an international tournament before. He was never the knockout specialist some seemed to assume. Just take a look at his record. He’s a process guy. And we are now right in the middle of that process.View image in fullscreenLewis Hall has enjoyed a fine international break and looks to be first choice for England at left-back.Photograph: Darko Bandić/APSo what has changed? Most obviously makingJude Bellinghamthe hub of this team is an excellent idea, and not just because of his astonishing talent. Rallying around Bellingham is Tuchel’s version of Southgate’s inflatable unicorns, the talk about Spitfires, the away-days with the SAS crawling through an assault course made entirely from Cheddar cheese and Eccles cakes.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHow do you make players want to play for England? Here’s a short cut. Give them aura, brand power, magnetism. Put the big guy right at the centre. Everyone’s turning up if Jude is loving it, and you have a chance for two weeks to exist in his forcefield.Then there’s the way England have played. There is always talk about “a Premier League style”, which has never been a single thing. But these players are definitely best suited to high-intensity, hard-running, duel-winning football. This wasn’t only there in successfully outmuscling an ageing Mateo Kovacic, who even in his pomp had the air of a frail Victorian child masquerading as an elite modern midfielder, shorts hiked up, skinny legs gamely covering the turf.England also played like this for half an hour against the world champions, andnarrowly lost a gamewhere they went 1-0 down after a minute and missed a late penalty. This felt like an evolved version of the “packet-ball” intensity that blew Croatia away at the World Cup for 20 minutes then could never quite click into gear again. The next Euros are in England. Cancel the heatwave, and they can play like this for longer.Then there is the issue of balance. Lewis Hall: yes, a proper left-back with a left foot. Jarell Quansah makes lots of sense now, offering something of the Kyle Walker-style recovery athleticism. Alex Scott looked really good in Rijeka, a genuinely smart, head-up, surging midfield presence.Tuchel is right. He can’t roll into a tournament with two first-choice midfielders. Scott offered something different in the exact area England lose these high-stakes, high-intensity games. He even knows who his back-up centre-forward is now, and it is of course Jude. Ask any question right now. The answer is likely to be the same.Lamine Yamal stars again as Spain see off Czechia and maintain perfect startRead moreHere is another unprovable counter-factual. England would have beaten that Argentina team in Atlanta with this team in Rijeka. This should not be a source of why-oh-why frustration. It’s forward momentum, learning new patterns, adding new tricks. Stick Bellingham up front in the second half, pack Scott into a three-man midfield, and they’ve got a far better chance of seeing that game out.The process is also far from done. England need competition on the right wing. Bukayo Saka is an excellent footballer. But he’s not a weapon other teams will fear. Add an England-issue Michael Olise, for example, and this team looks entirely different in its threat levels. Max Dowman is still just a very nice idea at this point. But there’s time. And he doesn’t need to be perfect.Finally, and back to the key figure in this cycle, there is the total weaponising of Bellingham, whose role in the team is now beautifully clarified. Station him in forward areas and he will still press and harry and add a defensive function. But turning, running, breaking in transitions, making risky creative passes, he is just a supreme footballer. Not to mention a one-man mission statement of the way this team wants to play.Tournaments aren’t won with a 7-0 win on the Adriatic coast in front of 6,000 over-caffeinated schoolchildren. But there is progress here. And that time will pass in a wink.Explore more on these topicsEnglandCroatiaNations LeagueThomas TuchelJude BellinghamcommentShareReuse this content

title: Cavan Sullivan’s stunner makes him youngest-ever USMNT scorer in romp over Mexico | USA | The Guardian
description: Sullivan became the youngest-ever goalscorer in USMNT history, while Julian Hall and Malik Tillman added to a signature result
Author: Jeff Rueter
Headline: Sullivan became the youngest-ever goalscorer in USMNT history, while Julian Hall and Malik Tillman added to a signature result
Content: Cavan Sullivan scored with an audacious and fortuitous chip in the second half.Photograph: Vanessa Luna/ISI Photos/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenCavan Sullivan scored with an audacious and fortuitous chip in the second half.Photograph: Vanessa Luna/ISI Photos/Getty ImagesUSACavan Sullivan’s stunner makes him youngest-ever USMNT scorer in romp over Mexico17-year-old scores brilliant long-range chipJulian Hall and Mailk Tillman also grab goalsUS have scored 11 goals in last three gamesAs it happened: USA 3-0 MexicoJeff Rueterat State Farm StadiumSun 4 Oct 2026 00.35 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 16.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe first time the United States andMexicoplayed at this building, Jimmy Conrad and Landon Donovan provided the goals in one of several 2-0 wins for the US. On Saturday, the US squad included eight players who hadn’t yet been born when that happened.This young US team went one better than their forebears, though, silencing a sizable pro-Mexico contingent ina composed 3-0 triumphthat fully announced the arrival of an exciting new generation of players. Cavan Sullivan, just a few days after turning 17, became the youngest goalscorer in the history of the program with an eye-catching long-range chip. Julian Hall, 18, scored his third goal in as many games. Malik Tillman capped the scoring in the 85th minute, humbling a 10-man Mexico after they’d opened the match with far more strength.The US haven’t played an away game since 2024, but Saturday may be as close as they’ve gotten with the heavily pro-Mexico crowd. The tailgates cooked up far more fajitas than frankfurters, and the red seats of State Farm Stadium were filled by a hearty influx of green jerseys as the anthems commenced for Tyler Adams’s first shift as Mauricio Pochettino’s captain.The disparity of support was a fitting embodiment of the match’s early balance. Mexico came out of the gates with intent, while the hosts struggled to get the ball off their feet. Despite fielding a backline that could credibly be considered the first-choice options to start the cycle, all four US defenders struggled to pass through Mexico’s aggressive man-marking scheme.After five minutes of Mexico maintaining a steady attack, the US adjusted. Leaning into Diego Kochen’s experience playing out from the back, the hosts opted for short restarts with Auston Trusty prodding goal kicks to his young keeper. The conservative approach took the sting out of El Tri’s attack, but hardly helped activate their own. After 15 minutes, Mexico had managed to take 38 touches in the opposing half, to the US’s five.By the 28th minute, as the hosts worked to keep Mexico off the ball, the crowd at State Farm Stadium had been lulled into quiet observation.Then, the US struck.Sebastian Berhalter lobbed a ball to the right flank to Alex Freeman, who drew Mexico’s focus as he headed toward the corner. He feigned a retreat before deftly rolling a through-ball between two opponents, with Gio Reyna collecting the ball in-stride inside the box. Reyna tried to center the ball in search of a target, leaving Raúl Rangel to flub his attempt to claim the low cross, shanking the ball directly to a lurking Hall. The New York striker made no mistake with his connection, slotting his first-time attempt across goal and far from Rangel.The 18-year-old turned to the crowd and cupped his ears in front of the American Outlaws, cheekily acknowledging the silenced Mexican support. Hall had his third US goal in as many caps to bolster his case for a regular place in the squad.Mexico strove to regain control of the match, fouling Tillman whenever he tried advancing upfield. Playing without the dynamic midfield duo of Gilberto Mora and Hirving Lozano, Mexico struggled to turn ample possession into genuine quality, with just four shots taken after 40 minutes and none landing on frame. The sea of green shirts began to ripple, with waves of Mexico fans beating the lines for concessions and restrooms with five minutes left in the half.Their impatience kept them from witnessing Mexico’s best chance of the half. A speculative effort by Luís Romo to the far post forced Kochen into a clumsy diving save. Much like the sequence leading to Hall’s opener, his spill fell right to Santiago Giménez, giving Mexico a golden chance to equalize from inside six yards. Instead, the Porto loanee shanked his effort well wide of goal, sparing US blushes just before half-time.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice weeklySign up toSoccer DeskJonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAllow content provided by a third party?This article includes content hosted onembed.bsky.app. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as the provider may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content,click 'Allow and continue'.Allow and continueThe hosts weren’t shy once play resumed, spraying the ball to Sullivan down the right flank and up the channel to Tillman or Reyna. Mexico finally put a shot on goal in the 58th minute, with Roberto Alvarado attempting a half-volley on a redirected corner kick. Kochen parried it over the bar with youthful ease, keeping his side in control with half an hour remaining.Both teams saw their intensity wane a bit as the half progressed, leading to some carelessness in possession. Just after the hour mark, Rangel collected a back pass from Érik Lira and took his time finding his next target for distribution while positioned far upfield. His undercooked pass to Diego Campillo instead found Sullivan, the leader of the US’s makeshift press and as instinctive a player as anybody in the US pool.Players with rare spatial awareness like Sullivan’s tend to manifest moments like these more often than most. Rather than look to retain possession, as his team had so often after turnovers, Sullivan snared the ball then used his preferred left foot to chip Rangel, curling his effort underneath the crossbar. Sullivan was beyond jubilant, clattering into the corner flag as his teammates converged before patting the US crest over his heart.Sullivan’s first international goal was always bound to be a staple of his and the team’s highlight reels, an occasion years in the making as the nation’s latest wunderkind. The quality of his solo effort warrants ample replays on its own merit, making his nation’s great rival aware of his threat from his very first shift.Something of a Mexican meltdown ensued as they struggled to return to their former state of control. Substitutes collided in the 67th minute, with Yunus Musah’s attempt to dribble upfield being thwarted by a Mateo Chavez kick. The foul brought both teams together in a confrontation, and Chavez was sent off.For years, El Tri fans have soundtracked opponents’ goal kicks bychanting a homophobic slur. After considerable mistakes on both goals, the supporters instead bellowed the bigoted cry on Rangel’s restarts, with the stadium operators declining to follow through on their pre-match threats to stop the game if the chant emerged. The fans also took to booing Rangel’s every touch, taking one item off a hosting fanbase’s usual list of responsibilities.Perhaps inevitably, Rangel struggled. Another poor backpass, this time from Álvaro Fidalgo, rolled right into the box with Rangel staying near his goalline in hopes a center-back would collect. Instead, Tillman strode on to the loose ball and placed it into the upper corner, turning what once looked like a comfortable day for Mexico into downright humiliation.In the lead-up to the game, Adams spoke about how the winner of this matchup tends to be seen as the region’s current power. On Saturday, the US took that power because it was given, and taken advantage of.Explore more on these topicsUSAMexicoUS sportsmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Denmark sink Wales as Rasmus Højlund makes Danny Ward pay for blunder | Nations League | The Guardian
description: A Rasmus Højlund penalty in the second half after a Danny Ward error handed Denmark a 1-0 win in Wales in the Nations League
Author: Ben Fisher
Headline: A Rasmus Højlund penalty in the second half after a Danny Ward error handed Denmark a 1-0 win in Wales in the Nations League
Content: Danny Ward brings down Gustav Isaksen to concede the decisive penalty.Photograph: John Sibley/Action Images/ReutersView image in fullscreenDanny Ward brings down Gustav Isaksen to concede the decisive penalty.Photograph: John Sibley/Action Images/ReutersNations LeagueDenmark sink Wales as Rasmus Højlund makes Danny Ward pay for blunderBen Fisherat the Cardiff City StadiumSun 4 Oct 2026 16.52 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWales crave momentum but, a few days after surely the sweetest high of Craig Bellamy’s two-year reign, a sapping international window ended on a bum note. At least until Bellamy was informedPortugal’s comeback victory over Norwaymeans Wales will spend the next six weeks in third, and not bottom of Nations League A4 owing to their superior head-to-record. “That’s actually quite nice,” the Wales head coach said, slowly digesting the silver lining about half an hour after the final whistle. “That’s brightened up a real rubbish moment.”Bellamy suggested lastThursday’s victory over Norwayblew the group wide open with a hand grenade but Danny Ward detonated one to give Denmark a second-half penalty and Rasmus Højlund’s flawless spot-kick ultimately proved the difference. The galling thing for Ward was that until his moment of madness, he had kept his country in the game, his best stop a sublime right-hand save to deny Gustav Isaksen. A first clean sheet since beating Liechtenstein last November also went out of the window for Wales. The life of a goalkeeper, eh?Wales v Denmark, Republic of Ireland v Israel and more: Nations League – liveRead moreThe difficulty forWaleswas always going to be trying to replicate the all-action performance from their triumph over Norway, the obvious caveat that their opponents played almost all of the second half with 10 men. The emotions felt after that game were always going to be hard to match but despite the awkward 7.45pm kick-off on a Sunday night, the Barry Horns, the brass brand who enthusiastically soundtrack Wales matches, made a racket and contributed to a fine atmosphere. Even without a full house, the anthem was stirring if not spine-tingling.Bellamy said it was impossible to keep the same XI owing to the toll of four matches across 11 days but in the end Daniel James was the only player to make way, Brennan Johnson taking his place on the wing. Ben Davies, whose only minutes for Tottenham came against a Charlton Athletic B team in the Carabao Cup, started a fourth successive game this window, together with Neco Williams and Ethan Ampadu, whose Leeds team visit Arsenal in Saturday’s early kick-off when the Premier League resumes. Ward also made it four in a row and in doing so has played four times as many games for his country as he has this season for his club, Wrexham.It is a familiar problem for Wales and Bellamy, who is hopeful Joe Rodon will return from a hamstring injury in time for next month’s trip to Oslo and home date with Portugal. “We started well and then as the game unfolded, the intensity started to drop for us,” said the 47-year-old. “We couldn’t sustain the intensity, we couldn’t get the energy up enough to be able to have a bigger say in the game. I felt it in the first half: we’re not moving enough now. We tried to make one or two substitutions to freshen it up. We shouldn’t really have played Ben – I’m just hoping he’s not injured but he’s a warrior. We don’t have enough players playing week in, week out, certainly not at the top level. When you don’t do this week in, week out, it’s a shock to the system. It was a touch of reality.”View image in fullscreenRasmus Højlund celebrates his second-half winner for Denmark.Photograph: Ulrik Pedersen/NurPhoto/ShutterstockWard’s first real save, to deny Højlund at the start of the second half, was smart but his second was phenomenal. Joakim Mæhle raced down the left and before reaching the byline flung into the box a feathery, hanging cross. Isaksen, of Lazio, tracked the ball all the way and cleverly adjusted his body position to pick his spot, the target the bottom right-hand corner of Ward’s goal. Isaksen appeared to have executed the perfect header but Ward got a brilliant right hand to the ball and pushed it on to his right post. At that point, Ward was Wales’s hero.But then, out of nothing, Ward conceded a clumsy penalty. Ben Cabango shifted the ball to his goalkeeper, from right to left, but Ward, looking to move the ball on again, inadvertently shovelled a miskicked pass straight to Isaksen. A panicked Ward tried to make amends but his desperation got the better of him and he clattered into Isaksen and the damage was done. Højlund waited for Ward to dive to his left and slotted the ball into the opposite corner.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSorba Thomas threatened on the left flank, intermittently destroying theDenmarkright-back Rasmus Kristensen and Liam Cullen, now of Leicester, was industrious as a playmaker. But Wales failed to test Mads Hermansen, a former Leicester clubmate of Ward’s. It was almost as if this was the fourth game in a marathon camp. “Physically, it makes no sense,” Bellamy said. “We know it’s a complete disadvantage to us … I think, really, it is designed for the elite.”Explore more on these topicsNations LeagueWalesDenmarkmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Nations League roundup: Haaland limps off in Norway’s loss to Portugal | Nations League | The Guardian
description: Erling Haaland limped off in Norway’s 2-1 defeat by Portugal in the Nations League as the holders sealed their place in the quarter-finals
Author: Guardian sport
Headline: Erling Haaland limped off in Norway’s 2-1 defeat by Portugal in the Nations League as the holders sealed their place in the quarter-finals
Content: Erling Haaland may have added to Manchester City’s problems.Photograph: Luis Vieira/APView image in fullscreenErling Haaland may have added to Manchester City’s problems.Photograph: Luis Vieira/APNations LeagueNations League roundup: Haaland limps off in Norway’s loss to PortugalPortugal victory seals place in quarter-finalsGreece hold Germany to goalless drawAgencies andGuardian sportSun 4 Oct 2026 17.42 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 18.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTitle-holdersPortugalmaintained their 100% record in the Nations League with a 2-1 home win overNorwayon Sunday to seal a place in ⁠the March quarter-finals, while Manchester City’s problems may have got worse afterErling Haalandlimped off for the visitors.Portugal hope their victory at the Estádio Do Dragão shifts the focus further away from Cristiano Ronaldo’s abrupt exit from the squad last week. Gonçalo Ramos netted 11 minutes from time to ensure they secured a top-two ⁠finish in Group A4 as ⁠they moved six points ​ahead of second-placed Denmark,who won 1-0 at Wales.The home side in Porto were still under a cloud from Ronaldo’s dispute with coach Jorge Jesus, although they were triumphant without himin Denmark ⁠last Thursdayafter he walked out on the squad, and continued their winning ways on Sunday.Denmark sink Wales as Rasmus Højlund makes Danny Ward pay for blunderRead moreNorway took the lead in ​the 36th minute from centre-back Kristoffer Ajer, who hit a ‌dipping half-volley from the edge of ‌the box. But if that effort was sumptuous, João Cancelo’s thrashing effort to equalise two minutes later was even more awe-inspiring.Ramos’s ‌winner came off his calf after João Félix had headed across goal for him to score.Portugal’s win was soured by a red card for Francisco Conceição four minutes from time. He gave the referee a cynical thumbs up after receiving a yellow card and was immediately shown a second.Afterwards, Jesus said Ronaldo can return to the squad if he wishes: “If he wants to, he’ll return to the national team … we can talk before the next call-up, but Cris is the one who’s going to decide.”View image in fullscreenGonçalo Ramos knocks down the corner flag in delight after scoring.Photograph: SPP/ShutterstockThe Netherlandstook over at the top of Group A2, after beatingSerbia2-1 in Eindhoven, but only on goal difference from ⁠Greece, who held on grimly for a goalless draw at home toGermanyin Thessaloniki.With their captain Virgil van Dijk celebrating a 100th cap, the Netherlands went ahead againstSerbiawhen Teun Koopmeiners’s 31st-minute free-kick evaded all in the penalty area and ​crept into the corner. However, the visitors were level within four minutes as Aleksa Terzic crossed for teenager Mihajlo Cvetkovic to rise over Koopmeiners and head in his first international goal.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIt took until the 72nd minute to go back ahead when Denzel Dumfries’s low cross was turned back across the goal by Tijjani Reijnders, sliding in at the far post, and tapped in by Joshua Zirkzee, who ⁠received a late call-up to the Dutch squad last week.Germany dominated away against Greece, but Jürgen ​Klopp’s inexperienced side could not find the net, ​and they have won only one of ​their first four games under the new coach.Austrianeeded a late equaliser to draw 1-1 atKosovo​but still have a three-point ‌lead at the top ​of Group B3 after the ​Republic of Ireland and Israeldrew 1-1 behind closed doorsin the Serbian town of Backa Topola.In Group D2, Abdulakh Khaybulayev’s first-half goal was enough to sendAzerbaijantop of the standings with a 1-0 win over previously unbeatenLithuania, while veteran Teddy Teuma came on as a second-half substitute to handMaltaa 1-0 home win overAndorrain Group D1.Explore more on these topicsNations LeaguePortugalNorwayErling HaalandNetherlandsSerbiaGermanynewsShareReuse this content

title: Shaw seals thrilling win over Arsenal to extend Manchester City’s 100% WSL start | Women's Super League | The Guardian
description: Manchester City came from behind twice to win a six-goal thriller against Arsenal and continue their 100% start to the WSL season
Author: Tom Garry
Headline: Manchester City came from behind twice to win a six-goal thriller against Arsenal and continue their 100% start to the WSL season
Content: Manchester City's Bunny Shaw scores the fourth goal to seal victory over Arsenal and top spot in the WSL.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PAView image in fullscreenManchester City's Bunny Shaw scores the fourth goal to seal victory over Arsenal and top spot in the WSL.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PAWomen's Super LeagueShaw seals thrilling win over Arsenal to extend Manchester City’s 100% WSL startTom Garryat the Etihad StadiumSun 4 Oct 2026 14.07 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleArsenal’s under-pressure head coach Renée Slegers still believes they will turn their form around, despite falling 10 points behind Manchester City with Sunday’s defeat in an absorbing six-goal thriller against the defending champions.Arsenal were last season’s runners-up in the Women’s Super League and had high hopes of mounting a strong challenge this term but their chances of lifting a first WSL title since 2019 now appear to be hanging by a thread after five rounds of fixtures, while City maintained their 100% start by coming from behind twice to beat Slegers’ struggling side.Manchester City 4-2 Arsenal: Women’s Super League – liveRead moreThe 37-year-old Dutchwoman, who in January signed a new contract until the summer of 2029, said on Friday that she felt the full support of the club. Asked, after this pivotal 4-2 defeat, whether she would be the one in charge after this month’s international break, she replied: “All I know so far is that the last couple of days we’ve been together as a club, as a team, with support, aligning on the direction. Of course, this result is disappointing, but I’m here, I’m full of energy and I care a lot for the club.”Slegers added she feels the international break will come at a good time to change environments and that there will be a “big review of our season so far” during the break. She continued: “We see solutions and we see the closeness. It’s not that we’re totally off it. It’s been consistently about margins – when we get them on our side, I think we’re going to be really good.”The match was the first to be played at the Etihad Stadium since the Premier League published the guilty verdict against Manchester City and there was something of a subdued atmosphere outside the stadium in the buildup to kick-off. That quickly changed once the game started, and was wholly different in the second half as the hosts began to take control and their supporters were thoroughly enjoying themselves.City had frequently insisted their women’s team were treating this as “business as usual”before their draw with Real Madridon Thursday. There were very few references to the ongoing saga here on Sunday, aside from some Arsenal fans chanting “same old City, always cheating” during the first half, and one City fan – sitting just in front of the media seats – who defiantly shouted about which part of the anatomy people could “stick your 115 charges”, but nobody else joined in. Matters on the pitch were more interesting.City will have felt aggrieved about the nature of Arsenal’s opener, as replays showed that Lisa Baum appeared to be offside when Lotte Wubben-Moy headed goalwards. Baum was the quickest to get to the rebound after Ayaka Yamashita’s save and poked home. The visitors could not hold on until the break, however, as Lauren Hemp’s deflected strike found its way into the far corner.Arsenal went back in front shortly after half-time when Yui Hasegawa lost the ball inside her own area and Alessia Russo pounced, curling a terrific finish into the far corner. It was her first league goal of the campaign. Arsenal appeared to be in control until a triple substitution from Andrée Jeglertz, including the introduction of Kerstin Casparij, changed things.View image in fullscreenAlessia Russo pounces to make it 2-1 to Arsenal at Manchester City.Photograph: Ed Sykes/Action Images/ReutersThe 26-year-old, playing as an inverted full-back, latched on to a loose ball and curled in a delightful strike to equalise and soon afterwards Hemp tucked a tidy finish through Anneke Borbe’s legs to make it 3-2. Suddenly Arsenal’s body language changed and City were on top. They added a clinical fourth when Shaw latched on to Aoba Fujino’s excellent through-ball and her low finish was superb.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMoving the GoalpostsNo topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionJeglertz was full of praise for Casparij and his centre-back pairing of Jade Rose and Alex Greenwood. Asked about Arsenal’s woes, he said he still expects them to have a strong campaign, saying: “They have great football players - I’m pretty sure that when we are coming into spring that they will definitely be one of the teams battling.”Arsenal’s problems were exacerbated by their midfielder Mariona Caldentey going off with a suspected hamstring injury. The Arsenal defender Wubben-Moy said there was unity as she told Sky Sports the players “fought for ourselves, for Renée and for the fans - but ultimately the result didn’t do that justice”, adding: “This is an unprecedented position for Arsenal to be in. It’s up to us to get ourselves out of it.”Her words may offer some solace to Slegers. So will the sight of the 2,000 travelling fans applauding her after the game. The upcoming “review” will determine whether or not that was a farewell.Explore more on these topicsWomen's Super LeagueManchester City WomenArsenal WomenWomen's footballmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Clàudia Pina hits four as Barcelona score seven goals to demolish Real Madrid | European club football | The Guardian
description: Clàudia Pina scored four times as Barcelona thrashed Real Madrid 7-0 in the women’s Clásico
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Clàudia Pina scored four times as Barcelona thrashed Real Madrid 7-0 in the women’s Clásico
Content: Clàudia Pina scores her fourth goal of the evening.Photograph: Alberto Estévez/EPAView image in fullscreenClàudia Pina scores her fourth goal of the evening.Photograph: Alberto Estévez/EPAEuropean club footballClàudia Pina hits four as Barcelona score seven goals to demolish Real MadridBarcelona 7-0 Real MadridLead at the top stretched to five pointsAgence France PresseSun 4 Oct 2026 18.28 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 18.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleClàudia Pina smashed in four goals as Barcelona demolished Real Madrid 7-0 to earn a five point lead at the top of Liga F on Sunday over their rivals.The 25-year-old Spain international was in lethal form in front of goal as a dominant Barça won the Clásico battle with ease at the Camp Nou in front of over 40,000 fans, continuing their perfect start to the campaign. The match was pushed back by two hours after torrential rain in the Catalonia region over the weekend.Moving the Goalposts | Women’s Ballon d’Or 2026 power rankings: will a new winner be crowned?Read morePina put Barcelona, who have won the league seven seasons running, in the driving seat after just four minutes with a neat finish after breezing into the area.The Catalan side controlled the ball and Madrid found it hard to pry it away from them, although managed to fend them off until Pina’s second in the 28th minute, the first of three goals in around five minutes.Ewa Pajor’s shot was blocked and Pina polished off the rebound, completing her hat-trick a few minutes later by blasting into the top corner.European champions Barça immediately struck again through Caroline Graham Hansen, who skipped past a defender before slotting home.Pina scored her fourth with a blast inside the near post before the interval as Barca yet again pulled apart Madrid’s defence. The fifth came early in the second half for Pere Romeu’s side, through Polish striker Pajor.Three-time Ballon d’Or winner Aitana Bonmatí came on for the final 30 minutes as she continues her return to full fitness following a broken leg.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMoving the GoalpostsNo topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSwiss midfielder Sydney Schertenleib scored a stunning seventh from long range to round off Barça’s rout late on.Real Madrid have beaten Barca just once in 25 meetings between the sides across all competitions. Madrid’s women’s team began in 2020 after taking over CD Tacon.Explore more on these topicsEuropean club footballBarcelona WomenReal Madrid WomenWomen's footballnewsShareReuse this content

title: Alexander’s absence weighs heavy as Bradford try to keep promotion push on track | League One | The Guardian
description: The Bantams faced Reading after manager left for Preston and ‘were a little unsettled’, according to caretaker Mark Trueman
Author: Sam Cunningham
Headline: The Bantams faced Reading after manager left for Preston and ‘were a little unsettled’, according to caretaker Mark Trueman
Content: Bradford had to deal with life after Graham Alexander in their draw at Reading.Photograph: Steve Bailey/ProSports/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenBradford had to deal with life after Graham Alexander in their draw at Reading.Photograph: Steve Bailey/ProSports/ShutterstockLeague OneAlexander’s absence weighs heavy as Bradford try to keep promotion push on trackThe Bantams faced Reading after manager left for Preston and ‘were a little unsettled’, according to caretaker Mark TruemanSam Cunninghamat the Select Car Leasing StadiumSun 4 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt was a bruising start to the week for Bradford City when news filtered through to the players that Graham Alexander had stepped down as manager. They were top ofLeague Oneand his departure was a sudden and unexpected blow for a side that had started to let imaginations run wild about a return to the second tier for the first time in 23 years.The coaches Mark Trueman and Colin Doyle took interim charge and called a meeting with the squad last Monday. “Some of the players were a little unsettled, didn’t know what was going on or who was taking the team,” Trueman said. “But the players have just got on with business and that’s the key. It shows the mentality of the team. This could quite easily derail them, but they’ve continued to do the right things.”Robbie Savage steps up to take Peterborough job: ‘All I want is a chance’Read moreIf any caretaker can keepBradfordon track, it is Trueman, who has now stepped in temporarily five times since joining the club as an Under-18 coach six years ago. This time, though, is different. Previously, his job was to raise the team during low periods. Now the task is to maintain the upward trajectory that began the moment Alexander arrived in 2023.Bradford were stuck in the bottom tier of the EFL and sitting in 16th when Alexander took over. They finished ninth in his first season, then third in his second to earn automatic promotion, followed by a stunning fourth-place finish back in League One, losing in the playoff semi-finals last May.It has been a thrilling ride rarely enjoyed by Bradford fans. They twice reached the EFL Trophy semi-finals in successive seasons. At one stage, they won 10 consecutive home games, breaking a club record set in 1953.Last year they had the best home record of any side in Europe’s top five leagues. Alexander won 79 times in 158 games – the best win rate of any Bradford manager in charge for at least 65 games.The chief executive, Ryan Sparks, said Alexander and the assistant manager Chris Lucketti, who has followed him to Preston, delivered “some of the most incredible moments in our recent history”.They looked set to deliver more, with Bradford top of League One when the Preston opportunity came out of the blue. Alexander told the club he had ambitions to manage in the Championship, but you wonder if he might have achieved that with Bradford had he stayed. Perhaps he believed that two promotions in two years would risk them becoming relegation fodder in the Championship, whereas Preston presents a more stable platform. Ultimately, the lure of a club that he once captained – playing 400 games during an eight-year spell from 1999 to 2007 – d in the city where his children were raised proved too strong.View image in fullscreenGraham Alexander’s sudden departure has left Bradford to rebuild early on in the season.Photograph: Paul Thompson/ProSports/ShutterstockOn forums and social media, fans shared a mixture of sadness, anger and anxiety. Most believe Alexander has left the club stronger, but frustration is shared among a sizeable minority about the timing – less than two months into a season after a summer spent recruiting specifically for his aggressive, direct, high-pressing football. After Jake Beesley headed Bradford into a fourth-minute lead atReadingon Saturday, the 1,118 supporters who made the 400-mile round trip sang about being top of the league, but did not chant for their departed manager once.Rapid developments in the space of a few weeks leave a huge hole. Bradford now find themselves in unfamiliar territory: it is the first time in 43 years they have lost a manager mid-season, and fans are nervous about the executives’ aptitude for finding a suitable replacement, given the shaky record before landing Alexander.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn the opposition dugout at Reading’s Select Car Leasing Stadium stood one of the favourites to take over. Before the match, Leam Richardson faced questions about whether he was interested. His response – that he would be in the Reading dugout for the match – neatly sidestepped the prospect that he might not be beyond this weekend, though he insisted he had not been contacted. Meanwhile Michael Duff, sacked by Wycombe last month, is also being heavily linked.Nonetheless, Sparks and the head of football, David Sharpe, would have been watching closely from the directors’ box to see whether Reading showed signs of a style of football that would fit the framework Alexander built. Plenty makes Richardson a logical candidate. He previously worked with Sharpe, who was chair at Wigan when Richardson was manager, and he has also coached Callum Connolly, in the Bradford starting XI, and Nick Powell, who came on from the bench.Others are in the frame, including the Plymouth manager Tom Cleverley, the former Manchester United midfielder – a Premier League winner in 2013 – who at 37 has quietly built his managerial reputation these past two years. Udoka Godwin-Malife’s second-half equaliser meant Plymouth moved above Bradford on goal difference. The next appointment is crucial. Getting Alexander so right makes getting it wrong so much more costly.Explore more on these topicsLeague OneBradfordReadingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Australia’s Marnus Labuschagne set for South Africa Test after first ton in 11 months | Australia cricket team | The Guardian
description: Stalwart Marnus Labuschagne has showed his readiness for Australia’s first Test in South Africa with a warm-up century in Potchefstroom
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Stalwart Marnus Labuschagne has showed his readiness for Australia’s first Test in South Africa with a warm-up century in Potchefstroom
Content: Marnus Labuschagne scored a century to put him in the frame to retain his No 3 position for the Test series in South Africa.Photograph: James Ross/AAP/APView image in fullscreenMarnus Labuschagne scored a century to put him in the frame to retain his No 3 position for the Test series in South Africa.Photograph: James Ross/AAP/APAustralia cricket teamAustralia’s Marnus Labuschagne set for South Africa Test after first ton in 11 monthsBatter makes 111 against Cricket South Africa Invitation XIThree-match Test series starts in Durban on FridayAustralian Associated PressSun 4 Oct 2026 18.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe indefatigable Marnus Labuschagne has responded to all the hand-wringing over whether he merits a place in Australia’s Test future by just doing what he likes doing best – scoring runs.After a difficult year, the under-pressure 32-year-old chose the most timely moment to score his first century in any form of cricket for 11 months in Potchefstroom, just five days before Australia play their first Test in South Africa since the 2018 ball-tampering scandal.Australia deny South Africa series sweep as Carey returns to form in rain-affected third ODIRead moreFormer skipper Ricky Ponting has led the chorus that Labuschagne’s Australia place has become “untenable” after three years and 43 Tests without a Test ton, capped by three failures in the recent Bangladesh series.Yet the South Africa-born batter looks sure to fill the No 3 spot once more in the first Test that starts in Durban on Friday after his swift century against a modestCricketSouth Africa Invitation XI attack on Sunday.Labuschagne was largely untroubled as he raced to a 76-ball ton, going on to 111 from 89, decorated with 19 fours, before retiring to let his colleagues also get in some batting practice on the final day of the two-day warm-up match.They enjoyed the opportunity too, with Steve Smith also retiring after making 61 while Alex Carey, fresh from his fine form in the third ODI, hit another half-century (57) as Pat Cummins’ Australian side rattled up 6-368 in the drawn procession.Smith, who received a 12-month ban when captain for his role in altering the condition of the ball with sandpaper at Cape Town on the infamous tour eight years ago, is back with a group of other survivors from that tour – Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Nathan Lyon and Matt Renshaw, all of whom could play on Friday.Renshaw declared he was good to go after a knock to his right wrist in the final ODI, but he missed out by being dismissed for 32 off his 50 balls, as did fellow opener Travis Head (21 off 22 balls), while Beau Webster brushed off a few cobwebs with his 42 before he retired.All eyes, though, were on Labuschagne, who even had a bit of local support as he took the crease at Senwes Park, a venue less than 50km from where he was born in Klerksdorp and the emotional scene of his first ODI hundred for Australia back in 2020.“Really nice. Looks like he’s got a lot of energy at the crease, it’s the Marn that I know that’s batting well,” enthused Renshaw, who gave himself a clean bill of health for Durban. “Really nice to see him getting the runs and doing what he wants to do. Really nice positivity, his feet were moving well and he was just reacting.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe SpinSubscribe to our cricket newsletter for our writers' thoughts on the biggest stories and a review of the week’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAustralia will see it as a useful outing after they gave 11 bowlers a run-out on the Saturday when the Invitation XI declared on 318-7 after a century from former Proteas’ captain Neil Brand.Meanwhile, South Africa paceman Anrich Nortje is in line for a remarkable return to first-class cricket after an absence of three-and-a-half year to help the injury-hit Proteas’ attack.With fitness doubts over key strike bowler Kagiso Rabada and three others, Nortje could return to Tests for the first time since March 2023 after a series of back and hip problems that left him concentrating on white-ball formats to reduce the strain on his body.“I’ll be very excited if I can put my Test cap on again. Growing up, ⁠it’s the format you want to play,” he said on Sunday, the day before he’s expected to be named in South Africa’s Test squad of 15.Explore more on these topicsAustralia cricket teamCricketAustralia sportnewsShareReuse this content
