title: Evans ends Britain’s wait for world rally title after Solberg crashes two corners from glory | Rallying | The Guardian
description: Welshman Elfyn Evans is the first British winner of the title since Richard Burns in 2001, emerging victorious after Oliver Solberg careered down a bank
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Welshman Elfyn Evans is the first British winner of the title since Richard Burns in 2001, emerging victorious after Oliver Solberg careered down a bank
Content: Elfyn Evans speeds towards a dramatic first World Rally Championship title on Sunday – he had been runner-up five times in the last six years.Photograph: Nikos Katikis/DPPI/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenElfyn Evans speeds towards a dramatic first World Rally Championship title on Sunday – he had been runner-up five times in the last six years.Photograph: Nikos Katikis/DPPI/ShutterstockRallyingEvans ends Britain’s wait for world rally title after Solberg crashes two corners from gloryElfyn Evans becomes first British winner since 2001Oliver Solberg’s hopes shattered by tumble down bankReutersSun 4 Oct 2026 14.14 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 15.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google⁠Elfyn Evans ended years of heartache, and a quarter-of-a-century wait for Britain, by winning the World Rally Championship title with Toyota after a dramatic season ⁠finale in Sardinia on Sunday.The ⁠Welshman had been ​championship runner-up five times in the last six years but emerged triumphant after a final Powerstage duel with teammate Oliver Solberg ended with the charging Swede crashing ⁠out two corners from the finish while on course to take the crown.‘Insane’: F1 drivers unite over engine regulations after chaotic Bahrain GPRead moreSolberg, 25, ran wide and careered down a bank before getting the car back on the road. ⁠He still won the rally but lost the crucial bonus points on offer for the top five in the ​final stage.Evans, with co-driver Scott Martin at his side, ‌became the first British world ‌rally champion since Englishman Richard Burns in 2001 and only the third since Scottish driver Colin McRae became ‌the first in 1995.Sweden’s Solberg, son of Norway’s 2003 champion Petter, ended the season as runner-up. The final standings left Evans on 243 points, Solberg on 238 and Sami Pajari on 237 in what was also the end of an era for the sport with new regulations in force next year.View image in fullscreenOliver Solberg is consoled by his co-driver Eliott Edmondson after his title dreams evaporated.Photograph: Nikos Katikis/DPPI/ShutterstockEvans said: “It hasn’t sunk in. I was sure it was over. I didn’t drive the best ‌stage but threw everything at it but it wasn’t clean. I feel for Oliver. He had an incredible weekend.” The Welshman completed his final run first and had to ​watch and wait to see whether he had done enough to take the title.“I don’t really know what my reaction is, it’s surreal with how it happened. It’s a relief. It wouldn’t be my proudest way of winning it, but it’s job done,” added the 37-year-old, who finished fifth in the gravel rally.Evans had started the rally – the ⁠final round after Saudi Arabia’s finale was cancelled due to conflict in the region – ​17 points clear of Finland’s Pajari, ​also in a Toyota, and 21 clear ​of Solberg.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenElfyn Evans (right) sprays spectators alongside his co-driver Martin Scott after sealing the title.Photograph: Nikos Katikis/DPPI/ShutterstockThe Swede took control of the rally on Saturday, knowing he had nothing ​to lose and all to ‌gain, and started ​the final day 33.6 seconds ​clear of the field and the momentum swinging his way.That feeling was reinforced when Evans lost time changing a wheel on Sunday’s penultimate stage, leaving the championship outcome hanging on the short final stage and the title going to which of the pair finished ahead of the other.Toyota had already won the manufacturers’ championship.Explore more on these topicsRallyingMotor sportnewsShareReuse this content

title: Tuchel says Alex Scott’s emergence gives England – and Rice – ‘high level’ competition | England | The Guardian
description: Thomas Tuchel praised Alex Scott’s all-round display in the 7-0 win in Croatia, saying: ‘We will not survive on two central midfielders. The more the better’
Author: Jacob Steinberg
Headline: Thomas Tuchel praised Alex Scott’s all-round display in the 7-0 win in Croatia, saying: ‘We will not survive on two central midfielders. The more the better’
Content: Alex Scott dominated the Croatia midfield alongside Elliot Anderson.Photograph: Bradley Collyer/PAView image in fullscreenAlex Scott dominated the Croatia midfield alongside Elliot Anderson.Photograph: Bradley Collyer/PAEnglandTuchel says Alex Scott’s emergence gives England – and Rice – ‘high level’ competitionTuchel praises Scott’s all-round display in Croatia win‘We will not survive on two midfielders. More the better’Jacob Steinbergin RijekaSun 4 Oct 2026 14.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThomas Tuchel warned that there is competition for Declan Rice’s place in England’s midfield after Alex Scott marked his first international start with an outstanding displayduring the 7-0 away win against Croatia.Rice, who struggled with neural pain in his upper hamstring during the World Cup, withdrew from the camp because of load management and the vice-captain’s absence at the start of the side’sNations Leaguecampaign has allowed Tuchel to broaden his options alongside Elliot Anderson in midfield.Bellingham stands out for high-grade England but Uefa sends out wrong message on racism | Barney RonayRead moreEngland’s head coach has added youth to the squad and enjoyed the competition between Myles Lewis-Skelly and Scott during the past fortnight. Lewis-Skelly did well after starting the3-2 defeat by Spainand the2-0 win against Czechiabut the Arsenal midfielder was outshone by Scott, who partnered Anderson in Croatia and delivered a performance full of energy, speed and quality on and off the ball.It was Scott’s second cap – he also impressed after coming on against Czechia in Prague – and the 23-year-old’s excellence was one of many positives on an important night for Tuchel. The manager can feel a newEnglandemerging after the pain of their World Cup defeat by Argentina. The squad has been refreshed and it was interesting that Tuchel used a question about Jordan Pickford’s spot as the No 1 goalkeeper last Friday to suggest, unprompted, that Rice does not necessarily have a guaranteed place in the team.The bigger picture is that Rice, who has helped England reach two major finals, remains part of Tuchel’s best XI. However, Tuchel delivered another pointed response when asked if the Arsenal midfielder will feel his place is under threat after seeing Scott’s performance in Rijeka.“Of course, and he does, we need performances like this,” the German said. “This is just the nature of it. We will not survive on two central midfielders. The more the better – and it’s always about the guys who are in camp.“Declan knows about his importance, and he’s one of the very best midfielders in Europe. Nothing will change that. But it’s exactly what we need. We need more, more, more, more variety. We need more, more, more options. Then it’s always about the guys who are in camp. Alex was in the highest level.”Anderson and Scott dominated against the experienced pairing of Luka Modric and Mateo Kovacic. The England youngsters built on playing together when Lee Carsley’s under-21 side won theEuropean Championship last year.“I guess it helps,” Tuchel said. “Not only as players but even in their character. They’re a good mix and match. Alex had a fantastic match, and we need to be strong in the middle of the pitch. I’m very happy with the level that Alex trained at.”View image in fullscreenThomas Tuchel said Alex Scott’s commanding performance in Croatia was ‘exactly what England needs’.Photograph: Bradley Collyer/PAScott explained his partnership with Anderson. “We work really well together,” he said. “We saw that last year at the Euros and we’ve been speaking about it ever since, playing this midfield together.“I love playing with Elliot. He makes life so easy for me. He’s one of the best midfielders in the world. We bounce off each other very well. We like getting on the ball, aggressive off the ball, we suit each other. Playing next to him is great and I know he enjoys it as well.”It is easy to see why Bournemouth were determined not to lose Scott last summer. Arsenal asked about the former Bristol City player’s availability, Manchester United were interested and Chelsea had multiple bids rejected.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTuchel sees Scott as one of the best midfielders in England. That assessment adds to the sense that not taking him to the World Cup was a mistake. England lacked cover for Anderson and Rice, who made 69 appearances for club and country last season. Tuchel gave no minutes to Kobbie Mainoo and lost Jordan Henderson when the 36-year-oldbroke a wristduring the celebrations after the last-16 win against Mexico.But Scott, who may well have ended Henderson’s hopes of a recall, refused to sulk. He used his World Cup disappointment as motivation and has started the season well.“It gave me more hunger but there’s so many top players for this country,” Scott said. “There was no bad feelings about not going to the World Cup. I went to the prep camp, I wanted to learn as much as I can and it helped me coming into this camp.”England’s triumph inCroatiakeeps them in second place in their Nations League group, three points behind Spain and well placed to reach the quarter-finals in March. They close this extended international break at home against Czechia Harry Kane will expect to equal Peter Shilton’s record of 125 caps and is playing brilliantly with Jude Bellingham.“They were good in the World Cup,” Tuchel said. “They get better and better. They love playing with each other. They understand each other better.”Tuchel could rotate against Czechia and has found out more about his squad. The Manchester City full-back Rico Lewis has been added to the senior squad for the Czechia game. “The level, the attitude, from the bench is good. Morgan Gibbs-White had a fantastic training week. Morgan Rogers got a goal. Eberechi Eze is good and is pushing. We need that.”Explore more on these topicsEnglandNations LeagueThomas TuchelCroatianewsShareReuse this content

title: Daryz makes history with back-to-back Arc de Triomphe triumphs | Prix de l'Arc de Triomphe | The Guardian
description: Daryz became the first colt for 48 years to win the Prix de l’Arc de Triomphe in successive seasons with a brilliant victory at Longchamp
Author: Greg Wood
Headline: Daryz became the first colt for 48 years to win the Prix de l’Arc de Triomphe in successive seasons with a brilliant victory at Longchamp
Content: Mickaël Barzalona riding Daryz to win the Prix de l'Arc de Triomphe.Photograph: Alan Crowhurst/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMickaël Barzalona riding Daryz to win the Prix de l'Arc de Triomphe.Photograph: Alan Crowhurst/Getty ImagesPrix de l'Arc de TriompheDaryz makes history with back-to-back Arc de Triomphe triumphsWinning rider Barzalona hails ‘exceptional horse’Stud beckons over bid for unprecedented third winGreg Woodat LongchampSun 4 Oct 2026 12.47 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt was a very different, distinctly brutalist Longchamp that last saw a colt go back-to-back in the Arc, and 48 years on from Alleged’s second victory in 1978 with Lester Piggott holding the reins, the uber-modernist new grandstand rose to acclaim its first legend here on Sunday as Daryz produced the same overwhelming turn of finishing speed down the straight that had carried him to victory in the Prix de l’Arc de Triomphe 12 months ago.Daryz and Mickaël Barzalona did not hit the front until inside the final furlong, but they had been closing on Bay City Roller, who had disputed the lead for much of the way, to such effect from well over a furlong out that the result was in no real doubt.Daryz wins back-to-back Prix de l’Arc de Triomphes at Longchamp – as it happenedRead moreOisin Murphy had worked wonders to get Bay City Roller into contention from stall 15, and likewise Christophe Soumillon, on Aidan O’Brien’s Diamond Necklace, who finished strongly into third from the widest draw of all. But unlike some recent runnings of the Arc – Enable’s narrow defeat of Sea Of Class in 2018, for instance – there was no sense that swapping the draws might have changed the result. Daryz, quite simply, proved himself a class apart.“To win this kind of race twice proves that Daryz is an exceptional horse,” Barzalona said. “It was a really tough race, it didn’t go as we expected but he showed his talent and that made the difference in the end.“The pace was not strong, it was a rough race and nothing went to plan, but the horse deserved to win again and he’s proved all season he is the best one.”For Francis-Henri Graffard, Daryz’s trainer, the win set the seal on another remarkable, championship-winning season in which he has won more than twice as much prize money as the runner-up, André Fabre.“He’s a champion,” Graffard said. “It’s rare I’m confident before a race as it is so hard in a race like this, but I knew things were going right and he’d be very hard to beat. I was confident but I was putting so much pressure on myself [before the race] and you can make yourself look a fool, so it is easier not to speak and not say anything.“We kept losing position early, we were too far back, but we were lucky Daryz has good acceleration.”The only real disappointment on an otherwise perfect, sun-drenched afternoon at Longchamp was a clear hint afterwards that becoming only the sixth colt in Arc history to record back-to-back wins is as much ­history as Daryz will be able to make. No horse has ever won the Arc three times and Daryz seems sure to be completing his first season as a stallion with the Aga Khan Studs when the racing clans gather again in Paris next year.View image in fullscreenBarzalona celebrates after victory on board Daryz in the Prix de l’Arc de Triomphe.Photograph: Frank Sorge/racingfotos.com/Shutterstock“We’re breeders,” Princess Zahra Aga Khan, who has taken over the running of Aga Khan Studs since the death of her father in 2025, said afterwards. “You get to the point where you’re taking a risk every time you run the horse. He’s improved with age, that’s true, and the dam [Daryakana] did, but would we want him to train on for another year? I’m not sure. I think he has other things to do.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn the likely absence of Daryz, it will be up to the beaten horses in Sunday’s race to represent the form in 12 months’ time, and George Scott’s Bay City Roller seems sure to be back next October after his fine run into second from out wide, on ground that was quicker than ideal.Quick GuideGreg Wood's Monday tipsShowYarmouth1.15 Eightthreeone 1.50 Awwjaan 2.25 Zhuri 3.00 Chaise Longue 3.35 Evening Call 4.05 Lucky Hero 4.40 Media Legend (nb)Pontefract1.30 Narrjoo 2.05 Floral Maid 2.40 Fiscal Policy 3.15 American Gulf 3.50 Physique 4.21 Selection 4.56 Noble Grace 5.33 Jojo RabbitStratford-On-Avon1.41 No More Bolero 2.16 Arcturus Flame 2.51 Stellarmasterpiece 3.26 Another Folly 4.00 Pescatorius 4.35 TurbogeistKempton4.10 Shareek 4.45 Footstepinthewoods 5.15 Pursuit Of Love 5.45 Sax Avoidance 6.15 Moving Force 6.45 Buccabay 7.15 Ararat 7.45 Ridger 8.15 Super HitWolverhampton4.26 Solar Swing 5.00 Dreams Galore (nap) 5.30 Iron Dome 6.00 Lady Branksome 6.30 Apex Star 7.00 Faeberon 7.30 Kaaranah 8.00 Alkaios 8.30 Alfa WhiteburdWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.“I could see Daryz coming, but it was an incredible run,” Scott, who saddled a Group-race double on ­Saturday’s card here, said afterwards. “What an amazing racehorse he is and what an amazing ride. He wears his heart on his sleeve, and he’s got all the talent and ability to go with it. Second in the Arc, but we need to go one better.”By then, Daryz will likely be ­completing his first covering ­season at stud, but if Sunday’s race was indeed his final flourish on the track, the sight of his first foals ­setting foot on a racecourse in 2030 will at least summon up memories of an ­outstanding colt and a special afternoon at Longchamp.Explore more on these topicsPrix de l'Arc de TriompheHorse racingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Daryz wins back-to-back Prix de l’Arc de Triomphes at Longchamp – as it happened | Prix de l'Arc de Triomphe | The Guardian
description: Daryz pips Bay City Roller to victory, a second consecutive win at Lonchamp. Greg Wood was watching
Author: Tony Paley
Headline: Daryz pips Bay City Roller to victory, a second consecutive win at Lonchamp. Greg Wood was watching
Content: 10.29 EDTDaryz wins back-to-back Prix de l’Arc de TriomphesDaryz became the first colt for almost 50 years to win Europe’s most prestigious race, the Qatar Prix de l’Arc de Triomphe, in successive seasons with a brilliant victory at ParisLongchamp.Not since the Vincent O’Brien-trained Alleged and Lester Piggott in 1977 and 1978 has a colt managed to defend his title, but once Mickael Barzalona pulled the Francis-Henri Graffard-trained Daryz out to make his run the result looked inevitable.Winning jockey Mickael Barzalona told Sky Sports Racing: “To win this kind of race twice he has to be a remarkable horse. It’s always a tough race and it didn’t go to plan but he deserved to win.”Meanwhile, trainer Francis-Henri Graffard was relieved and stated: “He’s a good horse – he’s a champion. It’s so hard a race to win – I was upset with myself for putting so much pressure on myself. The horse was really well and his rider was confident. He rode a beautiful race.“All my family is here – I am so happy for [the owner] Princerss Zahra. I wish I could be allowed to win the race with him for third time but I don’t think I will be allowed to.”Daryz crosses the line for victory in the Prix de l’Arc de Triomphe.Photograph: Steven Cargill/racingfotos.com/ShutterstockShareUpdated at11.48 EDT

title: Jonathan Taylor’s double earns Colts win against Commanders in London | NFL | The Guardian
description: The running back scored touchdowns either side of half-time to give Indianapolis a 30-13 win against Washington at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium
Author: Graham Searles
Headline: The running back scored touchdowns either side of half-time to give Indianapolis a 30-13 win against Washington at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium
Content: Jonathan Taylor ran for 95 yards and scored two touchdowns at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium.Photograph: Hugo Philpott/UPI/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenJonathan Taylor ran for 95 yards and scored two touchdowns at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium.Photograph: Hugo Philpott/UPI/ShutterstockNFLJonathan Taylor’s double earns Colts win against Commanders in LondonIndianapolis 30-13 WashingtonTreylon Burks scores 47-yard TD for WashingtonGraham Searlesat the Tottenham Hotspur StadiumSun 4 Oct 2026 14.28 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“Welcome to the NFL’s home away from home,” was the rallying cry from former running back and current in-stadium hype man Ronde Barber before the league’s 19th year holidaying in the UK began. And welcome Washington’s injury bug which must have stowed away on the flight to London. The mighty Commanders defense that overwhelmed the Colts at times could not overcome having another quarterback knocked out of commission. Indianapolis capitalised on the misfortune with crafty running back Jonathan Taylor carrying them to a 30-13 victory.The Commanders were already missing starting quarterback Jayden Daniels with an elbow injury and their pesky interloper wasn’t satisfied that Washington had endured enough torment. The game-defining moment came early as a knee injury forced backup passer Marcus Mariota out of the contest after a strong start. Rookie third-stringer Athan Kaliakmanis replaced him and though he delivered the play of the game with an incredible showcase of vision and accuracy on a 47-yard touchdown throw, it was too much, too soon for the 23-year-old.Watson and Browns hold off Steelers’ fightback on last-gasp 56-yard field goalRead moreWashington’s brutal defense, fresh fromtoppling the Super Bowl championslast week, burst out of the traps as defensive tackle Odafe Oweh drove his opposite number Bernhard Raimann straight into Colts quarterback Daniel Jones. The stunned signal caller fell backwards while coughing the ball up to the Commanders who had a turnover after two plays and three points after a 31-yard field goal from Drew Stevens.From then on it mattered little that Jones continued to struggle in the face of Washington’s ferocious front seven. The Colts passer would finish with 19 completions from 34 attempts for 143 yards, no touchdowns and an interception. Lucky for Indianapolis that they have the capable legs of Taylor who picked up the quarterback’s slack with 95 yards on the ground and a pair of touchdowns either side of half-time. His game-winning efforts sandwiched a 48-yard Spencer Shrader boot that put the Colts 17-6 up at the break and out of sight.Meanwhile Kaliakmanis was dealing with the pressure of being thrust into his first professional game. The crowd noticeably quietened at defeat looming far too early as veteran running back Austin Ekeler edged the Commanders to midfield. Those in burgundy and gold had accepted their fate after the unknown QB had started the second half with an ominous interception that set up Taylor’s second score.The backup’s backup quickly restored some faith though with a breathtaking throw. Kaliakmanis saw Treylon Burks breaking down the left sideline and drove the arcing pass just ahead of the sprinting receiver’s path. Burks made the grab in stride for the touchdown. The crowd could not believe it. Neither could Kaliakmanis as he grinned from ear to ear after giving his team a fleeting spark to sit 17-13 behind.View image in fullscreenTreylon Burks runs into the endzone after a throw from Washington Commanders quarterback Athan Kaliakmanis.Photograph: Mickael Chavet/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockThe rookie continued to receive help from his impressive defense as Indianapolis favoured conservative play calling to avoid any more costly turnovers as they added a field goal from Shrader. Alarm bells from the early fumble and interception had been silenced with Taylor taking care of the ball.Then for a few seconds it looked as if Kaliakmanis could be delivering a quarterback debut for the history books as his receiver Antonio Williams raced 80 yards for another touchdown that would have levelled the scores. To the crowd’s deafening ire it was not to be due to an illegal shift penalty.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |FortnightlySign up toThe HotspotA new fortnightly newsletter covering the intersection of sport and the climate crisisEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAs the final quarter began it was the reliable Taylor again at the controls. Two 12-yard rushes moved the Colts to the goalline. A faked handoff to their linchpin then allowed Jones to tuck and run for a score to add some much-needed positivity after his arm wilted under Washington pressure.Indianapolis will be glad to escape London with a 2-2 record and realistic ambitions of making the playoffs after the rockiest of starts. Washington will lick their wounds hoping Daniels is back soon to revive their season.Explore more on these topicsNFLIndianapolis ColtsWashington CommandersUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: NFL today: How to watch Chiefs v Raiders, TV channels & live stream Sunday 4 October | NFL | The Guardian
description: How will the Chiefs and Raiders fare today? Here is what to know, including kick-off time, TV channels and live stream options
Author: Alex Kirshner
Headline: How will the Chiefs and Raiders fare today? Here is what to know, including kick-off time, TV channels and live stream options
Content: Patrick Mahomes and the Chiefs are looking back to their best this season.Photograph: Kim Hukari/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenPatrick Mahomes and the Chiefs are looking back to their best this season.Photograph: Kim Hukari/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockNFLNFL today: How to watch Chiefs v Raiders, TV channels & live stream Sunday 4 OctoberHow will the Chiefs and Raiders fare today? Here is what to know, including kick-off time, TV channels and live stream optionsAlex KirshnerSun 4 Oct 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 12.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDisorienting as it may sound given the past 12 years of Chiefs-Raiders matchups, their game Sunday in Las Vegas is one of the blockbusters of the youngNFLseason. Kansas City have used Las Vegas (and before that, Oakland) as a doormat since the 2015 season, when Patrick Mahomes was a sophomore at Texas Tech. The Chiefs took both games from the Raiders that year and began a run of 18 wins in the teams’ last 22 contests, an unusual run of AFC West dominance in a league that adores parity.The Chiefs are favored again this week, but by less than a touchdown. The Silver and Black come in sporting a matching 3-0 record with their Missourian visitors. Kirk Cousins has found the fountain of youth at 38, keeping No 1 draft pick Fernando Mendoza in an understudy’s role for at least a while longer. The 38-year-old has averaged at least 7.5 yards per pass attempt in each of the team’s three wins, two of which came on the road. The Raiders have benefited from a light opening schedule, taking advantage of games against the moribund Dolphins and Saints. Now comes a stiff test in the desert.Chiefs at RaidersTime:4.25pm ET/9.25pm BSTStadium:Allegiant Stadium (Las Vegas, Nevada)How to watchUnited States:Watch on CBS andFuboCanada:Stream onDAZNandFuboUnited Kingdom:Watch onSky Sports NFL or Sky Sports Football, or stream withNOW.What to watch forJust how back is Patrick Mahomes? The answer might be “extremely.” The franchise QB was having the worst season of his career last year even before it ended a few weeks early because of a torn ACL. But now, Mahomes looks both accurate and unusually spry, like a man who’s gained mobility from chasing a bunch of little kids around his house. He is also benefiting massively from the arrival of Super Bowl MVP Kenneth Walker at running back. Walker is the league’s leading rusher, with 360 yards in his first three games with K.C. It’s not just volume, either; his 5.8 yards per touch are a career best.Cousins is getting the publicity, but the Raiders’ greatest strength to date is one that should come in extra handy against Mahomes: their sublime pass rush. Only one club, the Vikings, have generated more pressures than Vegas,according to Pro Football Reference. The biggest chunk of those (13) have come from the freakishly good Maxx Crosby, who only remains with the team because the Ravens backed out ofa tradethe teams had agreed to in March. It’s a team effort, though: Crosby only has two of the Raiders’ 10 sacks to date, a figure that places them tied for fourth. Mahomes will be minding his blind side.Explore more on these topicsNFLKansas City ChiefsLas Vegas RaidersUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Cable robs Padres of potential home run in bizarre playoff loss to Brewers | MLB | The Guardian
description: Brewers manager Pat Murphy credited the team’s legendary late broadcaster Bob Uecker for an unlikely boost in the ninth inning to help preserve a 3-2 victory
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Brewers manager Pat Murphy credited the team’s legendary late broadcaster Bob Uecker for an unlikely boost in the ninth inning to help preserve a 3-2 victory
Content: Ty France and William Contreras discuss the shot that hit a cable at the Brewers’ stadium.Photograph: Chris Carlson/APView image in fullscreenTy France and William Contreras discuss the shot that hit a cable at the Brewers’ stadium.Photograph: Chris Carlson/APMLBCable robs Padres of potential home run in bizarre playoff loss to BrewersTy France’s ninth-inning drive hits roof cableBrewers go on to win NLDS opener 3-2AgenciesSun 4 Oct 2026 08.04 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 09.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBrewers manager Pat Murphy credited the team’s legendary late broadcaster Bob Ueckerfor an unlikely boostin the ninth inning to help preserve a 3-2 victory over visiting San Diego in ⁠the opener of their playoff series on Saturday.With one out in the ninth and the Brewers clinging to a one-run lead, San Diego had a runner on first when Ty France hit a drive to left field ⁠off closer Trevor Megill. But the ball struck a roof cable, stayed in play and was caught by Jackson Chourio for the second out. Megill then retired Jackson Merrill on a fly ball to right field to ⁠give Milwaukee the victory.“I think the only thing that you could probably figure on the ball that everybody’s going to be talking about is that [Uecker] decided to put his hand on it and swat it down so Chourio ⁠could catch it,” Murphy said. “So thanks, Ueck.”Uecker, who was the radio voice of the Brewers for more than 50 ​years, died last year at the age of 90.The ground rules ‌for Milwaukee’s American Family Field say that a ‌batted ball that strikes the roof, roof truss, roof cable or any cabling over fair territory is in play. If caught by a fielder, ‌the batter is out. If the ball strikes any of those same structures over foul territory, it’s a dead ball. A third rule says if the ball strikes those structures over fair territory and lands foul, it’s a foul ball.MLB playoff predictions: are the Dodgers heading for an inevitable fall?Read moreThe Padres challenged whether the ball was fair or foul, but the on-field call that it was an out was upheld.Padres manager Craig Stammen thought the ball would have been a home run if it had not hit the cable, while Murphy believes it would have gone foul.“We joked about it at the umpire meeting today ‌about what would happen if the ball hit the roof,” Stammen said after the game. “And it was unlikely, but it happened. The rule is if they deemed the ball to be fair and it comes down you can catch it. If it ​hits off the roof foul, then it’s a foul ball. So they ruled that it hit the roof fair and the outfielder caught it.“Unfortunately, a bad break for us. Looked like it was a possible home run. Just didn’t go our way. Second time that’s happened this year to the Padres.”Murphy said from his vantage point, the ball wouldn’t have stayed fair for a homer.“It was going to be a foul ball for sure,” Murphy said. “I’m ⁠standing right on that line, a hitter that talented.”Chourio, who hit a game-tying, two-run homer earlier in ​the game, said he was just trying to make ​sure he made the play.“I wasn’t all that ​sure of what the rule was, and I wasn’t really all that sure that it actually did hit anything,” ​Chourio said. “I ‌thought I had a chance ​on that ball kind of ​the whole time off the bat. Then the only thing I kind of realized, it changed direction a little bit, but I thought I had a bead on it for the majority of the time.”As Stammen said, it also wasn’t the first time this season the Padres lost a potential home run to a stadium’s unique ground rules.In August, Xander Bogaerts’s drive struck the catwalk at Tampa Bay’s Tropicana Field and was caught by Rays third baseman Junior Caminero. Bogaerts’s drive had been projected by Statcast to go 386ft.“You would think with all the technology and data and everything we have now, we’d be able to make a clear call on that,” France said. “I don’t know if that’s ever been done before, but yeah, there should be something put in place right there. That shouldn’t be an out.”In Saturday’s other division series openers, the Rays shut out the Yankees for a 1-0 win, the Dodgers overcame the Braves 5-3 and the White Sox beat the Guardians 3-0.Explore more on these topicsMLBSan Diego PadresBaseballMilwaukee BrewersUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘We are in a kind of war’: row over viral Amsterdam chip shop lands in court | Netherlands | The Guardian
description: Neighbours say crowds drawn to Fabel Friet are clogging the picturesque canal street and attracting litter, gulls and rats
Author: Senay Boztas
Headline: Neighbours say crowds drawn to Fabel Friet are clogging the picturesque canal street and attracting litter, gulls and rats
Content: People living near the chip shop have referred to the ‘TikTok queue’ that builds outside the premises on Runstraat.Photograph: Judith Jockel/The GuardianView image in fullscreenPeople living near the chip shop have referred to the ‘TikTok queue’ that builds outside the premises on Runstraat.Photograph: Judith Jockel/The GuardianNetherlands‘We are in a kind of war’: row over viral Amsterdam chip shop lands in courtNeighbours say crowds drawn by TikTok to Fabel Friet are clogging the picturesque canal street and attracting litter, gulls and ratsSenay Boztasin Amsterdam. Photographs by Judith JockelSun 4 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePeople living in one of Amsterdam’s most exclusive neighbourhoods have taken the city to court for licensing a chip shop thathas gone viral on TikTok.View image in fullscreen‘It has polluted the whole area’ … Thomas van Leeuwen, who lives near to Fabel Friet.On busy days, the queue for Fabel Friet on Runstraat stretches across a bridge on the Keizersgracht – one of Amsterdam’s most famous canals – a court was told last week. The narrow street itself is crowded by tourists waiting for their orders seven days a week. And loitering with intent – on parked cars, on the street itself, and on steps and porches – gulls wait to swoop.“We are in a kind of war where a very unwelcome chip shop has polluted the whole area,” said Thomas van Leeuwen, who lives nearby. “Eating in the street is a shameful behaviour. It gets filthy food on our doorsteps and mayonnaise in the beautiful stone. The herring gulls have moved in as residents, and the worst thing is the rat infestation.”Nineteen neighbours have formally protested against the business licence for Fabel Friet, whose signature product is fries topped with parmesan cheese and truffle mayonnaise. Niek van der Heijden, the lead plaintiff, said the problem was the takeaway’s small size.“What we call the ‘TikTok queue’ for Fabel Friet causes the most nuisance,” he said. “The business takes place on the street: waiting to order, waiting to be served, eating. We want Fabel to go to a place where there is enough room to have clients inside.”In a packed courtroom on Tuesday morning, a lawyer for Amsterdam city council acknowledged that the city’s mayor, Femke Halsema, can refuse a licence to operate if the “residential and living environment” is negatively affected by a business.View image in fullscreenNiek van der Heijden, the lead plaintiff in the case.Photograph: Judith Jockel/The GuardianWhile the chip shop, she said, sticks to its licence obligations to manage the queue and clear litter “it has been going on for a long time, the impact remains severe, and you have to ask: how long can we tolerate this?” For the current licence, she said, the city would be guided by the court’s ruling.The shop’s owners, Abel Klatser and Floris Feilzer, said they employed a cleaning service seven days a week, four times a day, and that year-on-year visitor numbers had dropped by 23% this August after they openedfour new locations. “A few neighbours have experienced nuisance, but other people enjoy eating chips,” said Gertjan Teeuwen, their lawyer. “It can be busy, but there are peaks and troughs.”View image in fullscreenThe queue outside Fabel Friet, which occupies a small premises.Klatser and Feilzer said in a public statement that they felt unfairly attacked while doing their best to be good neighbours. “Fabel Friet is our child, and we have put our heart and soul into it,” they said. “It is painful if people talk about our business negatively.”View image in fullscreenHerring gulls have been attracted to the area by the leftovers and waste.Photograph: Judith Jockel/The GuardianThe case goes beyond irritations about so-called performative tourism, where tourists flock to a place to post images on social media. “The tiny streets might be charming, but actually the space is not designed for so many people,” said Lisa-Bobbie Kamp, a lawyer for the neighbours. “This is a question of taking space, who owns the place and whether you can just use public space.”Marije Peute, a PhD student at the University of Amsterdam, has studied the effects of “viral urbanism” in the neighbourhood. “The municipality should really think about how they want to act, because this is about the public space. A lot of much older retail spaces have lost their local clients because they don’t want to go there any more,” she said.Rogier Havelaar, a councillor from the Christian Democratic Appeal party, said that, while Fabel Friet should probably be offered a “flagship store” licence in a more suitable location, the benefits of tourism to the city should not be overlooked. “Amsterdam would never have as many museums, restaurants, going-out spots and theatres if they were only for the residents,” he said. “And tourism provides 70,000 jobs. Amsterdam would have a gigantic financial problem if tourism went away.”View image in fullscreenA customer with a portion of Fabel Friet’s signature fries topped with parmesan cheese and truffle mayonnaise.Photograph: Judith Jockel/The GuardianStanding on the bridge over the Keizersgracht, some German laboratory apprentices drawn by TikTok were enjoying their chips. Natalie Stübben said crowd managers had just asked them to move away from people’s houses. “It’s pretty hard to get through here with a car or just by walking,” she said. “I don’t think we were thinking about annoying the neighbours, but it makes sense.”View image in fullscreen‘I don’t think we were thinking about annoying the neighbours’ … Natalie Stübben.Some of those neighbours will be pleased if the business location has had its chips after the court verdict on 12 November. “There’s something very alarming about the fact that these people are all led by their higher power – influencers – and call themselves followers,” said van Leeuwen. “It’s Orwellian. This court case is part of the parasitic industry that lives on tourists.”Explore more on these topicsNetherlandsTikTokEuropeFood & drink industryChips (french fries)featuresShareReuse this content

title: OpenAI safety leader quits, warning AI company’s culture is ‘broken’ | OpenAI | The Guardian
description: David Robinson joins other insiders in urging industry to take more care over rapidly developing technology
Author: Dan Milmo
Headline: David Robinson joins other insiders in urging industry to take more care over rapidly developing technology
Content: David Robinson said AI firms were not ‘being nearly careful enough’ about developing the technology.Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersView image in fullscreenDavid Robinson said AI firms were not ‘being nearly careful enough’ about developing the technology.Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersOpenAIOpenAI safety leader quits, warning AI company’s culture is ‘broken’David Robinson joins other insiders in urging industry to take more care over rapidly developing technologyDan MilmoGlobal technology editorSun 4 Oct 2026 03.48 EDTFirst published on Sat 3 Oct 2026 15.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA safety leader atOpenAIhas quit the company, warning that its culture was broken and that AI firms were not “being nearly careful enough” about developing the technology.David Robinson, who led the writing of safety reports that accompanied the ChatGPT developer’s product releases, explained his resignation in an essay headlined: “I quit OpenAI because its culture is broken.”Robinson wrote that a cultural overhaul was needed at cutting-edge AI firms and incidents such as a “swarm” of OpenAI agents – AI programmes operating autonomously without human oversight –attacking the AI startup Hugging Facewere “typical of the industry, given the speed and flexibility with which people operate”.Writing inthe Atlantic magazine, Robinson wrote: “I agree with other recently departed staff that the companies building this technology aren’t being nearly careful enough. But I believe that we need to look deeper than specific rules or new laws. We need to talk about culture.”Referring to OpenAI’s pace of development, he wrote: “As the company sprints from one launch to the next, it is failing to achieve the level of care that I believe is needed.”OpenAI has shown signs of caution in recent weeks, after the Hugging Face incident and the revelation that it has notified more than 100 organisations about rogue agent activity. This week it announced it wasscrapping the release of a next-generation ⁠AI modelafter researchers raised safety concerns ⁠during internal testing. OpenAI hasalso paused trainingof its most advanced models.Geoffrey Irving, who worked at OpenAI and was chief scientist at the UK government’s AI Safety Institute before joining the AI safety researchcompany Resolution, also issued a warning on AI on Saturday.Writingin Time, he said: “Recent warnings about the potential destructive power of AI are understating the severity of the situation. I believe there’s about a 50% chance we all die because of the development of smarter-than-human AI systems, and that our actions over the next two to 10 years will determine the outcome.”The warnings follow the resignation of Jacob Coxon, a researcher at the OpenAI rival Anthropic, who quit the Claude chatbot developer last month. He said he believed AI “could kill us all by the end of the decade” – and wasbacked up by an Anthropic employee warningthere was a more than 10% chance AI would wipe out humanity within the next decade. Critics of such warnings have cautioned, however, thatthey are unscientificbecause they cannot be verified or falsified.Robinson wrote that Silicon Valley lacked an awareness of “how to handle dangerous technology” and “what it means to care for people”. Warning that OpenAI had “unimpeded optimism” about solving problems as they arose, he wrote that this internal culture meant safety failures would only grow as systems became more capable.“Imagine ‘rogue’ agents that work like teams of hackers (for example, holding hospital computer systems for ransom) but never need to sleep,” wrote Robinson.Robinson called for two safety changes: that AI firms rely on safety expertise in other fields such as nuclear and aviation, and that they develop “new science” that ensures powerful systems in the future are capable of being reined in when they are operating autonomously.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Given today’s risks, frontier labs need to run like nuclear power plants or busy airports, with layers of redundancy and careful, time-consuming planning, so that the occasional and inevitable human error does not open a door to disaster,” he wrote.An OpenAI spokesperson said the company was continuing to “strengthen our safety and security practices to address the risks we see today”, while working on dealing with the risks that might be created by future AI breakthroughs.“We’re making sure our models don’t become more capable than we can safely manage and secure, and we pause training or hold back models when we need to slow down,” said the spokesperson.Get in touchContact us about this storyThe best public interest journalism relies on first-hand accounts from people in the know. If you have something to share on this subject, you can contact us confidentially using the following methods:Secure Messaging in the Guardian appThe Guardian app has a tool to send tips about stories. Messages are end to end encrypted and concealed within the routine activity that every Guardian mobile app performs. This prevents an observer from knowing that you are communicating with us at all, let alone what is being said.If you don’t already have the Guardian app, download it (iOS/Android) and go to the menu. Select ‘Secure Messaging’.SecureDropIf you can safely use the tor network without being observed or monitored you can send messages and documents to the Guardian via ourSecureDrop platform.Our guide attheguardian.com/tipslists several ways to contact us securely, and discusses the pros and cons of each.Show moreExplore more on these topicsOpenAIAI (artificial intelligence)ComputingData and computer securityEthicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump names intelligence chief Jay Clayton as new White House AI czar | Trump administration | The Guardian
description: Clayton had said AI was a ‘gamechanger’ but also posed ‘a threat’ during his confirmation hearing
Author: Ariana Baio
Headline: Clayton had said AI was a ‘gamechanger’ but also posed ‘a threat’ during his confirmation hearing
Content: Donald Trump with Jay Clayton, the director of national intelligence, in Washington DC on 29 September.Photograph: Alex Brandon/APView image in fullscreenDonald Trump with Jay Clayton, the director of national intelligence, in Washington DC on 29 September.Photograph: Alex Brandon/APTrump administrationTrump names intelligence chief Jay Clayton as new White House AI czarClayton had said AI was a ‘gamechanger’ but also posed ‘a threat’ during his confirmation hearingAriana BaioSun 4 Oct 2026 13.45 EDTFirst published on Sun 4 Oct 2026 09.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trump on Sunday namedJay Clayton, the director of national intelligence, to also serve as the new White House AI czar.Clayton,who leads the US’s 18 intelligence agencies, previously served as the top federal prosecutor in Manhattan and led the Securities and Exchange Commission during Trump’s first term.During hisSenate confirmation hearing, Clayton said AI was a “gamechanger” but it also posed “a threat”.“When something’s both an opportunity and a threat, you better get your arms around it,” Clayton told lawmakers when asked about AI.CBS News was the firstto report that Clayton would be appointed White House AI czar.In a social media post on Sunday, Trump announced that Clayton would lead what the US president called “the Super Intelligence Force (SIF)”.Trump’s post also said the SIF would “coordinate the federal government’s engagement with consumers, public interest groups, religious organizations, critical infrastructure providers, and super intelligence companies”.Among those reacting on Sunday to Trump’s invoking the term “super intelligence” was SpaceX chiefElon Musk. Musk said on his social media platform X that SI was “better” than AI – and that he wasrenaminghis aerospace company’s AI unit from SpaceXAI to SpaceXSI.Senator Mark Warner, a Virginia Democrat who is vice-chair of the Senate select committee on intelligence, cautiously welcomed the appointment of Clayton, while noting that “the administration hasresistedmeaningful safeguards without offering a serious alternative for addressing the national security risks posed by increasingly powerful AI systems”.“I look forward to working with Director Clayton on ensuring the United States stays ahead of China and other adversaries, strengthening the security and resilience of our most advanced AI systems, and establishing rigorous testing and safeguards so that increasingly powerful systems remain secure, reliable, and under human control,” Warner added.In September, Trumpannouncedhe wascreating an “AI Force”and a czar to oversee the technology’s growth and monitor for “bad” development. The announcement came aftertech industry leaders warned that AI was developing too rapidlyto control and that it could harm humans.The president has largely brushed asideconcerns about AI developmentand the construction of datacenters, which power the technology.Trump has insisted continued development is paramount to defeating China in the global AI race.But to address concerns, the president created an advisory committee in addition to the czar – whom he previously promised would be led by a “high IQ” individual. Trump also recently met with AI industry leaders to discuss concerns.On Tuesday,Trump and six executives signed an AI accordat the White House, promising to create internal and external monitors to ensure the technology is used as intended and any safety issues are addressed.Trump had initially created the AI and cryptocurrency czar position when he returned to the White House in January 2025.David Sacks, the venture capitalist and tech businessman, served as the administration’s AI and cryptocurrency czar until March 2026, when he reached his employment limit under his designation as a “special government employee”.Sacks still co-chairs the President’s Council of Advisors on Science and Technology.Trump previously floated Clayton’s name as a potential AI czar, tellingAxiosin September that Clayton was “a good man” and the prospect of appointing him was “a good idea”.Explore more on these topicsTrump administrationAI (artificial intelligence)Donald TrumpUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Rural Queenslanders have seen gas projects come and go – but a 725-hectare datacentre poses a whole new level of ‘stupidity’ | Queensland | The Guardian
description: Residents of Dalby may soon live beside a $31bn datacentre. The premier sees ‘opportunity’ for the state – but others fear AI’s global creep
Author: Andrew Messenger
Headline: Residents of Dalby may soon live beside a $31bn datacentre. The premier sees ‘opportunity’ for the state – but others fear AI’s global creep
Content: Denver Kanowski believes the datacentre to be built to power Anthropic’s Claude will go beyond harming the environment by disconnecting people from the things that really matter.Photograph: Andrew Messenger/The GuardianView image in fullscreenDenver Kanowski believes the datacentre to be built to power Anthropic’s Claude will go beyond harming the environment by disconnecting people from the things that really matter.Photograph: Andrew Messenger/The GuardianQueenslandRural Queenslanders have seen gas projects come and go – but a 725-hectare datacentre poses a whole new level of ‘stupidity’Residents of Dalby may soon live beside a $31bn datacentre. The premier sees ‘opportunity’ for the state – but others fear AI’s global creepAndrew MessengerSun 4 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 16.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFrom the veranda on his bush block, Denver Kanowski has watched resources companies come and go from ruralQueenslandfor 70 years.The home cost him $800, and lets him live how he likes, in nature. It’s also in the middle of a gasfield, not far from theLinc Energy contamination site, down the road from a coalmine and three gas power plants.Last month came the biggest scheme yet, a $31bn datacentre to power Claude, the large language model developed by global AI giant Anthropic.If built, Australia’s largest datacentrewould be about 15 minutes’ drive away from Kanowski’s home, outside Kogan, near Dalby, about 180km west of Brisbane.In a community that has seen the boom and bust of coal seam gas, the response from many has been the same as Kanowski’s:once bitten, twice shy.“This is the power of money and the power of greed and shortsighted stupidity,” Kanowski says.“I’ve read this book before.”Anthropic’s project is to be built on a 725-hectare plot of land now occupied by a 24,000-head feedlot, surrounded by gas wells.According to Singapore-based developer Zerra DC, its cooling system will be far less water intensive than that used in most existing datacentres, generating about the same demandas an average shopping centre.View image in fullscreenThe site of what is planned to be Australia’s biggest datacentre is, today, a feedlot on a rural road 30km outside Dalby, surrounded by coal seam gas wells and three gas power plants.Photograph: Andrew Messenger/The GuardianBut like all AI, it will require an enormous amount of energy. The Western Downs datacentre will require a peak power capacityequal to about a quarter of total state energy demand, 2.16GW. It would also employ thousands during construction, with about 1,400 long-term jobs,according to the company.The proposal was made public just last month.Within days, Dalby travel agent Mordechai Winters had made up his mind: he didn’t want it.“I was crushed. You know, it’s very disappointing that the council and also the government would consider it,” he says.Issues like energy demand, noise and poor siting have drivena massive backlash against datacentresin the United States. Three-quarters of Americans now oppose them, and more than 500 counties have imposed a ban.At least thousands have a similar view in Australia.A petition that Winters helped to launch has been signed by more than21,500 people– mostly from the area – in just a few weeks, he says.Sign up for a weekly email featuring our best readsHe believes the project’s benefits are exaggerated and will trigger the same boom-bust cycle as gas.Cecil Plains farmer Liza Balmain remembers the big – and eventually unrealised – promises of the gas industry when it arrived.View image in fullscreenLiza Balmain fought for years to keep coal seam gas off her land in Cecil Plains near Dalby. She says she can see ‘huge similarities’ with the proposed datacentre.Photograph: Andrew Messenger/The GuardianThe industry brought massive change; academics later concluded that its scale and pace in a small agricultural community “was likely unprecedented anywhere in the world”. There was a huge influx of workers, with the high wages of gas attracting labour away from farms and local business.Then – because setting up a gas well requires a lot more labour than operating it – the industry leftjust as quickly as it had arrived,leaving business owners with debts they couldn’t pay on investments they no longer needed. Some academics believe the industryleft the region worse off.Others think it was a slim net positive.Plan for controversial $1.2bn datacentre in Sydney scrapped due to ‘emerging’ regulationsRead moreBalmain, wholed a long campaign against the gas industry, says she can see “huge similarities” between the coal seam gas era and the proposed datacentre.Australians across the country are concerned. Jo Shulman, CEO of the Environmental Defenders Office which has long helped communities fight resources projects such as coal seam gas, says the group had seen a 250% increase in queries about datacentres to the service’s free legal advice line since January.“I would say the datacentre is the new frontier,” she says.“Communities are concerned about [their] impacts on the environment and their wellbeing”.Shulman says datacentres will form an essential part of the clean energy transition – but called for a pause to allow national standards to catch up.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFive Great ReadsEach week our editors select five of the most interesting, entertaining and thoughtful reads published by Guardian Australia and our international colleagues. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Saturday morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“We think that there should be a moratorium on any further datacentres, or they risk repeating the same things that we saw with the coal seam gas boom,” she says.Big job for a small councilThe Dalby mayor, Andrew Smith, says the ultimate authority over the region’s largest ever project should rest with the Western Downs regional council, which services a population of 35,452. Speaking to Guardian Australia last month, Smith said council did not expect the project to be taken over by the state coordinator general.View image in fullscreenCunningham Street, Dalby. The town’s mayor says coal seam gas ‘diversified our economy … It’s created jobs.’Photograph: David Kelly/Photograph David Kelly/The Guardian“We did ask the question, but our understanding is it will stay with local government,” he says.But then, on Friday, things changed. The state announced it would take datacentres out of the hands of local councils, under a new planning framework to ensure “a consistent and transparent framework across the state,” similar to thegovernment’s renewables planning policy.“We will treat these projects no worse and no better than we do mining, renewables or tourism projects. Any deals done must be with the backing of councils and communities,” a spokesperson for planning minister, Jarrod Bleijie, says.“The state government will become the responsible assessor and coordinator of any data centre applications, instead of local councils”.If given the green light, the project will be worth more to the local community than coal seam gas, Smithsays.“In general, the coal seam gas industry has been wonderful for our region. It’s diversified our economy, which we talk about a lot. It’s created jobs,” he says.“Prior to coal seam gas, we were exporting a lot of our clever kids, because the opportunities weren’t back in the region.”Anthropic wants to start using the centre as early as next year. But Smith says the planning couldn’t be rushed – and was careful not to endorse or oppose the project.The Queensland premier,David Crisafulli, lobbied the company to invest in the state during a recent trade mission, he told parliament last week.Crisafulli said the state would help the council assess the project, but said it had done an excellent job with the gas industry and could do so again.“They see the same opportunity I do, and that opportunity is to make sure that there are jobs, very good jobs in regional areas, and if we get it right,lower power bills for every other Queenslander as well. I see a really good play with that,” the premier said.Toowoomba and Surat Basin Enterprise chief executive officer, Jo Sheppard, says most residents of the area had not yet made up their minds about the project, but that it was important for the developer to maintain their social licence.She added it was a “a once in a generation opportunity for Western Downs region and our broader region,” with the power to transform the town from a “fairly quiet” farming community to something more, adding to booms triggered by gas, and then renewables.“Someone actually did say to me the other day: ‘Gosh, should we all be buying a house in Dalby?’”Kanowski says there was something different about the datacentre compared with coal and coal seam gas schemes. He believes it will go beyond harming the environment by contributing to an online “fantasy” world, disconnecting people from the things that genuinely matter.“[The datacentre developers] don’t even see the trees. They don’t understand the relationship between all the things. This is my world, I love it,” he says.“This is not a datacentre … This is part of a network that these money-crazed idiots are planning to put all over the planet.”Explore more on these topicsQueenslandDatacentres - AustraliaAI (artificial intelligence)AnthropicDavid CrisafulliQueensland politicsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The AI industry is booming. Women are getting left behind | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Women hold just a fraction of new AI jobs but are overrepresented in roles with high risk of AI disruption
Author: Arielle Pardes
Headline: Women hold just a fraction of new AI jobs but are overrepresented in roles with high risk of AI disruption
Content: ‘AI is creating some of the fastest growing, highest paying … jobs in the global economy. Women are just strikingly underrepresented.’Composite: The Guardian/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘AI is creating some of the fastest growing, highest paying … jobs in the global economy. Women are just strikingly underrepresented.’Composite: The Guardian/Getty ImagesReworkedAI (artificial intelligence)The AI industry is booming. Women are getting left behindWomen hold just a fraction of new AI jobs but are overrepresented in roles with high risk of AI disruptionSupported byAbout this contentArielle PardesSun 4 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 09.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere’s a common fear among people who work in Silicon Valley: snag one of the fast-growing, high-paying jobs in artificial intelligence, or get trapped in the “permanent underclass”, a phrase describing the fate of those who won’t have upward mobility in the age of AI.The phrase usually describes a future in which AI automates human jobs. But for women in tech, it’s starting to look like the present.“A lot of people say: ‘Oh, AI is lowering barriers, it’s equalizing the playing field for women,’” said Urvashi Batra, co-founder and CEO of Prioriwise, an AI platform for IT service providers. “I actually think it’s the opposite.”Batra said people take her less seriously as the founder of an AI company than her male co-founder. When pitching investors, she and her co-founder have learned that they are more likely to get an investment if he does the pitching.Women made up only about a quarter of new hires in AI roles in the last year, compared to 50% of new hires in non-AI roles, according to a recentreportfrom LinkedIn. In executive roles, that number drops to just 13%. At the same time, LinkedIn’sresearchshows that women are more likely to work in roles with high exposure to AI disruption, like customer service, meaning they are also at higher risk for job loss due to AI.AI jobs, whose postings have doubled since 2023, come with a salary premium, on average paying more than twice as much as roles that don’t involve working with AI, according to LinkedIn’s research. But women who do have jobs in AI are disproportionately concentrated in low-paying roles, like data annotators, said Sarah Steinberg, the head of global public policy partnerships at LinkedIn. Across all AI occupations, men have $45,000 higher median pay than women, partly due to the types of jobs they are likelier to have.“AI is creating some of the fastest growing, highest paying and most consequential jobs in the global economy,” said Steinberg. “Women are just strikingly underrepresented.”The ongoing trend could produce the greatest gender pay gap in generations and leave women out of building a technology that shaped the economy, advocates for women in tech said.“What we’re witnessing is a sort of backsliding,” said Brenda Darden Wilkerson, president of AnitaB.org, a non-profit devoted to advancing women in tech jobs.Initiatives to promote women in the tech industry have been ongoing for years, with mixed results. Women now holdabout one-thirdof tech jobs in the US. Butresearchhas found that women leave the tech industry at a much higher rate than their male counterparts, citing factors like non-inclusive cultures and barriers to advancement.‘I’ve seen so many women fall through the cracks’Women working in AI may face even greater challenges. “AI moves extremely fast, and the pressure to keep up is immense,” said Jayeeta Putatunda, an AI engineering lead at investment firm Turing. “I have seen throughout my career so many amazing women I know kind of fall through the cracks.”Putatunda said it’s not uncommon to be the only female engineer on a team, and that when women are outnumbered, they have to speak up louder to make their ideas known. Mentorship in the AI field, especially by other women, can be hard to come by. And the breakneck pace of AI advancements means anyone working in the field should expect to put in long hours in order to keep up.“If you have very ambitious career goals in this field, there will be seasons when you work beyond normal hours,” she said, noting that a culture of working 12-hour days to keep up was not uncommon. “I don’t think there is always a neat shortcut around that than to put in the hours.”Those kinds of work expectations can make it impossible for everyone to stay in the field. “I went onmaternity leave for four months, and by the time I came back, there were completely different frameworks and levels of models,” Putatunda said. Getting caught back up was overwhelming. She said it was only possible with the help of supportive co-workers and a husband who equitably split childcare.“That is one way women get pushed out of AI,” she said. “They don’t lack the interest or ability to keep up. They may lack the infrastructure that makes keeping up possible.”The AI industry is so new and fast-moving that it should in theory be more meritocratic. No one has a decade of experience working with a model developed one year ago, which should mean everyone has a level playing field. But instead the field has indexed more on personal networks and other loose signals, according to some women who work in AI.“Companies are hiring at a breakneck speed, but they’re finding people through the same networks, the same referrals, the same filters that they’ve always used,” Wilkerson said. “Generally, that’s not given women the same sort of exposure they should have.”When people have tried to address these tech industry problems in the past, the solutions have largely come down to giving women more mentorship and implementing diversity programs with goals around representation. But in recent years, companies have aggressively scaled back their diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) programs, largely in response to a political climate that discourages them. That has left fewer companies with institutional programs to hire and promote women.The political climate has made it more challenging to get AI companies to support initiatives focused on women, said Felicia Newhouse, founder of AI Powered Women, an organization that promotes women’s participation and leadership in AI. Newhouse, a product marketer who has worked in technology companies for two decades, points to the Department of Justice targeting corporations with DEI programs, claiming the initiatives violate anti-discrimination laws. Companies like Accenture, Deloitte, IBM and PayPal have all agreed to pay multimillion-dollar settlements under this enforcement.“It is getting harder to go into companies being called AI Powered Women,” Newhouse said. “And our advocates inside those companies are also struggling with having women-focused initiatives.”Still, she said the risk that women are left behind in the AI workforce was something that kept her up at night. “We’re talking about who captures a major new source of economic mobility,” she said. “The deepest risk is that a participation gap becomes a power gap.”Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)ReworkedfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Hegseth is obsessed with increasing testosterone. If anything, the US could use less | Dave Schilling | The Guardian
description: Maybe the key to life is being able to bench press 300lb at 75. But do we need more muscle-bound, angry guys around?
Author: Dave Schilling
Headline: Maybe the key to life is being able to bench press 300lb at 75. But do we need more muscle-bound, angry guys around?
Content: ‘Will testosterone regrow my hair? I’d at least consider it if it did, but apparently, it makes hair lossworse.’Illustration: Fortunate Joaquin/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘Will testosterone regrow my hair? I’d at least consider it if it did, but apparently, it makes hair lossworse.’Illustration: Fortunate Joaquin/The GuardianOpinionPete HegsethHegseth is obsessed with increasing testosterone. If anything, the US could use lessDave SchillingMaybe the key to life is being able to bench press 300lb at 75. But do we need more muscle-bound, angry guys around?Sun 4 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 19.22 EDTShareI loathe going to the doctor.Not a controversial opinion, compared to some of the other ones in this section of the Guardian. I’m not exactly arguing for universal basic income or for Manchester City to be relegated to the Saudi Pro League here. No one looks forward to a doctor visit, with its recriminations for bad habits or various intrusive blood tests. People don’t have cocktail parties to celebrate their yearly check-up, and yet, it seems like every day, there’s a new reason to go get prodded by a stranger in a lab coat.Our collective fascination with testosterone levels is just another instance of me (specifically me) being shamed into more medical tests.The defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, and others in the Trump administrationhave been prattling onabout testosterone for years now, claiming it’s the key to maintaining what’s left of our civilization. Hegseth wants to test soldiers for T levels, and offer testosterone replacement therapy (TRT) to those who don’t have sufficient medically verifiable machismo. He sees this as “restoring and optimizing your natural capabilities, protecting your longevity, and ensuring you have the biological foundation required to sustain the fight”.Pete Hegseth wants testosterone for his soldiers. Finally, some gender-affirming care | Arwa MahdawiRead moreThe health secretary,Robert F Kennedy Jr, removed limits on TRT in June of this year, so that more men could be legally prescribed testosterone rather than, say, buying it at a gas station or from the back of a 2007 Dodge Caravan in the parking lot of an Arby’s.The science behind the perceived benefits of testosterone replacement therapy for cisgender men are hotly debated – a debate I’m simply too stupid to wade into. I have a hard time doing long division. How am I going to understand what injecting hormones into my body is going to do? Maybe testosterone will make me smarter. Probably not. I think that’s probably the one thing we can agree it doesn’t do.It’s bad enough that I have to be tested for blood pressure, cholesterol, A1C and eyesight. Why throw another thing on the pile of stuff I have to worry about? And is this actually worth my concern?Testosterone allegedly makes you more athletic, more virile, and more sexually active. First of all, I’m not a professional athlete. I don’t need to dunk a basketball or dominate my gym’s racquetball league. I’m a writer. My fingers work just fine.Do I need to function better sexually? If anything, I wouldn’t mind my libido toning down a bit. Will testosterone regrow my hair? I’d at least consider it if it did, but apparently, itmakes hair lossworse. What good will a bit more muscle mass be if I end up looking like Steve Harvey without the millions of dollars that make Steve Harvey attractive? If you give me a million dollars, I’ll take testosterone. There, the offer is in writing.While fightinghormone therapy for trans troops, the Trump administration is simultaneously suggesting to cis men like me that I should be taking it instead, even if I don’t actually want it. Or need it. Considering my high interest in sex, perfectly acceptable athletic ability, and generally sedentary lifestyle, if anything, maybe I have too much testosterone.I’m perpetually angry – about someone cutting me off in traffic, the escalator at the AMC Burbank 16 that never works, and the Lakers’ starting lineup. Would I be a more valuable member of society if I got out of my car and walloped the guy who swerved in front of me? Should I be bashing the escalator at the AMC with an aluminum baseball bat until the police arrive?Hegseth confirms plan to cut 20% of US top military brass and rails at ‘beardos, weirdos and wimps’Read moreLike any normal person my age, I take my aggression out in video games. Whenever I get too apoplectic to function, I turn on my Playstation 5 and queue upRoboCop: Rogue City, a game where you play as the titular cybernetic lawman of the future – blasting criminals with a high-powered, rapid-fire pistol. The only thing more satisfying than a robot eviscerating drug-addled gutter punks inside a game is when you get to issue parking citations and arrest people for public urination. Yes, you can do that in the game. It never gets old.I’m sure this is not whatPete Hegsethmeans when he talks about “lethality”, but this is as close as I’m going to get – wiping out a street gang with a rocket launcher. I assure you I don’t need more testosterone for that.Underneath much of this tedious discourse and my own dread of seeing a doctor, though, is the fundamental premise that there’s something wrong with the natural progression of the human body. That, for some reason, we need to fix people who aren’t sick – as though we’re in some Jean-Claude Van Damme movie and need to be turned into a biologically enhanced weapon so we can swim more laps or something.Is the key to life being able to bench press 300lb at the age of 75? For some, sure. I salute them. And yet, we are destined to age, to be rendered irrelevant, and to die. No matter what you inject or swallow from the pharmacist, it’s going to happen. That’s as normal as a stiff breeze. There’s no conquering reality. Just ask your doctor.Dave Schilling is a Los Angeles-based writer and humoristExplore more on these topicsPete HegsethOpinionHealthTrump administrationUS militaryMenRobert F Kennedy JrcommentShareReuse this content

title: Trump wants control of South America. If Bolsonaro Jr wins in Brazil, that could become a reality | Steve Bloomfield | The Guardian
description: The US president has taken credit for far-right victories across Latin America, but those wins have had more to do with fears of gang crime than his meddling, says journalist Steve Bloomfield
Author: Steve Bloomfield
Headline: The US president has taken credit for far-right victories across Latin America, but those wins have had more to do with fears of gang crime than his meddling, says journalist Steve Bloomfield
Content: Flavio Bolsonaro at a rally in Campo Grande, Rio de Janeiro state, Brazil, 3 October 2026.Photograph: Bruna Prado/APView image in fullscreenFlavio Bolsonaro at a rally in Campo Grande, Rio de Janeiro state, Brazil, 3 October 2026.Photograph: Bruna Prado/APOpinionBrazilTrump wants control of South America. If Bolsonaro Jr wins in Brazil, that could become a realitySteve BloomfieldThe US president has taken credit for far-right victories across Latin America, but those wins have had more to do with fears of gang crime than his meddlingSun 4 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 16.29 EDTShareDonald Trump has enjoyed very few foreign policy victories since returning to power. From failed wars to failed peace processes, his second term in office has been marked by one costly blunder on the world stage after another. In Latin America, though, the US president has a different story to tell.His administration’s national security strategy outlined how the US wanted to “restore American preeminence in the Western Hemisphere”. It was a brazen document, laying out how his government would interfere in the political life of countries it considered part of its sphere of influence, rewarding governments and movements that are “broadly aligned with our principles and strategy”.To this end, Trump bailed out Argentina to the tune of $40bn and threatened to withdraw the funding if President Javier Milei’s party lost the midterm elections. In Colombia, he repeatedly bullied and threatened the leftwing president, Gustavo Petro, hitting him with personal sanctions and accusing him of being an “illegal drug leader”. And most dramatically, he invaded Venezuela and kidnapped its president. The day after Nicolás Maduro was brought to the US, the state department posted a picture of Trump above the slogan “This is OUR hemisphere”.Over the past 18 months, seven rightwing or far-right candidates have won presidential elections across Latin America. In most of them, Trump openly backed the winning candidate. “We’re doing very well in South America,” Trump said last month. “Lots of people that I got elected.”This weekend, he will be hoping to add the greatest prize of all: Brazil, South America’s biggest country and its largest economy. Flávio Bolsonaro, son of the former far-right president Jair Bolsonaro, is neck and neck with the leftwing incumbent,Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. If he wins, Trump wins – and the hemisphere really will be his.View image in fullscreenFlávio Bolsonaro, centre, on the campaign trail in São Paulo last week.Photograph: Allison Sales/APThe White House has not simply been watching the election from afar. Since Trump returned to power in January 2025, administration officials and Maga-world allies have been doing what they can to damage Lula and boost the Bolsonaros. Initially, the aim of the support was to keepJair Bolsonaroout of jail. Like Trump, he had not accepted defeat at the ballot box when he lost in the 2022 general election. Like Trump, his supporters stormed government buildings. But there were two crucial differences in Brazil – the seriousness of Bolsonaro’s attempt to hold on to power, and the determination of Brazilians that he should be held to account.Investigators uncovered asprawling conspiracyled by Bolsonaro and seven of his closest allies to keep him in power. It included an astonishing plot to kill Lula and his running mate, as well as a supreme court judge. A draft decree had been written that would overturn the result. The military would step in and ensure Bolosnaro returned to power. But the plot failed and Bolsonaro and allies, including his defence minister and the navy chief, were arrested and put on trial.In response,Trump threatenedin July 2025 to impose a 50% tariff on all imports from Brazil, arguing the case against Bolsonaro was a “witch hunt”. This blatant attempt at interfering in the judicial procedure of another country backfired. Lula made clear he wouldn’t bow to US pressure, the trial went ahead and Bolsonaro was found guilty and sentenced to 27 years in prison. Lula also received a bump in the polls after standing up to Trump.In July, as the election campaign was kicking into gear, Trump tried his tariff trick again, imposing a new 25% rate on some Brazilian goods. The state department then tried to dispatch two officials toBrazilto investigate “electoral integrity” – Brazil denied them visas, accusing the officials of coming to “meddle in Brazil’s elections”.In the final weeks of the campaign, Lula has leaned into those accusations. A recent advert accused Flávio Bolsonaro of being “Trump’s candidate” and said the US president wants “to colonise Brazil, take our riches, steal our future and leave us in the dust”. What remains unclear is whether the White House’s strategy in Brazil is working. “Some in Brazil joke that Lula’s most effective surrogate is Trump,” Brian Winter, editor in chief of Americas Quarterly, told me.Indeed, while Latin American countries have undoubtedly moved to the right in the past 18 months, US interference, despite Trump’s boasts, has arguably had little direct impact. In Peru and Chile, the Trump-aligned candidates were careful not to seek his endorsement for fear it would cause more trouble than it was worth.
