In Bolivia, the leftwing Mas government wasresponsible for its own downfall, winning just 3.16% in last year’s election after 20 years of increasingly chaotic rule.3:43How Trump is meddling in Brazil’s election – explainerThe biggest reason countries have moved to the right has nothing to do with the US and everything to do with safety and security at home. Organised crime gangs, many of them linked to drug trafficking, are increasing in power. AsCrisis Group put it in a report last year, while drug-related organised crime has been a problem across the continent for decades, “never has it spread so wide, and rarely has it penetrated so deeply into states and communities”. The failure of leftwing governments to deal with the problem has hurt them more than Trump’s attempts at interference.If there is a foreign president whose policies are having an influence on Latin America, it’s El Salvador’s Nayib Bukele. His authoritarian clampdown, which has involved arresting tens of thousands of people, mostly without legal process, has become a model for other rightwing leaders in countries beset by gang and drug cartel-related violence.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionDemocracy has been eroded andhuman rights trampled upon, but Bukele claims that his strategy – best described as “security populism” – has turned one of the most violent countries in the world into one of the safest. Other rightwing populists have found success in vowing to emulate him.In Brazil, Flávio Bolsonaro has made a crackdown on drug cartels and organised crime gangs the centrepiece of his campaign. “We’re going to give the streets back to the Brazilian people,” he said at a recent campaign stop, vowing to chemically castrate rapists and reduce the age of criminal responsibility.The Guardian view on Lula v the Bolsonaros: the decision of Brazilian voters will affect us all | EditorialRead moreOn this issue, Trump may have an influence. The US decision in May to designate two criminal organisations – the Red Command and First Capital Command (PCC) – asterrorist organisationshas put Lula on the back foot. Bolsonaro has campaigned relentlessly on the issue, accusing Lula of weakness. Lula has talked about targeting the crime boss “who lives in a penthouse”, but has been more comfortable campaigning on improvements he wants to make in education and health. Bolsonaro Jr, should he win, will almost certainly sign Brazil up to Trump’s Shield of the Americas, a coalition of 18 rightwing Latin American and Caribbean heads of state that promises to use “lethal military force to destroy the sinister cartels and terrorist networks”.Trump arguably paved the way for this new generation of Latin American political leader. His first victory in 2016 showed that posing as an outsider, using coarse language and embracing authoritarianism could be popular. Jair Bolsonaro was the first to emulate him, embracing the “Trump of the Tropics” tag. If Flávio Bolsonaro wins this month – either on Sunday or in the probable second round on 25 October – Trump’s ideology will dominate the continent.It is likely to outlast the man himself. The rise of organised crime has spread fear across the continent and, at the moment, the security populists are the only ones who voters believe have the answer. As long as that remains, the right’s grip on Latin America will only get stronger, regardless of who is in the White House.Steve Bloomfield is the former international editor of the ObserverExplore more on these topicsBrazilOpinionDonald TrumpUS foreign policyAmericasLuiz Inácio Lula da SilvaJair BolsonaroDrugs tradecommentShareReuse this content

title: It’s never been so easy to find answers. But sitting with uncertainty can ultimately bring wisdom | Muhammad Abdulsater | The Guardian
description: Even the greatest prophets had questions but they learned to wait to see the full picture
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Even the greatest prophets had questions but they learned to wait to see the full picture
Content: ‘We interpret delays as failures and endings as defeats. We rarely consider that we may simply lack the vantage point from which the full picture can be seen.’Composite: Getty images/Guardian DesignView image in fullscreen‘We interpret delays as failures and endings as defeats. We rarely consider that we may simply lack the vantage point from which the full picture can be seen.’Composite: Getty images/Guardian DesignMaking sense of itReligionIt’s never been so easy to find answers. But sitting with uncertainty can ultimately bring wisdomMuhammad AbdulsaterEven the greatest prophets had questions but they learned to wait to see the full pictureSun 4 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 16.50 EDTShareWe live in an age that has become profoundly uncomfortable with not knowing.A delayed email reply becomes a source of anxiety. A medical symptom is immediately searched online. We refresh news feeds, ask AI for instant explanations, and expect the answers to life’s biggest questions to arrive at the same speed as food deliveries.Modernity has conditioned us to believe that uncertainty is a dilemma to be solved.Perhaps that is why one of the Qur’an’s most remarkable stories, involving Prophet Moses and al-Khidr, feels so unexpectedly relevant today.In the story, Prophet Moses embarks on a journey to learn from a mysterious servant of God known as al-Khidr, otherwise known as the “Green One” or “Green Man” . Before the journey even begins, al-Khidr warns him: “You will never be able to remain patient with me.” It is a curious statement. Moses is one of the greatest prophets, a man of extraordinary faith and wisdom. If anyone should possess patience, surely it is him.My dad’s determination to choose life despite his cruel illness has taught me gratitude | Nomi KaltmannRead moreBut the lesson is not about Moses’s character. It is about the limits of human understanding. As they travel together, Moses witnesses some deeply troubling events. Among them, al-Khidr deliberately damages a boat belonging to poor fishers. He repairs a crumbling wall for a town whose people had refused them hospitality, without asking for any payment.Each time, Moses objects. Each time, he judges what he sees according to justice, compassion and reason. Each time, he is gently reminded that he does not yet possess understanding of the whole story.Only at the end of this story are the hidden reasons revealed. The damaged boat was saved from confiscation by a tyrannical king. The wall protected an inheritance belonging to orphaned children.The story is not asking us to suspend thinking or rational inquiry. Rather, the narrative exposes something far more subtle: our tendency to mistake partial knowledge for complete understanding.That tendency feels particularly familiar today.Our lives are increasingly shaped by technologies that promise certainty. Artificial intelligence summarises complex subjects instantly. We have become accustomed to immediate explanations, immediate diagnoses and immediate conclusions.The great paradox of our age is that although information has become ubiquitous, our tolerance for uncertainty has never been lower. We increasingly expect life itself to function like a search engine with immediate output in response to our input.The Quranic story of Prophet Moses and al-Khidr gently suggests that reality does not work that way.One of the most overlooked aspects of this story is that understanding arrives only after patience. The explanations are deliberately delayed. Had al-Khidr explained each event before it occurred, there would have been no lesson at all. The transformation lies precisely in learning to remain faithful before understanding appears.This challenges one of modernity’s deepest assumptions, that peace comes from having all the answers.The Islamic spiritual tradition proposes something different. Peace is not born from eliminating uncertainty but from learning how to inhabit it without despair.This is not an invitation to passive resignation or to explain away suffering. What the story offers is humility about the limits of our own knowledge and perspective.Most of us are living somewhere in the middle of our own stories. We judge our lives from chapter three without knowing chapter 20. We interpret delays as failures and endings as defeats. We rarely consider that we may simply lack the vantage point from which the full picture can be seen.That is why the story continues to resonate across centuries. It reminds us that there is a profound difference between something that is meaningless and something whose meaning has not yet become apparent.In a culture that rewards instant opinions and relentless certainty, perhaps one of the most radical spiritual practices is learning to say: “I do not yet understand.”Not because reason has failed. But because wisdom sometimes arrives more slowly than information.And perhaps faith begins, not when every question has been answered, but when we discover the courage to keep walking before the explanation arrives.Dr Muhammad Abdulsater holds a PhD from the school of law and business at the University of Notre Dame Australia where he is a sessional academic. He is also a student of Islamic sciences at the eHawza international school of Islamic theologyExplore more on these topicsReligionMaking sense of itPhilosophycommentShareReuse this content

title: The demands of Welsh devolution are simple: just give us what Scotland has | Will Hayward | The Guardian
description: Andy Burnham is a Westminster leader whom Welsh nationalists could finally work with - but only if he stands up to the devo-sceptics in UK Labour, says Guardian columnist Will Hayward
Author: Will Hayward
Headline: Andy Burnham is a Westminster leader whom Welsh nationalists could finally work with - but only if he stands up to the devo-sceptics in UK Labour, says Guardian columnist Will Hayward
Content: Rhun ap Iorwerth at Plaid Cymru’s annual conference in Llandudno, 2 October 2026.Photograph: Peter Byrne/PAView image in fullscreenRhun ap Iorwerth at Plaid Cymru’s annual conference in Llandudno, 2 October 2026.Photograph: Peter Byrne/PAOpinionWelsh politicsThe demands of Welsh devolution are simple: just give us what Scotland hasWill HaywardAndy Burnham is a Westminster leader whom Welsh nationalists could finally work with - but only if he stands up to the devo-sceptics in UK LabourSun 4 Oct 2026 08.21 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 11.22 EDTShareAs I sat in the firstPlaid Cymru conferencesince the party won the Welsh election and started leading the Welsh government, I heard things I had never heard before. I have been to a lot of Plaid conferences and not once have I heard people being really positive about a UK Labour leader. But there was no mistaking it: the Welsh nationalist party feels that Andy Burnham is a man it can work with.When I interviewed Welsh first ministerRhun ap Iorwerth, he indicated he was hopeful – in a way he never was under Keir Starmer – that there was a prime minister who had a genuine desire to give Wales meaningful concessions when it comes to additional powers.Inhis speech in Llandudno,the first minister saidthat the prime minister had“looked me in the eyes and promised he would not [bypass the Senedd]”. He said he had written to Burnham with a “formal ask” for “a new deal for Wales”.There were five demands from the Welsh government to Westminster: powers over policing and justice, powers over rail infrastructure, control overthe crown estate, “fiscal fairness” and control of welfare. Seems like a pretty long shopping list, right? Well, it can actually be summarised in just five words: “Give us what Scotland has.”The Scots have control of the crown estate, a better funding settlement, with moremoney through the Barnett formula,heavy rail is devolved, and the Scottish government controls policing and justice, as well as havingpartial control of welfare spending.Slowly then all at once: this emboldened Celtic alliance could spell the end of the UK | Simon JenkinsRead moreWhen you look at it from that perspective, it’s not as if the Welsh government is asking for something unprecedented. The UK government only has to look north to see the precedent.You don’t have to be a Welsh nationalist to think it’s unfair that Wales’s government is equipped with fewer tools than its Scottish counterparts to meaningfully tackle Wales’s challenges. Wales has lessborrowing capacity than a local counciland, as mayor of Greater Manchester,Burnham had more power over policingin his area than the first minister of Wales does.The stars are aligning forWalesto get more parity with Scotland. If Burnham follows his own devolution logic – that decisions should be taken closer to the people they impact –then how could he defend a region of England getting more autonomy than a nation?Though figures within Plaid clearly believe that Burnham is genuinely open to giving Wales more powers, they have real concerns that the more devo-sceptic figures within both the UK Labour party and the civil service will hinder their attempts. These fears are not unfounded. A leaked memo from Starmer revealed thathe warned his cabinetagainst being “overly deferential” to devolved governments. In December 2025,11 Labour Senedd members wroteto the then PM accusing him of “rolling back” devolution.View image in fullscreenRhun ap Iorwerth meets Andy Burnham for bilateral talks in Glasgow, 23 July 2026.Photograph: Alastair Grant/Pool AP/APThis fear led to one of the better lines in ap Iorwerth’s speech, where he said that if Burnham fails to give Cymru concessions:“Wales will know again that our best interests will never be served by Westminster, and that it matters little whether who lives in No 10 Downing Street is an Evertonian or an Old Etonian.”With all the talk of “the Burnham bounce”, one thing that I think is being missed in the wider media is the total collapse of Labour’s status in Wales. Before the Senedd election in May, Welsh Labour was themost successful democratic partyin history, having been the largest party in Wales at every general and Senedd electionsince 1922.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhen Labour was struggling in England and Scotland against the Tories, led by both David Cameron and Boris Johnson, Welsh Labour was winning election after election. But now Labour’s dominance in Wales is over. In a 96-seat Welsh parliament,Labour now has just nine seats.AtLabourconference in Liverpool, speaking to people on both the Welsh and UK sides of the party, it was clear to me that they were facing very different trajectories. UK Labour members were full of hope, optimism and excitement for what is to come: the conference was like an engagement party, to celebrate a union with their new partner.Meanwhile, Welsh Labour members had just broken up with their partner of 27 yearsand were totally cut up about the divorce. They were at the engagement party, trying to keep a stiff upper lip while nursing a can of strong lagerand wondering how they were going to afford to furnish their new one-bed flat.But this is a very bad time for Welsh Labour to have an identity crisis. All of the demands made by Plaid to Burnham arelongstanding Welsh Labour policies. For so long, Welsh Labour and devolution were synonymous with each other, but now the mood music is very different. Welsh Labour’s new leader,Ken Skates, has actively criticised Plaidfor pursuing the very policies Labour previously sought around more devolution.There is a chance for the people of Wales to get more direct tools to improve their own prosperity, but to do so they need all their representatives to understand the value of devolution and be united in their fight for it, regardless of the party they represent.Will Hayward is a Guardian columnist. He publishes aregular newsletteron Welsh politicsExplore more on these topicsWelsh politicsOpinionDevolutionWalesRhun ap IorwerthPlaid CymruLabourAndy BurnhamcommentShareReuse this content

title: Own a mobile phone? Then you’re paying the ‘app tax’. It’s a racket and it’s time the UK faced Apple and Google down | Chi Onwurah | The Guardian
description: A deep-seated duopoly allows the tech giants to exploit the public and developers. But the regulator has powers to stop this abuse – it should use them, says Labour MP Chi Onwurah
Author: Chi Onwurah
Headline: A deep-seated duopoly allows the tech giants to exploit the public and developers. But the regulator has powers to stop this abuse – it should use them, says Labour MP Chi Onwurah
Content: With no alternative platforms, app developers simply have to accept the terms set by Silicon Valley.Photograph: Yui Mok/PAView image in fullscreenWith no alternative platforms, app developers simply have to accept the terms set by Silicon Valley.Photograph: Yui Mok/PAOpinionSmartphonesOwn a mobile phone? Then you’re paying the ‘app tax’. It’s a racket and it’s time the UK faced Apple and Google downChi OnwurahA deep-seated duopoly allows the tech giants to exploit the public and developers. But the regulator has powers to stop this abuse – it should use themChi Onwurah is the Labour MP for Newcastle upon Tyne Central and West and chair of the parliamentary science, innovation and technology committeeSun 4 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 15.28 EDTShareDebates around big tech and digital regulation can sometimes feel distant from the everyday concerns of voters. But the power that a small number of global tech companies hold over our lives goes far beyond what most people realise.As chair of the parliamentary science, innovation and technology committee, I have spent years raising concerns about this: from the data they harvest and the digital “twins” they build of us, to the algorithms that decide what our children see.But there’s a much less visible example of this imbalance of power sitting in the pocket of almost every smartphone user in Britain: the app tax. Apple and Google control the two app stores through which almost every mobile app in this country reaches its customers, and that position lets them set terms for app developers that most businesses would never accept from a supplier. Sell a subscription, game or piece of software through either app store and both companies now charge a commission of up to30% on purchases made inside apps, regardless of what the product is or what it costs to make. With no alternative platforms, developers simply have to accept the terms set by Silicon Valley.Leave big tech behind! How to replace Amazon, Google, X, Meta, Apple – and moreRead moreDevelopers are also prevented from telling users that a cheaper option exists elsewhere, known as “steering”. That restriction is enforced by Apple andGoogleto protect their own profits. For small British developers who might struggle to absorb the cost, that could be the difference between hiring their next engineer or not, investing in a new product or shelving it, or growing their business here or uprooting and building overseas instead.Consumers pay the price, too. Research commissioned by the Coalition for App Fairness, asreportedin the Daily Mail, indicated that British consumers pay approximately £700m per yearto Apple and Google, a full £232m more than the companies paid in UK corporation tax last year combined. This is equivalent to around £55 annually for a household with four smartphone users. It is a cost built into the price of the product, invisible on any receipt, that has far more to do with market control and bolstering profits than anything the companies actually did to earn it.My last job before coming into parliament was with Ofcom, the regulator for communications markets. I was responsible for assessing the competitiveness of markets, because it is through competition that consumers get choice. The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) has found thatAppleand Google’s mobile platforms hold an effective duopoly, with at least 90% of UK mobile devices running on their mobile platforms. App developers have no choice but to distribute their product through the Apple App Store or the Google Play Store. If a developer happened to dislike Apple’s terms and another app store existed, they would take their app, and their customers, elsewhere, and the price would fall. But there is no alternative app store on an iPhone, and no practical route for Android users outside Google Play either. Apple and Google set the rules unchallenged.Parliament anticipated this problem when, in 2024, it passed theDigital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act(DMCCA) with cross-party support, giving the CMA genuine powers to force dominant platforms to change their behaviour. But, so far, the CMA has resorted to weak, voluntary commitments from Apple and Google rather than requirements it is actually obliged to enforce.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionStop shaming people for using AI. Start organizing to prevent our obsolescence | Garrison LovelyRead moreIts consultation on “steering”, which would finally let developers point users to cheaper options elsewhere, has now closed and a decision is due soon. Many are rightly nervous that this could end up with another voluntary gesture, rather than a binding rule, deemed acceptable.But this moment also represents an opportunity. It will be one of the first serious decisions this government makes on big tech, and will likely determine the direction it takes on this issue. The prime minister has been clear, both before and since entering Downing Street, that tech sovereignty means reducing our dependence on a handful of overseas platforms. I want to see that instinct applied to decisions such as this.This is not about being anti-technology or anti-growth. It is about whether British consumers, British developers and British regulators are able to shape the terms on which technology operates in our own market and influences our society. I urge the CMA to use the powers we gave it, and I urge my colleagues in government to back it in doing so.Chi Onwurah is the Labour MP for Newcastle upon Tyne Central and West and chair of the parliamentary science, innovation and technology committeeExplore more on these topicsSmartphonesOpinionAppsGoogleAppleMobile phonescommentShareReuse this content

title: Ninety years on, the lessons of the antifascist battle of Cable Street have never felt more relevant | Sarah Sackman | The Guardian
description: With sectarian forces increasingly seeking to divide us, we must come together to fight for security, fairness and tolerance, says Labour MP for Finchley and Golders Green Sarah Sackman
Author: Sarah Sackman
Headline: With sectarian forces increasingly seeking to divide us, we must come together to fight for security, fairness and tolerance, says Labour MP for Finchley and Golders Green Sarah Sackman
Content: Supporters of Danny Tommo (Daniel Thomas), self-styled leader of the ‘Patriot Platform’, stand outside the offices of the Daily Mail in London, 9 September 2026.Photograph: Denise Laura Baker/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSupporters of Danny Tommo (Daniel Thomas), self-styled leader of the ‘Patriot Platform’, stand outside the offices of the Daily Mail in London, 9 September 2026.Photograph: Denise Laura Baker/Getty ImagesOpinionAntisemitismNinety years on, the lessons of the antifascist battle of Cable Street have never felt more relevantSarah SackmanWith sectarian forces increasingly seeking to divide us, we must come together to fight for security, fairness and toleranceSarah Sackman is the Labour MP for Finchley and Golders GreenSun 4 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 06.16 EDTShare“Nopasarán!” – they shall not pass. It’s the rallying cry that strikes at the core of my identity. The same anti-fascist slogan heard by my Spanish grandmother, who endured the horrors of that country’s civil war, echoed in London where my Jewish paternal grandparents lived. Ninety years ago, it was this cry that united tens of thousands of East Enders, who stood tall against Oswald Mosley’s Blackshirts at thebattle of Cable Street.The story is well known. In 1936, disparate communities came together to block the far right from marching – Jewish residents, Irish dockers, Somali seamen, trade unionists, independent socialists and communists alike.These groups were not uniform in identity, background or belief. Their solidarity was the expression of a tolerant Britishness, where neighbours look out for one another. When Mosley’s fascists wanted to rid British society of them, they stood together to defend their right to be different, while finding common cause in a Britain that had given them sanctuary.Ninety years later, the contest to define Britishness is with us again.We see it in thebalaclava-clad mobsin Dover and Portsmouth, and scenes of immigrants beingburned out of their homes in Belfast. Much like Mosley’s Blackshirts, these extremists push a narrow ethnonationalism with no space for different faiths or backgrounds.After Golders Green, this is what British Jews need from the government, the police – and the rest of society | Dave RichRead moreAnd it is not just the far right that threatens a tolerant, inclusive Britain. The extremism of recent years also comes from extreme Islamist sources and perpetrators of violent hate crimes.Earlier this year, in my constituency,Jewish volunteer ambulances were torched. A month later,two visibly Jewish men were stabbed. My community, where I was born and raised, came under attack.I condemned, with clarity, sectarian ideology and violent intimidation for what it is: un-British and antisemitic. As I said in the aftermath, an attack on Britain’s Jews is an attack on Britain itself.The Labourgovernment’s response to new extreme threats must be hard-edged and decisive.We proscribedIran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) –suspected of beingbehind the ambulance attack – and made record investment in local policing.But we must also champion a new, progressive patriotism. Extremists and sectarians create division in order to exploit it – be it the Islamist extremist whomurdered Jews in cold bloodat Heaton Park, Manchester, or the far-right thugs who assault police officers on marches. Responding by fuelling culture wars and inciting further violence, as some political leaders did, makes things worse. So-called anti-racist groups staying silent on the antisemitic violence on our streets makes things worse.We must instead win the argument about what it means to be British. We must model a politics that is curious about difference, not frightened of it. One that embraces those who trace their roots to the Domesday Book as well as the granddaughter of Jewish and Spanish immigrants. A dynamic patriotism that accepts that some things will change, and others will endure.We cannot be naive about the threat to our shared values. We must tackle those who seek to undermine our way of life, without demonising entire communities. But patriotism cannot only be about what we are against – it has to be a vision we are fighting for.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn 2013, the Somali Bravanese Muslim community centre in Barnet, north London, was burned to the ground, and theletters EDLwere found sprayed on the building. Finchley Reform Synagogue (FRS)opened its doors for the Somali Bravanese communityto pray and to heal. And, in 2026, afteran attempted arson attack on the FRS, the Somali Bravanese community showed upin force for the Friday night Shabbat service. Somali and Jewish communities were resilient, together, in defence of our home in Britain – just like at Cable Street.That’s the Britain I fight for. A tapestry of different cultures that creates a rich, proud, resilient British identity. When sectarian forces seek to divide us, our challenge is to fight for security, fairness and tolerance.As the prime minister, Andy Burnham, said in his party conference speech, we need to build a country of solidarity, not separation. That is the spirit of Cable Street. And we must declare once again to those who see violent intimidation as the answer: “No pasarán!” – they shall not pass.Sarah Sackman is theLabourMP for Finchley and Golders Green and minister of state for courts and legal servicesDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.Explore more on these topicsAntisemitismOpinionIslamophobiaFar rightImmigration and asylumOswald MosleyReligionLondoncommentShareReuse this content

title: Star Wars actor John Boyega on the day his 10-year-old school friend Damilola Taylor was killed: ‘It kept me up at night because I was just with the guy’ | Damilola Taylor | The Guardian
description: The star was just eight when his friend was stabbed. Decades on, he’s ready to talk about that day – how it shaped him, and how, as he becomes a father himself, it will shape him as a dad
Author: JN Benjamin
Headline: The star was just eight when his friend was stabbed. Decades on, he’s ready to talk about that day – how it shaped him, and how, as he becomes a father himself, it will shape him as a dad
Content: John Boyega:Photograph: Austin Hargrave/Austin Hargrave / AUGUSTView image in fullscreenJohn Boyega:Photograph: Austin Hargrave/Austin Hargrave / AUGUSTDamilola TaylorStar Wars actor John Boyega on the day his 10-year-old school friend Damilola Taylor was killed: ‘It kept me up at night because I was just with the guy’The star was just eight when his friend was stabbed. Decades on, he’s ready to talk about that day – how it shaped him, and how, as he becomes a father himself, it will shape him as a dadJN BenjaminSun 4 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 08.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“Ifeel a bit nervous,” confesses John Boyega, as he sits down in front of the camera. “Speaking about it could possibly help. I haven’t revisited this in a long time. Yeah, my heart is just beating.” The Attack the Block and Star Wars actor is talking in the opening scene of a new BBC Two documentary about the killing of 10-year-old schoolboyDamilola Taylor.On 27 November 2000, Damilola was stabbed in the leg with a broken bottle and left to die in a concrete stairwell, attacked as he walked home from an after-school club at Peckham library in south London. It took six years and three separate trials at the Old Bailey, costing a total of £16m, to secure a manslaughter conviction. His death shocked the nation not only because he was so young, but because all the suspects were also children. Boyega was one of the last people to see Damilola alive. The pair had enjoyed a close friendship since Damilola’s move to the UK from Nigeria in August of that year.View image in fullscreenDamilola Taylor, who was just 10 when he was killed.Photograph: PAWatching the film at a Bafta screening a few weeks before its premiere, it’s striking how young and vulnerable the 34-year-old actor looks as he talks about the death of his friend. Boyega is more often seen looking assured and confident, be that his impassioned, impromptu address to thousands of people at a Black Lives Matter protest in Hyde Park, posing for the Pirelli calendar, or portraying an African king in a Hollywood movie. Usually he stands tall, with broad shoulders supported by a proud stance. But in revisiting the memories of that day, it feels as if he has almost reverted to the eight-year-old child he was nearly 26 years ago when he found out his friend had died.A couple of hours later I reconvene with him at BBC New Broadcasting House to discuss the show. In person, Boyega is unassuming, with a calm demeanour and a welcoming smile. He has just returned from a trip to New York fashion week and looks surprisingly fresh-faced for somebody who has not long stepped off a transatlantic flight.Boyega is sitting comfortably with his father Samson, his mother Abigail and an older cousin. It’s a lively space – Boyega lives in Los Angeles now and I get the impression that everybody is excited to snatch a bit of time with him while he’s in London. We immediately get into a five-way conversation about the criminal proceedings around Damilola’s death. Everybody is talking at once.The first trial collapsed after the judge ruled that the prosecution’s key witness was unreliable and there was controversy about items of crucial evidence that were excluded from the proceedings. The family closely followed all three trials – in the second, the jury failed to reach a verdict for two of the three defendants on a charge of murder – and there is a sense of frustration at the opportunities missed when it came to bringing the killers to justice.“You would have thought the influence of the Stephen Lawrence case would have been way stronger, if they had actually learned something. It didn’t come across like that,” Boyega sighs. The police investigation was heavily criticised after it was found to have made a number of significant mistakes.The whole Boyega family knew Damilola; but the actor has previously said very little about him in public. Boyega has worked consistently since his 2011 debut in sci-fi cult classic Attack The Block, including a gamechanging role as a lead in Disney’s Star Wars franchise. His most recent projects, The Woman King (2022) and They Cloned Tyrone (2023), were both critically acclaimed. He has said that his professional success is in no small part due to being inspired by the way Damilola lived his short life.View image in fullscreenBoyega in 2011 film Attack the Block.Photograph: Optimum Releasing/ Sportsphoto/AllstarHe has been deeply involved in the documentary. “The first time I watched a rough cut I was in my living room and it was bright out. Since then, we’ve been watching daily edits, y’know, on a phone, on a laptop, on a little TV. But viewing it in the cinematic setup hits different – it was an emotional hill to get over, seeing the film like that. I feel really impacted by it.” Throughout the 75-minute screening, crying and sniffling could be heard around the room. “It’s one of those films I wouldn’t watch multiple times because of my personal relationship to it, but it’s definitely a film I will refer to – when my child comes of age I will show him this film. You need to know the realities of your lineage.”On Damilola Taylor’s first day at Oliver Goldsmith primary school in Peckham, shortly after his arrival in the UK, a teacher assigned Boyega’s sister Grace to be his chaperone. She says in the documentary: “My teacher was like, ‘Grace, there’s a new guy and he’s from Nigeria and obviously you’re Nigerian so you understand the language – you can show him around.’” They became a trio, because Boyega and his sister were inseparable at the time.“The only reason I was around him a lot was because I was always with my sister – I inherited Damilola,” Boyega tells me, laughing. “I stayed because I found him hilarious.”double quotation markThe psychological impact is something that definitely stayed with meView image in fullscreenBoyega in a still from the documentary about Damilola.Photograph: BBC/Optomen TVHis father chimes in with a poignant memory: “John don’t have many friends – at least not boys. John had girls surrounding him. And I remember asking, ‘John, why are you hanging around girls?’ and he said, ‘Dad, boys are dangerous – they’ll beat me up.’” At lunchtimes, the three of them would run around the playground together.Boyega describes the day Damilola died as a transformational moment for him. “The psychological impact is something that definitely stayed with me, but now it’s expressed through appreciation. Every time I wake up and I’m here, I appreciate it.” He smiles as he says of talking to his friends: “I’ll tell my boys, ‘Hey, a bullet don’t look at you and be like, “You’ve done movies before,” and swerve you!’” As a child, though, his thoughts were less positive. “When I would hear that anybody had been stabbed or whatever, it just felt like it was getting closer and closer and that awareness became part of day-to-day life. I was very scared of that.”Boyega was eight when Damilola was killed; he had previously thought that death “only happened to old people”. He was bewildered by it – “like when babies fall and everyone goes, ‘Oh my gosh!’ and then the baby [seeing the response] decides to cry? It was like that.” As the news sank in, he found it difficult to comprehend that bad things could happen to good people. “I was trying to compute what that meant. I thought about the practicality of it. The last breath. Does it hurt? I remember with Grace we would have conversations where I’d be like, ‘Do you think death is sleep?’ or, ‘Maybe they go for 20 years and then, they come back?’ It kept me up at night because I wasjustwith the guy, y’know?”In the aftermath of Damilola’s death, Boyega spent a lot of time at home in his bedroom. Sometimes friends would knock for him and he would tell his mother to relay the message that he didn’t want to go out. “The hand of death is influencing kids to kill kids. I’m like, ‘Damn, I’m a kid, let me stay where I feel the most safe.’ I had a home that granted extreme safety and my parents didn’t shy away from showing concern.”This played out in many ways, including their choice for his secondary school. Instead of the options in their home borough, he was sent to Westminster City School – almost an hour away by bus. Was getting out of the area a response to Damilola’s death? Boyega’s father answers: “Before John says anything, I went to his teacher when he was going to secondary school and he said to me, ‘Mr Boyega, why do you have to choose Westminster?’ And I never said to him what I saw: that the environment here will corrupt this guy,” he says, pointing at his son. “I saw what was coming, that in the future this environment is going to be very, very dangerous.” This was in 2003. By the end of the decade, 188 teenagers had been murdered on the streets of London.I direct the conversation back to Boyega. Did he have therapy back then? He lowers his chin and looks at me with a furrowed brow. What he appears to be conveying is there’s no such thing as therapy in an African household – especially not a 1990s African household. We both laugh. At this point I am conscious that my question could easily be construed as a criticism of his parents, who are sitting on the sofa opposite us in the suddenly quite claustrophobic room. We quickly move on.Over the years there have been numerous documentaries focusing on various aspects of Damilola’s killing, from a 2002 BBC Panorama special to most recently one fronted by broadcaster Yinka Bokinni to mark the 20th anniversary of Damilola’s death. This latest project focuses much of the narrative on the 24 hours leading up to his killing.We hear from a number of people who were critical to the investigation in its early stages, including the estate maintenance worker who first found Damilola as he lay bleeding in the stairwell. There were several months of discussions between Boyega and the director, Alex Thomas – who also directed the award-winning Sky Original documentary Bibaa and Nicole: Murder in the Park, about the 2020 killings of Bibaa Henry and Nicole Smallman. “It fell to me to decide who was coming from my world to sit down and talk,” says Boyega. “That’s when I decided that Grace would be more appropriate to discuss Damilola than me because that was her direct friend – they were around the same age. And I think her perspective on it was quite important.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThat was the easy part. More difficult was deciding how to address the ecosystem of bullying and fear on the streets of Peckham that led up to and ultimately underpinned Damilola’s killing. In the final edit, much of this element of the storytelling is omitted.It doesn’t go unnoticed. During a Q&A after the screening, a Bafta member in the audience queries the lack of backstory included about the lives of the two boys convicted of Damilola’s manslaughter. In August 2006, brothers Danny and Ricky Preddie were each sentenced to eight years in youth custody after the third trial. The questioner pointed out that the brothers appeared at the Old Bailey unattended by any family. “I’d love to know why you left that out,” they said, referring to the brothers’ troubled childhoods. It was well known that their single mother struggled immensely while raising them. The pair were eventually placed in a local authority children’s care home. “We did look at the option of interviewing the two brothers,”said Boyega, who explained a general concern within the team that it might be viewed as being too empathetic to the perpetrators. In the end, the decision was made not to approach them.But Boyega agrees that some elements of their backstory do have a place in the narrative, in particular when it comes to the debate about how to end youth violence. “Family. Discipline,” he says decisively. “The fact that you don’t have an adult at home that holds you accountable is a very important thing, especially for boys. Especially for boys.” He repeats the last sentence a little slower to emphasise its importance. “But y’know, you could have two parents at home and the child still goes out and does what they need to do, so there’s obviously a more nuanced conversation. Even in the sense that someone showed you that they loved you, that they cared about what you did or whether or not you made a mistake. What that person [in the screening Q&A] said made me think about what it meant – that they didn’t have that. Not even a social worker.”double quotation markI didn’t know I was poor until I was in year 7. When you’re super-young, you’re not really thinking about that. When you get to school, you start to see where you are in the food chain of lifeThere’s an extended silence when I ask Boyega what was difficult about making the documentary. “Poverty,” he replies, eventually. He means it brought back memories of the poverty he experienced as a child. Growing up, he lived in a small flat on Sceaux Gardens estate just off Peckham Road, with both his parents and his elder sisters – Grace, who appears in the documentary, and Blessing, who generally keeps a much lower profile. His mother was a care worker and his father a Pentecostal minister. “I didn’t know I was poor until I was in year 7. When you’re super-young, you’re not really thinking about that. And then when you get to school, you start to see where you are in the food chain of life, and that’s when you start to compare yourself with other children and other kids.” The process of filming the documentary brought that world back into focus.Boyega recalls being keen not to stand out for the wrong reasons in his first year at Westminster City School, and begging his mother to buy him a pair of Kickers. She took him to Barrie Howard, a shoe shop on East Street in Walworth – a strategic rite of passage for any south Londoner who hoped to survive the brutal transition from primary to secondary. But once he had the shoes he felt bad, because he could tell how much it cost her. “I never asked for Kickers from my mum again – I wore Clarks for the rest of school.” Recounting these memories, plus seeing the archive footage of Peckham and the burgundy Oliver Goldsmith school sweater, brought back the distinct feeling that he had so much less than many of his peers. “I did work hard to get out of that. In making this film I had to revisit who I used to be, and that bothered me.” The interviews took place while he was on location in the Isle of Skye making a supernatural horror movie,The Punishing, in which he stars alongside Cara Delevingne (it is currently in post-production). The surroundings served as a physical reminder of how far he’s come in life.View image in fullscreenBoyega with Oscar Isaac in Star Wars: The Force Awakens, 2015.Photograph: Disney/Lucasfilm/AllstarView image in fullscreen… and with his family at the London premiere of Star Wars: The Last Jedi, 2017.Photograph: PA Images/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.Boyega had some reservations about being involved in the project. His main concern was that he wanted to make sure that Damilola’s brother – Tunde Taylor, chair of the Damilola Taylor Trust – was happy with the way Damilola’s life is portrayed. “I’ve been in the public eye for a minute now and from my experience, you have to be very careful, because you don’t know which journalist is being stressed by an editor. You don’t know which person wants to grab a story and not use it with the right intentions. You don’t know if they’re gonna be respectful to the people who are really involved.” But he was reassured by meeting producer Nelson Adeosun, a childhood family friend, and fellow contributor Leroy Logan. Logan is the founder and former chairman of the Black Police Association, whom Boyega portrayed in the film Red, White and Blue, from Steve McQueen’s 2020 anthology series, Small Axe. The performance won him a Golden Globe award.Settling down thousands of miles away from Peckham has inevitably changed Boyega’s relationship with the place that made him who he is. “South is still familiar, but if I go now, people have to guide me … it’s so, so different,” he says, referring to the gentrification of the area. For him, though, the heart of the place is in the people who remember what it was like when he was growing up. We do a little reminiscing about which legendary hangouts have survived. He is pleased to note that Bagel King is on the list.Somebody pokes their head round the door to tell us we need to wrap up. Boyega’s on a tight schedule. I ask a final question. Tell me about your jewellery, I say, indicating towards his left hand. “Oh yeah, this is my wedding ring,” he says casually. “I’ve been married for coming up to two years now.” He doesn’t give any detail about his wife, but does say they had a small ceremony, joking that he got married the way Braveheart did, while miming the action of planting a sword in the ground. He continues by reaching to the deepest depth of his vocal range and bellowing, “Will you come with me?”His eldest sister has now joined us and the room has erupted into a chorus of unrestrained laughter. I note that the ring he is wearing is different from the one he wears in the documentary. “Yeah, this is our very sentimental ring,” he says of the two-toned band. “This is the one we decided to pick up spontaneously because I just wanted the ring on my finger, so we went to Walmart to get this. It was a lovely trip to Walmart. Shout out, Walmart Canoga Park!” he laughs. I am surprised to learn that he didn’t have a traditional Nigerian ceremony. “I would love to have a wedding celebration. We both like the idea of celebrating something established, rather than celebrating the entry. And by then, we’ll have to shut Nigeria down!”It occurs to me that the child he mentioned earlier in the conversation may not be hypothetical. Are you about to hard launch a baby, I inquire tentatively. “My baby’s on the way. We got a baby cooking.” And you said my son earlier – is that because you’re having a boy? He confirms this and that he also has a young stepson. “So, you know, my life is completely, completely fulfilled in terms of family. It’s been so nice with the timing.”Getting used to the new dynamic away from the public eye has obviously served him well – and perhaps this is why he is now ready to speak publicly about his friendship with Damilola. “I do think it’s important to reach back and tell people the grounded realities of your origins, because it wasn’t until I knew the grounded realities of other people’s origins that I decided to pursue something more.” When thinking about the kind of father he wants to be, it’s all still sinking in. “Us being parents is funny! I just want to make sure I’m present, I’m consistent and full of love.”These personal milestones explain why he’s been less visible in recent years. “I’ve tried to as much as possible – especially following periods when I’ve worked a lot – to de-centre my career. There have been certain moments when I’ve known that this is a time for family. Y’know, there’s stuff to do.” In this moment he’s clear that his purpose is to love his wife and sons and invest in the support system that he knows he is lucky to have had.Damilola: The Untold Story is on BBC Two and iPlayer from 5 OctoberExplore more on these topicsDamilola TaylorJohn BoyegaDocumentary filmsDeath and dyingChildrenFriendshipKnife crimefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘It’s OK to love somebody when they’re not perfect’: how John Cena conquered Hollywood – and why he refuses to abandon Vince McMahon | Movies | The Guardian
description: By embracing the role of amiable lunk, the wrestler turned actor has become an unlikely, and very modern, leading man. But does his relationship with the WWE, and its controversial former owner, risk tarnishing his brand?
Author: Sasha Mistlin
Headline: By embracing the role of amiable lunk, the wrestler turned actor has become an unlikely, and very modern, leading man. But does his relationship with the WWE, and its controversial former owner, risk tarnishing his brand?
Content: Mass appeal … John Cena.Photograph: Joe PuglieseView image in fullscreenMass appeal … John Cena.Photograph: Joe PuglieseMoviesInterview‘It’s OK to love somebody when they’re not perfect’: how John Cena conquered Hollywood – and why he refuses to abandon Vince McMahonSasha MistlinBy embracing the role of amiable lunk, the wrestler turned actor has become an unlikely, and very modern, leading man. But does his relationship with the WWE, and its controversial former owner, risk tarnishing his brand?Sun 4 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 10.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleImust admit, I was apprehensive about meeting John Cena. The WWE wrestler turned actor has built an enviable Hollywood career playing idiots – capable idiots with real heart, but dimwits nevertheless. Still, Cena is obviously nobody’s fool; fools don’t rise from humble beginnings to become their generation’s answer to Hulk Hogan or The Rock. Would the Cena who appears on my computer screen be the real one? Or something closer to the comic-book characters he embodies so well: guileless, silly and fond of a deliberate misunderstanding?It is immediately clear that this is no manchild. Perfectly punctual, he greets me with a lavish formality befitting a man who made his film debut as the title character in The Marine. Within a minute he has volunteered, unprompted, that “a core value of mine is respect”. Cena, 49, is speaking to me on behalf of Matchbox: The Movie, a film extension of the Mattel toy car brand for Apple TV, and for 45 minutes he is generous, funny, complimentary and elusive without ever being evasive. It’s a genuinely radical thing for a man built like a chest freezer – having only recently retired from wrestling after 26 years – to be so relaxed about being ridiculous, and in an age of such joyless online strongmen as Trump, Musk and Andrew Tate, his buff charm is welcome.John Cena is a company man. The word “loyalty” comes up often, and about everything from his friends back home to the wrestling to the US itself. Admirable, no doubt. But Cena’s loyalty has drawn him into some uncomfortable positions, and for 20 minutes our good-natured chat about reliability, discipline and what it means to owe everything to something bigger than yourself has set us on a collision course with one of the most disgraced figures in modern entertainment.View image in fullscreenCar trouble … John Cena in Matchbox: The Movie.Photograph: Jasin BolandIn January 2024, Vince McMahon, the all-powerful chairman and CEO of WWE, resigned from the organisation and its parent company TKO Group Holdings following a slew of sexual assault allegations and pending lawsuits that made his position in the company he’d spent his life building untenable. The final straw was a suit filed by a former WWE employee, Janel Grant, alleging that McMahon sexually assaulted her and pressed her into sexual acts during her time at the company, sent explicit images of her with other men without her consent, and passed her to others – in one instance, the filing says, to help secure a wrestler the company hoped to sign. McMahon denies all the allegations and in June, the litigation between him, the WWE and Grant was transferred voluntarily by all parties from the federal court into confidential private arbitration.McMahon was a mentor to Cena, and as well as sponsoring his career, provided him a second family amid the travelling circus of 00s wrestling. “I have no guilt nor shame about my friendship and my relationship with Vince McMahon,” he says, swiftly followed by “you’re obviously going to put this in [your] article”. He’s right, of course. What is strange isn’t that he foresaw this line of questioning – it’s that Cena took such an unequivocal stance in the face of something so potentially damaging. He is audibly proud of the association, revelling in the idea that he’s abiding by his principles in the face of what he calls “the storm”. “It’s OK to love somebody when they’re not perfect,” he says.Cena was born in West Newbury, Massachusetts, in 1977, one of five boys in a household that watched every dollar. His grandma and grandpa lived in an adjoining house. “There was a lot of ‘How are we going to pay the bills, how are we going to keep the lights on?’” Cena says. He worshipped the movie action men of the era – Schwarzenegger, Stallone, Willis – but he also loved hip-hop, which in suburban Massachusetts made him a target for bullies. Bodybuilding was the answer, and it doubles as an origin story – the boy bullied for dressing like a white rapper, growing up to become an icon for the next generation of suburban youth.Still, when I raise it, Cena is quick to correct the emphasis: the bullying wasn’t the point; his response to it was. “I didn’t treat hostility with hostility,” he says. “I got bullied for the way that I dressed, so I dressed more outlandish.” The muscle was a visible deterrent. “I’ll just project a physical sense of: Man, I don’t want to press my luck with that guy,” he says.After college, he drove to California in 1999 with about $500 to follow Schwarzenegger’s playbook to bodybuilding glory. He worked on the shop floor at Gold’s Gym in Venice Beach for six dollars an hour, and for a stretch, slept in the back of his 1991 Lincoln. A wrestler who worked out at Gold’s steered him towards the industry and in 2000 he made his debut in WWF (now WWE) as The Prototype, a robotic character whose deliberate speech was a clear nod to his idol Arnie. He was paid $250 a week “which meant I spiralled into debt”. To Cena’s credit he understood that the short-term loss had the potential to lead to long-term gain. “I’ve been pretty astute at understanding when luck arrives,” he says.View image in fullscreenLord of the ring … John Cena at a WWE event in Toronto in 2024.Photograph: WWE/Getty ImagesWhat followed was a 24-year stint as a WWE superstar, a period Cena describes without irony as “service”. “You can’t fake that,” he says. “If you’re in the business of bullshit, somebody’s going to see through it.” He stumbled on a character that stuck: a jersey-wearing, battle-rapping white kid from Massachusetts, who literally went by the name John Cena. Despite some distrust from fans – over his general clean-living, wholesome persona – and fellow wrestlers who initially ostracised him for not engaging in the hard-boozing that was par for the course, the gimmick worked. In fact it was so successful that it led to the slightly odd ongoing situation where Cena doesn’t own his own name.“John Cena is who I am as a human being,” he says, “and there is a company – WWE/TKO – that has invested hundreds of millions of dollars in the intellectual property of the character John Cena. And rightfully so; they have earned their share of ownership of that.” In Cena’s words he read and understood the agreement and he thought it was fair. However, the lingering sense that a career at the top of WWE requires a deal with the devil prevails (Dwayne Johnson onlygot his own moniker, “The Rock”, back in 2024, and now sits on the board of TKO). But Cena explicitly rejects the idea that he has had to make sacrifices along the way. “I prefer to use the word choice … When we say yes to something, we say no to everything else.” In effect, he gave up his name for the rare chance to live his dream.And for more than a decade he did. Cena was beloved throughout the 2000s and early 2010s primarily as an avatar for a certain brand of flag-waving, white masculinity that was firmly in tune with the climate of post-9/11 America but is maybe less so now. Donald Trump was a recurring presence in WWE during this period, memorably shaving McMahon’s head after besting him at WrestleMania and even “buying” flagship brand Raw as part of the pair’s staged rivalry. The DNA of today’s toxic masculinity can be seen in the WWE’s Attitude era: Muslim performers were painted as would-be terrorists; female wrestlers, known as “divas”, were sexualised, fighting in “bra and panties” matches; and scandals around steroid abuse and traumatic head injuries were raised in lawsuits.double quotation markRather than trying to take the reins of a movement or be the poster child for something, I’m just trying to be meThe miracle of Cena’s career is that the man who spent a decade as the straight-faced embodiment of American masculinity proved to be equally good at sending it up. After a handful of underwhelming action and sports film roles, he was cast against type by Judd Apatow for the 2015 romcomTrainwreck, playing a musclebound hunk whose attempts to be threatening just sound homoerotic. Then as the pumped-up Peacemaker, first in superhero movieThe Suicide Squad(2021), then in the comedyspin-off seriesnamed after the character, Cena managed to strike a balance between serious man and silly goose that would be tricky without a healthy amount of self-awareness. This quality was on full display during Cena’s small but charming turn as a merman inBarbie, a commitment to the bit that was all the more admirable given his agents tried to talk him out of the role.Matchbox, his latest film, is a vague attempt to recapture Barbie’s magic in the more contained format of a traditional action comedy. Cena admits feeling relieved when he read the script and found the cars to be “so far down the list of things they were doing with the IP”. He plays Sean, an undercover operative whose entire life is a performance. When I wonder aloud whether the part sits close to the bone, he eagerly connects the dots himself: “How does someone who thinks they’re always being watched act in a public place? That I got a little bit of familiarity with.”Cena’s onscreen persona is an intriguing model of masculinity: the strongman remade as softie. What’s more, his wall-to-wall presence in the childhoods of millennial men makes him a far more credible advocate of positive manhood than a Joe Rogan or a Jordan Peterson. But he is reluctant to assume the mantle. “Rather than trying to take the reins of a movement or be the poster child for something, I’m just trying to be me,” he says, before offering his own diagnosis of why so many people are in the business of selling a personal vision of masculinity. “The appetite for a certain kind of manhood is just supply and demand,” he says. To the people clamouring for it, “my advice would be: go get it”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenHero move … John Cena and Danielle Brooks in Peacemaker.Photograph: HBOPerhaps Cena’s lack of desire to be cast in the role is emblematic of why it would suit him. The system, he says, “is real fragile … if I say I’m going to be the showcase of masculinity and the supply-and-demand chain pivots in five minutes, I’m shit out of luck.” He is keen to underscore how much he “loves the United States and admires its military force that makes the vow to, under the ultimate sacrifice, protect that piece of paper that says ‘We the People’. To me, that’s extremely heroic.”Cena’s own heroism came into question in 2021 when, while promotingFast & Furious 9, he referred to Taiwan as “a country”. The Chinese audience took offence, and he filmed a contrite apology in Mandarin, a language he had been learning for six years in an attempt to grow the WWE’s presence in China. In the US, the grovelling video read less as an apology than a capitulation to the weight of China’s economic might. The fan backlash was so intense that he told James Gunn he’d understand if he had to be fired from Peacemaker. He takes full responsibility for the episode. “Just because you know the language doesn’t mean you know the culture,” he says, admitting, “I got way too overconfident. I thought I was the smartest guy in the room.” Part of what frightened him was the very real possibility of “the termination of employment that I love”. The same reflex to remain loyal to the brand has carried him, without complaint, to numerous events in Saudi Arabia. “WWE offers a universal language of diplomacy,” he says. “So, to your question of: ‘Hey, the thing that you’re in is sometimes criticised for the moves that it makes as an entity – is that difficult?’ Of course it is, especially when you believe in the entity.”For a man who prides himself on saying yes, it is revealing what he has time and time again said no to. Cena does not want children, and the reasoning is entirely in keeping with his sense of discipline: they’d simply require too much of him. From 2002 to 2015 he was home “about 15 days a year and even now it’s maybe 70”, he says. “If I said yes to children, I have to say no to everything else.” His engagement to fellow wrestler Nikki Bella – his co-star on the reality show Total Bellas – collapsed in 2018, in large part over whether to have them. Cena, who’d had a vasectomy, offered to reverse it, but the relationship ended shortly after.“I really enjoy my life,” he says. Cena has granted more than 650Make-a-Wishwishes, more than anyone alive. He sees his ability to do so much work for the organisation as inextricably linked to being child-free. “If I have a family of my own, I don’t have those 650 moments … I’m flying with just my partner on this one.” Cena married Shay Shariatzadeh, an Iranian Canadian tech product manager, in 2020, after meeting in Vancouver while he was shooting a film. They had only been together a year but he’s said he would have proposed after three months. “I have a loving connection that people don’t see,” he says. “I don’t need the world to totally know me as a person.”Wrestling With Trump review – the president gets an almighty smackdown!Read moreHe remains on the WWE’s books as a “brand ambassador”, a reflection of his gratitude to the company, but also an unresolved transition back into civilian life. Next up, he will star in One Attempt Remaining, a comedy from Kay Cannon (director of Blockers and the writer-producer behind the Pitch Perfect series). He plays one half of a divorced couple who is forced to team up with his ex in order to track down the lost password to a crypto account worth millions. Whereas Dwayne Johnson has become a brand bigger than his wrestling fame, you get the sense Cena will never fully escape his WWE persona, his screen performances a callback to the exaggerated version of himself he’s been playing since 2002.Perhaps that’s what it is to be a company man: not an empty suit or a servile mouthpiece but a person so thoroughly committed to the brand it is simply who he is. Present, punctual, polite and perfunctory. The job is done and it’s back to the gym.Matchbox: The Movie premieres on Apple TVon 9 October.Explore more on these topicsFilmWrestlingCelebrityinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I can’t listen to Pink Floyd - I find their music dreary’: Elvis Costello’s honest playlist | Elvis Costello | The Guardian
description: The singer-songwriter owes a lot to Georgie Fame and likes the romantic side of Jimi Hendrix – but which ringtone song can put him in a bad mood?
Author: Rich Pelley
Headline: The singer-songwriter owes a lot to Georgie Fame and likes the romantic side of Jimi Hendrix – but which ringtone song can put him in a bad mood?
Content: ‘Karaoke? Certainly not. I do this for a living’ … Elvis Costello.Photograph: Mark SeligerView image in fullscreen‘Karaoke? Certainly not. I do this for a living’ … Elvis Costello.Photograph: Mark SeligerHonest playlistElvis Costello‘I can’t listen to Pink Floyd - I find their music dreary’: Elvis Costello’s honest playlistThe singer-songwriter owes a lot to Georgie Fame and likes the romantic side of Jimi Hendrix – but which ringtone song can put him in a bad mood?As told toRich PelleySun 4 Oct 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe first song I fell in love withThe Wind Cries Mary by Jimi Hendrix, which came out in 1967 when I was 12. Hendrix was known for outgoing music, but I was a romantic soul, so the emotional side of his music led to that strain in my own writing.The song I do at karaokeKaraoke? Certainly not. I do this for a living. Would you have made my great-grandfather dig ditches for fun? I prefer to live vicariously through Bill Murray singing (What’s So Funny ’Bout) Peace, Love and Understanding in Lost in Translation.The song I inexplicably know every lyric to’Cross the Green Mountain by Bob Dylan is a bit hidden away, but in the very top tier of his songwriting. It’s full of images from the American civil war: conflict, overwhelming love, officers being shot, mothers receiving terrible news. It’s poignant and involving.The first single I boughtI saved my pocket money to buy the Fame at Last EP by Georgie Fame from Potter’s Music Shop in Richmond. He introduced me to Gerry Goffin and Carole King, Louis Jordan, Ray Charles, Big Joe Turner, Mose Allison, Willie Dixon and Lambert, Hendricks & Ross – which was a lot of education for an 11-year-old who didn’t play an instrument.The song I can no longer listen toAnything by Pink Floyd. Never could, never will. I find their music dreary. I love the imagination and playfulness of See Emily Play, but after Syd Barrett left they just never appealed to me.The best song to have sex toHow impertinent.The song I secretly like, but tell everyone I hateI’ve written a few songs that I secretly hate, but I can’t think of anything I secretly like apart from Milkshake by Kelis – and I don’t think that’s a secret.The best song to play at a partyI haven’t been to a party since I was 15. Then it would have been Double Barrel by Dave & Ansel Collins.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe song that changed my lifeMy mother claimed I’d request I’ve Got You Under My Skin by Frank Sinatra before I could form sentences. I can still visualise the record player we had in our basement flat near Olympia, which had a red eye on the front and looked a bit like a robot.The song that gets me up in the morningArmagideon Time by the Clash. I found having Good Morning from Singin’ in the Rain as my ringtone put me in a bad mood.The song I want played at my funeralKeepin’ Out of Mischief Now by Louis Armstrong.My Aim Is True (49th Anniversary Edition) is out now.Explore more on these topicsElvis CostelloHonest playlistPop and rockJazzReggaefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘We have been dispossessed’: Nick Hayes on land rights and a peaceful revolution at the real Toad Hall | Books | The Guardian
description: The co-founder of the Right to Roam campaign and author of The Book of Trespass discusses the Oxfordshire riverside community he calls home and how Hardwick Hall has been taken back by the people
Author: Patrick Barkham
Headline: The co-founder of the Right to Roam campaign and author of The Book of Trespass discusses the Oxfordshire riverside community he calls home and how Hardwick Hall has been taken back by the people
Content: Nick Hayes at the Hardwick Estate.Photograph: Megan Eagles/The GuardianView image in fullscreenNick Hayes at the Hardwick Estate.Photograph: Megan Eagles/The GuardianBooksInterview‘We have been dispossessed’: Nick Hayes on land rights and a peaceful revolution at the real Toad HallPatrick BarkhamThe co-founder of the Right to Roam campaign and author of The Book of Trespass discusses the Oxfordshire riverside community he calls home and how Hardwick Hall has been taken back by the peopleSun 4 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn the banks of the Thames in South Oxfordshire, the Hardwick estate has been owned by the Rose family for generations. When Sir Charles Rose, a banker, sportsman, yachtsman and aviator, sped through the lanes in his Rolls-Royce in the early days of motoring, heinspired Kenneth Grahameto create Mr Toad in The Wind in the Willows. Grahame’s character became a symbol of decadent aristocracy whose foolishness leads to the temporary loss of a fine house to weasel-socialists.Now Toad Hall has been taken over for good and Nick Hayes, artist, writer and co-founder of the Right to Roam campaign, has had a riverside view of this striking turn of events. When Hayes, who lives on a beautiful wide-beamed barge on the Thames, became the Hardwick estate’s artist-in-residence, he discovered that Rose’s heirs are, in effect, disinheriting themselves. The estate is gradually being turned into a charity which will be run by the tenants and the alternative community that has grown up in its shelter.The story of this peaceful revolution unfolds in his new book, The Medicine Tree, a sweeping alternative history of England that reaches across the globe for examples of colonial oppression and Indigenous enlightenment. Hayes poses some big questions. Why do English people lack a culture of connection with their land? And how might we forge a new one?Indigenous societies have stories, songs, philosophies and religions that bind them to their terrain. Such sacred traditions are still alive in many countries and can encourage modern societies to live sustainably, resist pollution and extraction, or create assertive legal rights for nature, as established on New Zealand’s Whanganui River. It is “an act of extreme exceptionalism to suppose that we were the only country on Earth not to have had a spiritual, mythopoetic relationship with the land,” Hayes writes.“If we were to look at English history through a colonial prism, we’d start to see ourselves as people that have been dispossessed as well,” he says, as we talk inside his cosy boat, swallows dipping over the water. “Community and ecology are the two big losses. England is in desperate need of repair in terms of epidemics of loneliness, in terms of one in six species going extinct.”There was no one moment when England’s land culture was lost, Hayes argues, but “a very steady letting of England’s veins” over 2,000 years: Christianity took away animism, while myth and folklore was lost with enclosure and the agricultural and industrial revolutions. The Medicine Tree is his attempt to plot a recreation of a useful English land culture: not nationalistic, not nostalgic and not off-the-peg folklore as invented by, say, Robert Graves in The White Goddess.Hayes was inspired by poet and storyteller Hugh Lupton’s idea of “restorying the landscape” to take one local tree, his “medicine tree”, as a symbol of his story. This soaring tree, beside the busy Thames path, turns out to be a hybrid of a (native) black poplar and an eastern cottonwood, brought to Europe from North America by French colonists. It invites a comparison between disparate cultures, not least because in both Indigenous and old European societies the poplar stood for community.Hayes grew up near here in the 80s and 90s. When we meet he is wearing a grubby pink vest adorned with an image of the Cerne Abbas giant and has just watched two boys jump into the water from the pretty, white-painted bridge that dinks over the river at Pangbourne. The elder boy led the way with a back-flip; his nervous younger brother eventually following with a maiden jump. “Did you see that?” he says. “It was so beautiful.”It is an idyllic scene but it is also bittersweet. The Thames has sewage discharged into it by privatised water companies and the bridge, nicknamed “the troll bridge” by locals, is an anachronistic privately owned toll bridge, which causes traffic jams every morning as motorists queue to pay 60p to cross the Thames. The bridge belongs to a company owned by a family who can trace their ancestry to one of William the Conqueror’s barons. Hayes estimates this local waster of everyone’s time enriches the company by more than £1m each year.View image in fullscreen‘I wanted to lean into the whole story as a fairytale, a folktale’ … Nick Hayes.Photograph: Megan Eagles/The GuardianThe English mostly accept such states of affairs as normal, natural and possibly even desirable. When Hayes was young, he couldn’t wait to escape this “affluent, middle-class” suburban environment and assumed he would never return. He had no real connection with the land, or nature, until university, where he was taught by Robert Macfarlane. After reading Macfarlane’s book The Wild Places, he cycled from Cambridge to wild-camp on the Gog Magog hills outside the city. “I felt like a weirdo bedding down, had a joint because I didn’t know if I’d sleep, and woke up having had a gorgeous night. The membrane burst in my head,” he says. He began camping with friends in fields and forests, trespassing, and learning more about the land.In 2020, he and Guy Shrubsole founded the Right to Roam campaign, seeking a responsible right of access to the 92% of land in England and Wales we are now excluded from. Hayes put his vision inThe Book of Trespass, a strikingly original, bullishly well-written declaration of the benefits and responsibilities that could flow from people being granted more access to private land. In the years since, Right to Roam has held more than 15 peaceful mass trespasses and defended attempts to restrict access by major landowners, including a court battle by a hedge fund manager seeking to curb wild camping rights on Dartmoor.double quotation markWhen people come to the country, it doesn’t take them long to shed their need for a mobile phone, to shed their post-industrial mindThe Medicine Tree follows Hayes’s journey home, living on his boat (because no artist could afford a house in this London commuter belt), and discovery of Hardwick, where an alternative community of around 90 tenants renting on the estate has slowly coalesced over several decades. On learning how their family wealth was ultimately derived from colonial extraction and exploitation in North America, the sibling heirs to the land have decided to turn it into a charity, andEngland’s first community-owned estate.In The Medicine Tree, the members of this community are named only after their occupations: the Dyer, the Head Grower, the Heiress. “I wanted to lean into the whole story as a fairytale, a folk-tale,” says Hayes. Unlike much contemporary nonfiction, Hayes does not fill the book with himself but instead directs his rage at the “taxidermied corpse” of English heritage, with its country houses that are “decorative manhole covers on a system of sewerage that drained, and still drains, the wealth of England and the world”.Hayes strikes me as a natural rebel, but he bristles at this for the same reason he doesn’t like being described as “a campaigner”: he thinks it diminishes taking a rational stand against an issue by suggesting it is a personality trait. That said, he read Christopher Hitchens’s Letters to a Young Contrarian “about 15 times”. He has always opposed “unfair or pointless rules. The big thing for me is orthodoxies so deep-set that they don’t even seem to be rules any more.” He points to a “Danger! Adders in this area” sign, one of many trophies that ornament his boat. “The purpose of that sign is to keep people out of their land, not warn people of adders. I would suggest that most adders are unsigned. All of these things can embed in our operating system.”What’s also embedded in England’s exclusionary, profit-making system of land ownership are landowners’ rights. Hayes tells of his community’s (daring, futile) attempts to stop the no-fault, short-notice eviction of the Carver and his family from their home on a neighbouring estate. “Losing a family who have done nothing but contribute to this valley for 26 years made me realise that eviction is not just an action against one family but an action against a community. The thing that makes me contrarian is that we just accept it. There doesn’t have to be a society where eviction is seen as the landowner’s right.”How do we reforge a culture of connection with the land? More land rights would help, says Hayes, but so would more time on the land. “I’m not suggesting that everyone needs to be a basket weaver, but when people come to the country from the town, it does not take them long to shed their need for a mobile phone, to shed their post-industrial mind.”As night falls, people from all over Hardwick emerge from the darkness to gather in a circle on the banks of the Thames beside Hayes’s boat. They bring guitars and accordions and even a saxophone. Songs are played and stories are told.“I’m wondering if land culture just grows like weeds,” says Hayes. “This English obsession with ancient heritage is tripping us up. Put people together with a certain amount of freedom, rights and responsibilities – work, duties, stuff to do on the land. People are going to start talking. People are going to start singing.”The Medicine Tree: Repairing the Rotten Roots of England by Nick Hayes is published by Allen Lane. To support the Guardian order your copy atguardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.Explore more on these topicsBooksScience and nature booksfeaturesShareReuse this content
