title: Mike Nelson review – a waking nightmare of derelict dunes and desert island despair | Art | The Guardian
description: Entropy and hopelessness become thrillingly confrontational in this ambitious show, which recreates Nelson’s studio, shacks and sand dunes in dilapidated form
Author: Eddy Frankel
Headline: Entropy and hopelessness become thrillingly confrontational in this ambitious show, which recreates Nelson’s studio, shacks and sand dunes in dilapidated form
Content: ‘The whole thing is an illusion. It always was’ … Mike Nelson, Double Negative (The Clown), 2026.Photograph: Dan Weill/Modern Art Oxford/courtesy the artist and 303 Gallery, New York; Galleria Franco Noero, Turin; Matt’s Gallery, London; and neugerriemschneider, BerlinView image in fullscreen‘The whole thing is an illusion. It always was’ … Mike Nelson, Double Negative (The Clown), 2026.Photograph: Dan Weill/Modern Art Oxford/courtesy the artist and 303 Gallery, New York; Galleria Franco Noero, Turin; Matt’s Gallery, London; and neugerriemschneider, BerlinArtReviewMike Nelson review – a waking nightmare of derelict dunes and desert island despairModern Art OxfordEntropy and hopelessness become thrillingly confrontational in this ambitious show, which recreates Nelson’s studio, shacks and sand dunes in dilapidated formEddy FrankelSun 4 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 05.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt’s either a cry for help or a scream into the void. Whichever it is, Mike Nelson’s latest exhibition is the English artist at his most frustrated, scared, introspective and personal. This is a show filled with rot and dilapidation, insanity and dereliction. It’s big, ambitious, immersive, complex and very, very good.It’s not Nelson’s first time at Modern Art Oxford.He was last here in 2004, with a crumbling shack in the process of being swallowed by desert dunes. The shack is back, rebuilt in the same gallery, as if it never actually left – just temporarily blinked in and out of temporal existence. But it’s different now, more weathered, more broken. And that vast pile of sand is different too – you can see that it’s not a real dune, it’s a thin layer of sand held up on carpets and a rusted metal frame. The whole thing is an illusion. It always was, we just couldn’t see it.He’s recreated his old studio in the first gallery too, but stripped of the ephemera and materials that make up an artist’s work space. Now it is largely empty, its shelves bare. A projector flips through slides of self-portraits next to a broken mirror and a human skull. Nelson is feeling pretty damn self-reflective, clearly.View image in fullscreen‘Things have only got worse’ … Mike Nelson, Double Negative (The Clown), 2026.Photograph: Dan Weill/Modern Art Oxford/courtesy the artist and 303 Gallery, New York; Galleria Franco Noero, Turin; Matt’s Gallery, London; and neugerriemschneider, BerlinAnd who can blame him? Returning to the site of an early major exhibition 22 years later he’s taking stock, asking what has changed. And the answer is not very much. When he first built that desert shack, it was back in the early days of the Iraq war. He was dealing with ideas of power, destruction and protest, and hoping desperately for change. Now in 2026, are things any better? We’ve got wars in Iran, Sudan, Ukraine, Israel and Gaza, we’ve got madmen in power, we’ve got conspiracy theories being taken as gospel. All these years later, things have only got worse.So now the shed has crumbled further into the desert, now it is littered with socialist party pamphlets and broken crucifixes. Now the foundations have been exposed and everything you believed in has been shown to be a lie.So all you can really hope for is escape. In a side gallery, an invigilator locks you in a bedroom with a single metal cot and shelves lined with travel books. You can’t travel to Thailand or New Zealand from here but, in this filthy, miserable little room, you can dream about it, and that’s better than nothing. The last time I saw this work it felt claustrophobic and overbearing, as if I’d been imprisoned with only my thoughts and dreams of travel for company. This time, with all the dilapidation in the galleries outside, it feels like a sanctuary.View image in fullscreen‘I’ve never seen him this clear and obvious and concise’ … Mike Nelson, Double Negative (The Clown), 2026.Photograph: Dan Weill/Modern Art Oxford/courtesy the artist and 303 Gallery, New York; Galleria Franco Noero, Turin; Matt’s Gallery, London; and neugerriemschneider, BerlinNelson’s big into the idea of desert islands these days. There’s a photocopy of an introduction to a book about Robinson Crusoe pinned to a door, there are vast white sculptures that are half-skull, half-conch shell plonked around the place, as if Nelson is imagining isolation in tropical paradise as the only way out of this societal nightmare.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toArt WeeklyYour weekly art world round-up, sketching out all the biggest stories, scandals and exhibitionsEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe spaces are connected by a rickety mining shaft which spits you out into a Lynchian cinema foyer, where most doors lead nowhere. Normally, Nelson shows feel like you’re stumbling across fragments of novels and trying to piece things together, but I’ve never seen him this clear and obvious and concise. Or this nakedly personal. Sure, the show is kinda like a Mike Nelson’s Greatest Hits compilation, but I think he’s looking back at his past, comparing it with his present, and feeling nothing but total, utter despair. It’s brutally affecting, and dizzyingly overblown. Cry for help or scream into the void, whichever it is, it’s miserably relatable.AtModern Art Oxford, 3 October to 11 AprilExplore more on these topicsArtInstallationExhibitionsSculpturereviewsShareReuse this content

title: Antigone Exits review – emotions run high in experimental reworking of Greek tragedy | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Nina Segal’s revisiting of the Sophoclean story is pleasingly experimental – but not all the ideas work in Jeff James’s fourth-wall breaking production
Author: Holly O'Mahony
Headline: Nina Segal’s revisiting of the Sophoclean story is pleasingly experimental – but not all the ideas work in Jeff James’s fourth-wall breaking production
Content: Blurred boundaries … Max-Bennett as Creon in Antigone Exits.Photograph: Andy ParadiseView image in fullscreenBlurred boundaries … Max-Bennett as Creon in Antigone Exits.Photograph: Andy ParadiseTheatreReviewAntigone Exits review – emotions run high in experimental reworking of Greek tragedyMinerva theatre, ChichesterNina Segal’s revisiting of the Sophoclean story is pleasingly experimental – but not all the ideas work in Jeff James’s fourth-wall breaking productionHolly O'MahonySun 4 Oct 2026 06.43 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLibations were typically poured to appease the gods and honour the dead in Ancient Greece, but as a black, tar-like substance is dribbled here, forming a runny circle on a bright yellow stage, the image conjures danger. It’s befitting for the court of this particular King Creon (Max Bennett), whose condemnation of his niece Antigone (Nina Cassells) after she defies him in retrieving her brother’s body for burial, is framed as an inability to even question let alone reconsider his own laws. The tar circle becomes a dividing line, separating the hypothetically welcome from the unwelcome in Thebes. The line is eventually crossed in more ways than one, and the oily substance spreads, smearing those irrevocably affected by the mess.Nina Segal’s revisiting of the Sophoclean tragedy is keen to explore the far-reaching consequences of our actions and their trickle-down effects. It’s pleasingly experimental, but not all ideas coalesce in Jeff James’s production, in which a combination of fourth wall breaking and direct address sees the boundaries blur further. Cast members break away from their Greek characters to relay anecdotes that could well be their own. Reaching for a mic that hangs suspended above the stage, one tells of watching a fox decompose, another of a husband dying and another of his teenage daughter’s suicide. The stories are moving, even if links to Antigone’s own plight are somewhat tenuous.View image in fullscreenTimeless appeal … Alex Lowde’s set.Photograph: Andy ParadiseAn emphasis is placed on emotions over actions, but having each key player describe their anger, fear or sadness, rather than showing us, has a distancing effect that prevents this production from striking the chords it might. Watching them mine seemingly personal memories in order to find a connection to these centuries-old characters is a little like watching a workshop in method acting.There’s a timeless appeal to Alex Lowde’s set, which features a giant hollowed-out eggshell structure, out of which the cast emerges one by one to take up their positions, as if born into the play. Later it becomes the cave through which Antigone vanishes, and as the rest look on, we’re reminded again of what lingers – physically and emotionally – after death.Antigone Exitsruns at the Minerva theatre, Chichester, until 17 October.Explore more on these topicsTheatreSophoclesChichester Festival theatrereviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Undertones review – silver-haired fans get Teenage Kicks once more | Punk | The Guardian
description: Derry’s answer to the Ramones play 30 songs in a breakneck and breathless ride through the punk humour and new-wave surrealism of their repertoire
Author: Katie Hawthorne
Headline: Derry’s answer to the Ramones play 30 songs in a breakneck and breathless ride through the punk humour and new-wave surrealism of their repertoire
Content: Far from sentimental … Paul McLoone and Michael Bradley in the Undertones.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenFar from sentimental … Paul McLoone and Michael Bradley in the Undertones.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianPunkReviewThe Undertones review – silver-haired fans get Teenage Kicks once moreCorn Exchange, EdinburghDerry’s answer to the Ramones play 30 songs in a breakneck and breathless ride through the punk humour and new-wave surrealism of their repertoireKatie HawthorneSun 4 Oct 2026 08.09 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 08.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“This is the first record we ever made. Still sounds good to me,” smiles bassist Mickey Bradley, deliberately downplaying the song released in 1978 that secured the Undertones’ legacy for almost 50 years and counting. Played hard and unceremoniously tonight, Teenage Kicks still sounds lonely, horny, thrilling: it’s the stuff of raw teen spirit, but has also aged poignantly with the Derry band and their now silver-haired audience, with something moving to say about the weight of nostalgia.When brothers John and Damian O’Neill’s guitars crash to a halt, many in the crowd are hugging – but the Undertones are already on to the next. This anniversary tour is far from sentimental: ripping through 30 songs in 90 minutes, it’s a breakneck ride through the punk humour, new-wave surrealism and open vulnerability of their first two albums.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSleeve NotesGet music news, bold reviews and unexpected extras. Every genre, every era, every weekEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenCrashing guitars … lead guitarist Damian O’Neill, whose brother John plays rhythm.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianYou’ve Got My Number (Why Don’t You Use It!), with its bouncing, fidgety frustration, remains an all-timer about waiting by the phone, while Male Model rages against a penny-pinched fashion crisis with a tongue-in-cheek, Ramones-y chorus. There’s surfy guitar and barbershop harmonies on (She’s a) Runaround, mixed with slice-of-life commentary about a girl dithering her life away, and the quiet tragedy of Jimmy Jimmy buried beneath that earworm melody. All the while drummer Billy Doherty is flying, holding the band to a breathless pace.The first incarnation of the Undertones lasted just eight years, and when they returned in 1999 it was without quivery-voiced frontman,Feargal Sharkey. Singer Paul McLoone was a savvy recruitment – he pulls off the shaky, brittle vocals that some of their classics demand, but is otherwise an entirely distinct performer. Tonight he’s flamboyant, cutting flamenco shapes with his arms twisted in the air, and his richer voice brings out the hip-shaking, even glam, qualities of rock’n’roll tracks such as Get Over You and (relatively) newer cut 2003’s Thrill Me.Despite its morbid title, unreleased newbie Time is Terminal accelerates faster still – as if the band are playing to outrun that teenage legacy, rather than indulge it. Are teenage dreams so hard to beat? Bus-pass punk feels just as essential. Here’s to the next 50 years.The Undertonesare touring the UK and Ireland.Explore more on these topicsPunkPop and rockreviewsShareReuse this content

title: TV tonight: Eric Morecambe’s children’s book comes to life | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: The Reluctant Vampire is a fun story starring Lenny Rush. Plus: secrets are spilled in juicy divorce drama The Split Up. Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Hollie Richardson
Headline: The Reluctant Vampire is a fun story starring Lenny Rush. Plus: secrets are spilled in juicy divorce drama The Split Up. Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: No biting … The Reluctant Vampire on BBC One.Photograph: BBCView image in fullscreenNo biting … The Reluctant Vampire on BBC One.Photograph: BBCTV tonightTelevision & radioTV tonight: Eric Morecambe’s children’s book comes to lifeThe Reluctant Vampire is a fun story starring Lenny Rush. Plus: secrets are spilled in juicy divorce drama The Split Up. Here’s what to watch this eveningHollie Richardson,Priya Elan,Phil Harrison,Graeme VirtueandSimon WardellSun 4 Oct 2026 01.15 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 01.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Reluctant Vampire6.40pm, BBC OneFifteen-year-old Valentine (Lenny Rush) grew up thinking he was a really rubbish vampire. But his mother (Sian Clifford) is about to tell him the reason why he doesn’t have bloodlust: he’s actually a human. She asks him not to tell his loving but despairing father (Tom Davis) – the vampire king! Can poor Valentine pull off being the heir to the vampire throne? Neil and Rob Gibbons – the team behind Alan Partridge – have done a fun job of adapting Eric Morecambe’s much-loved children’s book.Hollie RichardsonWagging Rights8pm, U&WHalfway through the competition and we’re into the freestyle challenge. It’s a fully choreographed routine or, as Rhod Gilbert explains, “It’s like Strictly Come Dancing, but with a human and a dog.” With the judges wanting clarity as well as a full spin, will Sara Pascoe and Mouse manage to retain their, erm, lead?Priya ElanThe Split Up9pm, BBC OneView image in fullscreenWedding woes … The Split Up on BBC One.Photograph: BBC/Sister PicturesThe penultimate episode of Ursula Rani Sarma’s family law firm drama arrives, and it’s the morning after the eventful night of spilled secrets before. Aria wakes up in Luke’s bed – and the day ahead involves them working hard on a meaty divorce case with Aria’s husband-to-be. Concludes on Monday.HRThe Blame9pm, ITV1It’s notable how many cop shows currently involve internal malfeasance. Ahead of the return of Line of Duty, this generic but sturdy drama continues to intrigue. This time, Michelle Keegan’s implacable DI Crane finds a suspect slipping through her fingers. But this strengthens her conviction that the real problem lurks within Wakestead station.Phil HarrisonStar Trek: Strange New Worlds10.15pm, ITV1In the year of Star Trek’s 60th anniversary, it’s pleasing that this vibrant streaming hit – a direct prequel to the original series – is getting beamed down to terrestrial TV. Season two begins with Spock (Ethan Peck) behaving in a very Kirk-like fashion by stealing the USS Enterprise to save a crewmate.Graeme VirtueThree Women11pm, Channel 4In a series based on Lisa Taddeo’s nonfiction book, Shailene Woodley plays a writer who follows three women who “had the audacity to believe that they deserved more”. They are homemaker Lina, who starts an affair, Sloane, who is in an open marriage, and Maggie, who had a sexual relationship with her high-school teacher.HRFilm choiceThe Deb,6.15am, 5.45pm, Sky Cinema PremiereView image in fullscreenBrush up! … The Deb on Sky Cinema Premiere.Photograph: Vertigo ReleasingRebel Wilson’s directorial debut is the subject of long-running legal disputes but you wouldn’t know it from watching this sweet, simple musical comedy. It’s set up as a city v country clash: rebellious Sydney teenager Maeve (Charlotte MacInnes) is banished to the bush to stay with farming cousin Taylah (Natalie Abbott) in “the town where feminism has come to die” – and where the debutante ball is still a thing. Issues of body positivity and stifled ambition are showcased in songs with a certain Aussie pep (the first one is titled Fuck My Life).Simon WardellThe Order,10pm, BBC TwoJude Law adds to his recent run of interesting character choices (Putin, Henry VIII, a Star Wars villain) in Justin Kurzel’s gripping fact-based crime thriller. He plays FBI agent Terry Husk, whose new posting to rural Idaho comes with an Aryan Nation splinter group, led by Nicholas Hoult’s charismatic Robert Jay Mathews, who are progressing from counterfeiting and bank robbery to something much bigger. Law’s Husk is a convincingly raddled near has-been but he’s a dog with a bone when he gets a sniff of Mathews’s racist plot.SWThe Crime Is Mine, 12.50am, BBC TwoProlific French director François Ozon is the master of many genres, and the comic melodrama – of which this is his latest – is his most effortlessly enjoyable. In 1935 Paris, struggling actor Madeleine (Nadia Tereszkiewicz) is falsely accused of killing a famous theatre producer. However, aided by her flatmate, lawyer Pauline (Rebecca Marder), she plans to confess to “legitimate defence”, hoping the publicity will be good for both their careers. That is, until Isabelle Huppert’s wrecking ball of a silent film star pops up.SWLive sportWomen’s Super League Football: West Ham v Chelsea, 1.30pm, Sky Sports Main EventMan City v Arsenal is at 4.15pm.Uefa Nations League Football: Wales v Denmark, 7.30pm, BBC TwoAt Cardiff City Stadium.Explore more on these topicsTelevision & radioTV tonightfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Once Upon A Time In Sokoto review – exuberant history lesson on intra-African slavery | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Inua Ellams displays a Stoppardian or Fraynian relish in turning complex topics into enjoyable theatre in his latest play
Author: Mark Lawson
Headline: Inua Ellams displays a Stoppardian or Fraynian relish in turning complex topics into enjoyable theatre in his latest play
Content: Expansive narrative … Will Atiomo, Adeola Yemitan and Antonia Layiwola in Once Upon A Time In Sokoto.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianView image in fullscreenExpansive narrative … Will Atiomo, Adeola Yemitan and Antonia Layiwola in Once Upon A Time In Sokoto.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianTheatreReviewOnce Upon A Time In Sokoto review – exuberant history lesson on intra-African slaveryRoyal and Derngate, NorthamptonInua Ellams displays a Stoppardian or Fraynian relish in turning complex topics into enjoyable theatre in his latest playMark LawsonSun 4 Oct 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 11.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOver the last decade, Inua Ellams has written inventive and educational plays centred on modern Nigeria, starting withBarber Shop Chroniclesin which hair care allowed cutting commentary on masculinity and politics.AlthoughThe Half God of Rainfallhad a detour to Mount Olympus, typical of Ellams’s structural fun, the focus was postcolonial Nigeria, his superb relocation of Chekhov’sThree Sistersto 1960s Africa showing ructions resulting from British imperial ruler Lord Lugard coercing the playwright’s birth nation from multiple cultures.Across 24 scenes set from 1865 to 1903, when Lugard crushed local resistance, Ellams’s new play, Once Upon A Time In Sokoto, maps pre-colonial history, mainly around the many emirates of the Sokoto Caliphate in West Africa but with diversions to Libya and Egypt.Using aspects of traditional storytelling – the audience learns a call-and-response chant in the Hausa language – the expansive narrative is anchored to Zinari (Antonia Layiwola), a matriarchal upper-class entrepreneur, and Nafisa (Adeola Yemitan), her former slave who fights for more agency. Suggesting a precocious feminism in the culture, Ellams also illustrates its limits. When Zinari chooses to be childless, her husband, Hadiru, (Bayo Gbadamosi) cites religious law to take Nafisa as a second, fecund wife.For many, the play will be a history lesson, though more exuberant and engaging than most schools. Ellams’s international curriculum, though, teaches much deeper.View image in fullscreenTragedy and comedy … Atiomo and Layiwola  in Once Upon A Time In Sokoto.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianMoral horror about slavery, in this case intra-African, incorporates a cold-eyed account of its economics: “Nafisa’s value has quadrupled 433% to one million, one hundred and forty thousand.” The currency is cowries, sea snail shells, showing how this economy – including literal shell companies– develops competition, taxation, inflation and a catastrophic crash when international predators – represented by the British-schooled Yusufu (Will Atiomo) – flood the market with imported cowries. This felt to me more fiscally astute than James Graham’s JM Keynes play,The Standard Of Living.Another subject tackled is philology, developing languages shown through clashes over rival alphabets and the colonisers’ import of exotic metaphors: “Many ways to skin a cat” alarms pro-feline Egypt. We learn the meaning of “Boko Haram”, later claimed by a Nigerian jihadist group.The fabular note in the title Once Upon A Time In Sokoto also often inflects the text. Anticipating modern advertising, Zinari adlibs an “ancient” legend to raise sales of her indigo cloth. Later, she and Nafisa conduct a late-19th-century poetry slam in a market square, the former’s Koranic verse trumped by the latter’s more populist quasi-rap.Scattering incidental but engaging data – the introduction of the lip kiss to a forehead-rubbing culture, the colonial significance of Millwall FC shorts – Ellams shows a Stoppardian or Fraynian relish in enjoyably compressing complex topics. His cast adept at tragedy and comedy, director Roy Alexander Weise brings characteristic grace and pace, a domestic conversation transitioning within seconds to a funeral.At theRoyal and Derngate, Northampton, until 10 October,then touring.Explore more on these topicsTheatreInua EllamsNigeriaBritish empireSlaveryreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Wakaliga Uganda review – a blistering superhero movie with hardboiled cops and a nefarious ‘girl with a voluminous bum’ | Art and design | The Guardian
description: A young man possessed by the spirit of a mythical Buganda warrior leads the film-making collective’s explosive new diatribe against the theft of cultural artefacts – with the help of a ‘video joker’
Author: Ben Eastham
Headline: A young man possessed by the spirit of a mythical Buganda warrior leads the film-making collective’s explosive new diatribe against the theft of cultural artefacts – with the help of a ‘video joker’
Content: A message without jeopardising the entertainment … Wakaliga Uganda: Kibuuka Omumbaale.Photograph: Courtesy of the artistView image in fullscreenA message without jeopardising the entertainment … Wakaliga Uganda: Kibuuka Omumbaale.Photograph: Courtesy of the artistArt and designReviewWakaliga Uganda review – a blistering superhero movie with hardboiled cops and a nefarious ‘girl with a voluminous bum’Chisenhale Gallery, LondonA young man possessed by the spirit of a mythical Buganda warrior leads the film-making collective’s explosive new diatribe against the theft of cultural artefacts – with the help of a ‘video joker’Ben EasthamSun 4 Oct 2026 03.04 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 03.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWakaliga Uganda makes action movies with a cast from the Kampala streets, props built out of scrap, desktop special effects and a bucketload of wit. The studio’s breakout hit,Who Killed Captain Alex?, followed a martial arts master on a mission for revenge against the mafiosi who killed his brother, a Ugandan military officer sent to clean up the capital’s slums. Featuring helicopter gunships, shootouts and kung fu showdowns, and reportedly made for a few hundred dollars, this blockbuster bears little relation to the films you might expect to find in an art gallery (setting aside the shoestring budgets). Which is to say, it is very good fun to watch.Founded by Harriet Nakasujja and Isaac Nabwana, the film studio also known as Wakaliwood came to the attention of the wider art world in 2017 when it was included in the German art festivalDocumenta. That influential show was part of a general turn towards the culture being made by independent collectives outside Europe and North America, especially those that pioneer unconventional ways to fund their activities (indicatively, the studio used the money to install fibre-optic cables in its neighbourhood). Its entry on to the international art circuit brought higher production value and – if the new commission now showing at the Chisenhale is any guide – a subtle shift in direction and purpose.View image in fullscreenDesigned to provoke emotions … Kibuuka OmumbaaleBecause while its previous films addressed the residents of the Wakaliga neighbourhood,Kibuuka Omumbaalespeaks to an international – and specifically British – audience. The 40-minute film is named after a mythical warrior of the Buganda kingdom (now a region in Uganda that includes Kampala) whose relics were removed by an Anglican missionary to Cambridge University in 1906. The remains were returned to Uganda the year before its independence in 1962, setting a precedent for the restitution of looted objects that UK museums have proved notoriously reluctant to follow.Clearly, there is the material here for a lecture on the evils of colonial expropriation and the ethical imperatives of restitution. Yet Wakaliwood has produced something considerably more complex and persuasive, designed to provoke its audience’s emotions as well as prick their consciences. In practice, this means telling the story as a blistering superhero movie featuring hardboiled detectives, courageous women, corrupt politicians, a nefarious “girl with a voluminous bum” and much else besides. It begins when a young man visiting the remains of Kibuuka Omumbaale is possessed with the warrior’s spirit. There is an important precedent for this: in the 1950s, a Ugandan truck driver had the same experience and became a key figure in the anticolonial resistance.View image in fullscreenReady for a showdown … Kibuuka OmumbaaleHis possession enables him to fly around the city and, according to a liberal reinterpretation of the warrior’s powers, zap death rays from his fingers. Unfortunately, the negative aspects of Kibuuka have been incarnated in another young man, a doppelganger bent on evil. Concerned journalists look to local folklorists and museum curators for answers, allowing the film-makers to embed some history lessons without jeopardising the entertainment. As the president calls in the helicopter gunships, it becomes clear that the disaster can be averted only by reconciling good and bad aspects of the past – by means of an explosive showdown.Essential to the film’s appeal and meaning (as in all good art, they are inseparable) is that it comes with two soundtracks. Over the conventional mix of dialogue, sound effects and music plays a disembodied voice that tells jokes, makes asides, casts aspersions and offers a running interpretation of what’s happening. This device derives from the tradition of screening films in Kampala to the live accompaniment of “video jokers” (VJs), whose entirely free translations of foreign-language films make them local celebrities.View image in fullscreenThey seize control of the narrative … Kibuuka OmumbaaleIn earlier Wakaliwood productions, the VJ might, for example, play for laughs by suggesting that a torture victim is being punished for the unforgivable crime “of watching Nigerian films”. On this occasion, Kampala’s first English-language VJ (most speak Luganda) mixes very funny interjections with repeated reminders that “this is how we watch films in Uganda!”. Shown without frills on a screen before painted bleachers, it is nonetheless hard to avoid the sense that this new work lacks some of the anarchic local energy of the original films. But this is something of which the film-makers are acutely aware: there is a history, after all, of the British removing cultural artefacts from the country to exoticise them.So they seize control of the narrative, and the opportunity to speak back. Yet rather than simply railing against the theft of a cultural artefact, they draw on everything from Cantonese kung fu to Hollywood popcorn movies to bring that heritage back into the cosmopolitan present. In the process they reclaim a local hero from the mausoleum of the colonial museum and put him back into the service of the Wakaliga community (battling corruption, femicide, inequality) without shying away from the ethical conflicts of precolonial history. As 20th-century art movements from cubism to expressionism were invigorated by indigenous traditions, so artists in Kampala and elsewhere are transforming the moribund cultures of the west into something richer, stranger and better fitted to the historical moment. Wakaliga Uganda is the model of a thriving culture: fearless, hybrid, irreverent and popular.AtChisenhale Gallery, London, until 6 DecemberExplore more on these topicsArt and designUgandaColonialismMuseumsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Alone with the stars, lynx and wolves in ‘Empty Spain’ | Spain holidays | The Guardian
description: A world away from the tourist hotspots of the coast, Extremadura and Castile and León offer unpolluted skies, lower prices – and hope for the future of vulnerable wildlife
Author: Stephen Phelan
Headline: A world away from the tourist hotspots of the coast, Extremadura and Castile and León offer unpolluted skies, lower prices – and hope for the future of vulnerable wildlife
Content: Extremadura’s astrotourism initiative is called Buenas Noches.Photograph: Extremadura, Buenas NochesView image in fullscreenExtremadura’s astrotourism initiative is called Buenas Noches.Photograph: Extremadura, Buenas NochesSpain holidaysAlone with the stars, lynx and wolves in ‘Empty Spain’A world away from the tourist hotspots of the coast, Extremadura and Castile and León offer unpolluted skies, lower prices – and hope for the future of vulnerable wildlifeStephen PhelanSun 4 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 11.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs photographed at night from a satellite, or the International Space Station (ISS), the Iberian peninsula looks encrusted with lights along its coastal edges. Madrid forms a big pulsing cluster near the centre, while surrounding hinterlands appear as something of a void. Ever fewer people live out in Castile and León and Extremadura, adjoining regions that cover much of what is known asLa España Vacía, or “Empty Spain”.Not many visit either, or at least not compared with Barcelona and other glowing nodes of the tourist circuit. So, while the big ports and resorts struggle to manage surplus holidaymakers, there is room for plenty more out west, toward the Portuguese border. Some have been following the stars that way lately, under the auspices of an astrotourism initiative calledExtremadura Buenas Noches.View image in fullscreenA route map plotted point-to-point between optimal stargazing sites leads to distant outposts likeLa Siberia(so-called because it felt that remote to workers who laid down the first roads and railways in these parts) and the Corral de los Lobos, an ancient stone enclosure on a hilltop, built to trap wolves when they outnumbered the farmers and shepherds around here.Corral de los Lobos also lies in one of the rainier reaches of the Spanish interior, and the weather has mostly closed over the night sky when I go up to look. But even through breaks in the clouds, I can see the ISS pass in its elliptical orbit. Beyond that, Jupiter. And, much farther out, the Milky Way.View image in fullscreenThe Iberian lynx population is increasing in Monfragüe national park, in Extremadura.Photograph: imagebroker.com/Alamy“Big region, small population, almost no light pollution,” says forestry engineer and nature guide Alberto Garzón Fernández the next day, on a misty hike throughGarganta de los Infiernos, a nature reserve named for the fearsome sound of water through its gorges.There are no other forms of pollution either, it seems. We look down into gigantic cauldrons of granite known asmarmitas, where the River Jerte swirls like soup in a pot around eroded rock smooth as brushed steel. The lichen across the wet surface is a luminous green, “a bioindicator of clean air”.double quotation markThe Iberian lynx population is climbing steadily from dangerous lows of a few decades ago in Monfragüe national park“Extremadura is, no doubt, the most natural and healthy place to live,” Garzón says. His claim extends to non-human natives, not least the birds, and he points skyward to the ghostly profiles of honey buzzards and griffon vultures floating in the vapour off the peaks above. Thanks to “sound management”, as he puts it, the Spanish imperial eagle is now seen in much healthier numbers up there.The Iberian lynx population, meanwhile, is climbing steadily from dangerous lows of a few decades ago in neighbouring Monfragüe national park, where Garzón was born and raised. And the Iberian wolf – hunted and displaced almost to extinction before recent, belated protections – has been making a comeback over the flanking Gredos mountains.That’s close enough for their howls to be heard again from the Corral de los Lobos, on those same clear nights when “the stars look so close you could touch them”, says Garzón. The return of these signature species gives him hope for our own. “To me, they represent our capacity to do things right, but we so often wait until the last minute.”View image in fullscreenIn the River Jerte’s giant cauldrons of granite, water swirls like soup in a pot.Photograph: Manoli Perez/AlamyIf this region has felt the benefit of a minimal human presence lately, it’s hardly untouched by the increasing hazards of our time. The heatwave-borne wildfires of 2025 burned through nearly 20,000 hectares (49,400 acres) of the Jerte valley’s famous cherry orchards. All that damage is bound to affect the harvests to follow – one of the few events to draw a crowd to this area. “It will still be beautiful,” says Sara Cudero Morcuende at Alimentación Sara, a grocery store in the nearby mountain town of Valverde de la Vera.Her shop is so well stocked with local delicacies that the place would make a killing if transplanted to, say, east London: figs and olives from surrounding groves, sweet and hot paprika dried over open fires, all sorts of cherry jams and liqueurs. But her town, like many in the region, has lost thousands of residents in recent years.double quotation markYou can often eat and drink better and cheaper in ‘Empty Spain’ than in the country’s busier quartersThere’s a gothic-romantic hush to the cobbled streets below Valverde de la Vera’s ruined and overgrown castle. The quietude, the quasi-abandonment, may yet enhance the appeal to those passing through, though it can’t be good for business. “A few more customers would be nice,” says Cudero, but otherwise the town has only a couple of tapas bars, a few guesthouses, and no hotel.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFor my part, I make use of Spain’s state-ownedparadornetwork, which tends to offer surprisingly affordable rooms in converted convents and palaces, mostly within the medieval walls of the nearest comparatively big cities. The provincial capital, Cáceres; Trujillo, with its dreamlike hilltop fortress; and Plasencia, with its two half-cathedrals (one never fully demolished, the other forever unfinished), make good, solid bases.Fun fact: there are more pigs than people in these regions, including the black, acorn-fed pigs of thedehesaforest, whose meat becomes the world-renownedjamón ibérico.Including, too, the very chunky fellow I encounter in La Alberca, enjoying a siesta in a sty that is also a kind of shrine. Custom dictates that a single fat pig be allowed to wander and eat at its leisure for seven months of each year, until it’s raffled off for the feast of San Antón in January. In the past, that porker was invariably eaten, but some recent winners have apparently kept them as pets.View image in fullscreenThe city of Trujillo makes a good base for exploring  rural areas.Photograph: Ventura Carmona/Getty ImagesLa Alberca is also known for its gorgeous three-storey houses with half-timber facades, the legacy of Christian settlers from Burgundy, who came to occupy territory reconquered from the Moors 1,000 years ago. The encircling mountains are called the Sierra de Francia for that reason, their slopes thick with oak forests that yield many fine species of mushroom.“You can eat them all,” says biologist and guide Marino Esteban (La Albercavisitor centreoperates hikes into the forest), on a walk through woods that look more like French or even English countryside. “But some you can only eat once.” This is his way of saying that certain types are toxic. This is also to say that a massive meal at Meson de San Martín – a stonebuilt tavern that seems the only place open in nearby village San Martín del Castañar – is not all about the ham.‘So big and so close’: spotting endangered bears on a trip to northern SpainRead moreThere’s plenty of that, but also plenty of the freshly picked penny bun mushrooms grilled with garlic salt and olive oil, not to mention the chestnuts, cheeses, tomatoes and potatoes of surrounding farmlands, and the red wine made from native rufete grapes – as good as anything I’ve tried from more domineering production regions such as La Rioja and Ribera del Duero.And here’s the big secret I learn on this little road trip: you can often eat and drink better and cheaper in “Empty Spain” than in most of the busier quarters. This was one of the great lunches of my life, I tell the cheery chef, Alfonso Buenaventura Calvo. His wife and co-owner Belén answers for him: “Of course it was.”The trip was provided by theSpanishtouristoffice,Turismo ExtremaduraandTurismo Castilla Y León. Accommodation provided byParadores). For stargazing,seeextremadurabuenasnoches.com.Aventura Jerteofferstourswith Alberto Garzón FernándezExplore more on these topicsSpain holidaysEurope holidaysAstronomyWildlife holidaysfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Dante Mayfair, Claridge’s, London W1: ‘Are chips ever worth £11? Probably not’ – restaurant review | Food | The Guardian
description: The whole point of going to Claridge’s in the first place is to sweep in through the grand main hotel entrance
Author: Grace Dent
Headline: The whole point of going to Claridge’s in the first place is to sweep in through the grand main hotel entrance
Content: Dante Mayfair, London W1: ‘You could invite anyone here, at any time.’Photograph: Beca B Jones/The GuardianView image in fullscreenDante Mayfair, London W1: ‘You could invite anyone here, at any time.’Photograph: Beca B Jones/The GuardianGrace Dent on restaurantsFoodReviewDante Mayfair, Claridge’s, London W1: ‘Are chips ever worth £11? Probably not’ – restaurant reviewThe whole point of going to Claridge’s in the first place is to sweep in through the grand main hotel entranceGrace DentSun 4 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 11.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDante Mayfair, inside Claridge’s on Brook Street in London, has been created, the hotel’s management says, to become “the living room of Mayfair”. It’s a charming idea: pop in, have a cuppa or a bowl of pappardelle bolognese, or lie about on the fancy sofas wearing elasticated tracksuit bottoms and slurping soft-serve with s’mores. No, sorry, I’ve gone too far: it’s nowhere nearthatinformal.Still, like many well-used living rooms, this one has been rearranged, redecorated and repurposed many times over the years. I’ve eaten fancy-schmancySimon Rogan dinners here when it was Fera, as well as his table experience at Aulis during which venture capitalist “foodies” bored the pants off me over a 12-course meal in the kitchen itself. I’ve stared unmoved atDaniel Humm’s New York-style pomp at the short-lived Davies and Brook, and have visited several times since Claridge’s took matters in-house in the shape of a rather anonymous ye olde British brasserie.View image in fullscreenTuna tartare at Dante Mayfair, where ‘service is warm, slick, effusive and casual’.Now I’m here for Dante, and we’re back in New York again, this time in the hands of Linden Pride and Nathalie Hudson, with no named chef at all, although there’s absolutely definitely a man plinky-plonking his way throughJohn Legend’s Ordinary Peopleon the piano. Pride and Hudson are a husband-and-wife team from Sydney, Australia, who met at college, moved to New York and in 2015 boughtCaffe Dante, an institution of a Greenwich Village coffee house that’s been open since 1915.By 2019, the place had been named the world’s best bar. The couple’s new space on Brook Street is a restaurant site in need of stability and comprehensible finery, as well as of caviar tarts with champagne pearls, shrimp cocktails and lobster linguine, and of caviar martinis and vintage or chocolate negronis.If you like, you can enter via a small side door on Davies Street, but ignore that. The whole point of going to Claridge’s in the first place is to sweep in through the grand main hotel entrance past the men in top hats – you need to feel like Paddington, a little bear in a big city just making it on your own. Take a right turn, hand in your coat at the beautiful little cloakroom, then quickly powder your nose in the vintage loos where nice ladies polish the sinks. Order a marmalade sandwich … sorry, I mean dover sole meunière or veal milanese. For this part of Mayfair, the prices are weirdly reasonable – a bowl of fazzoletti with pesto may be £27, but you should see how much they charge for pasta atBacchanaliajust down the road – and a mini martini is a tenner between 3pm and 5pm.View image in fullscreen‘The sauce lacked depth and the pasta was a touch overcooked’: Dante’spappardelle al ragu, or house bolognese.Dante is useful for client lunches or intimate tête-à-têtes when you want to be heard perfectly and don’t want to be constantly interrupted by the waiting staff. After all, no one needs a tomato and peach salad with marinated feta and freekeh explained to them, even though this one is very fresh, very nicely arranged and whispers more of California than of Italy. A large plate of San Daniele prosciutto comes with baked mozzarella, and the iceberg salad features very neatly dressed lettuce wedges. Thepappardelle al ragu, or house bolognese, lacks depth and the pasta is a touch overcooked, but chickenalla diavolawith green goddess dressing is earthy and fresh. Are chips ever worth £11? Probably not, but then this is Claridge’s, not Clacton seafront.I do wonder, however, whether Dante’s most noteworthy offering is its “dessert cocktail” list, which is aimed squarely at that moment after the main course when customers wrinkle their noses at shelling out on “something sweet” but will happily carry on drinking. That’s when the rounds of honey bees (tequila, coffee liqueur, amontillado, raspberry, salted honey cream) are ordered. And wait, what? It comes with my own face printed on top of it!?! Dante has a piece of kit that stamps photographs on to the foam in edible ink, and I defyanyonenot to be exhilarated by that – or to think that it’s not perfectly sensible to have a nonna’s alexander or a grasshopper afterwards. We wanted pudding, too, though, and the waiter asked if we fancied the sticky toffee doughnut with whisky flambé. Yes. Yes, please. Yes, I would like you to set fire to things. It goes up like a firework and is a sweet, sticky mess.View image in fullscreenDante Mayfair’s sticky toffee doughnut with whisky flambé ‘goes up like a firework’.On this Tuesday lunchtime, Dante was probably the quietest place in Mayfair. A small, elegant wedding had taken over the side room, while a few hotel residents were eating burgers in the main room. Service was warm, slick, effusive and casual, and completely on it. The issue with a semi-casual restaurant inside Claridge’s is that the very name scares off the general public. But you could invite anyone here, and at any time; I’d use it for breakfasts and meet-ups. Dante is not a destination dinner, but it is, as promised, a living room. It won’t win prizes for its food, but it is friendly and handy as hell, which in Mayfair these days is exceptionally rare.Dante MayfairClaridge’s, Brook Street, London W1, 020-7629 8860. Open all week, noon-9.30pm (10.30pm Thurs-Sat); breakfast 8-11am. From about £60 a head à la carte, plus drinks and serviceExplore more on these topicsFoodGrace Dent on restaurantsRestaurantsAmerican food and drinkBritish food and drinkfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: How to make the perfect zuppa di cozze – recipe | Shellfish | The Guardian
description: A tomatoey, southern Italian alternative to moules marinière – but who makes the definitive version?
Author: Felicity Cloake
Headline: A tomatoey, southern Italian alternative to moules marinière – but who makes the definitive version?
Content: Felicity Cloake’s perfectzuppa di cozze.Photograph: Dan Jones/The Guardian. Food styling: Stevie Taylor.View image in fullscreenFelicity Cloake’s perfectzuppa di cozze.Photograph: Dan Jones/The Guardian. Food styling: Stevie Taylor.How to cook the perfect ...ShellfishHow to make the perfect zuppa di cozze – recipeA tomatoey, southern Italian alternative to moules marinière – but who makes the definitive version?Felicity CloakeSun 4 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 08.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAbundant, good value and ready in minutes, mussels are one of my favourite seafoods, but when it comes to preparing them, I rarely look farther than northern France. Italians, of course, also eat mussels, and this tomato-rich recipe is a particular favourite in the south –Neapolitans traditionally tuck intozuppa di cozzeon Maundy Thursday but it’s found on menus all year round. With its bold flavours and oily, garlicky sauce, it’s a great alternative to creamymoules marinières, and similarly needs no accompaniment but a hunk of bread to make a meal, though chips, of course, are rarely unwelcome.The musselsView image in fullscreen‘Specifically Neapolitan’: Giallo Zafferano’s zuppa di cozze. All thumbnail photographs byFelicity Cloake.There’s not much to say about the main ingredient, except to bemoan the increasing difficulty in getting hold of live mussels due to the disappearance of so many fresh fish vendors, and the subsequent closure of supermarket fish counters (another rant for another day). Any remaining fishmongers should have British mussels, orthey can easily be bought online. Don’t wash them until you’re ready to cook, when you should dump them in the sink and sort through them, discarding any with broken shells or that don’t close when you give them a sharp tap. Rinse with cold water; most mussels on the market are farmed, and rope-grown, so should be pretty clean, and I’ve never seen the point of scrubbing away at barnacles for hours when you’re not going to be eating the shells anyway (though please do enlighten me as to why I should bother). Remove any remaining trailing beards, though – I do have some standards!The Silver Spoondry-fries the mussels, then shells them to add to the soup later, while theGiallo Zafferano websitesteams them in garlicky oil and a little white wine, then removes them from the pot to be returned to the finished soup. It makes more sense to me to eat them as freshly cooked as possible – asElizabeth Davidcautions in Italian Food, these “final operations must be carried out only immediately before serving”. Not only does this leave less chance of the shellfish overcooking, but necessarily ensures that every last drop of that delicious mussel liquor makes it into the sauce; tipping it back and forth, as in the Zafferano recipe, risks sacrificing a little, and when there’s not a lot to start with, that’s a gamble I’m not prepared to take.View image in fullscreenFor her zuppa di cozze, Elizabeth David insists that the steaming of the mussels ‘must be carried out only immediately before serving’.Zafferano, whose recipe is specifically Neapolitan, includes octopus, squid and prawns alongside the mussels. Delicious as all those things are, we find the squid and prawns are overcooked and rubbery once they’ve been fried and then simmered in tomato sauce for 15 minutes. If you’d like to include them, I’d fry them briefly first, then return them to the pan right at the end (and buy the octopus ready-cooked, if you can).The baseDavid and the Silver Spoon are the only ones to use onions as the base of their dishes, with the former also including celery. More common is garlic in more or less generous amounts – Zafferano simply uses it to flavour the oil, whileMarcella Hazan, perhaps reflecting the more Italian-American milieu in which she was writing The Essentials of Classic Italian Cuisine, sticks in a whole teaspoon and a half of the stuff, finely minced. I like the fiery flavour, especially alongside the chilli she also includes, plus this feels like a dish that should pack a punch.View image in fullscreenBenedetta Rossi’s zuppa di cozze uses cherry tomatoes but is ‘a bit light on sauce’.And that also applies when it comes to the tomatoes. Hazan uses tinned, and reduces them to a jammy, oily sauce before adding the bivalves, a similar approach to David, but the latter’s more watery fresh fruit (and seeded summer san marzano plum tomatoes are about as far from watery as you’re likely to get) yields a lighter, fresher flavour. My favourites, however, are the cherry tomatoes suggested byBenedetta Rossiof the Fatto di Casa da Benedetta website, because they strike a good balance between the intensity of the tinned variety and the zingy acidity of plum tomatoes. My recipe uses a few more than Rossi’s, though, because we find her version a bit light on sauce, and cooks them for a little longer, in homage to Hazan.The Silver Spoon flavours the base with saffron, Hazan chilli and parsley (Rossi adds the stalks, reserving the leaves as a garnish), and David suggests fresh marjoram, thyme or basil. I really like the echoes of Mediterranean French fish soups that the saffron brings with it, but my testers are ambivalent as to its merits, so I’ll leave that one up to you. Herbs, I think, are better used on top; not only do they look pretty against the glossy black shells and vivid sauce, but the peppery flavour of the parsley gets lost in the heat.The liquidView image in fullscreenSilver Spoon’s zuppa di cozze is more of a soup that’s garnished with mussels.Not all recipes add extra liquid – the mussels give off enough to make a sauce, but it’s fairly scanty, so it makes sense to dilute it a little so everyone gets a decent spoonful alongside the shells. Wine is popular, used by David (who also adds a little water), Zafferano andEdinburgh’s Contini, while the Silver Spoon, whose recipe is more of a mussel soup garnished with a few actual bivalves than a pot of mussels, goes for fish stock. If you don’t drink, then this, with a spritz of lemon juice, is a decent substitute, but the zesty acidity of a crisp white is the ideal, not least because you can then drink it as an accompaniment.Serving suggestionView image in fullscreenFelicity Cloake’s perfect zuppa di cozze.Peppery parsley looks good, and tastes great, according to those who like it better than I do (if you share my aversion, you might like to experiment with mint, thyme or basil), and the garlicky toasts that pop up in the Silver Spoon, Hazan and Zafferano’s recipes are the perfect accompaniment, whether you want to spoon the mussels on top, so the bread soaks up their liquid, or serve it on the side to mop up the end of the sauce.Perfect zuppa di cozzePrep10 minCook15 minServes22 garlic cloves500g cherry tomatoes3 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil, plus extra to serve1 pinch dried chilli flakes(optional)1 pinch saffron(optional)Salt800g live mussels2 tbsp white wine, or dry vermouth or fish stock2 thick slices crusty bread1 small bunch flat-leaf parsley, to serveFinely chop one and a half cloves of garlic. Cut the tomatoes in half. Heat the oil on a medium flame in a saucepan large enough eventually to hold all the mussels, then fry the garlic and chilli, if using, until pale golden.View image in fullscreenFelicity Cloake’s perfect zuppa di cozzePhotograph: Felicity Cloake/The GuardianStir in the tomatoes, saffron, if using, and a pinch of salt, then turn down the heat a little and cook until soft and pulpy. You can prepare the dish ahead up to this point if needed.For this recipe, I’m assuming you’ve bought your mussels; should you have gathered them yourself, however, you’ll need to purge them in salt water overnight first, to get rid of any grit (havea look online for specific instructions).View image in fullscreenEither way, just before cooking, tip the mussels into a large colander and give them a good rinse with cold water. Sort through them, discarding any with broken shells or that don’t close when given a sharp tap (unless you can see the creature moving within). Scrub off any dirty patches (and barnacles, if you wish), and give any trailing beards (the weedy bits hanging out of the side of the shell) a sharp tug to pull them off.View image in fullscreenAdd the wine to the pan, turn up the heat, then tip in the mussels. Cover and leave to cook, shaking the pan occasionally, for five to eight minutes, until most of them have opened (discard any that do not).View image in fullscreenMeanwhile, grill or toast the bread, then rub it with the remaining half-clove of raw garlic and drizzle with oil. Finely chop the parsley.View image in fullscreenDivide the bread between serving bowls, then use a slotted spoon to scoop out the mussels and arrange on top (or serve the bread on the side). Bring the liquid back to a simmer, reduce slightly, taste for seasoning and ladle on top of the mussels. Sprinkle with parsley and devour immediately.Zuppa di cozze – how do you like yours, and can anyone explain the many regional variations that surely exist on Italy’s extensive coastline?
